Inherited from Latin tisana, variant of ptisana, from Ancient Greek πτισάνη (ptisánē, “peeled barley, barley gruel”).
Borrowed from Latin boreālis (“northern”), from Boreās, from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās, “personification of the north wind”).
Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbinem.
From turpe + -itudine, or borrowed from Latin turpitūdinem (“turpitude”), from turpis (“ugly; base”).

Borrowed from Old Occitan velhar (cf. Old French veiller), which was inherited from Latin vigilāre. Replaced the original Italian vegghiare, which was inherited from Latin. Also a doublet of vigilare, a learned borrowing from Latin.
Ultimately from Latin viscera n pl.
Borrowed from Latin victōriōsus. By surface analysis, vittoria (“victory”) + -oso.
From contra- + tempo. Cognate with Piedmontese contratemp.
Formed from Latin prehēnsus (and based on Italian prendere), with the suffix -ile.
From susino (“plum tree”), from Vulgar Latin *susīna, from Latin Sūsa (“ancient capital of Elam”).
From Latin spīnōsus, or from spina + -oso.
From New Latin rhachis, -is, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis, “spine, ridge”), with an unetymological -id- added to the stem.
Learned borrowing from Latin aureus. By surface analysis, aur- (“gold”, fossilized stem for oro) + -eo.
From Latin beātitūdinem (“happiness, blessedness, beatitude”), from beātus (“happy, blessed”).
Borrowed from French blocage, derived from bloquer (“to block”).

From cagione + -are or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *occāsionāre, from Latin occāsiāre. Cf. also accagionare, possibly from a root *accāsionāre. Compare Old French achoisoner, Romanian cășuna, cf. also Spanish ocasionar.
Borrowed from Late Latin ūsuālis, derived from Latin ūsus.
From Latin canistrum, from Ancient Greek κάναστρον (kánastron), κάνιστρον (kánistron). Compare English canister.
Borrowed from Spanish caníbal, from Taíno.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin catheter.
From cazzo + -eggiare. Compare with Sicilian cazzijari.
From polinomio + -ale. By surface analysis, poli- + -nomio + -ale.
From Latin collecta, probably a borrowing. Cf. colto, colta.
From comprare + -tore, or from Late Latin comparātōrem, from Latin comparō.
From Late Latin viscerālis; cognate with Piedmontese visseral.

From alveolo (“alveolus”) + -are (adjective-forming suffix), from Latin alveolus (“small cavity”), derived from alveus (“hollow, cavity”), from alvus (“belly, womb”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”).

Maybe from Old French felpe, feupe, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Late Latin faluppa (“straw, fiber, chip”) (perhaps of Germanic origin and borrowed from Frankish *felt), or from earlier ferpe, metathesized from fibra.

Formed from contratto, from Latin contractum (compare French contracter), past participle of contrahō (“to draw, bring or drag several objects together; collect, assemble, gather, amass; to bring about, accomplish, execute, get, cause, produce, make; to make a contract, conclude, transact, do business, contract”), from con- (“with, together”) + trahō (“to draw, to pull”).
Borrowed from French démoraliser. By surface analysis, de- (“removal”) + morale (“moral”) + -izzare (“to make”).
Borrowed from French démoralisation. By surface analysis, demoralizzare + -zione.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēsīderōsus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēvāstātiōnem. Cognate with Piedmontese devastassion.
From Latin diffīdentem, present participle of diffīdō (“to distrust”).
From Late Latin dignitōsus. Cognate with Piedmontese dignitos.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek διοίκησις (dioíkēsis, “administration”), derived from διοικέω (dioikéō).
Borrowed from Late Latin mūcōsus, from Latin mūcus.
From Ancient Greek δεσποτικός (despotikós), from δεσπότης (despótēs, “ruler, despot”).
From Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”). See also Old French dissenterie.
From dis- + umano; cognate with Piedmontese disuman.
Learned borrowing from Latin hebes (“blunt, dull”). Compare French hébété.

From Late Latin aeōnem (“age, eternity”), from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn), from earlier αἰϝών (aiwṓn), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂oy-u-Hō, derived from *h₂óyu (“long time; lifetime”), derived from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force, life, age, eternity”).
Borrowed from Late Latin aequivocāre, present infinitive form of aequivocō (“to call with the same name”). By surface analysis, equivoco (“ambiguous”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix).
From Late Latin extorsiōnem. Cognate with Piedmontese estorsion.
From Latin herbōsus. By surface analysis, erba + -oso.
From French galant. Doublet of galano.
From fasciare + -tura; cognate with Piedmontese fassadura.
Borrowed from Old French menestrel (compare modern ménestrel), from Late Latin ministeriāle(m), from Latin ministerium.
From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós). By surface analysis, ana- (“reversal”) + cron(o-) (“time”) + -ismo (“-ism”).
From anacron(ismo) (“anachronism”) + -istico (“-istic”). By surface analysis, ana- (“reversal”) + cron(o-) (“time”) + -istico.
From Latin pinacotheca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē). By surface analysis, pinaco- + -teca.
From Latin ventūrus (“about to come”), future active participle of veniō (“to come, approach”).
Borrowed from French systématique (adjective), from Late Latin systematicus, from Ancient Greek συστηματικός (sustēmatikós), from σύστημᾰ (sústēmă).
Inherited from Late Latin sanguinōsus, from Latin sanguis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin curativus. By surface analysis, curare + -ivo.
Borrowed from Late Latin liquefactiōnem, derived from Classical Latin liquefaciōnem (“to melt”).
Borrowed from Latin phalangem, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “battle order, array”). See also the related falanga and palanca.
Internationalism. Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολυφωνία (poluphōnía). By surface analysis, poli- + -fonia.

Borrowed from Late Latin patriarcha, from Medieval Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “-arch”).
From Latin quintuplus. Equivalent to quinto + -uplo.
Probably borrowed from Latin negōtiātōrem (“merchant, banker”), or a semi-learned term. Or formed from negoziare + -tore.
From Medieval Latin conceptuālis, derived from Latin conceptus. By surface analysis, concetto + -uale.
From Latin resīnōsus. By surface analysis, resina + -oso.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin respōnsōrium.
From Latin psalterium, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharyngem, from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx).
From crivello + -are, from Late Latin cribellum, diminutive of Latin cribrum. Cf. also Late Latin cribellāre (“pass through a sieve; sift”).
From Late Latin cribellum, diminutive of Latin cribrum.
From Late Latin decasyllabus, from Ancient Greek δεκασύλλαβος (dekasúllabos), from δέκᾰ (dékă, “ten”) + σῠλλᾰβή (sŭllăbḗ, “syllable”). By surface analysis, deca- + sillabo.
From Latin similitūdinem (“likeness, similitude; simile”). By surface analysis, simile + -itudine.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek συντακτικός (suntaktikós), from σῠ́ντᾰξῐς (sŭ́ntăxĭs, “syntax”) (compare sintassi).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin subtractiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin speculātīvus, from Latin speculor.
From Latin casula, a diminutive of casa.

From di- + ramo, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Romanian dărâma, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.
Borrowed from French blinder (“to reinforce”), derived from blinde (“piece of wood used as cover or protection”).
From Vulgar Latin ferrāmenta, from the plural of Latin ferrāmentum.
Inherited from Latin flaccus. Compare French flache, Portuguese fraco, Sicilian fraccu and Spanish flaco.
From fiore + -aio. Compare Portuguese floreiro, Romanian florar, Sicilian ciuraru, Spanish florero.
Borrowed from Late Latin repulsiōnem, from Latin repulsus.
Borrowed from Latin fluctus. Compare the inherited doublet fiotto.
From Latin fragor. Compare Spanish fragor.
Derived from Latin ēvolūtus (perfect passive participle of ēvolvō) + -ivo.
From Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “sovereign”), from αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) (combining form of αὐτός (autós)) + κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”) + -ης (-ēs).
Calque of English externality. First attested in 1987.
Borrowed from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).
From Latin subsidiārius. Compare with Friulian sussidiari.
From svalutare + -zione; cognate with Piedmontese svalutassion.
Probably a borrowing from French jeton.
Borrowed from French javelot, from Vulgar Latin *gabalottus (“spear”), derived from Gaulish *gabalos.
Borrowed from French gilet, itself from Italian giulecco.
From New Latin anthēra, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρά (anthērá), feminine form of ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”) from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower, blossom”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin incīsīvus.
Inherited from Latin carnōsus. By surface analysis, carne (“meat, flesh”) + -oso (“-y”).
From Latin dēciduus (“falling down or off”), from dēcidō (“fall down”).
Borrowed from Latin fruticem (“shrub”), of uncertain origin.
Borrowed from Latin Aethiopem, from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Latin involūtus. Doublet of involto, which was inherited.

From Late Latin hippocampus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea-monster”)). The anatomy sense is so named from its resemblance to the seahorse. By surface analysis, hippo- + campus.
Unadapted borrowing from French dépliant (“leaflet, flyer”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lavativus, derived from Latin lavō (“to wash”). Compare French lavatif.
Borrowed from Late Latin peltātus, derived from Latin pelta (a kind of shield).
Borrowed from Latin longitūdinem (“length, longitude”), from longus (“long”).
From ri- + piegare, cf. also Latin replicō, replicāre.

Probably borrowed from Latin tēgula as a semi-learned term, or simply evolved from the word while the doublet teglia developed from another variant without the 'u'. Compare French tuile, Portuguese telha and Spanish teja.
From Latin trānsgressiōnem, derived from trānsgressus, perfect passive participle of trānsgredior (“to go over”).

From Medieval Latin marchionissa, feminine form of marchion, from Late Latin marcha, from Frankish *markōn (“to mark, mark out, to press with the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *markō (“area, region, edge, rim, border”). Cognate with Sicilian marchisa.
From a- + buffare (“to blow; to huff”) + -are + -si.
Borrowed from English shaman, from German Schamane, from Russian шама́н (šamán), from Evenki шама̄н (şamān), сама̄н (samān).
From Latin somnolentus, derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
From Late Latin nārīcem, ultimately derived from Latin nāris.
From pagare + -abile; cognate with Piedmontese pagàbil.
From French lamantin, alteration of Spanish manatí.
Borrowed from English cybernetics, from Ancient Greek κυβερνητική (kubernētikḗ).
From Latin scoliosis, from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis, “twisting; torsion”).
Borrowed from English agnostic, derived from Ancient Greek ἄγνωστος (ágnōstos). By surface analysis, a- (“un-”, negative prefix) + gnostico (“gnostic”).
From New Latin glottidem, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).

From Late Latin epiglottidem, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγλωττίς (epiglōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, epi- (“above”, “over”) + glottide (“glottis”).
From Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos), from οἰσέμεν (oisémen), future form of φέρω (phérō, “I carry”) + ἔφαγον (éphagon, “I ate”).
From Ancient Greek μᾰρασμός (mărasmós, “withering”), from μᾰραίνω (măraínō, “to waste, wither”).
From biometria + -ico. By surface analysis, bio- + -metrico.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dīgestīvus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin formativus.
From Late Latin molīnārius, from molīnus, from Latin molō. Doublet of mulinaro, molinaro, and mulinaio, from regional variants. Compare French meunier.
From Latin amātōrem. Doublet of amateur.
From Latin apud with the confluence of ad post.
Borrowed from Latin gentīlicius. By surface analysis, gentile (in the historical sense “relating to a gens”) + -izio.
From Latin gentiana, possibly ultimately from Illyrian [Term?].
Borrowed from Late Latin contrādictōrius (“contradictory”), from Latin contrādīcō (“to speak against; contradict”).
Borrowed from Old French corocier, corucier, from Vulgar Latin *corruptiāre, from Latin corruptus, perfect passive participle of corrumpō (“to corrupt”). Doublet of crucciare.
Borrowed from Latin dēlinquere (“to fail in one's duty”), from de- + linquō (“to neglect”), present infinitive form of linquō (“to leave”).
Borrowed from Latin convexus, and adapted to Italian.
From Latin dēsuētus (“unused”), from dēsuēscō (“to disuse”).
From *fiorello + -ino (diminutive suffix), from fiore + -ello (diminutive suffix). Compare Sicilian ciuriḍḍuzzu.
From Ancient Greek ἐμφατικός (emphatikós), variant of ἐμφαντικός (emphantikós), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “I show, present”).
Borrowed from French minoritaire, from minorité. By surface analysis, minorità + -ario.
From Late Latin furnārius, from Latin furnus (“oven”). By surface analysis, forno + -aio.
Inherited from Late Latin ganathus, from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos).
Formed from percetto + -ivo (from Latin perceptus), based on French perceptif, or borrowed from Medieval Latin perceptivus.
Borrowed from Late Latin incrēdulitātem, from Latin incrēdulus.
Borrowed from Latin inūtilitātem (“uselessness”), derived from inūtilis (“useless”).
Calque of French similaire, from Latin simile + -are. Compare also Medieval Latin similāris.
Borrowed from French linguiste, from Latin lingua + -iste.
Borrowed from French légaliser. By surface analysis, legale (“legal”) + -izzare (“to make”).
From paglia + -aio, or from Latin paleārium.
Borrowed from Latin prĕcārius. See also preghiera.
From Latin Athenaeum, from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓θήναιον (Ăthḗnaion).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσυμμετρίᾱ (asummetríā). By surface analysis, a- + simmetria.
Inherited from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion).
Borrowed from Latin angelicus, from angelus (“angel”). By surface analysis, angelo + -ico.
From Latin amphitheātrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron). By surface analysis, anfi- + teatro.
Inherited from Late Latin appārēscente (“beginning to appear”, singular ablative present participle of appārēscō (“to begin to appear”), inchoative of Latin appāreō (“to appear”)).
Borrowed from Spanish achaque, from Arabic شَكَا (šakā, “to complain”).
From muscolo + -oso, or from Latin musculōsus.
From Latin alpēstris. By surface analysis, Alpi + -estre.
From French pachyderme, from Ancient Greek παχύδερμος (pakhúdermos), from παχύς (pakhús, “thick”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).
From a- (“to”) + guant(o) (“glove”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
From a- (“towards”) + moglie (“wife”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

From Latin lūcus (“grove sacred to a deity”), from Old Latin loucos, from Proto-Indo-European *lowkós (“open space, clearing”), derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include English lea (“meadow”), Hindi लोक (lok, “public” ← “world”), Lithuanian laũkas (“field”).
From ri- (“re-”) + mescolare (“to mix, stir, blend, shuffle”).
Borrowed from Latin althaea, from Ancient Greek ἀλθαία (althaía, “marshmallow, Althaea officinalis”), from ἀλθαίνω (althaínō, “to heal”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mendācem (“mendacious, lying, false”).
From rin- + culo + -are, calque of French reculer.
Learned borrowing from Latin scrība. Doublet of scrivano.
From giallo (“yellow”) + rosso (“red”), the colors of the flag of Rome and of the shirts of the Roma football/soccer team.
From Medieval Latin stigmatizō, from Medieval Greek στιγματίζω (stigmatízō). By surface analysis, stigma + -izzare.
From Latin suppositiōnem, from sub- (“under”) + positiō (“position; theme”).
Borrowed from Latin vorācitātem. Cognates include Catalan voracitat, French voracité and Spanish voracidad.
From in- + farina (“flour”) + -are. Compare Catalan enfarinar, French enfariner, Portuguese enfarinhar, Romanian înfăina, Sicilian nfarinari, Spanish enharinar.
From Latin apotheōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις (apothéōsis).
From French guinder (“to raise, hoist”, figurative “to emphasize”).
From Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).
Borrowed from Late Latin acēdia. Doublet of acedia.

From Latin angustus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰ-. The correspondence of Latin short /u/ to Italian /u/ (rather than Italian /o/ as in agosto, mosto) indicates that the form is possibly a semi-learned borrowing (compare gusto).
From Spanish bauprés, from French beaupré, from Dutch boegspriet.
From a- (“to, towards”) + quieto (“quiet, peaceful”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
From French cambuse, from Middle Dutch kabuys.
Borrowed from French caréner. By surface analysis, carena (“keel”) + -are.
From Latin āmanuēnsis. By surface analysis, a + mano + -ense.
Borrowed from Spanish hamaca (“hammock, swing”), from Taíno.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs).
From Latin apostasia, from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía, “defection, revolt”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin forāneus, from Latin foris. First attested 17th century.
From vendemmia (“grape harvest”) + -aio, calque of French vendémiaire.
From bruma (“mist, haze”) + -aio, calque of French brumaire.
From Ecclesiastical Latin baptistērium, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστήριον (baptistḗrion).
From Old Occitan beltat, from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem, derived from Latin bellus (“beautiful”).
From bottega + -aio. See also Latin apothecārius. Cognate with Sicilian putigaru.
From Latin bulla (“seal”) + -etta (diminutive suffix), from the resemblance.
From borro (“ditch”) + -one, the stem probably a northern form of botro.
Borrowed from Spanish marrano, from Arabic مُحَرَّم (muḥarram, “forbidden”).
From Latin nāvigium (with a change of suffix), or through a Late Vulgar Latin form *nāvilium (compare French navire (Old French navilie), Old Occitan navili). Doublet of navigio.
From Latin cālīgō, cālīginem (“fog”), of uncertain origin. Compare Portuguese caligem (“fog”) and Spanish calina (“haze”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cālīginōsus (“foggy, misty; dark”).

From Vulgar Latin *prōda, from Latin prōra (via dissimilation), borrowed from Ancient Greek πρῷρα (prōîra), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-, form of *por-. Doublet of prua and prora. Compare Spanish proa.
Borrowed from French propulsif, from Latin prōpulsus.
Borrowed from French rouler. Doublet of rotolare.
Borrowed from Latin Carthāginem, from Phoenician 𐤒𐤓𐤕-𐤇𐤃𐤔𐤕 (qrt-ḥdšt, “New City”).
From svantaggio + -oso; cognate with Piedmontese svantagios.
Borrowed from French calorique. By surface analysis, calori- + -ico.
From antropometria + -ico. By surface analysis, antropo- + -metrico.
From Ancient Greek ἄπολις (ápolis, “without city, state or country”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).
From Late Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos, “catarrh, head cold”).
From Latin catasta, from Ancient Greek κατάστασις (katástasis, “establishment, institution, method, condition”).
Borrowed from French caoutchouc, from Quechua kawchu.
Borrowed from Late Latin causālis, derived from Latin causa. By surface analysis, causa (“cause”) + -ale (“-al”, “pertaining to”).
Derived from Late Latin clāmorōsus. By surface analysis, clamore + -oso.
From 16ᵗʰ-century Spanish xícara (modern jícara), from Classical Nahuatl xīcalli.
Borrowed from Latin contumāx (“stubborn, obstinate”). Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese contumaz, English contumacious.
From Late Latin claustellum (“keyhole”), diminutive of Latin claustrum. Influenced by Italian chiave (“key”).
From Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”). By surface analysis, fiducia + -ario.
From Occitan chiminièra, from Old French cheminee.
Perhaps from vulgar forms like *sorcipiglio, *sorpiciglio, from Latin supercilium (“frown”). Compare sopracciglio (“eyebrow”).
Calque of French informatiser, from informatica + -izzare.
Borrowed from Latin inimīcitia, from inimīcus.
Borrowed from Latin collūctātiōnem. By surface analysis, colluttare (“to fight, scuffle”) + -zione.
From Latin mittentem, present active participle of mittō.
Borrowed from Latin pecūlātus, from Latin pecūlor (“to embezzle”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin persecūtōrem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin postilla, from post illa (verba) "after those words".
Borrowed from Latin quaesitus. Doublet of chiesto.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin rendita, from the past participle of Late Latin rendō (“to give back, yield”).
From Late Latin ārsūra, from Latin ārsus.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσφυξία (asphuxía, “stopping of the pulse”).
Borrowed from Latin augustus. Doublet of the inherited agosto.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θρόμβωσις (thrómbōsis, “curdling”), derived from θρόμβος (thrómbos, “clot, curd”).
From Latin benna (“carriage”), from Gaulish benna (“carriage”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bitūminōsus. By surface analysis, bitume + -oso.
From Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus.
Borrowed from Late Latin plēnārius, from Latin plēnus.
Inherited from Latin natāre (“swim, float”). Doublet of nuotare.
From the intermediate Vulgar Latin *ri(ji)one(m), from the masculinization of Latin regiōnem. Compare the borrowed doublet regione. Cognate with Sicilian rijuni.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin compūnctiōnem.
Blend of mieti(trice) (“harvesting machine”) + trebbiatrice (“threshing machine”). By surface analysis, mietere (“to harvest”) + trebbiare (“to thresh”) + -trice (female agent noun suffix).
Calque of French mouvementer, from movimento + -are.
From Latin concussiōnem (“shaking”, noun), derived from concutiō (“to shake violently”).
From Latin concupiscentia, from concupīscō (“to desire strongly, to desire eagerly; to covet”).
Borrowed from Old French oreillier, from oreille (“ear”). By surface analysis, orecchia + -are.
Borrowed from Old French ostel, from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospitale.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclūsīvus, from Latin inclūsus.
Borrowed from Latin pignorāre. Doublet of pegnorare, the inherited counterpart.
From proseguire + -mento; cognate with Piedmontese proseguiment.
Learned borrowing from Latin aurum, from earlier ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom (“glow”), derived from the root *h₂ews-. Doublet of oro.
Of Southern Italian origin, from Latin sapientem (“discerning, wise”), present active participle of sapiō (“to be wise”). Doublet of sapiente.
Borrowed from Latin silvestrem. Cf. salvastrella.
From coriandro + -olo, with loss of the second /r/.
Borrowed from Latin correctivus, from correctus.
From Latin corruptōrem, from corruptus, past participle of corrumpō, corrumpere (compare corrompere).
Learned borrowing from Latin trepidātiōnem (“agitation, trepidation”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis. Doublet of triste, a borrowing from Latin.
From tutto (“everything”) + fare (“to do”), calque of French (bonne à) tout faire.
Borrowed from Latin vitiōsus. Doublet of vezzoso.
From Latin cultōrem, derived from colō (“to cultivate; to inhabit; to worship”).
Borrowed from French décalquer. First attested in 1758.
From settanta + -enario. Cognate with French septantenaire.
Borrowed from Late Latin ficticius, from Latin fictus.
From centimetro + -are. Literally, “[to divide] into centimeters”.
From a- + casa (“house”) + -are. Compare also Spanish casar (“to marry”), Romanian căsători.
Borrowed from Latin acquiēscentem (“resting, acquiescing”), present active participle of acquiēscō (“to rest; to acquiesce”).
Borrowed from Latin tunica. Compare the inherited tonaca.
From aero- + -statico, on the model of French aérostatique.
Inherited from Latin adēscāre (“to feed, fatten”), from ad + ēsca (“food”).
From Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
Borrowed from French autodidacte, from Ancient Greek αὐτοδίδακτος (autodídaktos), derived from αὐτός (autós, “self”) + the root of διδάσκω (didáskō, “I teach”).
From Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”).
From Late Latin delavāre, from Latin de + lavāre.
From a- (“to, towards”) + mare (“sea”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
Borrowed from Latin andrōnem from Ancient Greek ἀνδρών (andrṓn).
From Latin anthrōpophagus, from Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποφάγος (anthrōpophágos).
From diritto + -tura or from Latin dīrēctūra.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin exsistentiālis.
From arma (“weapon”) + -aiolo (suffix indicating a profession or activity).
From a- + riccio + -are. Compare Spanish rizar, Portuguese riçar and French hérisser.
Borrowed from Latin aspidem, from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield; Egyptian cobra”). Doublet of aspe.
From assillo (“horsefly, gadfly; nagging worry”) + -are. Compare Sicilian siḍḍijari (often incorrectly written as siḍḍiari).
From a- + sottile (“thin”) + -are, or from a- + sottigliare (now obsolete), from Late Latin subtiliāre, from Latin subtīlis.
From astro- + -nautica, on the model of aeronautica.
From Ancient Greek ἄτονος (átonos), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + τόνος (tónos, “tension, tone”).
Borrowed from Latin aurifer. By surface analysis, auri- + -ifero.
Borrowed from French autocratie, from Medieval Greek αὐτοκρατία (autokratía).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin dēsertiōnem, from Latin dēsertus.
From dis- + inserire. First attested in 1940.
From dispetto + -oso; cognate with Piedmontese dispetos.
Borrowed from Old French bai, or Old Occitan, ultimately from Latin badius.
Via Latin balaustum, balaustium, from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Latin anguem, form of anguis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éngʷʰis (“snake”).
From battere (“to beat”) + -tore (“-er”, agent noun suffix).
From bevone, from Late Latin bibōnem, from Latin bibō, bibere + -ō, -ōnem. By surface analysis, bere + -one.
From bi- + camera + -ale, a calque of English bicameral.
Inherited from Late Latin drappus, probably of Germanic or possibly Celtic origin.
Deverbal from bilicare (“to balance”) + -o, itself inherited from Vulgar Latin *umbilicāre, derived from Latin umbilicus.
Inherited from Late Latin bisaccium, bi- + sacca. Compare dialectal English bysack.
From bi- (“bi-, two”) + Latin secāre (“to cut”). First attested in 1905.
Borrowed from Latin diūturnus (“long-lasting”), derived from diū (“continually, all day”).
From Latin Rudolphus, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþiwulfaz (literally “glorious wolf”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bonificāre. By surface analysis, buono + -ficare.
From Latin Zacharias, from Koine Greek, from Hebrew.
Borrowed from Late Latin duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō.
From Medieval Latin Bulgarus (“Bulgarian; swindler, usurer”) + -are.
From cane (“dog”) + -esco, using the root found in cagna (“female dog”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calidizāre. Derivable from caldo + -eggiare.
Borrowed from French calotte. Compare Portuguese calota.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “I explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “I lead, guide”).
From Latin mūnificentia, derived from mūnificēns (“bountiful”).
From Latin ēbrius, from Proto-Italic *ēɣʷrios, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ēgʷʰryos, derived from the root *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”).
From Ancient Greek τρίπτυχος (tríptukhos, “consisting of three layers, threefold”), from τρι- (tri-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “a fold”).
From Latin petrōsus or from pietra + -oso. Doublet of petroso.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin exemplificāre, from Latin exemplum (“example”).
Borrowed from French hématie, from Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin imperscrūtābilis.
From Latin efferātus, from efferō (“to brutalize”), from ferus (“wild”), related to Italian fiero.
Learned borrowing from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek σωματικός (sōmatikós, “bodily”), from σῶμα (sôma, “body”). By surface analysis, soma + -atico.
From Late Latin caprifolium, from Latin caper + folium.
Inherited from Late Latin farīnōsus, from Latin farīna. By surface analysis, farina + -oso.

From Latin epigonī, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγονοι (epígonoi), plural form of ἐπίγονος (epígonos, “offspring, descendant”), from ἐπιγίγνομαι (epigígnomai, “to come after”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”), from γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to become”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin hermeticus.
From Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -archia (“rule”, “government”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin retorsiōnem, derived from retorsus, alternative form of Latin retortus, perfect passive participle of retorqueō.
Borrowed from Late Latin exūberantia, derived from Latin exūberāns, present active participle of exūberō (“to abound or flourish”).
From Latin salix, from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥H-ik- (“willow”). Doublet of Salgari.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin temporizāre, from Latin tempus (“time”); adapted to the suffix -eggiare.
Inherited from Late Latin variola f, with a change in gender.

Uncertain. Most sources originate it from Late Latin faluppa (“chaff, waste”) (from which also the doublet faloppa), influenced from/crossed with a derivate of Latin volvere. Other sources theorizes a sole derivation from volvere. Lastly, it may be related to/based on Old French (en)velopper, which either derives from one of the previously mentioned roots or, through an unattested Vulgar Latin term, from Germanic (compare with the (unsourced) theories displayed for the english terms envelop, develop).
Inherited from Latin numerus (via old intermediary forms *nomero > *nombero > *nobero), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”). Doublet of numero, a borrowing.
(Possibly borrowed) from Latin opācus (“shaded, shady, dark”), itself of unknown origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *farrum, from Latin far (“emmer”).
From fiacc(o) (“exhaust, weary”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix). Compare Sicilian ciaccari.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin novilūnium.
Borrowed from Latin frātricīda. By surface analysis, fratri- (“brother”, fossilized stem of fratello) + -cida.
From Late Latin trepanum, from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “auger, borer”).
From the variant formicola of formica (“ant”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation suffix). Cf. also French fourmiller.
Borrowed from French frange, from Late Latin fimbria, from Latin fimbriae. Compare Sicilian frinza.
Borrowed from French jade, from Spanish piedra de ijada (“loin stone”), because of its purported property of curing kindney stones.
From lavare + -tura, or from a Vulgar Latin *lavatūra, from Latin lavō. Compare French lavure, Sicilian lavatura, Spanish lavadura, Romanian lături.
Borrowed from Latin locusta, of uncertain origin. Doublet of the inherited aragosta.
Learned borrowing from Latin ostentātiōnem (“exhibition, showing off”).
From Latin portentum, participle of portendere, from portendō (“to predict, to foretell”).
Borrowed from Latin Cȳrēnaeus, from Ancient Greek Κυρηναῖος (Kurēnaîos), from Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē) + -αῖος (-aîos).
From corniolo, ultimately from Latin cornus.
From discernere + -mento; cognate with Piedmontese disserniment.
Borrowed from Spanish fanfarrón, from Arabic فَرْفَار (farfār), perhaps via French fanfaron.
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin fulgor, fulgōrem (“lightning; flash”).
From Old French garant, probably from Frankish *werênd, *warjan, akin to German gewähren (“to grant”) and Old High German wërênt.
Borrowed from Old French joir. Doublet of godere.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impostūra.
Borrowed from Latin ineffābilis (“unutterable, unpronounceable”), derived from effābilis (“utterable”), derived from effor (“to speak, say out, utter”), derived from for (“to speak, talk, say”).
From Late Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; phlegm”).
Borrowed from Spanish flojo, from Latin fluxus. Doublet of frocio. Compare Sicilian froscia.
Inherited from Latin lībātiōnem. Compare libazione, a borrowing from Latin.
From Latin licentiōsus, from licentia (“license, freedom”).
From mentire + -tore, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *mentitōrem, from Latin mentior. Compare French menteur, Romanian mințitor.
Borrowed from Late Latin parasceue, from Ancient Greek παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ, “preparazione”).
From Latin perniciōsus. By surface analysis, pernicie (“disaster”, “ruin”) + -oso (“-ous”, suffix denoting presence of an attribute).
Inherited from Latin pēnsiōnem. Doublet of pensione, which was borrowed.
From Latin prīscus, from earlier *priuscus, derived from prior (“former”, “previous”), from Proto-Italic *priōs, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *per (“to go over”).
Borrowed from Late Latin prōclāmātiōnem, from Latin prōclāmō.
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin pulcher, pulchrum.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin sūdārium, from Latin sūdor.
From Latin tarmes, perhaps via intermediate Vulgar Latin *tărma. Doublet of tarlo.
From Latin tarsus (“tarsus”), from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “flat surface used for drying”).
From vano (“vain”) + -eggiare; cognate with Piedmontese vanegé.
Borrowed from Late Latin verbōsitās. By surface analysis, verboso + -ità.
From Latin verbōsus. Cognate with Piedmontese verbus.
Borrowed from Late Latin inductivus, from Latin inducō.
From carta (“paper”) + pesta (“crushed, ground, beaten”). Literally, “crushed paper”.
Borrowed from Late Latin chartulārius and adapted to native -aio. Doublet of cartulario.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin anacardium, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “on, upon”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”).
From Latin iuvencus (“young”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós, derived from *h₂yuh₁en-, derived from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force”, “life”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin excommūnicāre, from Latin ex + commūnicō.
From inquietare (“to worry, upset”) + -si (enclitic reflexive pronoun).
From in- (“into”) + castone (“collet, bezel, rim in which a jewel is set”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix).
Borrowed from Latin īnsipientem (“foolish”), derived from in- (“not”) + sapiēns (“discerning, wise”).
From Latin pistacium (possibly through Latin *pistaculum), from Ancient Greek πιστάκιον (pistákion). Of Iranian origin. See also πιστάκη (pistákē).
From sesso + -ato, with influence from sessuale.
From Latin sculptōrem. Cognate with Friulian scultôr, Lombard scultor, Piedmontese scultor.

From διαβάλλω (diabállō, “to slander”, from δια- (dia-, “through”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”)). For the meaning development, compare Russian кида́ла (kidála), кида́лово (kidálovo) related to кида́ть (kidátʹ).
From ἄρχω (árkhō, “to begin, to be first in order”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).

From ἔκκλητος (ékklētos, “summoned”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix), from ἐκκαλέω (ekkaléō, “to call forth, summon”), from ἐκ (ek) + καλέω (kaléō). The τ (t) changes to σ (s) by palatalization and assibilation, triggered by the following ι (i). Compare typologically Latin convocātio.
From Ἰουδά (Ioudá) + -ιος (-ios), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yəhūḏā(h), “Judah”).
From σῠ́νεδρος (sŭ́nedros, “sitting together”) + -ιον (-ion), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “with”) + ἕδρᾱ (hédrā, “seat”).
From συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather together”) + -ή (-ḗ), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead”).

From Θεσσᾰλός (Thessălós, “Thessalian”) + νῑ́κη (nī́kē, “victory”). The woman was named by her father, Philip II, in honor of his military victory in Thessaly, and later the city was named after her by Cassander, her husband.
From εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + ἀγγέλλω (angéllō, “to deliver”).

Resembles λεπίς (lepís, “scale”) + *-ρᾱ (*-rā), but with unclear morphology. Perhaps both words are ultimately Pre-Greek; compare λεβηρῐ́ς (lebērĭ́s, “shed skin”), and see λέπω (lépō, “to peel”) for more.
Perhaps from λέπω (lépō, “to peel”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, feminine suffix).
From παραβάλλω (parabállō, “to set side by side”) + -η (-ē).
Inherited from Middle French premier, from Old French premier, from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primaire.
From βᾰπτῐ́ζω (băptĭ́zō, “to baptise”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
The feminine substantive form of the adjective μεσοποτάμιος (mesopotámios) from μεσο- (meso-, “middle, between”) + ποταμός (potamós, “river”), compare with the Hebrew אֲרַם נַהֲרַיִם.
From διαδέω (diadéō, “to bind round”) + -μα (-ma, result noun suffix).
Compound of στρατός (stratós, “army”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead”) + -ος (-os). Cf. Proto-West Germanic *harjatogō, Proto-Slavic *vojevoda.
From φῐλόσοφος (phĭlósophos, “lover of knowledge or wisdom”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from φῐ́λος (phĭ́los, “beloved; loving”) + σοφός (sophós, “skilled with handcrafts; wise”).

From Ἰνδός (Indós, “the Indus river”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from Old Persian 𐏃𐎡𐎯𐎢𐏁 (hiⁿdūš), from Proto-Iranian *hínduš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *síndʰuš (“river”), of uncertain origin. Compare Persian هند (hend), Sanskrit सिन्धु (síndhu, “a river, stream”).
From Ἀχᾱΐᾱ (Akhāḯā, “Achaea”) + -ιος (-ios, adjective suffix). It is also attested as in the older forma Ἀχαιϝοί (Akhaiwoí), possibly coming via an intermediate form *Ἀχαϝyοί (*Akhawyoí).
From ἀγα- (aga-, “very”) + μέμνων (mémnōn, “steadfast”). See ἄγαν (ágan), μένω (ménō) and Μενέλαος (Menélaos).
From ἄναρχος (ánarkhos, “without leader”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix).
From ῐ̔στορέω (hĭstoréō, “to inquire”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from ἵστωρ (hístōr, “one who knows, wise one”).
From τρέφω (tréphō, “to maintain, support”) + -η (-ē, action noun suffix).
From ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “I strike with a stroke”) + -τικός (-tikós), from ἀπό (apó, “of, from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “I strike”).
PIE word  *h₁nómn̥ From ὄνομᾰ (ónomă, “name”) + -άζω (-ázō, denominative verb suffix).
From the phrase Κωνστᾰντῑ́νου (Kōnstăntī́nou, “Constantine's”, genitive) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).
From εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + βο- (bo-, “cow”) + -ια (-ia, “country of”), literally “good cow country”.
From ᾰ̓μφῐ́ (ămphĭ́, “on both sides”) + τρῡ́ων (trū́ōn, “harassing”), from τρῡ́ω (trū́ō, “to wear out; to distress”).

The theonym is found in Homer and Hesiod (c. 8th century B.C.). Traditionally it has been viewed as a compound, ᾰ̓φρός (ăphrós, “sea foam; froth”) + -δῑ́τη (-dī́tē), connecting the first part with the legend of the goddess' birth. This has not been accepted by modern scholars. There is no etymology generally accepted in scholarship. Some such as Beekes propose that the name in its entirety is a loan from a non-Greek language, of probable "oriental origin", possibly Cypriot Phoenician (such as in the Idalion bilingual). A connection to Akkadian 𒀭𒈹 (ᵈIštar) has been further proposed. An older, now rejected proposal of a Greek etymology connects -δῑ́τη (-dī́tē) with the verb δέᾰτο (déăto, “to shine, to appear, seem”) (Homeric δῆλος (dêlos, “visible, conspicuous, clear”)) and interprets the name as originating from an epithet of the dawn goddess Ἠώς (Ēṓs). More on Wikipedia.
According to scholars in classical Greece, from Cretan dialectal ἀρι- (ari-, “very”) + ἀδνός (adnós, “holy, pure”). Beekes, however, suggests a Pre-Greek Minoan origin.
Endearing form of *Ναυσικάστη (*Nausikástē). From ναῦς (naûs, “ship”) + κᾱ́ω (kā́ō, “burn”)
From καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”), probably from the aorist καλύψαι (kalúpsai) + -ώ (-ṓ).
From γρήγορος (grḗgoros, “watchful; alert; awake”) + -ιος (-ios), from ἐγρήγορᾰ (egrḗgoră) (perfect form used as present) of ἐγείρω (egeírō).
From δήϊος (dḗïos, “hostile, destroying”) + ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man, husband”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă), referring to her killing of her husband, Heracles.
A compound of εὐρῠ́ς (eurŭ́s, “broad”) + κλέος (kléos, “fame”) + -ια (-ia). Compare Ἀντῐ́κλειᾰ (Antĭ́kleiă) and Μεγᾰ́κλειᾰ (Megắkleiă).
From ῐ̔ερός (hĭerós, “holy; sacred”) + ὄνῠμᾰ (ónŭmă, “name”) + -ος (-os, adjective-forming suffix), literally “having a holy name”.
From ἶφι (îphi, “by force or might”, Epic adverb) + -γένειᾰ (-géneiă, “birth”). See also Ῑ̓φῐγόνη (Īphĭgónē).
From δῐᾰτῐ́θημῐ (dĭătĭ́thēmĭ); also analyzable as δια- (dia-) + -θήκη (-thḗkē)
Originally a comparative adjective, from ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + -ίων (-íōn, “-er”)
From θεός (theós, “ruler, god”) + κῦδος (kûdos, “glory”) + -ῐ́δης (-ĭ́dēs, patronymic suffix).
From καταρρᾱ́σσω (katarrhā́ssō) + -της (-tēs), the former from κατα- (kata-, “down”) + ῥᾱ́σσω (rhā́ssō, “to strike, dash”).
From δῐᾰφαίνω (dĭăphaínō, “to shine; to be manifest”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix).
From στέλλω (stéllō, “to clothe”) + -η (-ē). Compare deverbal English dress.
From ἀείδω (aeídō, “to sing”) + -ός (-ós, deverbal adjective and noun suffix).
From the root of κεράννυμι (keránnumi, “to mix”) + -σις (-sis).
From σείω (seíō, “to shake”) + -μός (-mós). The "earthquake" sense is an ellipsis of γῆς σεισμός (gês seismós, “shaking of the earth”).
From σῠ́μφωνος (sŭ́mphōnos, “agreeing in sound, harmonious”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā) and σῠν- (sŭn-, “with, together”) + -φωνίᾱ (-phōníā, “sound”).
From ἐπῐφᾰνής (epĭphănḗs, “in view”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă), from ἐπιφαίνω (epiphaínō, “to come into view”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, bring to light”).
From πρό (pró, “before”) + -τερος (-teros, contrastive or comparative suffix).
From ἐνεργής (energḗs) + -ιᾰ (-iă); for the former component, see ἐνεργός (energós, “at work; active”).
From the root of βιβρώσκω (bibrṓskō, “to eat”) + -μᾰ (-mă, object noun suffix).
Compound of λόχος (lókhos, “a lochus; a file in the phalanx”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead”) + -ος (-os).
From διαστέλλω (diastéllō) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix), from διά (diá, “apart”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “send”).

From βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + στροφή (strophḗ, “turning”) + -ηδόν (-ēdón, adverbial suffix), in reference to the back-and-forth course traced by boustrophedon text resembling the path taken by an ox ploughing a field.
Nominalization of verb φωνέω (phōnéō, “to produce a sound or tone”) + -μᾰ (-mă)
From μῠ́στης (mŭ́stēs, “one who has been initiated”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós).
From στέλλω (stéllō, “to send”) + -ος (-os). See also στολή (stolḗ).
From σῠνῐ́στημῐ (sŭnĭ́stēmĭ, “to place together, associate, unite”) + -μᾰ (-mă).

From an earlier *προτῐωπον (*protĭōpon, literally “what is opposite to the eyes [of the other]”), analyzed as προτῐ́ (protĭ́, “opposite”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”) + -ον (-on, “nominative neuter suffix”); for the first component, see πρός (prós, “towards”). In light of exact cognates such as Tocharian B pratsāko (“chest”) and Sanskrit प्रती॑क (prátīka, “face; appearance”), this compound may have been directly inherited from Proto-Indo-European *prótih₃kʷom, though it is equally possible it was formed independently of its cognates.
From τᾰ́σσω (tắssō, “I arrange”, “I order”, aorist passive participial stem: τᾰγ-, tag-) + -σῐς (-sĭs).
From φλέγω (phlégō, “to set on fire, inflame”) + -μα (-ma).
From γραφή (graphḗ, “drawing, painting, writing, a writing, description, etc.”) + -ικός (-ikós), from γράφω (gráphō).
From τέλος (télos, “end”) + *-ϳω (*-jō, denominative verbal suffix). Synchronically from τέλος (télos) + -έω (-éō).

From σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *sḱop-, the o-grade of *sḱep-, a metathesis of *speḱ-, from which also comes σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “to consider, think, speculate”).
From δῐπλόω (dĭplóō, “I double”) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).
From χαράσσω (kharássō, “to scratch, engrave”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, agent noun suffix). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀏𐀨𐀏𐀳𐀨 (ka-ra-ka-te-ra).
From μετέχω (metékhō, “to take part”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).

From αὐτόνομος (autónomos, “autonomous, independent”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-y, -ia”, nominal suffix), from αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) + νόμος (nómos, “usage, custom; law, ordinance”) + -ος (-os, adjectival suffix).
From φᾰ́ντᾰσῐς (phắntăsĭs) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from φᾰντᾰ́ζω (phăntắzō, “to make visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine”).
From the root of ἁμαρτάνω (hamartánō, “to miss, fail”) + -ίᾱ (-íā, abstract noun suffix).

Borrowed from Latin praecoquum (“precocious”), variant of praecox (“early-ripe”), apparently because the apricot was considered a "precocious" variant of the peach. βερίκοκκον (beríkokkon) (whence modern Greek βερίκοκο (veríkoko)) is traditionally connected and considered as a variant form; however, the details of its relation to and phonetic development from πραικόκιον (praikókion) are unclear.

Directly from τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, place”) + -σις (-sis). Although, it could either have been formed in Greek, or Proto-Indo-European. In the latter case, this would be from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tis, from *dʰeh₁- (root of τίθημι (títhēmi)). Cognates include Sanskrit अपिहिति (ápihiti), Avestan 𐬀𐬭𐬋𐬌𐬛𐬍𐬙𐬌 (arōidīti), Latin conditiō, and Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌳𐌴𐌸𐍃 (gadēþs). More at deed.
From σῠ́μμετρος (sŭ́mmetros, “symmetrical”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “with”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, σῠν- (sŭn-, “with”) + -μετρῐ́ᾱ (-metrĭ́ā, “-metry”).
From συμπαθής (sumpathḗs, “affected by like feelings; exerting mutual influence, interacting”) + -ια (-ia).
From ῠ̔ποτῐ́θημῐ (hŭpotĭ́thēmĭ, “to place under, set before, suggest”) + -σῐς (-sĭs).
From the root of προΐστημι (proḯstēmi, “to stand in front”) + -της (-tēs), the former from προ- (pro-) + ἵστημι (hístēmi).
τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”) + -ος (-os). Hypothetically inherited from Proto-Hellenic *tómos, from Proto-Indo-European *tómh₁-o-s, from *temh₁- (“to cut”).

From στέφω (stéphō, “to encircle, crown”) + -μα (-ma), with regressive assimilation (though others, including Beekes, instead take the word to stem from the root of στολή (stolḗ, “equipment, robe”) + -μα (-ma)).
Derived from μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “monarch”) + -ία (-ía, noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, μόνος (mónos, “sole, only”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “rule, government”).
From φαρμακεύω (pharmakeúō, “to use drugs”) + -ία (-ía), from φάρμακον (phármakon).
From ἀποτίθημι (apotíthēmi, “to put away”), from ἀπο- (apo-, “away”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put”).
From κλῆρος (klêros, “a lot, which is alotted, clergy”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós).
From φᾰντός (phăntós, “visible”) + -ᾰ́ζω (-ắzō), verbal adjective of φαίνω (phaínō, “I cause to appear, bring to light”).
From ἀξιόω (axióō, “to think or deem worthy”) + -μα (-ma).
From σκάπτω (skáptō, “to dig”) + -ος (-os). Compare, for more, σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).
From θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “I wait on, attend, serve, cure”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From στραβίζω (strabízō, “to squint”) + -μός (-mós), from στραβός (strabós, “distorted, squinting”).
From συντάσσω (suntássō, “to put together”) + -μα (-ma) and συν- (sun-) + τάγμα (tágma, “command, order”)
From εὔφορος (eúphoros, “bearing well”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear”).
From λειτουργός (leitourgós, “public servant”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun–forming suffix).
From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + πάθος (páthos, “feeling, suffering”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix).
From κόχλος (kókhlos, “shellfish with a spiral shell”) + -ῐ́ᾱς (-ĭ́ās, nominal suffix).
From πάνοπλος (pánoplos, “in full armour”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from πᾶς (pâs, “all, every”) + ὅπλον (hóplon, “armour”).

Usually interpreted as derived from πάγος (págos, “crag, rock”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”). However, this traditional etymology is unconvincing, like in σκίουρος (skíouros, “squirrel”). More probably this is a Pre-Greek word. Furnée compares also φάγρος (phágros, “red porgy”).
From σῠνᾰλλᾰ́σσω (sŭnăllắssō, “to have dealings with another”) + -μα (-ma). By surface analysis, συν- (sun-, “syn-, with”) + ἄλλαγμα (állagma, “something taken in exchange”).
From φωνέω (phōnéō, “to speak, produce a sound”) + -τικός (-tikós).
From φῐλέω (phĭléō, “to love; to kiss”) + -τρον (-tron, instrument noun suffix).
From ἀ- (a-, privative alpha) + μιαίνω (miaínō, “stain, defile”) + -τος (-tos).
From μοναστήριος (monastḗrios, “alone, made alone”) + -ιον (-ion, “-ium: forming places”), from μονάζω (monázō, “to be alone”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”).
From τραγῳδός (tragōidós, “singer and dancer in the tragic choir; tragic actor”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).

From ὦνος (ônos, “price”) + -έομαι (-éomai). The suppletive aorist ἐπρῐάμην (eprĭámēn) is from Proto-Indo-European *kʷreyh₂- (“to buy”). Cognates include Welsh prynu, Old Irish crenaid, Sanskrit क्री॒णाति॑ (krīṇā́ti) (root क्री (krī)), Old East Slavic крити (kriti).
From ἔπος (épos, “speech, song”) + ποιέω (poiéō, “to make, to do”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
From ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “to be an anachronism”) + -μός (-mós), from ἀνά (aná, “backwards”) + χρονίζω (khronízō, “to be located in time”).
From ᾰ̓νᾰ- (ănă-, “backwards”) + χρονῐ́ζω (khronĭ́zō, “to be located in time”).
From ᾱ̓θλέω (āthléō, “to contend”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From ἆθλος (âthlos, “contest, struggle”) or ἆθλον (âthlon, “prize, contest”) + -έω (-éō, “verbal suffix”). In the Attic form ᾱ̓θλῶ (āthlô), ᾰε (ăe) is contracted to ᾱ (ā).
From εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + δαίμων (daímōn, “god, destiny”), literally “possessed by a good genius or spirit”.
From φέρω (phérō, “to carry”) + -τρον (-tron, instrument noun suffix).
From αὐλέω (auléō, “to play the flute”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From ᾰ̓νᾰτείνω (ănăteínō, “to lift up, stretch forth”) + -σῐς (-sĭs).
From πολῠ́γᾰμος (polŭ́gămos, “married to many”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γᾰ́μος (gắmos, “marriage”).
From κᾰτήγορος (kătḗgoros) + -έω (-éō), or from κᾰτᾰ- (kătă-, “against”) + ἀγορεύω (agoreúō, “to speak in assembly”).
From ὡρολόγος (hōrológos, “Egyptian astrologer”) + -ιον (-ion), the former from ὥρα (hṓra, “hour”) + λέγω (légō, “to put in order”) + -ος (-os).
From ᾰ̓ντονομᾰ́ζω (ăntonomắzō, “to name instead, call by a new name”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
Formed as σῠν- (sŭn-, “with”) + ἕδρᾱ (hédrā, “seat; session”); the noun is a substantive use of the adjective.

From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μέθῠστος (méthŭstos, “drunken”), from μεθῠ́ω (methŭ́ō, “to be drunk on wine”), from μέθῠ (méthŭ, “wine”). Compare to εὐμέθῠστος (euméthŭstos, “easily made drunk”). The exact semantic development of the "stone" sense is uncertain. Beekes believes that the stone was named after the light color of diluted wine (that is, "non-drunk wine"), while others have proposed that the Greeks believed that the amethyst prevented intoxication.
From διαιρέω (diairéō, “take apart, cleave, divide”) + -σις (-sis), from δια- (dia-, “apart”) + αἱρέω (hairéō, “take, grasp”).
From ἐλέφας (eléphas, “elephant”) + -ινος (-inos, “-ine”). Compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀩𐀞𐀳𐀃 (e-re-pa-te-o), 𐀁𐀩𐀞𐀳𐀍 (e-re-pa-te-jo, “made of ivory”) formed with -εῖος (-eîos).
From σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”), possibly ultimately from the Old Chinese word for silk.

Derived from δέκᾰ (dékă) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs); compare δυάς (duás), τριάς (triás), τετράς (tetrás), χιλιάς (khiliás), μυριάς (muriás). Formal similarities with Proto-Slavic *desętь, Lithuanian dešimt, Latvian desmit (dental suffix indicating collectivity).
From μᾰκρόθῡμος (măkróthūmos, “long-suffering, patient”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from μακρο- (makro-, “long”) + θῡμός (thūmós, “soul; temper, passion”).
From δῐᾰγῐγνώσκω (dĭăgĭgnṓskō, “distinguish; discern”) + -σῐς (-sĭs), from δῐᾰ- (dĭă-) + γῐγνώσκω (gĭgnṓskō, “know”).
From εὔχομαι (eúkhomai, “to pray; to wish”) + -η (-ē, noun-forming suffix).
From ἄμβροτος (ámbrotos, “immortal”) + -ιος (-ios, adjective suffix). The τ changed to σ before ι by assibilation.
From ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “under”, “beneath”) + γῆ (gê, “land”, “earth”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, adjective-forming derivational suffix).
Derived from λήθᾱργος (lḗthārgos, “forgetful, lethargic”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, nominal abstract derivative suffix).
From εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). Euphemistically refers to "left" because bad omens came from the left side.
From the verb ῠ̔ποτῐ́θημῐ (hŭpotĭ́thēmĭ, “put down, pledge”). Morphologically, from ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + -θήκη (-thḗkē, “case, holster”).

Traditionally analyzed as ὗς (hûs, “swine”) + θρῐ́ξ (thrĭ́x, “hair”), or alternatively with the first element being the base of ῠ̔́στερος (hŭ́steros, “latter”), thus “(animal with) rising hairs”. However, Beekes cites the nasalization seen in the variant genitive plural form ῠ̔στρῐ́γγων (hŭstrĭ́ngōn, from ῠ̔́στρῐγξ (hŭ́strĭnx)) as proof of Pre-Greek origin.
From ὅμῑλος (hómīlos, “a crowd or gathering of people”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).

Traditionally derived from ὁμός (homós, “same, joint”) + ῑ̓́λη (ī́lē, “crowd”), the latter related to εἴλω (eílō, “to aggregate”). However, Beekes is skeptical and prefers to take the word as Pre-Greek, due to the presence of interchange -ιλ-ο-/-ιλλ-ο- in variants such as ὅμιλλος (hómillos), ὁμιλλει (homillei), as well as the word's phonetic structure and to some extent semantics resembling that of ἅμιλλα (hámilla, “competition”), which is probably also Pre-Greek.

The personification of λάχεσις (lákhesis, “obtainment by lot”), from λαχεῖν (lakheîn, “to obtain by lot”) + -σις (-sis, “-ing”), the former being the aorist of λαγχάνειν (lankhánein). The thing obtained is lifetime, represented by Lachesis allocating a certain length of the life-thread spun by Κλωθώ (Klōthṓ) to each individual.
Derived from μόνος (mónos, “single, only”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “ruler, leader”).
Derived from ἔπος (épos, “story, song”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
From ἐρᾰτός (erătós, “lovely”) + σθένος (sthénos, “strong”) + -ης (-ēs, masculine proper noun suffix)
From ἔνδον (éndon, “within”) + -γενής (-genḗs). Compare with Latin indigenus.

Traditionally regarded as a formation from τῠ́πτω (tŭ́ptō, “to strike, beat, smite”) + -ᾰνον (-ănon), similar to that of ὄργανον (órganon, “instrument, sense organ”). However, a borrowing from some other language such as Semitic seems likely; compare Hebrew תֹּף (top, “drum”), Ugaritic 𐎚𐎔 (tp, “drum”), with this borrowed element undergoing folk-etymological adaptation to τῠ́πτω (tŭ́ptō).
Αἰγεύς (Aigeús, “Aegeus”) + -αῖος (-aîos, adjectival suffix). The name might be connected to αἶγες (aîges, “waves”).
From ἀμείβω (ameíbō, “to exchange”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).
From αὐτάρκης (autárkēs, “self-sufficient”) + -ιᾰ (-iă, abstract noun suffix), from αὐτο- (auto-, “self-”) + ἀρκέω (arkéō, “to suffice”).
From ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to put, place, set”) + -τήρ (-tḗr), hence literally "that which sets, settles".
From ὀρχέομαι (orkhéomai, “to dance”) + -τρᾰ (-tră, “a suffix used to form instrument nouns (pl.)”).
From ᾰ̓́κρος (ắkros, “at the edge; extreme, outermost”) + πόλῐς (pólĭs, “city; the Athenian citadel”).
From προξενέω (proxenéō, “to manage on another's behalf”) + -τής (-tḗs).
From μέλπω (mélpō, “to celebrate with dance and song”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).
From μεταβάλλω (metabállō, “to change”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).
αὔταρχος (aútarkhos, “autocratic, absolute; autarchic”) + -ία (-ía), from αὐτ- (aut-, “self”) + ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule, govern”)

From μνήμων (mnḗmōn, “remembering”) + -ικός (-ikós, “relative to”); μνήμων (mnḗmōn) from μνάομαι (mnáomai, “to be mindful, remember”) (from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to mind; to think”)) + -μων (-mōn, suffix forming adjectives and agent nouns).
From πέτρος (pétros, “rock”) + σέλινον (sélinon, “celery”). So called because of being used to treat calculi.
From αὐτο- (auto-, “self-”) + νόμος (nómos, “usage, custom; law, ordinance”) + -ος (-os, adjectival suffix).
From κᾰτᾰ- (kătă-, denoting motion downwards) + λέγω (légō, “to choose, to say”).
From συν- (sun-, “with”) + λέγω (légō, “to choose, to say”).
From ῥᾰ́πτω (rhắptō, “to sew together, stitch”) + -η (-ē, action noun suffix).
From μετᾰ- (metă-, “in the midst of”) + ὀπή (opḗ, “hole, opening”).
From βᾰ́τρᾰχος (bắtrăkhos, “frog”) + -ῐον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix). Compare typologically Latin rānunculus (diminutive of rāna).
From πᾰρᾰ́ (părắ, “beside”) + σῖτος (sîtos, “wheat; corn”). Compare typologically Russian нахле́бник (naxlébnik) (< хлеб (xleb)).
From μελάγχολος (melánkholos, “dipped in black bile”) + -ία (-ía), from μέλας (mélas, “black”) + χόλος (khólos, “gall, bile”).
From οἶκος (oîkos, “house, home, estate”) + νόμος (nómos, “law, rule, authority”), equivalent to οἶκος (oîkos) + νέμω (némō) + -ος (-os).
From πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “I stick, I fix”) + -σις (-sis, suffix to form a feminine noun).
From ὑποκορίζομαι (hupokorízomai, “to call by endearing names”) + -ικός (-ikós). See also ὑπό (hupó, “below”) and κόρη (kórē, “girl”).
From ζῠγόω (zŭgóō, “to yoke or join together”) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominal suffix).
From ἐπι- (epi-, “after”, prepositional prefix) + γόνος (gónos, “fruit, product, seed; begetting, procreation”).
From μετα- (meta-, “concerning change of”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).
From ᾰ̓́λγος (ắlgos, “pain of the body or mind”) + -έω (-éō, verbal suffix).
From ἀφαιρέω (aphairéō, “I take away”) + -σις (-sis, nominal suffix), from ἀφ’ (aph’, apocopic form of ἀπό (apó, “from”)) + αἱρέω (hairéō, “I take”).
From στρέφω (stréphō, “I turn, I twist”) + -τός (-tós, “able to”).
From ἀξίωμα (axíōma, “honor, worth, self-evident principle”) + -ικός (-ikós, “of or pertaining to”), from ἀξιόω (axióō, “to think or deem worthy”) + -μα (-ma, nominal suffix).
From ἐμβάλλω (embállō, “to throw in; to burst in, rush in”) + -ος (-os, nominal suffix).
Borrowed from Latin citrum (“citron”) < citrus, itself probably via Etruscan from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, “cedar”).
From καρκινόω (karkinóō, “to suffer from cancer”) + -μα (-ma), from καρκίνος (karkínos, “crab”).
From καταλύω (katalúō) + -σις (-sis); also analyzable as κατα- (kata-) + λύσις (lúsis).
From πᾰρᾰλογῐ́ζομαι (părălogĭ́zomai, “to cheat; to use fallacies”) + -μός (-mós).
From ἀνᾰχωρέω (anăkhōréō, “to retire, withdraw”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From ῐ̔ερός (hĭerós, “holy”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “show”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent-noun suffix).
From ὁμός (homós, “same, common”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma) + -ος (-os), Doric/Aeolic variant of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
From σπᾰ́ω (spắō, “to draw (a weapon)”) + -ων (-ōn, nominal suffix).
Ellipsis of ἐλεγεία ᾠδή (elegeía ōidḗ, “an elegiac song”), from ἐλεγεῖος (elegeîos, “elegiac”), from ἔλεγος (élegos, “poem or song of lament”), perhaps from Phrygian.
From Koine προκοπ(ή) f (prokop(ḗ), “progress forward to prosperity; advancement toward success; improvement by diligence”) + -ῐος (-ĭos).
From συν- (sun-, with, together) + ἀλλάσσω (allássō, “to change, alter”).
From αὐτο- (auto-, auto-) + κράτος (krátos, “power, strength”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix).
From βόσκω (bóskō) + -τήρ (-tḗr, masculine agent noun suffix).

From ἐπι- (epi-, “on, upon; on top of; all over”) + κοινός (koinós, “common; general, public”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“beside, by, near, with”) + *-yós (suffix forming adjectives from noun stems). Compare γένος ἐπίκοινον (génos epíkoinon, “common gender”).
From εὐφημίζω (euphēmízō, “speak sounds of good omen”) + -ισμός (-ismós, “suffix forming abstract nouns”)
From ἀριθμέω (arithméō, “reckon, count”) + -τικός (-tikós, “a suffix added to verbal stems to form adjectives: relating to, suited to, skilled in, able to”)
From ἐξαιρέω (exairéō, “to take out, discharge [cargo], except, bereave [someone] of [something, e.g. life], transcend, claim [someone] as a freeman”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, suffix forming nouns of action).
From ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “turn away”, from ἀπο- (apo-) + στρέφω (stréphō)) + -ος (-os)
From the o-grade of στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist, turn”) + -ος (-os).
From σκληρόω (sklēróō, “to harden”) + -σις (-sis); also interpretable as σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”) + -ωσις (-ōsis).
From αἱμορροέω (haimorrhoéō, “to lose blood”) + -ῐς (-ĭs), from αἱμο- (haimo-, “blood”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”). Also serves as the feminine of αἱμόρροος (haimórrhoos, “flowing with blood”).
From the root of μνάομαι (mnáomai) + -μων (-mōn); compare μνήμη (mnḗmē, “memory”).
From θαῦμα, θαυματ- (thaûma, thaumat-) + -ουργός (-ourgós). Also substantivised.
From κόλυμβος (kólumbos, “little grebe”) + -άω (-áō, “verbal suffix”), due to the grebe's diving skills.

From τῆλε (têle, “at a distance, far off, far away”) + σκοπός (skopós, “one that watches; a target”). Piecewise doublet of τηλέσκοπος (tēléskopos, “far-seen, conspicuous”) with different accentuation and passive meaning.
From ἀντι- (anti-, “against”) + ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnízomai, “contend for a prize”).
From μέγας (mégas, big, grand) + -γραφία (-graphía, writing, drawing)
From the root of ἐρυθαίνω (eruthaínō, “to dye red, make blush”) and ἔρευθος (éreuthos, “redness, flush”) + -μα (-ma). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”).
From the root of θιγγάνω (thingánō, “to touch, grasp”) + -σις (-sis).
From ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”).
From χωρογρᾰ́φος (khōrogrắphos) + -ικός (-ikós). By surface analysis, χώρα (khṓra) + -γραφικός (-graphikós).
From πολυ- (polu-, “poly-”) + ὄνῠμᾰ (ónŭmă, “name”) + -ος (-os, adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, πολυ- (polu-) + -ώνυμος (-ṓnumos, “-onymous”).
Phono-semantic matching of Latin Rōma with ῥώμη (rhṓmē, “power, strength, might"”).
From λόγος (lógos, “computation, reckoning”) + -ῐ́ζομαι (-ĭ́zomai, denominative mediopassive verb suffix).
From γνω- (gnō-), the root of γῐγνώσκω (gĭgnṓskō, “to know”) + -μη (-mē).
From πόλις (pólis, “city”) + -της (-tēs). The ῑ from the stem of πόλις led to the backformation -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs), whence the reanalysis πολ-ῑ́της (pol-ī́tēs).
From ὄψ (óps, “eye”) + -σῐς (-sĭs). Diachronically from Proto-Hellenic *ókʷtis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ékʷtis, from *h₃ekʷ- (“eye, to see”).
From ἐπι- (epi-) + ἐντίθημι (entíthēmi, “to put in”), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, place”).
From παρα- (para-) + σκευάζω (skeuázō, “to make, prepare”) or παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ) + -άζω (-ázō).
From βούλομαι (boúlomai, “to wish; to will”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).
From ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnízomai, “I contend for a prize”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From μετα- (meta-, indicating change) + φέρω (phérō, “bear, carry”).

According to some scholars, from ἄγω (ágō, “to lead, draw out or down”) + -τιος (-tios) (perhaps via an unattested intermediate ἄξις (áxis, “weight”)), with sense development "draw down (in the scale)" > "weigh, import". Beekes expresses mild doubts about this, both in the semantics as well as no other morphological derivative of ἄγω (ágō) being in -τι- (-ti-), but tentatively accepts this etymology. For a semantic parallel, compare Latin exāmen (“tongue of a balance; examining”), from the same root.
From ἀπο- (apo-, “off”) + ὁρῐ́ζω (horĭ́zō, “separate”), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”) + -ίζω (-ízō, denominative verb suffix).
From ἔνθους (énthous), later contracted form of ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), + -ιάζω (-iázō, denominative verb suffix), influenced by οὐσία (ousía, “essence”).
From ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bring, bear, carry”).
From ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos, “old, ancient”) + -ίζω (-ízō, denominative verb suffix).
From δῐᾰ- (dĭă-, “in different directions, apart, asunder; dia-”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to walk, step”).
From ἐκ- (ek-, “out”) + λέγω (légō, “to choose”). Exact cognate in form and meaning to Latin ēligō (“to choose”).
From ἐνεργός (energós, “active, effective”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix).
From κατα- (kata-, “down, against”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to make stand, set up”).
From δύναμαι (dúnamai, “be able”) + -στης (-stēs, masculine agentive suffix).
From στᾰ́ζω (stắzō, “to drop”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, suffix to form a feminine noun).
From ἀπο- (apo-, “away, from, off”) + τρέπω (trépō, “turn”) from Proto-Indo-European *trep-.
From ἐξ- (ex-, “ex-, out-”) + αἱρέω (hairéō, “to take, seize”).

Inherited from Middle French digue, from Old French dike, diic, from Middle Dutch dijc (compare modern Dutch dijk), from Old Dutch diic, dīc, from Frankish *dīk, from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (“pool”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, stab, pierce, dig”). More at dig, dike, ditch.
Borrowed from Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê). Compare Spanish té. Doublet of chai.
From German Blinde, from blenden (“to dazzle, to blind”).
Inherited from Middle French pennache (“plume of feathers”), borrowed from Italian pennacchio, from Late Latin pinnāculum. Doublet of pinacle.
From Old French billette, from Latin bulla. See French boulette.
From English mohair. Doublet of moire.
Borrowed from German Vampir, from Serbo-Croatian vampir.
From an alteration, likely via Medieval Latin, of Italian gattopardo (“serval”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid, firm”)

Inherited from Middle French bloc (“a considerable piece of something heavy, block”), from Old French bloc (“log, block”), from Middle Dutch blok (“treetrunk”), from Old Dutch *blok (“log”), from Frankish or Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką (“beam, log”).
Inherited from Middle French blocus, bloccus, from Middle Dutch blochuus.
From the Late Latin clīnicus (“a bed-ridden person”, “one baptized on a sick-bed”, “a physician”).
Inherited from Middle French cotte, from Old French cote, Latin cotta, Proto-Germanic *kuttô.
Borrowed from Late Latin scholāris, from schola (“school”). Compare the doublet écolier.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coalitiōnem, from Latin coalitus (“fellowship, communion”).

Inherited from Middle French ouest, from Old French ouest, west, borrowed from Old English west (“west”). The English (rather than Dutch or Norse) origin of the French compass directions is evidenced by the vowel in est.
Inherited from Latin sagēna, from Ancient Greek σαγήνη (sagḗnē).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φωνητικός (phōnētikós).
Inherited from Middle French varieté, borrowed from Latin varietātem.

Inherited from Middle French garçon, from Old French garçon, garçun m (“servant, boy”), from Early Medieval Latin garciōnem, accusative of garciō m (“mercenary, servant, boy”), from Frankish *wrakkjō (“servant, boy”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, driven one”). Cognate with Modern German Recke ("warrior"), Old English wreċċa (“exile, outcast”), whence Modern English wretch.
Borrowed from Old Occitan cazerna, from Latin quaterna (neuter plural of Latin quaternus). Doublet of cahier, inherited from Latin, and quaterne, a later borrowing.
Borrowed from English wagon, from Middle Dutch wagen.
Coined in 1863 by Louis Pasteur, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”).
Inherited from Old French forge, from earlier faverge, inherited from Latin fābrica. Doublet of fabrique, which was borrowed.
From Latin pericarpium, from Ancient Greek περικάρπιον (perikárpion, “pod, husk, shell”), from περί (perí, “around”) + καρπός (karpós, “fruit”).
Inherited from Latin canīcula (“little dog”) (because of a caterpillar's head). Doublet of canicule.
From ᾰ̔γνή (hăgnḗ), the feminine of ᾰ̔γνός (hăgnós, “pure; chaste”)
Borrowed from Spanish cauchuc (an early variant of caucho), from Quechua kawchu. The final -c was formerly variably pronounced or silent, but is now always silent.

Borrowed from Portuguese feitiço (“feigned, false; spell, witchcraft, amulet”), from Latin factīcius (“artificial”). Compare the doublet factice (a borrowing directly from the Latin), as well as the inherited Old French faitis.

From Dutch vrijbuiter (“freebooter”). The spelling with fl- is often considered to be due to influence from Dutch vlieboot or a descendant of that word. The unetymological spelling with -s- began to appear in the early eighteenth century.

From Middle French losange, losenge, from Old French losenge (“a drawn shape on fabric, rhombus”), of obscure origin. Perhaps ultimately from Gaulish *lausā (“flat stone, stone slab”). Alternatively, perhaps from earlier Old French losenge (“flattery, deceitful praise”), from the notion the shape was reminiscent of the square flat slabs of tombstones upon which fulsome epithets of undue praise and flattery were written.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حلب (haleb), from Arabic حَلَب (ḥalab).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carving”). First attested in 1701.
Derived from glott(e) (“glottis”) + -al (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).
Inherited from Old French gorge, from Late Latin gurga, related to Latin gurges (“eddy, whirlpool; gulf; sea”).
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of water-closet.
Inherited from Middle French coucher, from Old French couchier, from Latin collocāre (“set in place”). Doublet of colloquer.
From a substantivation of Old French linge, from Latin līneus.
From the root of σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “to observe”) + -ός (-ós).
From κόσμησις (kósmēsis, “an adorning”) + -κός (-kós), from κοσμέω (kosméō, “I adorn”).

From ᾰ̓λέκτωρ (ăléktōr, “cock, rooster”) + -υών (-uṓn, an obscure suffix also appearing in ἀλκυών (alkuṓn, “kingfisher”)). The first element is the agentive noun of ᾰ̓λέξω (ăléxō, “ward off”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂lek-s-, an *s-derivative of *h₂lek- (“protect”). Compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀨𐀓𐀶𐀬𐀺 (a-ra-ku-tu-ru-wo /⁠Alektruōn⁠/).
From μή (mḗ, “not”) + δέ (dé, “and, but”). Compare οὐδέ (oudé, “but not, and not”).
From ἅπτω (háptō, “to kindle, set fire; to touch; to fasten”) + -ή (-ḗ).
From μόνος (mónos, “alone”) + μᾰ́χη (mắkhē, “combat”) + -ος (-os), literally “lone warrior”, from μάχομαι (mákhomai, “to fight, battle, contend”).

From ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + Κένταυρος (Kéntauros, “Centaur”). While "horse centaur" may seem redundant, it should be noted that Κένταυρος (Kéntauros) originally referred to a race of people, the Centaurs, who are associated in some myths with the origin of the creature "centaur". This term likely made the distinction between a person of the Centaur race and the creature, until later, when the word κένταυρος (kéntauros) simply referred to the creature. Note that while Wiktionary distinguishes between upper and lower case in Ancient Greek words, Ancient Greek did not (minuscules were not invented until the seventh century).
From Βοιωτός (Boiōtós) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). Possibly related to Βόιον (Bóion).

From ᾰ̓́χθομαι (ắkhthomai, “to be loaded”) + -ος (-os). It has been suggested that the ultimate root is Proto-Indo-European *h₂édʰǵʰ- (“to oppress, squeeze”), though another theory derives ᾰ̓́χθομαι (ắkhthomai) from Proto-Indo-European *h₂égʰdʰ-e-ti, a dental-aspirate present from *h₂egʰ- (“to be upset, afraid”) + *-dʰeti. If this alternative possibly is accepted, then ἄχθος (ákhthos) might have originated from ᾰ̓́χθομαι (ắkhthomai) by analogy with ἄχομαι (ákhomai) ~ ἄχος (ákhos, “distress, pain”).
From φαίνω (phaínō, “to bring to light, to cause to appear”) + -μα (-ma, nominal suffix) with -σ- from analogy to other -αίνω : -ασμα or from φάσις (phásis).
From χρῡσός (khrūsós, “gold”) + πράσον (práson, “leek”) + -ος (-os), in allusion to the greenish color (compare πρασοειδής (prasoeidḗs, “leek-green”)).
From μέλισσα (mélissa, “bee”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of, tend”) + -ος (-os).
From βαθύς (bathús, “deep”) + -ος (-os), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeh₂dʰ- (“to sink, submerge”) (though Beekes rejects the link to the Indo-European root).
παῖς (paîs) + *-ϳω (*-jō), i.e. "to act like a child" > "to play".
ὑπο- (hupo-) + εὔθῡνος (eúthūnos); see εὐθῡ́νω (euthū́nō, “to direct”) for more.
From τᾰ́σσω (tắssō, “to put in order, arrange”) + -ή (-ḗ).
From ἀ- (a-, privative alpha) + καθαίρω (kathaírō, “to cleanse”) + -τος (-tos).
From πόρος (póros, “way, bridge”) + -εύω (-eúō). From πείρω (peírō, “to pierce, pass through”).
From συνέχω (sunékhō, “to keep together, hold together”) + -ής (-ḗs).

Apparently from προσ- (pros-, “pro-”) + φατός (phatós, “slain”), thus originally a hunting or fishing term meaning "lately or freshly slain", with semantic broadening being facilitated once the second element's origin had become opaque to Greek speakers. However, Beekes is skeptical of the above interpretation of the first syllable as being equivalent to the prefix meaning "forward".
From ῑ̓́ς (ī́s, “muscle of the body”) + -ῐον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix).

From ᾰ̓- (ă-, “un-”) + θᾰ́νᾰτος (thắnătos, “dying”). Sense 4, referring to certain soldiers in Achaemenid Persia, has an uncertain origin. One suggestion claimed that "Immortals" were named by the ancient Greeks because wounded soldiers were quickly replaced, while another claimed that it was because Greek informants confused Old Persian *anauša- (“immortal, without death”) with Old Persian *anūšiya- (“companion, royal bodyguard”).
Borrowed from Latin tabla (“tablet, plank, table”).
From ὑποδέχομαι (hupodékhomai, “to welcome”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).
From ἐγκαλέω (enkaléō, “to bring a charge”) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).

From κᾰρόω (kăróō, “to plunge into deep sleep or torpor”) + -τῐ́δες (-tĭ́des, plural nominal suffix), from the fact that the carotid artery supplies blood to the brain, and interruption of this flow causes loss of consciousness.
From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τόλμα (tólma, “boldness, bravery”) + -ος (-os, adjectival suffix)
From μαδάω (madáō, “I fall off, am bald”) + -ρός (-rós).
From ἀμφι- (amphi-, “both”) + ἅλς (háls, “saltwater, the sea”) + -ος (-os), thus literally, “with the sea on both sides”.
From γράφω (gráphō, “to write”) + -εύς (-eús, “-er”, masculine agent noun suffix).
From ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) + ὤρα (ṓra, “care”) + -ος (-os, adjective forming suffix).
From ἀληθής (alēthḗs, “true”) + -ιᾰ (-iă, abstract noun suffix). Synchronically analyzable as ἀληθής (alēthḗs) + -εια (-eia).
From κᾰ́ρος (kắros, “heavy sleep, torpor”) + -όω (-óō, verbal suffix).
From προσ- (pros-) + μείγνῡμῐ (meígnūmĭ), alternative form of μῑ́γνῡμῐ (mī́gnūmĭ).
From δίκαιος (díkaios, “decent, righteous”) + -όω (-óō, “cause someone to be”, factitive verb suffix).
From λέξῐς (léxĭs, “speech, word”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós), from λέγω (légō, “I speak”).
From κῡ́ριος (kū́rios, “lord”) or Κῦρος (Kûros, “Cyrus”) + -ιλλος (-illos, diminutive suffix).
From προ- (pro-, “before, in front of”) + βόσκω (bóskō, “to feed, to graze”) + -ις (-is, suffix to form a feminine noun).
Verbal adjective, from πνῑ́γω (pnī́gō, “to choke, stifle”) + -τός (-tós).
σάνδαλον (sándalon) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive), of uncertain origin, possibly loaned from Parthian, Persian, or another substrate of Asia Minor.

From πορνεύω (porneúō, “to prostitute, to whore”) + -ίᾱ (-íā, “-ia: forming abstract nouns”), from πόρνη (pórnē, “prostitute, whore”) + -εύω (-eúō, forming verbs), from the Proto-Indo-European root *perh₂- (“to sell, to provide for a fee”).
From the root of δείκνυμι (deíknumi, “to show, point out”) + -σῐς (-sĭs).
From γλῠ́φω (glŭ́phō, “to carve, engrave”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).
From ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on, upon; over”) + ᾰ̓́ρχω (ắrkhō, “to begin; lead, rule, command”).
From the root of ἁμαρτάνω (hamartánō, “I miss, fail, am deprived of (a thing), fail to do, sin”) + -μα (-ma, “instance of”).
From ὀκνέω (oknéō, “to shrink, hesitate”) + -ρός (-rós, adjective suffix).
From κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “I discern, judge”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, “masculine agent suffix”).
From δίς (dís) + -άζω (-ázō), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“in two, twice, doubly”); cf. Latin dubitō, German Zweifel (“doubt”), and English second-guess.
From πτόλῐς (ptólĭs), variant of πόλῐς (pólĭs, “city”) + -θρον (-thron). Olsen calls the phonetic details "quite obscure."
From ἐμπειρία (empeiría, “experience”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós), from ἔμπειρος (émpeiros, “skilled”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πεῖρα (peîra, “a trial, experiment, attempt”).
From λῡπέω (lūpéō, “to grieve”) + -ρός (-rós). Compare also λῡπρός (lūprós).
From ψῆφος (psêphos, “pebble; counter; vote”) + -φόρος (-phóros, “-phore, suffix from φόρος (phóros), verb φέρω (“bring”)”).
ἀντι- (anti-) + θεός (theós) The meaning of ἀντί here is "exchangeable for, no better or worse than."
From ἀπράγμων (aprágmōn) + -σύνη (-súnē), from the root of πράσσω (prássō).
From ἐκπλήσσω (ekplḗssō, “to drive out one's senses by a sudden shock”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, nominal suffix), from ἐκ (ek, “out of”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike, to smite”).
From ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “I strike with a stroke”) + -τος (-tos).
κτῐ́ζω (ktĭ́zō, “found, build”) + -σῐς (-sĭs). Cognate with Sanskrit क्षितिज (kṣitija).
From φρονέω (phronéō, “to think”) + -σις (-sis); the former from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).
From πνῑ́γω (pnī́gō, “to choke, throttle, stifle”) + -ρός (-rós, adjective suffix).
From φέρω (phérō) + νῑ́κη (nī́kē), literally “bringer of victory”. Doublet of Βερενῑ́κη (Berenī́kē).
From ἤθω (ḗthō, “to strain, sift”) + -μός (-mós, nominal suffix).
πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent noun suffix)
From λυτρόω (lutróō, “to ransom”) + -τής (-tḗs, “a suffix forming agent nouns”)
From εὐ- (eu-, “well-”) + λαβεῖν (labeîn, “to take hold of”) + -ης (-ēs, adjectival suffix).
From εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”) + -ος (-os), from φημί (phēmí, “to speak, say”).
Derived from δύο (dúo) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs); compare τριάς (triás), τετράς (tetrás), δεκάς (dekás), χιλιάς (khiliás), μυριάς (muriás).
From κᾰρῡ́κη (kărū́kē, “rich sauce made of blood and spices”) + -εύω (-eúō, verb-forming suffix).
From ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + -εύς (-eús, suffix for masculine person concerned).
From κρῠπτός (krŭptós, “hidden”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, adjective forming suffix), from κρῠ́πτω (krŭ́ptō, “hide”).
From φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “to grow; to become; to be”) + -τός (-tós).
From φθείρω (phtheírō, “to spoil, ruin”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).
From Γερμᾱνός (Germānós, “German”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā) or borrowed from Latin Germānia.
From δᾰνείζω (dăneízō, “to lend money”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From προστάσσω (prostássō, “to place or post at a place”) + -μᾰ (-mă).
From ῥῑ́πτω (rhī́ptō, “to throw; to cast; to hurl”) + -ή (-ḗ).
From οὐρέω (ouréō, “to urinate”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, action noun suffix), from οὖρον (oûron, “urine”) + -έω (-éō, verbal suffix).
From ἀ- (a-, “a-, un-”) + πᾰραιτέομαι (păraitéomai, “to beg, entreat”) + -τος (-tos).
From ὁρμή (hormḗ, “start, impetus, rush, attack, effort”) + -άω (-áō, “verbal suffix”).
From λατρεύς (latreús, “hired servant”) + -εύω (-eúō), the former from λάτρις (látris, “hired servant, handmaid”) + -εύς (-eús).
ἐκτᾰ́σσω (ektắssō, “to draw out in battle-order”) + -τος (-tos), from ἐκ- (ek-) + τᾰ́σσω (tắssō).

Unknown. Ultimately either from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on”) + εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “go, come”) or from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on”) + εἰμῐ́ (eimĭ́, “be”). Possible etymologies include: # From the phrase ἡ ἐπῐοῦσᾰ ἡμέρᾱ (hē epĭoûsă hēmérā, “the following day”), essentially breaking down into ἐπῐοῦσᾰ (epĭoûsă, “next, following”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, adjectival suffix), where ἐπῐοῦσᾰ (epĭoûsă) is the feminine nominative singular of ἐπῐών (epĭṓn) the present participle of ἔπειμῐ (épeimĭ, “follow, come after”) from ἐπ- (ep-, “on”) + εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “go, come”). # From the phrase ἐπὶ τὴν οὖσᾰν ἡμέρᾱν (epì tḕn oûsăn hēmérān, “for the actual/current day, lit. for the day being”), essentially breaking down into ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on”) + οὖσᾰ (oûsă, “being, actual”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, adjectival suffix), where οὖσᾰ (oûsă) is the feminine nominative singular of ὤν (ṓn), the present participle of εἰμῐ́ (eimĭ́, “be”). # From ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on”) + οὐσῐ́ᾱ (ousĭ́ā, “essence, existence, substance”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, adjectival suffix), cognate with ἐπουσῐ́ᾱ (epousĭ́ā, “surplus”) from ἐπών (epṓn, “remaining”), the present participle of ἔπειμῐ (épeimĭ, “remain, be left over”) from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on”) + εἰμῐ́ (eimĭ́, “be”), but a separate Koine innovation of t
