Verbal noun from συλλογίζομαι (sullogízomai, “to compute, infer”) + -μός (-mós).
According to Zosimos of Panopolis it was named from its supposed inventor, Χύμης/Χήμης/Χείμης, but more probably it is from χῠ́μᾰ (khŭ́mă) + -είᾱ (-eíā).
From λῠτήρ (lŭtḗr, “who loosens, liberates”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, “pertaining to”, suffix)
From παρα- (para-, “beside, by”) + τείνω (teínō, “to stretch out”).
From μύρον (múron, “sweet juice or oil; muron”) + -ίζω (-ízō, “verbal suffix”).
From κλίνη (klínē, “bed”) + -ικός (-ikós), from κλίνω (klínō, “to lean, incline”).
ἐφίσταμαι [ἐπι-στα-] (ephístamai [epi-sta-], “stand on, over, or near”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent noun suffix): literally, one who stands on, over, or near something or someone.
From κᾰκοποιός (kăkopoiós, “doing ill, mischievous, maleficent”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from κᾰκόποιέω (kăkópoiéō, “I do evil”), from κᾰκός (kăkós, “bad”) + ποιέω (poiéō, “I do”).
From ἀ- (a-, without) + νόμος (nómos, “law, ordinance; melody”).
From ῠ̔περ- (hŭper-, “over”) + θῡμός (thūmós, soul; anger, wrath).
Borrowed from Latin Gallia. Greeks earlier called Gaul Γαλατία (Galatía), also the name for Galatia. Greeks still call France Γαλλία (Gallía).
From δαίμων (daímōn, “god, divine power, evil spirit”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, adjective suffix).
From περίοδος (períodos, “patrol around”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjectival suffix). See also περῐοδεύω (perĭodeúō, “to go round”).
From ἄπληστος (áplēstos, “insatiable, greedy”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix), ultimately from πίμπλημι (pímplēmi, “to fill”).
From Ἥρᾱ (Hḗrā, “Hera”) + κλειτός (kleitós, “glorious”), literally “glory of Hera”. Compare Ἡρακλῆς (Hēraklês).
From Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea; Pontus”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
From μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell tales”) + -ία (-ía), from μυθολόγος (muthológos, “legend”), from μῦθος (mûthos, “story”) + λέγω (légō, “to say”).
μετα- (meta-) + ἀνίστημι (anístēmi), itself from ἀνα- (ana-) + ἵστημι (hístēmi).
From Σᾰ́μος (Sắmos, “Samos, the other island whose people colonized Samothrace”) + Θρᾴκη (Thrāíkē, “Thrace, near which Samothrace is situated”).
Borrowed from Latin birrus, from Gaulish *birros, from Proto-Celtic *birros (“short”).
From αὐδή (audḗ, “human voice”) + *-ϳω (*-jō). By surface analysis, αὐδή (audḗ) + -ᾰ́ω (-ắō).
From χείμερος (kheímeros, “wintry, stormy”) + -ινός (-inós), or directly from Proto-Indo-European [Term?] and cognate with Latin hībernus.
From ῠ̔μνῳδός (hŭmnōidós, “singing hymns”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from ῠ̔́μνος (hŭ́mnos, “hymn”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ), contracted form of ᾰ̓οιδή (ăoidḗ, “song”).
From ᾰ̓γᾰθός (ăgăthós, “good”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work; deed”) + -έω (-éō, verb-forming suffix). Literally, “to do a good deed”.
From παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, “teacher, tutor”) + -ικός (-ikós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead”).
From ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + τοξότης (toxótēs, “archer”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agentive suffix).
From ὅπλον (hóplon, “instrument of war; arms or armour”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs).
From κεντέω (kentéō, “to prick, goad, spur on, stab”) + -τός (-tós).
τραῦμᾰ (traûmă, “wound”, stem: τραυμᾰτ-) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “of or pertaining to”, suffix forming adjectives)
Traditionally analyzed as τηρός (tērós, “a guard”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix), though Beekes considers τηρέω (tēréō) as the original formation and τηρός (tērós) as a back-formation.

From the verbal stem of προδίδωμι (prodídōmi, “to betray”) (προ-, the preposition, and -δω-, the verbal stem of δίδωμι) and the suffix -σια (-sia) (a suffix often used in nouns derived from verbs or adjectives) From προ- (pro-) and δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give, to deliver”).
From λῡ́ω (lū́ō, “loosen”) + -τός (-tós, “a suffix that creates verbal adjectives of possibility, either active or passive”).
From ἁλιεύω (halieúō, “I fish, am a fisher”) + -ίᾱ (-íā).

From δύσπνοος (dúspnoos, “short of breath”, adjective) (also δύσπνους (dúspnous) by contraction) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, suffix forming abstract nouns), from δῠσ- (dŭs-, “bad-, hard-, ill-”) + πνέω (pnéō, “blow, breathe”) + -ος (-os, suffix forming adjectives).
From the root of μᾰνθᾰ́νω (mănthắnō, “to learn”) + -σις (-sis, verbal noun suffix).
From ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + τέλλω (téllō, “to perform, accomplish, rise”).
From πρός (prós, “to, towards, with”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, hold”).
From ταῦρος (taûros, “bull”) + μᾰ́χη (mắkhē, “fight”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix).
σφᾰ́λλω (sphắllō, “to fall, to be cast down”) + -μᾰ (-mă, suffix forming neuter nouns)
From ᾰ̓πό- (ăpó-, “from”) + λέγω (légō, “to choose; to say”).
From ἀπο- (apo-, “out, away from”) + πτῡ́ω (ptū́ō, “spit out”).
From μῠ́στης (mŭ́stēs, “initiated one”) + -ῐον (-ĭon), from μυέω (muéō, “to initiate into mysteries”), from μῡ́ω (mū́ō, “to shut”).
From διαλέγομαι (dialégomai) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós, adjectival suffix), literally “related to conversation”.
From σμήχω (smḗkhō, “to wipe; to soap off”) + -μᾰ (-mă).
From ἁλιεύω (halieúō, “I fish, am a fisher”) + -τής (-tḗs).
From ᾰ̓πο- (ăpo-, “away, off”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) + -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō, denominative verb suffix).
From ᾰ̓γρεύς (ăgreús, “hunter”) + -εύω (-eúō, verb-forming suffix), from ᾰ̓́γρᾱ (ắgrā, “hunt”); doublet of ᾰ̓γρέω (ăgréō).
From κᾰτᾰ- (kătă-, “downwards, down”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, run, stream, gush”).
From μέδω (médō, “I rule over; I protect”) + -ων (-ōn).
From ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “to fall short, omit”) + -σις (-sis, verbal noun suffix), the former from ἐν- (en-) + λείπω (leípō, “to leave behind”). Compare ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis).
From ἀνάγκη (anánkē, “force, necessity”) + -άζω (-ázō, denominative verbal suffix).
From ἐν- (en-, “in”) + τυγχάνω (tunkhánō, “to happen (to), I succeed, I light upon, I obtain”).
From ἀπο- (apo-, “to, toward”) + σβέννῡμι (sbénnūmi, “to quench, to be quenched”).

From ἀνατέλλω (anatéllō, “rise, grow up”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + τέλλω (téllō, “I perform, accomplish, rise”), related either to τέλος (télos, “accomplishment, fulfillment”) or to ἔτλην (étlēn, “endure”).

From δίδωμι (dídōmi, “I give”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, “-er”). This suffixion uses the zero grade of the verb rather than its full grade, as in δωτήρ (dōtḗr). Formations of this kind follow the usual practice, which is why δοτήρ (dotḗr) is attested more often than δωτήρ (dōtḗr).
From ἀνδρεῖος (andreîos, “manly”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun–forming suffix). Compare ἠνορέη (ēnoréē).
From χᾰ́σκω (khắskō, “to yawn; to gape”) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).
Possibly from λοπός (lopós, “shell, scale; bark”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs). Ultimately from the same root of λέπω (lépō, “to peel”). See also λεπάς (lepás, “limpet”) for a similar derivation.
From ἀφ- (aph-, “apo-, away from”) + ἵημι (híēmi, “to send, throw”).
From ῥιζόω (rhizóō) + -μα (-ma). See Ancient Greek ῥῐ́ζᾰ (rhĭ́ză).
From πέλας (pélas, “nearby”) + -άζω (-ázō). Compare cognate πλησιάζω (plēsiázō) and old πιλνάω (pilnáō).
From λογίζομαι (logízomai, “I calculate”) + -μός (-mós, verbal noun suffix).
As if from *νουθέτης (*nouthétēs), from νοῦς (noûs) + τίθημι (títhēmi) + -της (-tēs), + -έω (-éō).
From ἀρκέω (arkéō, “to ward off, be enough”) + -τός (-tós).
From σῠμπότης (sŭmpótēs, “fellow drinker”) + -ῐον (-ĭon), from σῠμπῑ́νω (sŭmpī́nō, “to drink together”) + -της (-tēs), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “with, together”) + πῑ́νω (pī́nō, “to drink”).
From ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “upon”) + γνῶσῐς (gnôsĭs, “inquiry, knowledge”), or from ἐπῐγῐγνώσκω (epĭgĭgnṓskō) + -σῐς (-sĭs).

Irregularly formed from Εὔβο(ιᾰ) (Eúbo(iă), “Euboea”) + -εύς (-eús, suffix forming demonyms). The twelfth-century Etymologicum Magnum criticises the omission of the ι (i, “iota”), prescribing the form Εὐβοιεύς (Euboieús), whilst acknowledging that such omission is common in terms formed on iota-terminal stems suffixed with -εύς (-eús).
From προσ- (pros-, “to, towards, with”) + καλέω (kaléō, “to call”).
From τροπή (tropḗ, “a turn, turning, solstice, trope”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós).
From κείρω (keírō, “to cut short, shear, clip”) + -μα (-ma).
From Ἕλλης (Héllēs, “of Helle”, genitive of Ἕλλη (Héllē)) + πόντος (póntos, “sea”).
From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + συμπτωτός (sumptōtós, “falling in”), from συμπίπτω (sumpíptō, “to fall together”).
πωλέω (pōléō, “I sell or offer for sale”) + -ης (-ēs, suffix forming masculine agent nouns)
From ἀκρῑβής (akrībḗs) + -ια (-ia). Synchronically analyzable as ἀκρῑβής (akrībḗs) + -εια (-eia).
From γέννα (génna) + -ᾰ́ω (-ắō), poetic form of γένος (génos, “offspring”). Causal counterpart of γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be born, to become”).
ὀξῠ́ς (oxŭ́s, “sharp, keen, pointed”) + μωρός (mōrós, “dull, stupid, foolish”)
From Ἴων (Íōn, “Ionian”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). Compare Egyptian ywnj-ꜥꜣ (“Great Ionia”) i-i-w-n:y-aA:a-Y1
From θαυμάζω (thaumázō, “to admire, be surprised at”) + -τός (-tós, adjective suffix).
From πᾰρᾰλληλῐ́ζω (părăllēlĭ́zō, “to place side by side”) + -μός (-mós).
From βοή (boḗ, “shout”) + -ᾰ́ω (-ắō). Possibly cognate to Sanskrit जोगु॑वे (jóguve, “to sound; to shout; to proclaim”).
From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + σβεστός (sbestós), participle of σβέννυμι (sbénnumi, “to quench, quell”). The noun is shortened from ἄσβεστος τίτανος (ásbestos títanos).

Usually said to be from Latin sāpō, but borrowing from Galatian is also possible. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ (“soap”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyp-, *seyb- (“to pour, strain, trickle”). Cognate with Old English sāpe (“soap”). More at soap.
From ἐπι- (epi-, “on, upon”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, nominal suffix).

From γλῠ́φω (glŭ́phō, “to carve”) + -της (-tēs, suffix forming masculine agent nouns). The stem of γλῠ́φω (glŭ́phō) also occurs without aspiration, as γλῠπ- (glŭp-), in the verb’s third-person singular mediopassive indicative perfect – γέγλῠπται, ἔγλῠπται (géglŭptai, églŭptai) – and pluperfect – ἐγέγλῠπτο, ἔγλῠπτο (egéglŭpto, églŭpto) – forms.
From στυγέω (stugéō) + -ερός (-erós), from Proto-Hellenic *stugéō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“to hit, push”).
From δῐᾰ- (dĭă-, “across”) + οἰκοδομέω (oikodoméō, “to build a house”).
From πῑ́πτω (pī́ptō, “to fall”) + -μᾰ (-mă, resultative noun suffix). (corpse): Compare typologically Latin cadāver (< cadō), Russian па́даль (pádalʹ) (akin to па́дать (pádatʹ)).
From παροξύνω (paroxúnō, “to sharpen, irritate”) + -μός (-mós), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + ὀξύνω (oxúnō, “to sharpen”).
From βίος (bíos) + -όω (-óō). Doublet of inherited ζῶ (zô).
From κέρᾰμος (kérămos, “pottery”) + -εύς (-eús, suffix for person concerned). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀐𐀨𐀕𐀄 (ke-ra-me-u /⁠kerameus⁠/, “potter”).
From ᾰ̓- (ă-, “a-, not”) + σχολή (skholḗ, “leisure”) + -ος (-os, adjectival suffix).
From δόλῐχος (dólĭkhos, “long course in the arena”) + δρόμος (drómos, “race, running”).
From νοητός (noētós, “conceivable, perceptible, intelligible, comprehensible”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós, “verbal adjective suffix”).
From ᾰ̓́δῐκος (ắdĭkos, “unjust, wrong”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix).
From βρέχω (brékhō, “to rain”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).

From περιφερής (peripherḗs, “circular; rounded; revolving; wavering”) + -ια (-ia), from περιφέρω (periphérō, “to carry round; revolve; wander”), from περι- (peri-, “around, surrounding”) + φέρω (phérō, “to carry, bear”) from Proto-Hellenic *pʰérō (“to bear”) from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti.
From ἐπι- (epi-) + ἀγγέλλω (angéllō). (to promise): Compare typologically Latin prōmittō (< Latin mittō); Russian сули́ть (sulítʹ) (? akin to слать (slatʹ)).

From τράπεζα (trápeza, “money changer’s table, bank”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). Compare typologically English banker (via French, Italian, and further via Proto-Germanic *bankiz, akin to bench); Russian ла́вочник (lávočnik) (akin to ла́вка (lávka)).
From νοέω (noéō, “to intend, to perceive, to see, to understand”) + -μᾰ (-mă).
From ἀράομαι (aráomai, “I pray”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, masculine agent noun suffix).
From σῠν- (sŭn-, “with, together”) + φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “to bring forth, to produce”).

From σῠν- (sŭn-, “beside, with, along with”) + ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”), from Proto-Hellenic *wórwos (whence Mycenaean Greek 𐀺𐀺 (wo-wo)), from Proto-Indo-European *werw-; possible cognates include Latin urvō (“to trace, mark out bounds”).
From περῐπᾰτέω (perĭpătéō, “to walk around”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós, “verbal adjective suffix”).
From διασπείρω (diaspeírō, “to sow, to scatter”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).
From καρῡ́κη (karū́kē, “kind of sauce made with blood”) + -ῐνος (-ĭnos).
From ἐπείσοδος (epeísodos) + -ιος (-ios). Alternatively analyzed as ἐπι- (epi-) + εἰσόδιος (eisódios), from εἰσ- (eis-) + ὅδιος (hódios).
From the root of πείθω (peíthō, “I persuade”) + -νος (-nos, adjective suffix).
From φαρμακεύω (pharmakeúō, “to administer a drug or medicine”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós).
From τρέμω (trémō) + -ος (-os), from Proto-Indo-European *trem- (“to tremble”). Cognate with Tocharian B tremi (“anger”).
From λυτρόω (lutróō, “to ransom”) + -σις (-sis, “a suffix added to verb stems to form abstract nouns or nouns of action, result or process”)
From τρῑ́βω (trī́bō, “to rub away, wear away”) + -ακός (-akós).
From σῠγκᾰλέω (sŭnkăléō, “to call to council, convoke, convene”) + -τος (-tos). In the Byzantine sense, a semantic loan from Latin senātus.
From συν- (sun-, “with, together”) + πίνω (pínō, “to drink”). Compare Ancient Greek ἀναπίνω (anapínō).

From πάλαι (pálai, “long ago”) + -ος (-os, “adjectival suffix”). Likely cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀞𐀨𐀍 (pa-ra-jo), which has been argued to mean “old”; this connection points to a Proto-Hellenic *palai(y)ós and casts doubt on the popularly proposed etymology from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel-.
From φοιτᾰ́ω (phoitắō, “to visit”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent-noun suffix).
From ἀπο- (apo-, “from, away from”) + κρίνω (krínō, “to separate, distinguish, judge”).
From διακόπτω (diakóptō, “to cut in two, cut through”) + -ή (-ḗ). By surface analysis, δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + κοπή (kopḗ, “cutting in pieces”).
From πᾰρᾰ- (pără-, “by, near”) + ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “to come, go”).
From οὐρέω (ouréō, “to urinate”) + -ήθρᾱ (-ḗthrā, “body part; anatomical cavity; container; receptacle; opening”), from οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).
From αὐτο- (auto-) + κράτωρ (krátōr, “ruler”) (from κρατέω (kratéō, “to rule, command”) and -τωρ (-tōr, “masculine agent suffix.”), from κράτος (krátos, “power, strength”))
From Βῡ́ζᾱς (Bū́zās, “Byzas”) + -ῐον (-ĭon), after the city's legendary founder.
From ἀ- (a-, “-less”) + -πάτωρ (-pátōr, “father”, stem used in compounds). Compare ὁμοπάτωρ (homopátōr), another compound related to πατήρ (patḗr, “father”).
θεάομαι (theáomai, “to gaze at”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent noun suffix)
From γελᾰ́ω (gelắō, “to laugh”) + -τός (-tós). The apparent additional sigma is in fact part of the verb stem, and surfaces before consonants.
From συστέλλω (sustéllō) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix), from σύν (sún, “together”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “send”).
From παγκρατής (pankratḗs, “all powerful”) + -ιον (-ion), from πᾰν- (păn-, “all, every”) + κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”).
From Ἥφαιστος (Hḗphaistos, “Hephaestus”) + -εῖον (-eîon, “instruments or means of action”).
From μόνος (mónos, “single”) + ὄνῠξ (ónŭx, “nail, hoof”) via haplology.
From Λῆμνος (Lêmnos, “a Greek island Lemnos”) + -ίσκος (-ískos, noun-forming diminutive suffix).
From πρόξενος (próxenos, “public guest or friend”) + -ίᾱ (-íā), ultimately from προ- (pro-, “before”) + ξένος (xénos, “stranger, foreigner”). See also Latin hospitium (“hospitality”).
συντέμνω (suntémnō, “to cut down, cut short”) + -ος (-os), in the o-grade.

From τρεῖς (treîs, “three”) + -αινᾰ (-aină). Chantraine considers a folk-etymological transformation after the numeral. Furnée compares τρίναξ (trínax, “instrument used in agriculture”) and θρῖναξ (thrînax, “three-pronged fork”), and asks whether the word could be a transformation of a Pre-Greek loan for an agricultural tool.
From κᾰκός (kăkós) + πᾰτρίς (pătrís); in its archaic use, the second element may involve wordplay between πᾰτρίς (pătrís, “homeland”) and πᾰτήρ (pătḗr, “father, ancestry”).
From ἀπο- (apo-, “away from”) + φεύγω (pheúgō, “to flee, run off”).
From ἀν- (an-, “not”, alpha privativum) + ὄρεξῐς (órexĭs, “yearning”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract-noun-forming suffix).
From χλεύη (khleúē, “jest, joke”) + -άζω (-ázō, suffix to form a verb).
Denominal verb of ἁλιεύς (halieús, “fisher”); also analyzable as ἅλς (háls, “saltwater, seawater”) + -εύω (-eúō).
From κηδεύω (kēdeúō, “to care for”) + -είᾱ (-eíā). The sense of "care for the dead" > "funeral" developed in the Hellenistic Koine era.
From προσπᾰθέω (prospăthéō, “to feel passionate love for”) + -ειᾰ (-eiă) or προσπᾰθής (prospăthḗs, “impressionable”) + -ειᾰ (-eiă), both ultimately from the same roots.
From δοξόσοφος (doxósophos, “wise in one's own conceit”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
From ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).
From ἀ- (a-) + ῥήγνῡμι (rhḗgnūmi, “to break, shatter”) + -τος (-tos, adjective suffix).
From πυρετός (puretós, heat, fever) + -σσω (-ssō), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire, fever”).
From δια- (dia-, “through, between”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bring, carry”).
κατα- (kata-, strengthening prefix) + σκευάζω (skeuázō, “equip”), from σκευή (skeuḗ, “equipment”) + -άζω (-ázō, denominative verb suffix).
Abstract noun from σύμμαχος (súmmakhos, “fighting together”) + -ίᾱ (-íā, abstract noun suffix).
From φύω (phúō, “to grow, to be . . . by nature”) + -η (-ē, nominal suffix).
From σοφίζω (sophízō, “to become wise”) + -ιστής (-istḗs), from σοφός (sophós, “wise”).
Analyzable as By surface analysis, ἐπῐ- (epĭ-) + κλῆσῐς (klêsĭs) or as ἐπῐκᾰλέω (epĭkăléō) + -σῐς (-sĭs).
From μελῳδός (melōidós, “musical”) + -ία (-ía), from μέλος (mélos) "musical phrase" + ᾠδή (ōidḗ), contracted form of ἀοιδή (aoidḗ) "song".
From ᾰ̓́μνηστος (ắmnēstos, “forgotten, forgetful”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix), ultimately from μνάομαι (mnáomai, “remember”).
From εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + ἁφή (haphḗ, “sense of touch”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix).
From πτερόω (pteróō, “to feather”) + -τός (-tós, verbal adjective suffix).
From στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”) + -βᾰ́της (-bắtēs, “walker, from βαίνω (“to walk, to tread”)”).
From κάρφω (kárphō, “to dry up, to wither”) + -ος (-os). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐂓 (ka+po).
From ἀν- (an-) + ἔκδοτος (ékdotos, “given in marriage; published”).
From δῐηγέομαι (dĭēgéomai, “set out in detail, describe”) + -σῐς (-sĭs).
From γῠμνᾰ́ζω (gŭmnắzō, “to train, exercise”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From νω- (nō-) + ὄνυμα (ónuma). Compare the parallel formation ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “nameless”).
From ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive suffix), because it was used for dyeing the hair yellow.
From παιδεύω (paideúō, “rear a child”) + -ίᾱ (-íā), from παῖς (paîs, “child”).
From κρᾰτέω (krătéō, “to rule”) + -τωρ (-tōr, masculine agent nouns suffix).
From αἰσχρός (aiskhrós, “shameful, ugly”) + -της (-tēs, abstract noun suffix)
ὑπερ- (huper-, “over-, super-”) + βῐ́ᾱ (bĭ́ā, “strength, force”) + -ος (-os, adjectival suffix)
From ἐπι- (epi-, “epi-, on-”) + δόρπον (dórpon, “supper”) + -ίς (-ís, feminine nominal suffix),
From γέννα (génna, “descent, birth, origin”) + -ιος (-ios). Compare ἀγενής (agenḗs).
From μᾰκρήγορος (măkrḗgoros, “speaking at great length”) (from μακρο- (makro-, “long”) + ᾰ̓γορεύω (ăgoreúō, “to speak”)) + -έω (-éō).
From Ᾰ̓ντῐ́οχος (Ăntĭ́okhos, “Antiochus, name of several Seleucid kings”) + -ειᾰ (-eiă).
From τεῖχος (teîkhos, “wall, fortification”) + -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō, suffix used to form verbs from nouns, adjectives and other verbs).
From φυσιογνώμων (phusiognṓmōn, “judging of a person's character by their features”) + -ία (-ía).
From the root of τίθημι (títhēmi, “to set, place”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agentive suffix).
From λύω (lúō, “to set free, release”) + -τρον (-tron, “a suffix forming instrument nouns”).
From ᾰ̓κρᾰτής (ăkrătḗs, “powerless”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă), from ᾰ̓- (ă-, “not”) + κρᾰ́τος (krắtos, “strength, might”) + -ής (-ḗs).
From Μετᾰγείτνιᾰ (Metăgeítniă, “wedding feast”), a festival in celebration of emigration. Ultimately from μετά (metá) + γείτων (geítōn).
From ἀγάλλομαι (agállomai, “to be proud, exult in”) + -μα (-ma).
From πρεσβεύω (presbeúō, “to be elderly; to be ambassador”) + -εία (-eía, “nominal suffix”) and see πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder”).
From σφῐ́γγω (sphĭ́ngō, “to bind tight or fast”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, agent noun suffix).
From πᾰγκρᾰτῐᾰ́ζω (pănkrătĭắzō, “to practise the pankration”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From ᾰ̓- (ă-) + ληπτός (lēptós), from the root of λᾰμβᾰ́νω (lămbắnō).
From στέγω (stégō, “to cover”) + -νός (-nós), with sense development "covered" > "waterproof, clogged".
From the root of γῐ́γνομαι (gĭ́gnomai, “to be born”) + -της (-tēs, agentive suffix).
From εὐσεβής (eusebḗs, “pious”) + -ια (-ia), synchronically analyzable as εὐσεβής (eusebḗs) + -εια (-eia). The sense “dharma” is a semantic loan from Ashokan Prakrit 𑀥𑀁𑀫 (dhaṃma).
From μακρηγορέω (makrēgoréō, “I speak at great length”) + -ία (-ía).
Feminine form of Κλεόπᾰτρος (Kleópătros, “glory of the father”) + -ᾱ (-ā).
From βόσκω (bóskō, “to feed, tend”) + -ᾰ́νη (-ắnē, instrument noun suffix).
From the root of θάνατος (thánatos) and θνῄσκω (thnēískō) + -ιμος (-imos).
From παρατάσσω (paratássō, “to place side by side”) + -σις (-sis).
From δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + τρέφω (tréphō, “to breed, feed”).
From the stem of βασιλεύς (basileús, “king”) + -ίᾱ (-íā, abstract noun suffix).
From δονέω (donéō, “to shake”) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).
From περῐ- (perĭ-, “beyond”) + -φρων (-phrōn, suffix for adjectives relating to the mind or emotions).
From ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on, onto”) + λέγω (légō, “to choose, to say”).
From δῐᾰγρᾰ́φω (dĭăgrắphō, “to mark out lines, delineate”) + -ή (-ḗ).
From ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀλγέω (algéō, “feel bodily pain, suffer”) + -τος (-tos, adjectival suffix).
From ἐκλύω (eklúō, “set free”) + -σις (-sis, “a suffix added to verb stems to form abstract nouns or nouns of action, result or process”)
Compound of παῖς (paîs, “child”) + τρίβω (tríbō, “to use, to wear down”) + -ης (-ēs).
From γνώμων (gnṓmōn, “interpreter, discerner”) + -ικός (-ikós, suffix to form an adjective).
From the radical of σέβομαι (sébomai) + -νός (-nós), with regressive assimilation.
From ἆθλος (âthlos, “conflict, struggle”) + -ιος (-ios, “a suffix added to nouns or adjectives, forming adjectives: pertaining to, belonging to”)
From κατα- (kata-, back, down) + ἥκω (hḗkō, “to have come, be present”).
From ἐκλέγω (eklégō) + -τικός (-tikós), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λέγω (légō, “choose, count”).
From ὑποκορίζομαι (hupokorízomai, “to call by endearing names”) + -μα (-ma).
From πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “a thing done, a fact”) + -ικός (-ikós).
From προδίδωμι (prodídōmi, “to betray”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent-noun suffix).
οἶκος (oîkos, “home”) + -ίζω (-ízō, “a suffix forming a verb from a noun”)
From δολόω (dolóō, “to beguile, to ensnare”) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).
From βᾰρῠ́θῡμος (bărŭ́thūmos, “sullen”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from βᾰρῠ́ς (bărŭ́s, “heavy, grievous”) + θῡμός (thūmós, “soul”).
From μονο- (mono-) + κέρας (kéras). The long ω results from a contraction of Proto-Hellenic *-kerahos, from the s-stem *kéras plus an o-suffix.
From *μᾰστῐγϳ- (*măstĭgj-, stem of μάστιξ) + -όω (-óō, causative/factitive verbal suffix).
From the o-grade of the root of πλέω (pléō, “to sail”) + -ιον (-ion), or inherited directly from Proto-Indo-European *plówyom (“floating vessel”): compare Proto-Germanic *flawją (“ship, vessel”).
From δῐκᾰ́ζω (dĭkắzō, “to judge”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agent-noun suffix): Literally, “judger”.
From ῠ̔ποκρῑ́νομαι (hŭpokrī́nomai, “to answer (a fellow actor on stage), play a part, feign, pretend”) + -σῐς (-sĭs).
From ἀνδράποδον (andrápodon, “a slave”) + -ίζω (-ízō, “a suffix forming a verb from a noun”)
From ἀδάμᾱς, ἀ˘δᾰμᾰντ- (adámās, ădămănt-, “diamond; steel”) + -ῐνος (-ĭnos, suffix).
From ἀπομνημονεύω (apomnēmoneúō, “relate from memory, recount, remember”) + -μᾰ (-mă).
From παίζω (paízō, “I play”) + -της (-tēs) using an alternative stem παιγ- (paig-) which is also found in παῖγμα (paîgma).
From εὐχᾰ́ρῐστος (eukhắrĭstos, “thankful, grateful”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + χᾰ́ρῐς (khắrĭs, “grace”) + -τος (-tos).
From the zero-grade of τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).
From εὔπνοος (eúpnoos, “breathing well”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + πνέω (pnéō, “breathe, blow”).
From χρηστομᾰθέω (khrēstomăthéō, “be desirous for learning”), from χρηστός (khrēstós, “useful”) + μανθάνω (manthánō, “learn”).
From φροντίς (phrontís, “thought”) + *-ϳω (*-jō), superficially containing -ίζω (-ízō). Related to φρήν (phrḗn).
From πέκω (pékō, “to comb, to card; to shear”) + -ος (-os).
Bahuvrīhi compound of μεγᾰλ- (megăl-, “great”) + ἦτορ (êtor, “heart”). Compare Sanskrit महात्मन् (mahātman, “having a great soul”), from these two roots.
From μάγγανον (mánganon, “means of charming or bewitching, philtre”) + -εύω (-eúō).
From κᾰκόζηλος (kăkózēlos, “having bad taste”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from κᾰκός (kăkós, “bad”) + ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal”).

From ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “hypo-, under-”) + ἐρέτης (erétēs, “rower”), with the suffix ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-) invoking a sense of opposition to the higher κελευστής (keleustḗs, “boatswain”), rather than one who literally "rows under (a structure, etc.)". By surface analysis, ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “hypo-, below”) + ἐρέσσω (eréssō, “to row”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”).
From ᾰ̓ντῐ- (ăntĭ-, “without”) + κλέος (kléos, “fame”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă). Compare with Εὐρῠ́κλειᾰ (Eurŭ́kleiă) and Μεγᾰ́κλειᾰ (Megắkleiă).
From πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “I do, practice”) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).
From κρῐτήρ (krĭtḗr, “interpreter”) + -ῐον (-ĭon), from κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “I discern, judge”).
From ᾰ̓- (ă-, alpha copulativum) + κοίτη (koítē, “[marriage] bed”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, “a woman pertaining to —”).
From ᾰ̓ρῠ́ω (ărŭ́ō, “to draw (water, wine, etc.)”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, masculine noun suffix).
From δάπτω (dáptō, “to devour, consume”) + -ᾰ́νη (-ắnē). Compare semantically Latin damnum (“fine, mulct, penalty”).
From ἐκ- (ek-, “ex-, out-”) + παιδεύω (paideúō, “to raise, train”).
From πρῐ́ω (prĭ́ō, “to saw”) + -τήρ (-tḗr). Closely related to Mycenaean Greek *𐀠𐀪𐀁𐀳 (*pi-ri-e-te /⁠prihentēr⁠/).

From χαμαί (khamaí, “on the ground”) + λέων (léōn, “lion”); ultimately a calque of Akkadian 𒌨𒈤𒊭𒆠 (nēšu ša qaqqari, “chameleon, reptile”, literally “lion of the ground", "predator that crawls upon the ground”).
From ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “to play a part on stage”) + -τής (-tḗs).
From διαβάλλω (diabállō, “to calumniate”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).
From στενός (stenós, “narrow”) + -όω (-óō, “to make someone do or be something”).
From μορφόω (morphóō, “to form”) + -σις (-sis, verbal noun suffix).
From πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist; unit of length approximately equal to 1 foot”) + -αῖος (-aîos).

Via Late Latin Theodericus from a Germanic origin, likely via Gothic *𐌸𐌹𐌿𐌳𐌰𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (*þiudareiks) from Proto-Germanic *Þeudōrīks, from *þeudō (“people”) + *rīks (“king”). Etymologically unrelated to Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος (Theódōros, “Theodore”, literally “gift of God”), although medieval conflation of the Germanic and Hellenic names may have given rise to Medieval Greek Θεοδώριχος (Theodṓrikhos, “Theodoric”), Medieval Latin Theodōrīchus (“Theodoric”).
δοῦπος (doûpos) + -έω (-éō); earlier *γδουπέω (*gdoupéō) as shown by augmented aorist forms beginning ἐγδ- (egd-) as well as the prefixed form ἐπιγδουπέω (epigdoupéō).
ῐ̔κνέομαι (hĭknéomai, “to come”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agent-noun suffix): literally, “comer”.
From an o-grade of ἐρέφω (eréphō, “to cover with a roof”) + -ος (-os).
From βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”) + -ίζω (-ízō, “verbal suffix”), literally “to test with touchstone”.
From νοέω (noéō, “to perceive, to think”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, suffix forming deverbal nouns).
From συγκρητίζω (sunkrētízō) + -μός (-mós), or possibly from συν- (sun-) + Κρῆτες (Krêtes, “Cretans”) + -ισμός (-ismós, “-ism”) if the verb is a back-formation. First appears in Plutarch's Moralia.
From νέος (néos, “young”) + -της (-tēs). Diachronically from Proto-Hellenic *newótāts, from Proto-Indo-European *néwoteh₂ts (“newness”); cognate with Latin novitās, Sanskrit नवता (návatā).
Mediopassive of ῠ̔ποκρῑ́νω (hŭpokrī́nō), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “under”) + κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “to separate, judge, decide”).
From χορεύω (khoreúō, “to dance a choral dance”) + -τής (-tḗs).
From δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + εὐθῡ́νω (euthū́nō, “to make straight”).
From ἀνατέμνω (anatémnō, “to cut up”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).
Adverb from εὐθύς (euthús, “straight”) + -ως (-ōs), using the stem εὐθε- (euthe-).
From φορέω (phoréō, “to carry”) + -εύς (-eús, suffix for person concerned).
From διαζυγία (diazugía, “separation, parting”) + -ιον (-ion), the former from δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”) + -ία (-ía).
From *-ϝειδής (*-weidḗs), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form; appearance”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix).
From σκέλλω (skéllō, “to dry up, parch”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).
From διασκευάζω (diaskeuázō, “to revise, edit, prepare”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From φρᾱ́τηρ (phrā́tēr, “clansman, kinsmen”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *bràtrьja.
From δῐοικέω (dĭoikéō, “to manage, administer”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
From ἄγρυπνος (ágrupnos, “sleepless, wakeful”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix).
From the zero grade of ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to leave out”) + -ης (-ēs).
Superlative, possibly from *ἧκᾰ (*hêkă, “slightly”, attested as Epic ἦκᾰ (êkă)) + -ῐστος (-ĭstos).

ξένος (xénos, “guest”) + φῶν (phôn, “shining”), the latter contracted from φάων (pháōn), explaining the accentuation, participle of φάω (pháō, “to shine”). The word φῶν (phôn) was indirectly attested in the works of Hesychios of Alexandria, where the accusative form φῶντα (phônta) was equated to λάμποντα (lámponta) from λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”).
From ὑπερβάλλω (huperbállō, “to go beyond, exceed”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix), from ὑπερ- (huper-) + βάλλω (bállō).
From the root of τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, verbal noun suffix).
From δῐᾰ- (dĭă-, “across”) + ᾰ̓γωνῐ́ζομαι (ăgōnĭ́zomai, “contend for a prize”).
From the root of ῡ̔μεῖς (hūmeîs, “you”, plural) + -τερος (-teros, contrastive adjective suffix).
From πλησίον (plēsíon, “near”) + -ᾰ́ζω (-ắzō, “suffix for verbs”). Compare cognate πελάζω (pelázō) and old πιλνάω (pilnáō).
From Σεβαστός (Sebastós) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming place names”), from use of σεβαστός (sebastós, “venerable, august”) as a calque of Latin Augustus.
From ὑποδέω (hupodéō, “to bind underneath”) + -μα (-ma) (these were fastened to the feet with straps).
From Ἄρειος Πάγος (Áreios Págos, “Areopagus”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, masculine suffix for a member of a group).
From δικαιόω (dikaióō, “to set right, deem right”) + -μᾰ (-mă).
From νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”) + -ῖτις (-îtis, “a suffix forming a feminine noun, especially a technical term that pertains to the root word”)

From εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + βόσκω (bóskō, “feed, graze”, verb) or βοτόν n (botón, “a grazing beast”, noun) + -ος (-os, suffix forming second-declension compound adjectives); for the βοτ- (bot-) root, compare βοτᾰ́νη (botắnē, “pasture”) and βοτήρ (botḗr, “herdsman”).
From ᾰ̔́πτω (hắptō, “to fasten to”) + -σῐς (-sĭs), with compensatory lengthening of the final vowel *ᾰ̔ψσῐ́ς (*hăpssĭ́s) > ᾰ̔ψῑ́ς (hăpsī́s).
From στενόω (stenóō, “to confine, to contract”) + -σις (-sis, nominal suffix), from στενός (stenós, “narrow”) + -όω (-óō, “to make someone do or be something”).
From οὐρᾰνός (ourănós, “heaven, sky”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look, contemplate”).
From κράτος (krátos, “power, might”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix).
From προ- (pro-, “to, towards, with”) + καλέω (kaléō, “to call”).
From ἀποφθέγγομαι (apophthéngomai, “I plainly speak my mind”), from ἀπο- (apo-, “away”) + φθέγγομαι (phthéngomai, “to speak loudly”), + -μα (-ma, result noun suffix).
From τᾰρᾰ́σσω (tărắssō, “to disturb; to stir; to agitate”) + -ή (-ḗ).
From πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”) + -τός (-tós, verbal adjective suffix).
From ἐλπίς (elpís, “hope”) + *-ϳω (*-jō). Synchronically also analyzable as ἐλπίς (elpís) + -ίζω (-ízō).
From φᾰρμᾰκεύω (phărmăkeúō, “to administer a drug; practise sorcery”) + -εύς (-eús, masculine agentive suffix).
From ῐ̓́δῐος (ĭ́dĭos, “one’s own; peculiar”) + -της (-tēs, abstract noun suffix).
From ζεύγνῡμῐ (zeúgnūmĭ, “I join”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, abstract noun suffix).
From ᾰ̓μῡ́νω (ămū́nō, “to keep off; to ward off”) + -τωρ (-tōr, “-er”).
From γᾰμηλῐ́ᾱ (gămēlĭ́ā, “wedding feast”) + -ών (-ṓn), because it was the fashionable time for weddings.
Reduplication of τείνω (teínō, “I stretch, I pull tight”) + -ος (-os, adjective suffix).

From χρῑ́ω (khrī́ō, “to rub, smear; anoint”) + -τός (-tós, verbal adjective suffix), forming a verbal adjective denoting a resultant state (“fit for spreading or anointing; anointed”), often functioning semantically like a participle.
From νέμω (némō, “to pasture; to graze”) + -ός (-ós, deverbal nominal suffix). Compare ἀγρός (agrós).

From βᾰσῐλεύς (băsĭleús, “king”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, feminine ending), synchronically also analyzable as βᾰσῐλεύς (băsĭleús, “king”) + -ειᾰ (-eiă). Intervocalic ῐ (ĭ) developed from a sonorant cluster /wj/, which assimilated to /jj/, then became the second element in the diphthong ει (ei); the formation is thus *βᾰσῐ́λεϝϳᾰ (*băsĭ́lewjă) > *βᾰσῐ́λεϳϳᾰ (*băsĭ́lejjă) > βᾰσῐ́λειᾰ (băsĭ́leiă).
From δύναμαι (dúnamai, “to be able”) + -τός (-tós, verbal adjective suffix).

Perhaps from κεντέω (kentéō, “I goad, wound”) + ταῦρος (taûros, “bull”) either from bull-fighting or from herding. Often linked to the Indo-Iranian etymon of which Sanskrit गन्धर्व (gandharva) is a reflex, in which case substrate borrowing and/or substantial remodeling is indicated.
According to Strabo, from μάραθον (márathon, “fennel”) + -ών (-ṓn), referring to the prevalence of the plant in the area. This explanation appears to be implicitly accepted by Beekes.

Univerbation of né + meno, but may also continue Latin nē minimum (quidem) (literally “not even a little”), with the superlative replaced by the comparative, and nec minus (literally “nor any less, and just as much > and even”)).
From ἐκ (ek, “out”), formed on the model of ἐντός (entós, “within, inside”). Cognate with Old Irish acht (“but, provided that”), Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau, “or, otherwise”).

From πειράω (peiráō) (“to attempt, attack”) + -τής (-tḗs), from πεῖρα (peîra) (“trial, attempt”), ultimately from PIE *per- (“to try, risk”). Not related to περάτης (perátēs) (“wanderer”), from περάω (peráō) (“to cross”).
Derived from the verb τύφω (túphō, “to smoke”).

According to Beekes, the word is Pre-Greek — which Beekes claims is the case for all Greek words with the -αλλο- suffix. Contrary to this, the apparent semantic and phonetic relationship to κρύος (krúos, “cold; ice”), Latin crusta (“crust, bark”), and Old English hruse (“ground”) is striking - perhaps the word is a derivative of κρύος (krúos) with the addition of the Pre-Greek suffix.
PIE word  *dwís Nominal formation from δῐαιτᾰ́ω (dĭaitắō, “to treat, handle”).
From ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to send off”), from ἀπό- (apó-, “from”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to send”).

By surface analysis, ψῡ́χω (psū́khō, “to breathe, blow; to cool, chill; to dry”, verb) + -η (-ē, zero grade nominal suffix). The original meaning is thus supposed to have been breath. Compare the origins of Latin anima (“air, breath, life, soul”), as well as Proto-Slavic *dušà (“soul; spirit”) and Latin dusius (“kind of demon, goblin”). Compare Proto-Circassian *psa, Proto-Northwest Caucasian *pǝsA (literally “soul”).
From ra- + fine + -are; cognate with Friulian rafinâ, Piedmontese rafiné.
From αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) + χθών (khthṓn, “earth, soil”), sprung from the land itself.
From ἀνατίθημι (anatíthēmi, “to dedicate”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).
Inherited from Latin dolor, from doleō + -or.
Substantivized neuter singular of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “added on”), from ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi).
From dimenticare (“to forget”) + -toio. First attested in 1583.
Compound of κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”). Coined by 4th-century BC Greek Cynic philosopher Diogenes of Sinope.
From a- + gomitolo (“ball of fabric, etc.”) + -are.
From sarca(smo) + -stico; cognate with Piedmontese sarcàstich.
A noun use of the present participle of ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule”).
From a- (“to, towards”) + bacino (“bowl”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
Shortened from bevanda gazzosa, the second element from gazare + -osa (see gasa); compare French boisson gazeuse. Cognate with Sicilian gazzusa.
From ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to lead”) with Attic reduplication.
From a- (“to, towards”) + vampa (“heat; flame”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
From κᾰ́μηλος (kắmēlos, “camel”) + πᾰ́ρδᾰλῐς (pắrdălĭs, “leopard”); from the fact that a giraffe has a long neck like a camel and is spotted like a leopard.
Attested since at least 1793. Learned borrowing from Latin incunabulum.
See ᾰ̓́ρχω (ắrkhō, “to begin; to be first; to rule”).
From δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + λέγω (légō, “to gather, choose”).
From or closely related to ἐτεός (eteós, “true”).
From δρᾶσῐς (drâsĭs, “strength, efficacy”), from δράω (dráō, “I do”), + -τικός (-tikós).
Neuter substantive of τρίγωνος (trígōnos, “three-cornered”), from τρεῖς (treîs, “three”) + γωνία (gōnía, “corner, angle”)
By surface analysis, λούω (loúō, “to wash, bathe”) + -τήρ (-tḗr). Compare λουτρόν (loutrón, “bathing-place”).
Combining form of τρεῖς (treîs, “three”, cardinal numeral) and τρῐ́ς (trĭ́s, “thrice”, “three times”, adverbial numeral).
From ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to inject”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).
Ultimately from ὄξος (óxos, “poor wine, vinegar”) or ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, pointed”).
Prefix version of the preposition σῠ́ν (sŭ́n, “with”).
From the root of χράομαι (khráomai, “to use, desire”) + -ιμος (-imos, “-able, -like”).

Traditionally explained as a bahuvrihi compound of σκιά (skiá, “shade, shadow”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”), thus "(one who) generates shade with its tail", but this could be a folk etymology, and it might actually be Pre-Greek, if the -ουρος (-ouros) is a suffix rather than a standalone word.
Univerbation of εὖ (eû, “well”) + γε (ge, emphatic particle).
Substantivization of the neuter of αἰδοῖος (aidoîos, “modest, bashful”). Compare similar use of English shame.
Attic corruption, possibly by assimilation, of βῠβλῐ́ον (bŭblĭ́on).
Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna. Doublet of guaina.
From μῑμέομαι (mīméomai, “to simulate”) + -σις (-sis, verbal noun suffix).
A variant of φῡλή (phūlḗ, “tribe”), itself related to φύω (phúō, “to beget”).

From παθ- (path-), zero-grade of the root of πᾰ́σχω (pắskhō, “to feel; to suffer”). Compare the aorist ἔπαθον (épathon). Related to πένθος (pénthos), in the same way as βάθος (báthos) is related to βένθος (bénthos).
From genesi + -ico. Compare Ancient Greek γενητικός (genētikós), γεννητικός (gennētikós), derived from γεννάω (gennáō, “I beget”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin commerciālis. By surface analysis, commercio + -ale.
Learned borrowing from Latin multiplicātor. By surface analysis, moltiplicare + -tore.
Univerbation of non + ostante. Compare Portuguese não obstante, Spanish no obstante, French nonobstant.
From the stem of γυμνάζω (gumnázō, “to exercise”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), and -ιον (-ion), neuter of adjective suffix -ιος (-ios).
From ἐκτέμνω (ektémnō, “to cut out”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κρᾶσις (krâsis, “mixture, blending”). Compare the surname Craxi.
Abstract noun used only in compounds, equivalent to γρᾰφή (grăphḗ), from γρᾰ́φω (grắphō, “to carve, write”).
From pup(o) (“puppet”) + -azzo (derivational suffix for diminutive or pejorative nouns). Parallel formation to Middle French poupette, French poupée, Romanian păpușă.
Nominal form of the verb φθέγγομαι (phthéngomai, “to utter a sound, raise one's voice”).
From in- + furia (“fury, rage”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

Explained since antiquity as a compound of αἴθω (aíthō, “to burn”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “face”), though this is generally thought to be a folk etymology. Beekes argues that the first assumed root always has senses related to brightness and never to darkness, that the *-ί- as well as *-ο- instead of *-ώ- are unexplained, and that *-οπ- (*-οψ) is a typical Pre-Greek substrate suffix observed in ethnonyms like Δόλοψ (Dólops) and Δρύοψ (Drúops). The suffix is shaped differently in Mycenaean Greek 𐁁𐀴𐀍𐀦 (a3-ti-jo-qo). A connection to this colour however brings closer the native Ethiopian Semitic ዕጣን (ʿəṭan, “incense”) to explain the unsuffixed etymon. Frankincense had the primary characteristic of being white, so also the source of λίβανος (líbanos, “incense”) is a Semitic root related to whiteness. The word might ultimately refer to the incense trade passing from Abyssinia. The folk of Ethiopia was so noted for earning its living by olibanum commerce that the Arabs even derived a term حَبَشَ (ḥabaša, “to earn, to obtain for the household”) from their other ethnonym اَلْحَبَشَة (al-ḥabaša).
A nominalization of the verb πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “to stick, fasten, build, fix”), meaning "that what is built or fixed"; see also πάγη (págē, “snare, trap”) and Latin pagus.
From either σκεῦος (skeûos, “vessel”) or σκευή (skeuḗ, “equipment”) + -ᾰ́ζω (-ắzō), both ultimately of the same origin.
Derived from the root of ὄνᾰρ (ónăr) with a suffix *-yos.Cognate with Old Armenian անուրջ (anurǰ) and Albanian ëndërr.

Traditionally derived as a ᾰ̔́μᾰ (hắmă, “at once”) + ᾰ̓́ξ(ων) (ắx(ōn), “axle”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, nominal suffix), literally “one-axler”. Other theories include a relation to ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to lead; to guide”), as well as Tocharian B amäkṣpänte (“wagonmaster”). Beekes rejects these theories (noting that a "one-axler" formation makes less sense than a "two-axler" formation) and considers the word Pre-Greek, based on the Cypriot variant ἀβακλή (abaklḗ).
Back-formation from σολοικῐ́ζω (soloikĭ́zō, “to speak or write incorrectly”) or suffixed form of Σόλοι (Sóloi).
Ultimately from αἶσχος (aîskhos, “disgrace”). According to Beekes, a back-formation from αἰσχύνω (aiskhúnō, “to disgrace”).
From Θεό (Theó, “God”) + δοῦλος (doûlos, “slave”), literally “Slave of God”.
Substantivized verbal adjective of ἕρπω (hérpō). Compare Latin serpēns and Sanskrit सर्प (sarpá, “snake, serpent”).
From πολῠ́ς (polŭ́s, “much”) + μᾰθ- (măth-, root of μᾰνθᾰ́νω (mănthắnō, “to learn”)) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix).
Adverbial use of declination of πλησίος (plēsíos).
From ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp; sour”), with an analogous formation as ἦδος (êdos, “delight, pleasure”) to ἡδύς (hēdús, “pleasant, sweet”).
From mangiare + -toia. Cognate with French mangeoire, English manger, Occitan manjadoira, Galician manxadoira,
Diminutive of mozza (“a type of cheese”), related to the verb mozzare. Originally of southern Italian origin. Compare Neapolitan muzzarella.
Univerbation of qualche (“some”) + uno (“one”). Akin to French quelqu'un.
Diminutive of sigaro, modeled after French cigarette.
Compound of via + andante. Cognate with Piedmontese viandant.
Compound of sempre (“always”) + vivo (“alive”), an apotropaic nickname.
From so- + pesare (“to weigh”). Cognate with Portuguese and Spanish sopesar, French soupeser.
From micidio (“murder”, aphetic form of omicidio) + -ale (“-al, pertaining to”). Compare the archaic omicidiale.
Calque of Latin ātricapilla. By surface analysis, capo (“head”) + nero (“black”) + -a f.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin evangelista, borrowed from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs). By surface analysis, Latin evangelium + -ista.
From pesc(are) (“to fish”) + -ata (suffix indicating an instance of something).
From radice (“root”) + -ando, on the example of nouns like dividendo, moltiplicando, etc.
Univerbation of mala (“bad”) + pena. Emphasized form of appena.
Borrowed from Late Latin abstentiōnem, from Latin abstentus, from abstineō.
Inherited from Old French taupe, inherited from Latin talpa.
Borrowed from Algerian Arabic, from Arabic بِلَاد (bilād).
Learned borrowing from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin similāris, extended from Latin similis (“like”).

Inherited from Middle French desveloper, from Old French desveloper, from des- + voloper, veloper, vloper (“to wrap, to wrap up”), from Vulgar Latin base *vlopp-, *wlopp- (“to wrap”), from Proto-Germanic *wrappan-, *wlappan- (“to wrap, roll up, turn, wind”), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to turn, bend”) http://www.wordnik.com/words/envelop. Akin to Italian -viluppare, Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”); also Middle English wlappen (“to wrap, fold”) (Modern English lap (“to wrap, involve, fold”)), Middle English wrappen (“to wrap”), Middle Dutch lappen (“to wrap up”), dialectal Danish vravle (“to wind, twist”), Middle Low German wrempen (“to wrinkle, scrunch, distort”), Old English wearp (“warp”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κακοφωνία (kakophōnía), from κακόφωνος (kakóphōnos), from κακός (kakós) + φωνή (phōnḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin amātōrem (“lover”), from amō (“to love”). Displaced Old French ameor, which was inherited from the same source but disappeared by the 15th century.
Borrowed from Italian appartamento, from Spanish apartamiento.
Derived from Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi). See English kilo-.
Learned borrowing from New Latin elasticus.
Learned borrowing from Latin cataclysmus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κατακλυσμός (kataklusmós).
Inherited from Middle French dent f, with change of gender from Old French dent m, from Latin dentem m, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts.
Inherited from Middle French crud, from Old French cru, creu, from Latin crūdus (English crude).
Borrowed from Spanish carapacho (“carapace, shell”), of uncertain origin.
Inherited from Old French col, from Latin collum (“neck”). Doublet of cou.
Inherited from Old French fibre, borrowed from Latin fibra.
From Latin sēpia, from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía).

Inherited from Middle French soye, from Old French soie, earlier seie, from Latin sēta, saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”).
Borrowed from German Zirkon, formed in the 1780s from Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn). Doublet of jargon.
From a root of Latin crux (“cross”). The sense of "crucial" is a semantic loan from English crucial.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēmancipātiō. By surface analysis, émanciper + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin incandescens, present participle of incandesco (“to be heated, to glow”).
From the Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “metal”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

Inherited from Middle French bransler, from Old French bransler (“to shake (a sword at), move”), a contracted form of brandeler (“to wobble”), from Vulgar Latin *brandus (“firebrand, flaming sword, sword”), ultimately from Frankish *brand (“sword”), from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“burning, flash, firebrand, flaming sword”). Compare brandish. The supposed intermediary form, Late Latin *brandulare, also from Proto-West Germanic *brand (“sword”), is unlikely given that the suffix -ulāre had already fallen into disuse (i.e. was no longer productive) at the time of borrowing.
Borrowed from Italian caricatùra, from the verb caricàre (“to load; to exaggerate”), cognate with French charger.
Borrowed from Latin cilicium (“clothing made of goatskin”), from Cilicia where it originates from.
Learned borrowing from Latin sagācitās. By surface analysis, sagace + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin polīticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós).

PIE word  *médʰyos Borrowed from Italian mezzanino, from mezzano (“(adjective) middle; (noun) go-between”) + -ino (diminutive suffix). Mezzano is derived from Latin mediānus (“central, middle”, adjective), from medius (“mid, middle”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”)) + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin commūnālis, from Latin commūnis (whence commun). By surface analysis, commune + -al.
Learned borrowing from Latin domesticus (“of the house, domestic; familiar; native”), from domus (“home, house; place of one's birth or residence, native country”).

Borrowed from Provençal mascoto, from masco (“witch”), from Old Occitan masca, from Medieval Latin masca, from a stem *maska, *mask- (“black”) believed to be of Pre-Indo-European origin giving rise to words meaning "witch, wizard, sorcerer.".
Borrowed from Occitan nogat, from noga (“nut”).
Borrowed from Latin ēlogium, later influenced by confusion with eulogia (“eulogy”).

Borrowed from Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader of the chorus in an Ancient Greek drama”), from κορῠφή (korŭphḗ, “top of the head, crown”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head, top; horn”)) + -ῐος (-ĭos, suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘belonging to, relating to’).
From in- + flexibilité or from inflexible + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French moue, from Old French moe (“grimace”), from Frankish *mauwa (“pout, protruding lip”). Akin to Middle Dutch mouwe (“protruding lip”).

Inherited from Middle French pluvial. In the sense of “rain, rainy” since the late 15th century. The liturgical use is older and stems from Old French pluvial (12th c.), a borrowing from Latin pluviālis.
Inherited from Old French hospise, borrowed from Latin hospitium.
Borrowed from Latin līmināris, from līmen (“threshold”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin indisciplīna. By surface analysis, in- + discipline.
From Latin imbricātus, from imbricō, from imbrex.
Inherited from Middle French entre, from Old French entre, inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”). Doublet of inter-, a borrowing.
From Catalan galera, from Medieval Latin galēra, alternative form of galea, from Medieval Greek γάλεα (gálea). Compare galée, from Old French, directly from Latin galea.
Borrowed from Late Latin quadrumanus, from quattuor (whence French quatre) and manus (whence French main).
From Ancient Greek μωρόσοφος (mōrósophos), from μωρός (mōrós, “dull, stupid”) + σοφός (sophós, “wise”).
Borrowed from Latin imberbis. See in- + barbe.
Inherited from Old French camail, a borrowing from Old Occitan capmalh.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin abrasiōnem (“a scraping”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin proprietārius.
Borrowed from Italian bomba, from Latin bombus (“a boom”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin apologia.
From bombarde + -er, from Middle French bombarde, ultimately from Latin bombus.
From Late Latin ideālis (“existing in idea”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέᾱ (idéā, “idea”).
Inherited from Old French braciere (originally a lining inside armor to protect the arm, but later a garment), from Old French brace (“arm”). Equivalent to bras + -ière.
Inherited from Middle French selle, from Old French sele, from Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
Inherited from Middle French bourgois, from Old French borgeis (“town dweller”), from Late Latin burgensis. By surface analysis, bourg + -ois.
Borrowed from Late Latin competitiōnem, from Latin competō.
From Middle French passagier, from passage. Adjective derived from the noun.
Learned borrowing from New Latin mollusca, from Latin molluscus.
From Latin explosiōnem, accusative singular of explosiō.
Borrowed from Spanish alcoba or Portuguese alcova, from Arabic اَلْقُبَّة (al-qubba, “vault, chamber with vaulted roof”).
From Middle French balustrade, from Italian balaustrata.
From ambulant + -ance, after the earlier hôpital ambulant (literally “ambulant hospital”).
Inherited from Middle French entrepreneur, from entreprendre (“to undertake”) + -eur.
Borrowed from Latin caelibātus, from caelebs.
Learned borrowing from New Latin sēpalum.
Borrowed from Italian concerto, deverbal from concertare.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin repertōrium.

Learned borrowing from Latin anōnymus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “without name”, adjective), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma), Doric dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). By surface analysis, an- + -onyme (adjective-forming suffix).
From féminin + -isme, with haplology. In the original sense of “women's movement or advocacy”, probably directly derived from Latin fēmina (“woman”), as if from Neo-Latin feminismus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin commerciālis. By surface analysis, commerce + -ial.
Borrowed from Italian zecchino, from zecca (“mint”), from Arabic سِكَّة (sikka, “die for coining, coin”).
Inherited from Middle French rolle, from Old French role.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑποχονδριακός (hupokhondriakós).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin illegālis, from Latin legālis. Also il- + légal.
PIE word  *ḱóm  PIE word  *swé Borrowed from Italian costume, from Latin cōnsuētūdinem (“custom, habit”). Doublet of consuétude and coutume.
Borrowed from Italian facciata, a derivation of faccia (“front”), from Latin facies (“face”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin quaestiōnārius, from quaestiōnō, from Latin quaestiō.
Borrowed from Italian chiosco, from Ottoman Turkish كوشك (köşk), from Classical Persian کوشْک (kōšk, “palace, portico”), from Middle Persian kwšk' (kōšk).
Learned borrowing from Latin fossilis (“something which has been dug up”), from fodiō (“to dig up”).
Learned borrowing from Latin flōrālis, from flōs (“flower”) (whence fleur).
Borrowed from Italian balletto, diminutive form of ballo (“group dance”) (cognate with Old French bal), from Late Latin ballō (“to dance”). By surface analysis, bal + -et.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “agreeing, of one mind”). By surface analysis, homo- + -logue.
Inherited from Middle French limitrophe, from Latin limitrophus.
Borrowed from Italian risposta, from the verb rispondere (“to respond”).
From Spanish pastilla (“small roll of fragrant dough”), from Latin pastellum (“dough, paste”), a diminutive form of pasta (“dough, paste”). Doublet of pastel.
Inherited from Old French chaudiere, from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”).
Borrowed from Latin refectiōnem (“recovery, refection”), from reficiō (“restore, renew”).
Learned borrowing from Latin paedagogicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγικός (paidagōgikós), from παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, “teacher, tutor”). By surface analysis, pédagogie + -ique.
From New Latin deista, from Latin Deus (“God”) + -ista (“-ist”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin gȳrovagus (“wandering aimlessly”).
FromMedieval Latin calamīna, from Latin cadmī̆a, ultimately from Ancient Greek Κᾰδμείᾱ (Kădmeíā), from Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming related substances”).

Inherited from Old French scarifier, from Late Latin scarificāre, from Latin scarifāre (“to scarify”), from Ancient Greek σκαριφᾶσθαι (skariphâsthai, “to scratch an outline”), from σκάριφος (skáriphos, “writing, drawing, sketching”).
Borrowed from Italian guazzo (“water paint, splash”).
Learned borrowing from Latin īliacus, from īlia (“intestines, guts”).
From méta- + statique, as an adjective corresponding to métastase (“metastasis”), perhaps after Koine Greek μεταστατικός (metastatikós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”). Doublet of amande and mandorle.
From Middle French naufrage (15th c.), a borrowing from Latin naufragium.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin manūtentiō, from the past participle of manūteneō (“to maintain”).

From Middle French buron, from Old French buiron (“cabin, hut”), from Frankish *būr (“dwelling, residence”), from Proto-Germanic *būraz (“room, chamber, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to be, become, live, dwell”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Búur (“room, cage”), English bower, Swedish bur (“hutch, coop, cage”).
Inherited from Middle French couteau, costeau, from Old French costel. By surface analysis, côte + -eau.
The second sense is from Latin mascula, from Germanic (see English mascle for details). The first sense either has the same origin, or derives from macula (from Italic).
Learned borrowing from Latin proletārius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”).
Renaissance borrowing of Latin dictum, with francisation of the ending. Doublet of dit.
From Occitan sanqueta, from sang (“blood”) + -eta (diminutive suffix). By surface analysis, sang (“blood”) + -ette (diminutive suffix).
Learned borrowing from Latin acidus (“acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”).
From Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ) + -ème, coined on the model of phonème.

Inherited from Old French bruit, used as a noun of the past participle form of bruire (“to roar”), from a Proto-Romance alteration (by association with braire (“to bray; to cry out, shout out”)) of Latin rugītus (“brayed; bellowed, roared; rumbled”) (compare Vulgar Latin *brugitus, from Latin *brūgere). Compare also Spanish ruido, Portuguese ruído, French rut, and English rut.
Borrowed from Late Latin archaicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊκός (arkhaïkós).
Learned borrowing from Latin impersōnālis. By surface analysis, in- + personnel.
Inherited from Middle French lune, from Old French lune, from Latin lūna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, from *lewk- + *-sneh₂.
Coined by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1818 from Ancient Greek σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”)
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin adhaesivus.

Inherited from Middle French chasteau, château, chastel, from Old French chastel, from Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum. Cognate with Italian castello, Portuguese castelo, Romanian castel, Spanish castillo

Inherited from Old French antique, from antic, borrowed from Latin antīquus. Compare also the inherited Old French antive, from the Latin feminine antīqua, which analogically influenced a masculine form antif (compare a similar occurrence in Spanish antiguo).
From Italian utilizzare. By surface analysis, utile + -iser.
Learned borrowing from Latin fābrica. Doublet of forge.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin medicālis (compare Classical Latin medicīnālis, whence the French médicinal), from Latin medicus.

Inherited from Old French druide (13th c.), borrowed from Latin druidae, from Gaulish *druwits, from Proto-Celtic *druwits (“wise person”). The Old French form is definitely a borrowing and not inherited. The question poses itself, however, whether the word was inherited since then or borrowed again later on.
Borrowed from Italian spianata with influx from Spanish explanada, both from Latin explānātus.

From Middle French toupet (“small tuft of hair, forelock”), from Old French toupet (“small tuft of hair, forelock”), diminutive of toupe, top (“tuft of hair”), from Frankish *topp (“summit, crest, tuft of hair”), from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“summit, crest, tuft of hair”). Cognate with Old Dutch topp (“top”) (Dutch top), Old Frisian top (“summit, crest, tuft of hair”), Old English top (“summit, crest, tuft of hair”), Old High German zopf (“end, summit, tuft of hair”), Old Norse toppr (“tuft of hair, forelock”). More at top.
Borrowed from Italian isolato, past participle of isolare.
From Latin apoplēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληκτικός (apoplēktikós).
From Latin condylus, from Ancient Greek κόνδυλος (kóndulos, “knuckle”).
From Old French estude, borrowed from Latin studium.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin volitiōnem (“will, volition”), from Latin volō (“to wish, to will”).
Borrowed from Late Latin dēcapitāre, literally, “to de-head”.
Learned borrowing from Latin cupiditātem. Compare the inherited Old French coveitié. Compare also convoitise, convoiter, from related inherited roots.
Inherited from Old French covert, from Latin coopertus.
Borrowed from Latin euphonia, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (euphōnía).
Learned borrowing from Latin inānitās, from inānis.

Borrowed from Italian pasticcio (“pie, something blended”), from Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”), from παστός (pastós, “sprinkled with salt”). Doublet of pastis, which was borrowed through Occitan.
A scholarly, and adjectival, derivation ultimately based upon Latin iudicō.
Borrowed from Occitan mas, from Latin mānsum.

Coined by French chemist and pharmacist Henri Braconnot 1830s, from acide pectique "pectic acid", from Ancient Greek πηκτικός (pēktikós, “curdling”), from πηκτός (pēktós, “curdled”), from πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “stiffen”).
Borrowed from Portuguese macaco, of uncertain origin (see macaco for more).
Learned borrowing from Latin gangraena, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek γάγγραινα (gángraina).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin syndicus (“syndic”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos, “advocate of a defendant”).
Borrowed from Latin archīāter, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀρχιατρός (arkhiatrós).
Inherited from Middle French brut, from Old French brut, from Latin brūtus (“heavy, dull”).
Borrowed from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (paralutikós, “paralyzed”).
From Latin cērusa, variant of cērussa, q.v.
Learned borrowing from Latin sōlitārius. In Middle and Old French there existed the words soltain, soutain, inherited from Vulgar Latin *sōlitānus, from Late Latin sōlitāneus.
From the Roman name, Latin Diviōnem, from the name Divius (“godly, divine”); see divus.
Inherited from Old French tige, from Latin tībia. Doublet of tibia (“shin”), which was borrowed.
Inherited from Middle French venin, from Old French venim, from Vulgar Latin *venīmen, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum.
Inherited from Middle French armure, from armure, armeüre, from Latin armātūra. Doublet of armature, a borrowing.
From Late Latin balsaminus, from Latin balsamum.

From Occitan boumbouno m [from boumbo + -ouno, ultimately from Latin bombus and -ōnem], made feminine under the influence of French bonne (unrelated), and with change of bomb- to bonb- under the influence of French bonbon (also unrelated). By surface analysis, bombe + -on. Although less common, the spelling bombonne more accurately reflects the Latin bomb- root.
From dialectal Arabic سْلُوڭِي (slūgī, “greyhound”), from Arabic سَلُوقِيّ (salūqiyy, “greyhound”). See also English Saluki.
From partire (“I divide, part”), the rare, literary word, not its more common homonym meaning to depart.
From German Zander, from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *sǫdakъ.

Borrowed from Italian bergamotta, deemed a corruption of Ottoman Turkish بك آرمودی (beg armudu, literally “a lord's pear”), denoting originally a fattish kind of pear, whereafter the European word developed the sense of a fruit of a certain citrus cultivar in the late 17th century.
From orient + -er, from Old French oriant.
Probably from Occitan charrada, from charrar (“to chat”). Compare Italian ciarlare.

Inherited from Middle French pomme, from Old French pome, from Latin pōma, plural of pōmum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular, from Proto-Italic *poomos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”). Compare English pome.
Inherited from Middle French hacher, from Old French hacher, hachier, from Frankish *hakkōn, from Proto-Germanic *hakkōną (“to chop; hack”). More at hack.
Learned borrowing from Latin vēnālis (“for sale”).
A learned formation from the root of Latin cerebrum and the suffix -al.
Borrowed from Latin agitātiōnem. By surface analysis, agiter + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin herbivorus. By surface analysis, herbe + -i- + -vore.
From collaborer + -tion, from Late Latin collaboratio, from Latin com- (“with”) + labōrō (“work”).
Learned borrowing from Latin adeptus, the past participle of adipīscor (“to attain”).

Inherited from Middle French bresze, from Old French breze (“ember, burning coal, gleed”), perhaps from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐍃𐌰 (*brasa, “glowing coal”), from Proto-Germanic *brasō (“gleed, crackling coal”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to crack, break, burst”). Cognate with Swedish brasa (“to roast”), Icelandic brasa (“to harden by fire”).
Learned borrowing from Latin integrātiō. By surface analysis, intégrer + -ation.
From lorgner (“to take a sidelong look at”) + -ette, analogous to lunette.

Learned borrowing from Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περιπατητικός (peripatētikós, “given to walking around”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) + πατέω (patéō, “to walk”).
Verb-object compound, composed of gira (“to turn”) + Sole (“sun”), referring to the heliotropism of the plants when they are young.
From Latin obēsitātem, from obēsus (“fat”) (compare obèse).
From New Latin anthēra, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρός (anthērós).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnsecūtīvus, from Latin cōnsecūtus (“followed up”), from Latin cōnsequor (“to travel”).
Inherited from Old French mural, borrowed from Latin murālis.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French denier, inherited from Latin dēnārius. Doublet of dénaire.
Learned borrowing from New Latin cervicālis, formed from the root of Latin cervix (“the neck, nape of the neck”) and -alis (see -al).
Inherited from Old French praerie, from Vulgar Latin *prataria, from Latin prātum (“meadow”) + -aria. See also pré and -erie.
Inherited from Old French senile, borrowed from Latin senīlis (“relating to old age”), from Latin senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”).
Borrowed from Italian cascata, from cascare (“to fall”).
Feminine past participle of sortir; from Latin sortīrī (“cast lots, divide, receive”), possibly influenced by a derivative of surgō (“get up, arise”). Compare Italian sortire (“produce”).
Inherited from Middle French chanson f, from Old French chançon f, inherited from Latin cantiōnem f (“song, singing”).
Inherited from Middle French parler, from Old French parler, from Early Medieval Latin parabolāre (“to express”), from Latin parabola (“parable, comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin adaptātiōnem, from Latin adaptō (“to fit, adjust, modify; to adapt, fit or adjust to”).
Learned borrowing from Latin pudīcus (“chaste, pure”).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).

Inherited from Middle French braser, from Old French braser (“to burn”), either from a variant of Old French brese (“live coals”), of Germanic origin; or more likely from Old Norse brasa (“to braze, harden with fire”), from the same Proto-Germanic origin.
Borrowed from Spanish natrón, from Arabic نَطْرُون (naṭrūn), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron, “nitre”).
Earlier called sirop grenadin. From grenade (“pomegranate”) + -ine from Middle French grenade (“pomegranate”).
Borrowed from Italian piastra. Doublet of plâtre.
From pistole + -et. Ultimately from Czech píšťala (“whistle”).
Inherited from Old French chalemel, from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of Latin calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed”). Doublet of caramel.

From early modern French esbauche (“the first form of a work of art, a proto-type”), deverbal of Middle French esbaucher (“to rough-hew, frame”), alteration (due to Middle French bauche (“beam, wooden crosspiece”)) of Old French esbosquier, esboskier (“to rough-hew beams”), from es- (“out”) + bosc (“wood, firewood”), from Frankish *busk (“wood, firewood”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“wood, thicket”). Cognate with Old French esbochier (“to prune grapes”), French bois (“wood”), bau (“crossbeam”). More at bush, balk.
Learned borrowing from Latin amphibologia, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιβολία (amphibolía, “ambiguity”).

From Middle French matelot (“sailor”), from Old French matenot (“sailor, bunkmate”), most likely from Middle Dutch mattenoot (“bunk fellow”), corresponding to modern mat (“mat, rug, hammock”) + genoot (“companion”) or less likely Old Norse mǫtunautr (“food companion”) (from matr (“food”) + nautr (“companion”) << Proto-Germanic *ganautaz).

From Middle French arrestation. Equivalent to arrêter + -ation. The noun, being of a more formal register, was standardised with a Latinate pronunciation, while the verb has the popular form with loss of preconsonantal s.
Inherited from Latin mōrēs (“ways, character, morals”), the plural of mōs.
From the verb βδάλλω (bdállō, “to milk; to suck”).

From soigner (“to look after, take care of; to nurse, treat”) + -eur (suffix forming masculine agent nouns from verbs). Soigner is derived from soin (“care”, noun) (ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sunjō, *sunþijō (“care, responsibility; sooth, truth”), from *sunjaz (“real, true”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sónts, the active participle of *h₁ésti (“to be”), from *h₁es- (“to be”)) + -er (suffix forming infinitives of first-conjugation verbs).
Alteration of earlier malaguette, a borrowing of Portuguese malagueta, from Italian meleghetta.
Learned borrowing from Latin hyraulicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin conditiōnālis (“conditional”), from conditiō (“condition”).
Learned borrowing from Latin metrum, itself from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐκλεκτικός (eklektikós).

Inherited from Old French ogre, itself probably an alteration, with influence from words like bougre, of an earlier form *orc, from Latin Orcus (“the underworld; the god Pluto”), with metathesis. According to the Trésor de la langue française informatisé, first attested in the late 12th century meaning 'fierce non-Christian', and ca. 1300 meaning 'human-eating giant' (in fairy tales). Cognate with Old Spanish huerco (“the Devil”), Spanish huerco (“depressed man in the dark”), Italian orco (“ogre, orc”). Doublet of orque. See also French lutin (“imp, pixie”), possibly from Old French netun (“marine monster”), derived from Latin Neptūnus, and also Old French gene (“mischievous fairy”) and Romanian zână (“fairy”), both inherited forms of Latin Diāna. A sermon by Merovingian French bishop St. Eligius (died 659) advises people against belief in Neptune, Diana, Orcus and Minerva.
1765, from Latin quadrātus + -ique, form of quadrō (“to make square”), from quādrus (“square”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀφασία (aphasía).
Borrowed from Italian cartuccia, a diminutive of carta, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs).
Sax + -o- + -phone. Named after Adolphe Sax (1814–1894), its inventor.
From Latin apologus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόλογος (apólogos).
From New Latin psychologia (coined by Marko Marulić from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + Latin -logia (“study of”)).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin credibilitātem, from Latin credibilis. By surface analysis, crédible + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French par, from Old French par, from Latin per.
Borrowed from Italian carena (cf. Ligurian carena), from Latin carīna.
Borrowed from Italian zibetto, from Arabic زَبَاد (zabād).
Inherited from Old French pension, panssion, borrowed from Latin pēnsiōnem (“payment, rent”), from pēnsus, the past participle of pendō (“weigh, pay”).

From Ancient Greek κοσμητικός (kosmētikós), κοσμητής (kosmētḗs, “orderer, director, decorator”), from κοσμέω (kosméō, “to order, to arrange, to rule, to adorn, to equip, to dress, to embellish”), from κόσμος (kósmos, “world, universe”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós).
From juxta- + poser or from Latin iūxtāpōnō.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συνθετικός (sunthetikós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēditiōnem.
From Latin fūsibilitās. By surface analysis, fusible + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French lucratif, from Latin lucrātīvus (“profitable”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γεωδαισία (geōdaisía).
Inherited from Middle French explicite (attested since 1488), borrowed from Latin explicitus, variant of explicātus.

Past participle of blaser, from Middle Dutch blâsen (“to blow, sound, brag”), from Old Dutch *blāsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan (“to blow”). Cognate with German blasen (“to blow”), English blast.
From typographe + -ie, from Medieval Latin typographia.
1845, formed from Latin calor + -ie. Cf. also French chaleur.
Inherited from Middle French detergent, from Latin dētergentem.
Back-formation from the Old French verb ramper (“to go up, climb, ascend”).
Borrowed from Italian torrente, from Latin torrentem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin compatriota, itself likely a calque of Ancient Greek συμπατριώτης (sumpatriṓtēs). By surface analysis, com- + patriote.
Inherited from Old French pelice, from Late Latin pellicia, from Latin pellis (“skin”).
Learned borrowing from Latin factūra. Compare the inherited Old French faiture.
Formed from the root of Latin clāvis (whence French clef), with the suffix -ier. Cf. also Medieval Latin clāvārius.

Borrowed from Italian macramè, from Ottoman Turkish مقرمه (makrame), from Arabic مِقْرَمَة (miqrama, “ornamental fringe, embroidered veil”), from مِقْرَم (miqram, “bedspread”), from قَرَمَ (qarama, “to gnaw”), from Proto-Semitic *q-r-m.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an inversion of English walkie-talkie.
From New Latin Doryphora (the former genus of the Colorado beetle), from Ancient Greek δορυφόρος (doruphóros, “lance-bearing; lance-bearer”).
From Latin chamaedrys, from Ancient Greek χαμαίδρῡς (khamaídrūs, “ground oak”), from χαμαί (khamaí, “on the ground”) + δρῦς (drûs, “oak”).
Inherited from Late Latin arepennis (“surface of a field”), from Gaulish *are-penno- (“end, extremity of a field”).
From rouler (“to roll”) + -eur (suffix forming agent nouns from verbs).
From oblique stem of Latin comes, comitis (“count, earl, companion, comrade”) + -al.
From Ancient Greek μονόξυλον (monóxulon), see mono- & xylo-.
Inherited from Old French saucice, from Late Latin [farta] salsīcia, ultimately from Latin sāl (“salt”).
Learned borrowing from Latin actuālis (“active, practical”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitās, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”). Morphologically, from réel + -ité.

Inherited from Old French bast, from Vulgar Latin *bastum, derivative of *bastō (“to carry, serve as a support, suffice”), from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to lift, bear”). Displaced Classical Latin clitellae.
Learned borrowing from Latin foederātiōnem. By surface analysis, fédérer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτος (anékdotos, “unpublished”). Compare inédit.
From maraud + -er, from Middle French maraud (“rascal”), from Old French *marault (“beggar, vagabond”), from marir, marrir (“to trouble, stray, lose ones way, be lost”).
Learned borrowing from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Cognate with French charte.
Inherited from Middle French axonge, axungie, borrowed from Latin axungia.
Inherited from Old French chasse, from Late Latin capsa, from Classical Latin capsus, whence also the doublets casse and caisse.
Inherited from Middle French categorie, from Late Latin catēgoria.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δραματουργός (dramatourgós).
Inherited from Middle French feste, from Old French feste, from Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstum. Doublet of festin.
Learned borrowing from Latin lapis schistos, from Ancient Greek σχῐστός (skhĭstós, “divisible”). First attested in the 16th century.

Ca. 1600, borrowed in the musical sense from Italian fuga, itself a borrowing from Latin fuga. Doublet of fougue (from the inherited Italian cognate). The sense “flight” (18th c.) may be a new borrowing from the Italian.
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós).
Inherited from Middle French alphabetique, borrowed from Latin alphabēticus; equivalent to alphabet + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Latin ventrālis. By surface analysis, ventre + -al.
Inherited from Old French dragon, perhaps borrowed from Old Occitan dragon, from Latin dracō, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn). Doublet of drac.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin fragrantia, from fragrō, fragrāre. Related to flairer, which was inherited.
Learned borrowing from Latin ātrophīa, from Ancient Greek ἀτροφία (atrophía, “a wasting away”).
From Late Latin monoculus (“one-eyed”), from mono- (“single”) + oculus (“eye”).
From pet + -er. Compare Catalan petar, borrowed into Spanish as petar.
Borrowed from Occitan lusèrna (“glowworm”), a reference to its shiny seeds, from Latin lucerna (“lamp”).
Inherited from Old French sompnolent, borrowed from Latin somnolentus.
Borrowed from Italian zoccolo (“wooden shoe”), from Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“sock”).
Borrowed from Spanish caramelo, derived from Portuguese caramelo, probably derived from Late Latin calamellus, and therefore doublet of the inherited chalumeau.
From Russian кнут (knut), from Old East Slavic кнутъ (knutŭ), from Old Norse knútr (“knot”). Doublet of nœud.
Feminine of the Old French salier, saler, from Latin salārius.
Learned derivation from the root of Latin ludus suffixed with + -ique

Inherited from Middle French travail (“suffering, pain”), from Old French travail (“suffering, pain”), deverbal of travailler, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre, from Late Latin tripālium (“torture device made of three stakes”). The plural derives from Old French travauz, early travailz, with vocalization of the lateral before a consonant (/tʁavo/ < /tɾaˈvau̯s/ < /tɾaˈvaʎts/).

From chiffe + -on. Chiffe is from Middle French chiffe (“cloth, old rag”) from Old French chipe (“rag”), from Middle English chip, chippe (“chip, shard, fragment”) from Old English ċipp (“chip, splinter, shaving”), from Old English *ċippian (“to chip, shave, splinter”), from Proto-West Germanic *kipp-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵey- (“to split; divide; germinate; sprout”). More at English chip.
Inherited from Old French areste, from Latin arista.
Inherited from Old French Roem, from the Roman name, Latin Rotomagus, from the Gaulish name Ratumacos, from *rato- (of unclear origin - see Rouen) + *magos, from Proto-Celtic *magos (“field”).
Borrowed from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon). Doublet of organe, a later borrowing.
Learned borrowing from New Latin tetania. Compare tétanos.
Borrowed from Latin degustātiōnem, from degusto.
Borrowed from Late Latin cynismus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κυνισμός (kunismós).
Borrowed from Late Latin angaria (“forced service”).
From Latin siliqua. Compare English silique.

From Medieval Latin grātīcula, from Latin crāticula (“grating, grill”), from crātis (“hurdle; wickerwork”) (probably from Proto-Indo-European *kréh₂-tis (“fenced handiwork”)) + -cula (feminine form of -culus, a variant of -ulus (“diminutive suffix”)).
Inherited from Old French donter, from Latin domitāre. The p is unetymological, also seen in terms like Old French dampner (Latin damnō, Modern French damner).
Learned borrowing from Latin inēnarrābilis. Related to narrer.
Borrowed from Latin virgula, diminutive of virga (“rod, branch”).
From Middle French crequier, from Old French crekere, equivalent to crèque + -ier.
From Medieval Latin censivus and French recensement.
From Latin centipeda, centipēs, from centi- (“hundred”) + pēs (“foot”). By surface analysis, centi- + -pède.
From Old French epilepsie, from Latin epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψία (epilēpsía).
From Old French avenue, feminine past participle of avenir (“approach”), from Latin advenīre (“come to”), from ad (“to”) + veniō, venīre (“come”).

From Gascon Occitan basc, from Latin Vascō, Vascōnēs pl, a pre-Roman era tribe settled in the Atlantic Biscaian gulf and Pyrenean mountain region of south-western Europe, who were ancestors of the current Basque population.
Learned borrowing from Latin axis. Compare the inherited doublet ais.
From Italian gruppo, itself derived from Vulgar Latin *cruppus.
Learned borrowing from Latin avidus (“greedy; eager; hungry”), from aveō (“wish, desire, long for, crave”).
From Latin visa, neuter plural of Latin visus (“having been seen”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós).
