Learned borrowing from Latin vehiculum (“vehicle, carriage”).
From Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).
Alteration, on the model of Italian scellerato, of older scéléré, borrowed from Latin scelerātus.
From Latin colica, from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin dogmatismus.
From Latin diatriba (“learned discussion or discourse”), from Ancient Greek διατριβή (diatribḗ, “way of spending time, lecture”), from διά (diá, “through”) + τρίβω (tríbō, “to waste, wear out”).
Inherited from Old French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus.
Inherited from Old French corruption, borrowed from Latin corruptiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin modulus. Doublet of moule.
From Latin apathīa, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia).
Learned borrowing from Latin districtus. Doublet of détroit.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin facētiōsus. By surface analysis, facétie + -eux.
From méno- + -pause, coined by French physician Charles de Gardanne in 1821.
Learned borrowing from Latin glaciālis. Morphologically, from glace + -ial.
Inherited from Middle French comper, from Old French comper, conper, from Late Latin compatrem (“godfather”), from Latin com- + pater.
From modern Latin hyoides, from Ancient Greek ὑοειδής (huoeidḗs, “shaped like the letter υ (u)”).

An adaptation of the Castilian Spanish criollo (“homey, local yokel”), from Portuguese crioulo, diminutive of cria (“person raised in one’s house, servant”), from Portuguese criar (“to rear, to bring up”), from Latin creō (“to create”)

Inherited from Middle French prendre, from Old French prendre, prandre, from Latin prēndere, alternative form of prehendere (“to seize”), from prae- (“before”) + *hendō (“to take, seize”) (not attested without prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.

Learned borrowing from Latin cosmopolītēs, itself borrowed from Koine Greek κοσμοπολίτης (kosmopolítēs, “citizen of the world”), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”).

Substantive use of Old French grenate in pomme grenate (“pomegranate”), from dialectal northern Italian pom granat, from Medieval Latin pomum granatum (“seeded fruit”), from Latin grānātum. The -d- developed under influence from Spanish granada.
Inherited from Latin friābilis, from friō (“to crumble”).
From Catalan ganga, of imitative origin.
From Arabic طِلَّسْم (ṭillasm), from Ancient Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, “payment”).
Inherited from Old French brume, borrowed from Latin brūma (“winter”), possibly through the intermediate of Old Occitan bruma.
Inherited from Old French voiture, from Latin vectūra.
Inherited from Middle French reverer, ultimately borrowed from Latin reverērī (“to stand in awe (of), regard, respect, honor, reverence, revere”) (compare Catalan reverir), from re- + vereor.
Inherited from Middle French celeste, from Old French celeste, borrowed from Latin caelestis.
Borrowed from Italian torso, from Latin thyrsus. Doublet of thyrse.
Learned borrowing from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós).
Borrowed from Turkish sipahi, from Persian سپاهی (sepâhi, “horseman, soldier”), from سپاه (sepâh, “army”).
From Occitan bolhabaissa, possibly a compound of bolhir (“to boil”) + abaissar (“to lower [temperature]”). By surface analysis, bouillir + abaisser.

Inherited from Middle French coulpe, from Old French coupe, colpe, inherited from Latin culpa, which see for more. The expected form would be *coupe; the -l- was reintroduced in Middle French – first in spelling, then in pronunciation – after the Latin etymon, in part to avoid the homonymy with coupe (“cup”).
Borrowed from Latin pulsiōnem, from pulsus.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek βοτανικός (botanikós). The noun comes from the ellipsis βοτανικὴ [τέχνη].

Inherited from Middle French chancre, from Old French chancre, inherited from Latin cancrum, from Proto-Italic *kankros, dissimilation of *karkros (“enclosure”) (because the pincers of a crab form a circle), from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (“circular”), reduplication of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Doublet of cancer.

Inherited from Old French calament~calamente, borrowed from Medieval Latin calamentum, from Latin calaminthe, from Ancient Greek καλαμίνθη (kalamínthē, “an odoriferous plant”), of uncertain origin (either by haplology from *καλαμο-μίνθη (*kalamo-mínthē) or a loanword, which Beekes considers most likely to be from Pre-Greek). First attested in the twelfth century.
Borrowed from English goddamn, in reference to the English propensity for swearing. Originally used in the Hundred Years War.
Borrowed from dialectal Italian pavana, contraction of padovana, feminine of padovano, meaning from the city of Padua (Italian Padova, dialectal form Pava).
From Middle French stilet, borrowed from Italian stiletto.
From in- + aptitude, or from Renaissance Latin inaptitūdō.
Inherited from Middle French octroy, alteration of Old French otroi, from otroier (“to grant”), from Late Latin auctōrizāre.
Calque of Old Occitan retaule. Compare Catalan retaule.
From Middle French huron (“bristle-haired”), from Old French hure (“bristly, unkempt, shaggy”), of possible Germanic origin.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin myrias, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μυριάς (muriás).
Borrowed from Italian busto, from Latin būstum.

From Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, sour, acid”) + γένος (génos, “birth”). Coined by French nobleman and chemist Antoine Lavoisier in 1778 under the mistaken assumption that it was a constituent of all acids.
Inherited from Middle French Florence, from Latin Flōrentia, from flōrens (“flowering”) + -ia (suffix forming place names).
Learned borrowing from Latin centi-, from centum (“hundred”).
Inherited from Old French colp, cop, from Late Latin colpus, syncopated form of Latin colaphus, from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos).
Inherited from Middle French pere, from Old French pedre, pedra, pere, from Latin patrem, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

Formed, with the suffix -ible, from Latin ostēnsus, past participle of ostendō (“to show”), itself from obs- (“in front of”) (akin to Latin ob- (“in the way”), Ancient Greek ἐπι- (epi-, “on, at, besides, after”), Old English eofot (“crime”)) + tendō (“to stretch”); or borrowed from Medieval Latin ostēnsibilis.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνομία (anomía, “lawlessness”), from ἄνομος (ánomos, “lawless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”).
Coined 1923 by Gabriel Bertrand from Ancient Greek λῐ́πος (lĭ́pos, “animal fat”) + -ide.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin marginem, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs.
Learned derivation from Latin efflōrēscere with the suffix -ence.
Introduced into French from settlers visiting the Indies; from Spanish ananás, from Portuguese ananás, from Old Tupi naná (“pineapple”).
Inherited from Middle French début, deverbal of desbuter (“to move, begin”) (whence débuter).
Learned borrowing from Latin mūnicipālis (“of or belonging to a citizen or a free town”), from mūniceps (“a citizen, an inhabitant of a free town”), from mūnus (“duty”) + capiō (“to take”).
Learned borrowing from Latin globulus. By surface analysis, globe + -ule.
Inherited from Latin mantellum, diminutive of mantum. Compare Italian mantello.
Borrowed from Latin resēda, noun use of imperative form of resēdāre (“to heal”), from re- + sēdare.
Borrowed from Italian catafalco, from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “down”) + Latin fala (“scaffolding, wooden siege tower”), which is from Etruscan. Doublet of échafaud.
Inherited from Middle French moulin, from Old French molin, from Late Latin molīnum, from the adjective molīnus, from Latin molō.

From Italian merlone (“merlon”), from merlo (“merlon”) + -one (suffix forming augmentatives). Merlo is derived from Late Latin merulus, merlus, possibly from Latin merula (“blackbird”) (as merlons resemble a row of birds perched on a wall), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ems- (“black; blackbird”).
Learned borrowing from Latin lassitūdō (“faintness, weariness”), from lassus (“faint, weary”).
From Italian ptomaina, from Ancient Greek πτῶμα (ptôma, “corpse”).
From a Maghrebi form of Arabic قَصْر (qaṣr).
From Middle French delicatesse, equivalent to délicat + -esse, probably modelled on Italian delicatezza.

Inherited from Middle French, from Italian salone (“large hall”), augmented form of sala (“hall”), from Lombardic sala (“room, house, entrance hall”), from Proto-Germanic *salą (“dwelling, house, hall”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“human settlement, village, dwelling”). Cognate with Old High German sal (“room, house, entrance hall”), Old English sæl (“room, hall, castle”), Old Church Slavonic село (selo, “courtyard, village”), Lithuanian sala (“island”).
Borrowed from Portuguese talapão, from Mon တၠဳ ပိုဲ (tloe poi, “our lord”).
Borrowed from Occitan alhòli, contraction of alh (“garlic”) + òli (“oil”).
Borrowed from Italian caloiero, from Ancient Greek κᾰλόγηρος (kălógēros, “venerable”), from κᾰλός (kălós, “beautiful”) + γῆρας (gêras, “old age”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dēsinentia f, present participle of dēsinō (“to stop, end, close, make an end”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin graphiārius (“scribe, secretary”), from graphium (“stylus”). Compare greffe (“clerk's office”).
Inherited from Old French [Term?], inherited from Latin cōnfectus, the past participle of conficiō (whence confire).
Learned borrowing from Latin pudor (“modesty, chastity”).

From forcener (“to go mad, become enraged”), from Middle French, from Old French forsener (“to be mad with rage”) (compare Old French forsenede (“one who has lost his mind”)), from for- + sen (“sense, reason, mind”), from Frankish *sinn (“sense, mind, judgement”). Cognate with German Sinn (“sense, meaning, mind”), Dutch zin (“sense, desire”). Related to asséner.
Probably from Occitan vinassa, from Latin vīnācea. First attested in the mid–18th c. By surface analysis, vin + -asse.
From Latin phylactērium (“amulet, phylactery, gladiator's medal”).
Learned borrowing from Latin alexipharmacon (“antidote for a poison”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλεξιφάρμακος (alexiphármakos, “antidote”).
Inherited from Middle French menu, from Old French menu, from Latin minūtus (“minute, tiny”). Doublet of minute.
Clipping of inoxydable, itself an ellipsis of acier inoxydable.
Inherited from Old French naïf, inherited from Latin nātīvus. Doublet of natif. Semantical shift from "original; natural; simple" to "simple-minded".
First attested in Old French, from parer + -ure.
Inherited from Middle French bosse, from Old French boce (“protrusion, outgrowth, lump”), from Frankish *bottja. Compare Occitan bòssa, Italian boccia and bozza; cf. also Romanian bot.
From Old French querele, from Latin querella (“complaint”), from queror (“to lament, to complain”).
Inherited from Old French bordure, bordeüre, from border (“to border”), from bort, bord (“a border”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bord.

Inherited from Middle French glace, from Old French glace (“ice", also "glass, mirror, radiance”), from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”). The senses of "glass, mirror, radiance" were possibly derived from Frankish *glas (“glass”).
Inherited from Middle French cheval, from Old French cheval, from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin.

Inherited from Old French artillerie (“collection of military engins, crossbows, lances, etc.”), from artillier (“to equip, provide with contraptions”), alteration of atiller (“to arrange, adjust, put on clothes or, especially, pieces of armour”) (influenced by art), itself from a Vulgar Latin *apticlāre < *apticulāre, from Latin aptāre (“to make capable”).
Inherited from Old French ajorner, from the phrase a jorn (nome) (“to an (appointed) day”).
From symbole + -iste, coined by French poet Paul Verlaine in 1885.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin persōnālis. By surface analysis, personne + -el.
Inherited from Middle French vertu, from Old French vertu, from Latin virtūtem.
From Drais + -ienne, named after Baron Karl Drais (1785–1851).
Inherited from Old French osfraie, inherited from Latin ossifraga (“osprey”), from ossifragus (“bone breaking”). Doublet of ossifrage.

Inherited from Old French fermail (also fermeil, fermal), from Vulgar Latin *firmāc(u)lum, a noun derived from Latin firmāre (“make fast”). By surface analysis, fermer + -ail. Compare Occitan fermalh, Italian fermaglio.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). By surface analysis, manie + -aque.

From télé- (“far off”) + vision (“seeing”), first used by Constantin Perskyi in a paper ("Télévision au moyen de l’électricité") read to the International Electricity Congress at the International World Fair in Paris on August 25, 1900.
Inherited from Middle French contre, from Old French contre, from Latin contra.
Inherited from Old French seel, from Vulgar Latin *sitellus, from sitella (“kind of urn”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀργασμός (orgasmós, “excitement, swelling”).
From Middle French jambon, from Old French gambon, gamboun, jaumbeun; equivalent to jambe (“leg”) + -on.
Learned borrowing from Latin in-, from Proto-Italic *n̥-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-, from *né.
From Latin iactantia. Cognate with Spanish jactancia and Catalan jactància.
Inherited from Old French chapelet, from chapel (“hat”) + -et.
Learned borrowing from Latin reciprocitās. By surface analysis, réciproque + -ité.
Probably from Old French ancor, from Late Latin in hanc hōram (“until this hour”). Compare Catalan and Occitan encara, Italian ancora. Sense 5 is a semantic loan from German noch (adverb).
Inherited from Middle French goutren, from Old French catran, from Medieval Latin catarannus, from Arabic قَطْرَان (qaṭrān). Form influenced by Middle French goutte (see French goutte).
From Chine (“China”) + -ois (“-ese”). Sense 3 of the noun comes from the strainer's resemblance to a traditional Asian conical hat.
From Late Latin drappum (“cloth”), first recorded in Frankish ordinances (The Capitularies of Charles the Great). More at drape.
Borrowed from Italian capriola, initially as capriole, with a final -e to fit French norms.
From Old French resverie (“revelry”), from resver (“to dream, to rave”), of uncertain origin.
Inherited from Middle French duc, from Old French duc, borrowed from Latin ducem (“duke, commander”), from dūcere (“to lead”). Doublet of doge.
From Old French baterie, from batre (“to hit”).
Borrowed from Spanish almadraba, from Arabic مضربة (maḍraba), ضرب (ḍaraba). Attested since 1679.
From protester + -ant. Influenced by German Protestant.
Learned borrowing from Latin gravitās. Replaced the older inherited grieté, griéveté.
Inherited from Latin carbōnārius, from carbō. By surface analysis, charbon + -ier.
Inherited from Old French unde, onde, from Latin unda.
Borrowed from Italian collina, from Late Latin collina, from Latin collinus.

Inherited from Middle French mode, from Old French mode f, ultimately from Latin modus m. The masculine gender was reintroduced for some senses during the Middle French period under influence of the Latin. Doublet of mœuf.

Inherited from Old French chalivali (“noise from pots and pans”), from Late Latin caribaria, from carivaria, from Ancient Greek καρηβάρεια (karēbáreia, “headache”, from κάρη (kárē, “head”) + βαρύς (barús, “heavy”)).
From Latin animālitātem. By surface analysis, animal (adjective) + -ité.
Inherited from Old French perdriz, from Latin perdīcem, from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix).
From Franco-Provençal (Savoy) rimaye (“split, glacier crevasse”), from Latin rimari (“crack, split, open, search”).
Learned borrowing from Latin prōpēnsiōnem (“penchant, inclination”).
Learned borrowing from Latin observātiōnem. By surface analysis, observer + -ation.
Borrowed from Breton bizoù, bizou (“ring”), from biz (“finger”).
Borrowed from New Latin pupa, from a specialized use of Latin pūpa.
Inherited from Middle French lascher, from Old French laschier, from Vulgar Latin *lassicāre < *laxicāre, frequentative of Latin laxāre (whence French laisser).
Borrowed from archaic Italian todesco, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin theodiscus. Doublet of thiois.
Calque of Italian la Gioconda using Middle French joconde, feminine of jocond, from Latin iūcundus.
Borrowed from Late Latin Dominicus, derived from Dominus (“Lord”).
Inherited from Old French revers, from Latin reversus.

Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French pochete (“small purse, small bag”), diminutive (with suffix -ete) of puche (“purse, bag”), from Frankish *pokō (“pouch, bag”), from Proto-Germanic *puhô (“bag, pouch”). Reinforced by Old Norse puki, poki (“bag, pocket”), from Old Northern French. Cognate with Middle Dutch poke, Alemannic German Pfoch (“purse, bag”), Old English pohha, pocca (“poke, pouch, pocket, bag”). Compare English pocket, derived from an Anglo-Norman/Old Northern French variant.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praecautiō, from praecaveō.
Borrowed from Latin capillāris, from capillus (whence cheveu).
From Middle French oubliete [1372]. Compositionally oublier (“to forget”) + -ette (forms feminine nouns).
From Old French flambeier, inherited from Vulgar Latin *flammizāre (but influenced by flambe), derived from Latin flamma. Derivable from flambe + -oyer.

Inherited from Middle French bâtard, from Old French bastard (“child of a nobleman by a woman other than his wife”), from Medieval Latin bastardus (“illegitimate child”), from Proto-Germanic *banstuz, *bunstuz (“a bond”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie, bind”) + -ard. Cognate with Old Frisian bōst (“marriage”) and Middle Dutch basture (“whore, prostitute”) (from bast + hure).
Coined by French geologist Wilhelm Philippe Schimper in 1874, originally intended as being paléo- + Éocène, as he imagined this term to cover the earliest Eocene.
Inherited from Old French aiol, aiuel, from Vulgar Latin *aviolus, ultimately from Latin avus.
From Middle French plastique, borrowed from Latin plasticus. Doublet of plastic.
From couper + -on. Compare Italian tagliando (“coupon, voucher”) from tagliare (“to cut”) for a similar semantic shift.
From rond (adjective) + -eur (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns from adjectives).
Borrowed from Portuguese Zaire, a truncation of Kongo nzadi o nzere (“river swallowing rivers”) which refers to the Congo river; adopted in accordance with the Authenticity Movement.
From pique + nique, from piquer (“to pick”, verb) + nique (“small thing”).

Inherited from Middle French Londres, from Old French Londres, ultimately from Latin Londinium. However, it is not a natural evolution from Latin to French, as Londinium would render *Londin, *Londein. Thus, it is possible that it was borrowed or at least derived from Old English Lunden. The final syllable would have been weakened to -dn, later changing to -dr, which would yield an epenthetic -e. The -s would be added to fit Old French declension.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from English foot (“foot, to walk”) + -ing.
From Old French avantage. Derivable from avant + -age.
From the now archaic oxide, from a blend of ox(ygene) and (ac)ide, coined by G. de Morveau and A. Lavoisier.
] From Middle French chouette, from Old French choete, diminutive from choe (“jackdaw”), from Frankish *kâwa.
From barrique (“cask”) + -ade (“group”). So named after the first street barricades in Paris, which were composed of casks filled with earth, paving stones, etc.
From Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “spiral”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”). Coined in 1861 by Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt.
From guêpe + -ière, after the phrase taille de guêpe.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin pānārium (“breadbasket”), from pānis (“bread”).
From Dutch kermis, a bastardization of kerk (“church”) + mis (“mass”). Compare German Kirmes (“church mass”).
From bijou (“piece of jewelry”) + -erie, with intrusive -t-.
From Middle French decime, décime, decyme, borrowed from Latin decima (pars) (“tenth (part)”). Compare the inherited doublet dîme.
Borrowed from Breton maen-hir, from maen (“stone”) + hir (“tall”). Compare Cornish men hir, and Welsh maen hir.

Inherited from Middle French matinee f, from Old French matinee f, ultimately from Latin mātūtīnus (“of the morning”), from Mātūta f (“goddess of morning”). Equivalent to matin m (“morning”) + -ée (“contained by, duration of”).
An alteration of voussoyer (vous + -oyer), influenced by the v in vous and the form of tutoyer.
Borrowed from Occitan espardilha via metathesis, itself from espart (“esparto grass”). Compare Catalan espardenya.
Learned borrowing from Latin centenārius. Doublet of quintal.
Coined in the 19th century from anti- + -onyme (noun-forming suffix), modelled after synonyme.
Created from Latin prehēnsus, with the suffix -ile.

Inherited from Old French megre, meigre, from Latin macrum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. The variant dialectal form maire is the normal phonetic result; the main form with -gr- was perhaps influenced by analogy with aigre, or may be semi-learned.

Inherited from Middle French ayde, from Old French aide, aie, from aidier (modern Old French aider (“to help”)). The medial -d- would've been regularly lost, but was reinserted on the basis of the verb.
Borrowed from Italian bassone, from basso (“bass”) + augmentative suffix -one.
Inherited from Old French bourgesie, borgoisie (“citizenship”). By surface analysis, bourgeois + -ie.
Inherited from Middle French noir, from Old French noir, neir, from Latin nigrum. Doublet of nègre.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin firmatūra. By surface analysis, fermer + -ure.
From Middle French, from Old French bout (“a blow”), derivative of bouter (“to strike”), of Germanic origin. More at bouter.
From Latin margarīta (“pearl”), from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs).
From Ancient Greek Ἑλληνισμός (Hellēnismós, “imitation of the Greeks”), from Ἕλλην (Héllēn, “a Greek”).
Learned borrowing from Latin pneumaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Canicula and canicula. From the ancient association of Canicule (“Sirius, Dog Star”) with late summer heat. Doublet of chenille.
From Old French brunete, equivalent to brunet + -e.
From palme + -ite. Calque of Spanish palmito, from palma + -ito, from Latin palma.

Inherited from Old French droit (spelled dreit in Early Old French, such as the Oaths of Strasbourg), inherited from Late Latin drictus, syncopated form of Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direct. In Middle French, it was for a time spelled droict to reflect the original Latin etymology.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πορνογράφος (pornográphos).
Inherited from Old French debonaire et al, from de bone aire (“of a good bloodline”).
Inherited from Old French dous, from Latin dulcem (“sweet”).
Learned borrowing from Latin fōrmātor. By surface analysis, former + -ateur.
From rivière + -ain, literally “people living along a river”.
Learned borrowing from Latin pistillum. Compare Old French pestel.
From Old Occitan fat, from Latin fatuus.
First attested in the 17th century. From demi- (“half”) + teinte (“tint, shade”).
Inherited from Old French chous, from Latin caulis, itself akin to or derived from Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós).
Inherited from Old French escut, inherited from Latin scūtum, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, protect”) or Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, split”).
Borrowed from Spanish caracol, of unclear origin.
Borrowed from Latin galla, probably from Germanic. See gall.
From Old French estage: ester + -age (see also stage), or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *stāticum, from Latin stāre.
From in- + éligibilité or from inéligible + -ité.
From Latin puer (“child”) + culture; coined in 1863 by Alfred Caron by analogy with agriculture, apiculture, and the like.
First attested 1904, coined by French engineer and novelist Édouard Estaunié, from télé- (“far off”) + communication
From Middle French faciliter (15th c.), a borrowing from Italian facilitare.
From Latin anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “uneven, irregular, anomalous”).

Inherited from Middle French capitaine, from Old French capitaine, borrowed from Late Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput. Compare the inherited Old French chevetaine (whence English chieftain). Doublet of cheftaine.
From Medieval Latin clāvicymbalum (compare Italian clavicembalo), from clāvis (“key”) + cymbalum (“dulcimer, cymbal”).
From Jacquerie, from Jacques (derogatory nickname for peasants, literally “James”) + -erie.
From Medieval Latin stāminea (“kind of woollen cloth”), from stāmineus (“trimmed with thread”), from Latin stāmen (“warp (of a loom)”). The biological sense is by etymological analogy.
From Java + -ais, with the addition of the interfix (n) to prevent the sequence -aa-. Java + -n- + ais.

Inherited from Middle French blanc, from Old French blanc, branc, from Early Medieval Latin blancus, a borrowing of Frankish *blank, from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“bright, shining, blinding, white”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”). Akin to Old High German blanch (“bright, white”) (German blank (“polished, naked”)), Old Norse blankr (“white”) (Danish blank (“bright, shiny”)), Dutch blank (“white, shining”). More at blink, blank.
Borrowed from Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus.
From connaiss(ant) (stem of the present participle of connaître) + -eur.
Borrowed from Spanish vicuña, from Quechua wik'uña.
Inherited from Old French veneor, from Latin vēnātōrem.
Borrowed from Old Occitan radel, a diminutive of rat, itself from Latin ratis (“raft”).
Inherited from Middle French triumphe, from Old French triumphe (12th c.), borrowed from Latin triumphus, which see.

Inherited from Old French chaitif, caitif, from Vulgar Latin *cactivus, from a combination of Latin captīvus (“prisoner”) with Transalpine Gaulish *caxtos, from Proto-Celtic *kaxtos (compare Irish cacht, Welsh caeth). Compare also Italian cattivo (“bad”). See also French captif, a borrowed doublet.
Borrowed from Occitan bastida, past participle of bastir, cognate with French bâtir. Doublet of bâtie. Compare with bâtisse.
From faucon + -erie, or from Medieval Latin falconaria.
Inherited from Middle French douzaine, from Old French dozaine, from doze (“twelve”), from Vulgar Latin *dōdeci, from Latin duodecim. Equivalent to douze + -aine.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin traversus, from Latin trānsversus. Doublet of transverse. Compare Italian traverso.
Inherited from Middle French enveloppe, anveloppe, from Old French envelope (“that which envelops, a type of garment”), from envoloper, anveloper (“to wrap around, enfold, cover”).
From Latin exergum, from Ancient Greek ἐξ (ex, “from, out of”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

Inherited from Middle French chien, from Old French chien, from Latin canis, canem (“dog”). See cognates in regional languages in France : Bourguignon chein, Catalan ca, Corsican cane, cani, Franco-Provençal shin, tsin, Gallo chien, cun, qhun Norman quien, tchian, Occitan can, chin, Picard quien, tchien. See cognates in Romance languages outside France : Aromanian cãni, Galician can, Italian cane, Lombard can, Ladin cian, Portuguese cão, Romanian câine, Sardinian cane, Sicilian cani, Spanish can.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τρίπτυχος (tríptukhos).

Inherited from Middle French bœuf, from Old French buef, boef, from Latin bovem (“ox”), from Proto-Italic *gʷōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (compare English cow). The music sense derives from the expression “faire un Bœuf”, after the Parisian cabaret-bar Le Bœuf sur le toit where jam sessions were held.
From convenir + -able. Compare typologically Russian подходя́щий (podxodjáščij) (< подходи́ть (podxodítʹ), под- (pod-) + ходи́ть (xodítʹ)).

Inherited from Middle French mot, from Old French mot, from Late Latin muttum (“sound”), from muttīre (“mutter, make a mu-noise”), of onomatopoeic origin. Has almost entirely replaced parole in Modern French, perhaps because of its brevity. Compare Catalan mot.
From quinze + -ième, compare Late Latin quindecimus.
Borrowed from Latin exstinctor. See éteindre + -teur.

Inherited from Middle French ciboule, from Old French cibole, borrowed from Occitan cibola, itself from Late Latin cēpulla~caepulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa~caepa (“onion”), whence the inherited French cive (“chive”).
Back-formation from idéologie, equivalent to idée + -ologue. First attested in the 19th century.

Borrowed from Latin dēcīsiōnem (“agreement; settlement”). Cognate with Catalan decisió, Italian decisione, Occitan decision, Portuguese decisão, Romanian decizie, Sardinian detzisione, Sicilian dicisioni, Spanish decisión.
From Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin integer. Doublet of entier.
From Latin sabbatismus (“Sabbath observance", "Sabbath-keeping, Sabbathkeeping”), from Ancient Greek σαββατισμός (sabbatismós).
Inherited from Old French decembre, a learned borrowing from Latin decembrem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin crucifīxiō.
Inherited from Middle French querir, from Old French querre (with conjugation change), from Latin quaerere (“to seek”). Compare also Walloon cweri. Cognate with Portuguese querer and Spanish querer.
Inherited from Old French frume (“expression, mien”).
Learned borrowing from Latin calumniātōrem. By surface analysis, calomnier + -ateur.
Inherited from Middle French brunir, from Old French brunir (“to polish, make brown”).
Inherited from Middle French consyderer, from Old French considerer, borrowed from Latin cōnsīderāre (“to examine, look at, inspect; to consider; to investigate”).

From Middle French pause (14th c. in the musical sense), from Latin pausa. The Middle French form may be merely a relatinized spelling of Old French pose (“moment, period of time”, 12th c., whence Dutch poos), itself an early borrowing (if not inheritance) from the same Latin noun; at any rate both forms cannot be separated entirely.
Inherited from Middle French Taproban, from Latin Tāprobanus.
Borrowed from Late Latin tmēsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τμῆσις (tmêsis).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin gamma. Doublet of gamma.
Inherited from Old French fleume (with etymological re-formation), from Late Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma). Doublet of flemme.
From Old French salv, salf, inherited from Latin salvus. Cognate to Italian and Spanish salvo.
From Middle French interrompre, partial relatinization of Old French entrerompre, itself a calque of Latin interrumpere.
Inherited from Middle French and Old French pasnage, from Medieval Latin pāstiōnāticum (“the right to feed on mast”).
Borrowed from Catalan paella or Spanish paella, from Latin patella. Doublet of poêle.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French grain, grein, from Latin grānum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin irremissibilis.
From Old French chierté, itself either inherited from Latin cāritātem or newly formed from cher (“dear, expensive”) + -té. Doublet of charité (“charity”).
Learned borrowing from Latin camelīnus. Compare the inherited doublet chameau, with palatalization.
From Old French aumosnier, itself inherited from Late Latin eleemosynārius.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ūsūrpātor. By surface analysis, usurper + -ateur.
Inherited from Old French ardour, ardor, ardur, borrowed from Latin ardorem (according to the TLFi etymological dictionary).
From New Latin cercus, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”).
Inherited from Middle French paroistre, from Old French paroistre, pareistre, from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre.
Borrowed from Spanish macho, from Latin masculus. Doublet of mâle. :* c. 1952 :* c. 1962
Inherited from Old French curreie, from Latin corrigia.
Inherited from Middle French naturel, from Old French natural, a borrowing from Latin nātūrālis. By surface analysis, nature + -el.
Learned borrowing from Latin dogmaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós).
Inherited from Old French gru ?, from Frankish *grūt. Cognate with English grout, groats.
Borrowed from Italian infanteria and fanteria, from infante (“child”) (cognate with French enfant).
Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Petunia.
Learned borrowing from Latin particula. Doublet of parcelle.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēnūntiātor. By surface analysis, dénoncer + -ateur.
Borrowed from Latin perplexus, composed by per- + plexus, past participle of the verb plectere.

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French essai, from Late Latin exagium (“weighing”), hence English assay (compare also Spanish ensayo), from Latin exigō; the original sense of "trial" (if the gold is good) drifted towards a general meaning of "attempt". The literary meaning is given by Michel de Montaigne's masterpiece.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin frāternālis, from Latin frāternus, from frāter (“brother”) (whence frère).
Inherited from Middle French mathematique, from Latin mathematicus.
From Ancient Greek ψελλισμός (psellismós, “stammering”), from ψελλός (psellós, “faltering”).
Borrowed from English script. Doublet of écrit.
Calque of Occitan empegar, from pega (“glue”)
Borrowed from Occitan pineda, from Latin pīnēta.
Inherited from Old French repeter, borrowed from Latin repetere. Cf. also the Old French form repeir.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin triangulāris. By surface analysis, triangle + -aire.
Learned borrowing from Latin diametrālis. By surface analysis, diamètre + -al.
Learned borrowing from Latin prīmōrdiālis (“of the beginning”).
From Middle French regret, from Old French regret (“lamentation, complaint”), deverbal of regreter (“to lament”).
From Latin elleborum, from Ancient Greek ἑλλέβορος (helléboros), possibly from ἄλκη (álkē, “fawn”) βιβρώσκω (bibrṓskō, “to eat”).
From Latin topazus, from Koine Greek τόπαζος (tópazos), variant of τοπάζιον (topázion).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin fideī commissum (literally “trust of faith”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin irremediābilis. By surface analysis, in- + remédier + -able.
Inherited from Middle French caisse, borrowed from Occitan caissa, from Latin capsa. Compare the etymological doublets châsse and casse.
Inherited from Middle French loy, from Old French loi, lei, from Latin lēgem, from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s < *leǵ-.
Learned borrowing from Latin prōcrāstinātiō. By surface analysis, procrastiner + -ation.

From Late Latin euphemismos (“euphemism”), from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός (euphēmismós), from εὐφημίζω (euphēmízō), from εὔφημος (eúphēmos, “uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φάναι (phánai, “to speak, say”).
From Ancient Greek δύσπνοια (dúspnoia), from δυς- (dus-) with πνεῖν (pneîn).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin persecutor, from Latin persecutus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin rādīcālis.
Inherited from Old French pyoine (with epenthetic /-v-/), borrowed from Latin paeōnia, borrowed from Ancient Greek παιωνία (paiōnía, “peony”).
Alteration, under the influence of orne, of Old French ordiere, inherited from Vulgar Latin *orbitaria, from Latin orbita.
Inherited from Middle French oingnon, from Old French oignon, from Latin ūniōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin inefficāx. By surface analysis, in- + efficace.
* Most meanings: Learned borrowing from Latin forum. * Internet: Borrowed from English forum.
Inherited from Middle French apparoistre, from Old French aparoistre, from Late Latin appārēscere (“begin to appear”), from Latin appareō.

From Hindustani لشکر / लश्कर (laśkar), itself from Persian لشکر. Originally a nickname given in the early 19th century to Indian seamen on French ships travelling in the East Indies. With time, the term became somewhat pejorative.
Borrowed from New Latin stasis, derived from Ancient Greek στᾰ́σῐς (stắsĭs).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vayrola, from Latin variola.
Borrowed from Spanish armadillo (“armadillo”) and armadilla (“small naval armada”), with the sense of "woodlouse" being a semantic loan from taxonomic name Armadillo (“genus of isopods”).
Learned borrowing from Latin artificiālis. By surface analysis, artifice + -iel.
Learned borrowing from Latin cremātor, from cremō + -tor. By surface analysis, crémer (“to cremate”) + -ateur.
Learned borrowing from Latin dēviātiō. By surface analysis, dévier + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French dot (16th c.), a borrowing from Latin dos. Doublet of dose.
Unadapted borrowing from American English cheeseburger.
Learned borrowing from Latin canonicus. Doublet of chanoine.
Inherited from Middle French operatif, from Latin operātīvus.
First attested in the eleventh century as Old French comandement. By surface analysis, commander (“to order”) + -ment.
Learned borrowing from Latin theātrālis. By surface analysis, théâtre (“theatre”) + -al.
Borrowed from Latin cytisus, from Ancient Greek κύτισος (kútisos, “tree-medick, Medicago arborea"; "bastard ebony, Laburnum anagyroides”), of uncertain origin (probably Pre-Greek).
Borrowed from Renaissance Latin flōrilegium, calque of Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”).

Inherited from Middle French navire, from Old French navirie, variant of navilie, probably from Vulgar Latin *navilium (compare Old Occitan navili), alteration of Classical Latin navigium (whence also Old French navoi, navie). Cognates with Catalan nau, Galician nave, Italian nave, Occitan nau, Portuguese navio, Romanian naie, navă, Sicilian navi, Spanish nave.
Borrowed from Latin parasītus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos).
Borrowed from Latin pugilatus, from pugil.
Borrowed from Latin admittātur (“let him be admitted”), the third-person singular present passive subjunctive form of admittō (“to let in, to admit”).
Inherited from Middle French lycanthrope, from Ancient Greek λυκάνθρωπος (lukánthrōpos, “human-wolf”).
Inherited from Old French cas, borrowed from Latin cāsus.
Learned borrowing from Latin phthisis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek νεκρόπολις (nekrópolis, “city of the dead”). By surface analysis, nécro- + -pole.
From Old French testament, from Latin testāmentum.
Inherited from Old French seing, inherited from Latin signum, of Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of signe and tocsin.
First attested in Old French. From rouille + -er.
Learned borrowing from Latin indigestus. By surface analysis, in- + digeste.
Inherited from Middle French renouvelable (attested since 1461). By surface analysis, renouveler + -able.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin essentiālis.
From Vulgar Latin *tempula, from Latin tempora, originally an accusative plural form of tempus.
Learned borrowing from Latin gigantomachia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek γιγαντομαχία (gigantomakhía).
From Latin, from Ancient Greek, analyzable as dia- + -mètre.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin divisiōnem, noun of process form from perfect passive participle divisus (“divided”), from dīvidō (“divide”).
From sérène + -ité or borrowed from Latin serēnitātem.
Inherited from Old French dolor, from Latin dolor (“pain”), from doleō + -or.
Learned borrowing from Latin nōrmālis. By surface analysis, norme + -al.
Inherited from Old French humor, humour, borrowed from Latin hūmōrem. Doublet of humour.
Borrowed from English boycott, from Charles Boycott.
From Latin fluere (“to flow”) (with change to first conjugation).
Inherited from Middle French famille, borrowed from Latin familia.
Inherited from Middle French pet, from Old French pet, from Latin pēditum.
Learned borrowing from New Latin obstētricālis. By surface analysis, obstétrique + -al.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek προπερῐσπώμενος (properĭspṓmenos).

From the oblique case of Old French sire (see also French sire), from Vulgar Latin *seior (“lord, elder”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”) (whence also seigneur, from the accusative form), from senex (“old”). Cognate with Spanish señor, Italian signore, etc. Also a doublet of senior and sire.
Learned borrowing from Latin nātīvus. Doublet of naïf.
Inherited from Middle French extremite f, inherited from Old French estremité f, borrowed from Latin extrēmitātem f. By surface analysis, extrême + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French dextre, borrowed from Latin dextra or dextera; replaced the popular/inherited Old French form destre.
From Roumanie, based on analogy with romain (“Roman”), itself from Latin romānus; cf. Romanian român (older rumân). Compare also Italian rumeno, Spanish rumano, etc.

Inherited from Middle French fleuve, from late Old French flueve (12th cent.), according to the traditional view, a dissimilated form of fluive, fluie, a re-borrowing of Latin fluvius (“stream”). Alternatively, confluence with Old French fluet, flot ("river, flood"; from Frankish *flōd) and/or borrowing from Old Norse flóð (“tidal flood, estuarine river or flood”) cannot be ruled out. See flot. Replaced native Old French fluns, flum, from Latin flūmen (compare Occitan flume, Romansh flüm, Italian fiume).
With a change of suffix, from Old French piler, from Vulgar Latin *pilāre, from Latin pila.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin velleitātem, from velle (“to will”).
Inherited from Middle French tradition, from Old French, borrowed from Latin trāditiōnem, from the verb trādere. Compare trahison.
Inherited from Old French chastier, castier inherited from Latin castīgāre.
From Latin rūminātiōnem (“chewing the cud”); see ruminer.
Inherited from Old French salaire, from Latin salārium, probably a semi-learned borrowing. Cf. also the inherited Old French salier, saler (and modern salière).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin entitātem.

Borrowed from Late Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha) (Α,α) and βῆτα (bêta) (Β,β) (the first two letters of the Greek alphabet), from Phoenician aleph 𐤀 (ʾ, “ox”) and beth 𐤁 (b, “house”), so called because they were pictograms of those objects, having developed from the Egyptian hieroglyphs F1 (𓃾) and pr (𓉐).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diversiōnem, from Latin divertō (“to divert”); see divert.
Borrowed from Italian cavaliere, itself borrowed from Old Occitan cavalier, from Late Latin caballārius. Doublet of chevalier, which was inherited.
From quasi + -ment. Cognate with Italian quasimente.
Inherited from Middle French montant; equivalent to a deverbal of the modern verb monter (“to mount, go up”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan cadera, cadieira, from Latin cathedra (“chair”). Doublet of cathèdre, chaire, and chaise.
Learned borrowing from Latin excellentia. By surface analysis, exceller + -ence.

Inherited from Middle French moult, from Old French mut (with a silent ⟨l⟩ inserted per the Latin etymon), from earlier Old French mult~molt, from Latin multus, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). After having largely disappeared from the spoken language, where it was replaced by beaucoup, the term is now occasionally heard again, often with a spelling-pronunciation.
Learned borrowing from Latin vēsīcula, diminutive of vēsīca (whence vessie).
Inherited from Old French sappe, from Latin sappa. Compare Italian zappa, Friulian sape, Romanian sapă.
From Ancient Greek ὄντος (óntos), from ὤν (ṓn), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “I am”).
Inherited from Middle French nul, from Old French nul, from Latin nūllus.
Inherited from Old French certain, from Vulgar Latin unattested form *certānus, extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”).
Borrowed from Latin substantia (“substance, essence”), from substāns, present active participle of substō (“exist”, literally “stand under”), from sub + stō (“stand”).
Inherited from Middle French loyer, loiier, loier, from Old French loier, from Latin locārium.
Inherited from Old French miche, from Vulgar Latin *mīcca, from Latin mīca (“crumb”) via expressive gemination of /k/. Doublet of mie and mica.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impostūra.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēducātiō. By surface analysis, éduquer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin industriōsus. By surface analysis, industrie + -eux.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation, explanation”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin abstrāctiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin abductor, from abdūcō + -tor.
From déchirer (“to tear; to rip up”) + -ment.
Inherited from Middle French tarpee, from Latin Tarpēius.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin incorruptibilis. By surface analysis, in- + corruptible.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin indurātiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French globe, borrowed from Latin globus.
From Middle French satire, from Old French, from Latin satira, from earlier satura.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin indigestiō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praeludium.
From the New Latin polyadenus, from the Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”, stem: ἀδεν-, aden-).
From Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “great, large, mighty”).
Borrowed from Late Latin decimālis, from Latin decimus.
From earlier mangrore, borrowed from English mangrove.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐρώμενος (erṓmenos).
From Vulgar Latin *pincta (“mark used to indicate level on vessels”), from Latin pictus (“painted”), from Latin pingō (“paint”, verb).
Borrowed from Latin hymenaeus, from Ancient Greek ὑμέναιος (huménaios).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cordiālis.
Borrowed from Latin philtrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φίλτρον (phíltron). Unrelated to filtre.
English pyjama, from Urdu پایجامه (pāyjāma) / Hindi पैजामा (paijāmā), from Persian پایجامه (pâyjâma) / پاجامه (pâjâma, “leg garment”).
Inherited from Old French vair, veir, from the accusative singular masculine form of Latin varius.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποειδής (anthrōpoeidḗs, “human-looking”). By surface analysis, anthropo- + -oïde.
Inherited from Late Latin frīgorōsus, from Latin frīgus, or from a Vulgar Latin *frigidulōsus (contracted to *fridlōsus), from frigidus. Compare Romanian friguros.
From Old French demonstrer, from Latin dēmōnstrō.
Inherited from Middle French verdeur, from verd + -eur. By surface analysis, vert + -eur.
Inherited from Middle French honneste, from Old French honeste, a borrowing from Latin honestus, from honor.
Borrowed from Latin agricola. Equivalent to agri- + -cole.
Borrowed from Russian президиум (prezidium), from Latin praesidium.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin excentricitas. By surface analysis, excentrique + -ité.

Inherited from Middle French guere(s), from Old French gaire(s), guaire(s) (“much”), from Frankish *waigaro (“much”), related to *waigr (“resistant”). Compare Middle High German unweiger (“not much”), which corresponds closely to the French construct. Romance cognates are Occitan and Catalan gaire, Italian guari.
English subliminal, itself a calque from German unterschwellig.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Late Latin divisibilis, from the verb Latin dividō.

Inherited from Middle French fronce, from Old French fronce, fronche (“frown, wrinkles, small creases in cloth”), from Frankish *hrunkwiju (“wrinkle, rumple”) from Proto-Germanic *hrunkwijō, *hrunkwǭ (“fold, wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Akin to Old High German runza (“fold, wrinkle, crease”) (German Runzel (“wrinkle”)), Middle Dutch ronse (“frown”), Old Norse hrukka (“wrinkle, crease”) (Icelandic hrukka (“wrinkle, crease, ruck”)). More at ruck.

From Old French pute (nominative singular of putain) – perhaps from:. * a Vulgar Latin *pūtta, from a supposed Latin *puta (“girl”), female form of putus (“boy”) (a hapax legomenon of dubious reading) * from the feminine form of put (“stinking, fetid”), from Latin pūtidus (“stinking”), therefore effectively inherited from Latin pūtida; this is the preferred etymology of the Trésor de la langue française informatisé Cognate with puta in the Gallo-Romance and Ibero-Romance areas (including Catalan puta, Spanish puta, Portuguese puta, Galician puta, Asturian puta), as well as Old Italian putta (“girl”).
Borrowed from Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos).
First attested circa 1073, from re- + tirer.
Borrowed from English igniter. By surface analysis, Latin ignītum (supine of igniō) + -eur.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παρέγχῠμα (parénkhŭma, “anything poured in beside”).
Learned borrowing from Latin benignitas. By surface analysis, bénin + -ité.
From Ancient Greek στενός (stenós, “narrow”) and ὀπή (opḗ, “hole”).
Inherited from Old French [Term?], borrowed from Latin fortitūdō (“bravery, strength”), from fortis (“brave, strong”).
Borrowed from Italian medaglia. Doublet of maille.

Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French agriper (“to snatch”), from Frankish *angrīpan (“to seize”), from Proto-Germanic *ana- (“on-”) + *grīpaną (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to take, seize, rake”). Cognate with Middle Dutch aengrīpen (“to grasp, seize”), Old High German anagrīfan (“to touch, grasp”), Old English grīpan (“to seize, snatch, take, apprehend”). More at grip.
Learned borrowing from Latin iniūriōsus. By surface analysis, injure + -(i)eux.
Inherited from Old French allegorie, from Latin allegoria, from Ancient Greek ἀλληγορία (allēgoría).
A calque of English survivalism, survival + -isme.
Inherited from Middle French Egypte, from Old French Egypte, borrowed from Latin Aegyptus, from Ancient Greek Αἴγυπτος (Aíguptos).
Inherited from Old French ver (with the suffix -at), from Latin verrēs.
Inherited from Old French pirate, borrowed from Latin pīrāta.
Learned borrowing from Latin recreātiōnem. By surface analysis, récréer + -ation. In the education sense compare Spanish recreo and Italian ricreazione.
Borrowed from Occitan muge, from Vulgar Latin *mūgō (cf. Italian muggine), a noun based on Latin mūgil (“mullet”).

From Middle French meurtre (“murder”) from Old French murtre, mordre (“murder”) (compare Medieval Latin murdrum (“murder”)), both from Frankish *murþar (“murder”) from Proto-Germanic *murþrą (“murder, killing, death”), from Proto-Indo-European *mrtro- (“murder, death”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to die”). Akin to Old High German mord (“murder”) (German Mord), Old High German murdren (“to kill, murder”) (German mördern (“to murder”)), Old English morþor (“death, murder”), Old English myrþrian (“to murder”). More at murder.

Borrowed from Italian ciao (“hello, goodbye”), from Venetan ciao (“hello, goodbye; your (humble) servant”), from Venetan s-ciao (“servant, slave”) or s-ciavo (“servant, slave”), from Medieval Latin sclavus (“Slav, slave”), related also to Italian schiavo, English Slav, slave and Old Venetan S-ciavón (“Slav”), from Latin Sclavonia (“Slavonia”).
Learned borrowing from Latin interpretātiō. By surface analysis, interpréter + -ation.
Inherited from Old French continuel, created from Latin continuus with the suffix -el.
Learned borrowing from Latin collector. Reanalyzable as collecter + -eur.
Inherited from Old French resurrection, borrowed from Late Latin resurrēctiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin senior. Doublet of sire, seigneur, and sieur.
Learned borrowing from Latin hostia. Compare Old French oiste.
Learned borrowing from Latin articulātiō. By surface analysis, articuler + -ation.
Internationalism. Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἰσο- (iso-, “equal”).
Borrowed from Latin animal. Compare the archaic inherited doublet aumaille and its variant armaille, both from the Latin neuter plural animālia.
Learned borrowing from Latin intelligentia (“discernment, intelligence”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cohors, cohortem. Doublet of cour (“courtyard”), which was inherited, and court.
Borrowed from Breton plouk, from Breton ploue. First attested in c. 1880s.
From Ancient Greek ἄπατρις (ápatris, “without country”). By surface analysis, a- + patrie + -ide.
Inherited from Old French paon, from Latin pāvōnem.
Inherited from Middle French innovation, from Old French innovacion, borrowed from Late Latin innovātiōnem, from Latin innovāre.
Borrowed from Latin sambūca, from Ancient Greek σαμβύκη (sambúkē), ultimately from Aramaic סַבְּכָא (sabbəḵā).
Inherited from Old French sentence, itself borrowed from Latin sententia.
From Middle French crane (14th c.), a borrowing from Medieval Latin crānium.
From Latin obsessiōnem (“a besieging”), from obsidere (“to besiege”); see obsess.
Learned borrowing from Latin vīvācem (“lively, vigorous”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trānsversālis, from Latin trānsversus (whence transverse and travers).

From Old French driade (“wood nymph”), from Latin Dryadem (“dryad”), from Ancient Greek Δρυάς (Druás, “dryad”), from δρῦς (drûs, “oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *derew(o)- (“tree, wood”); cf. Proto-Indo-European *dóru.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ēlūcubrātiō, from ēlūcubrō.
Borrowed from Latin cancer. Doublet of chancre, which was inherited, and cancre.
Learned borrowing from Latin prophēticus. Morphologically, from prophète + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δευτεραγωνιστής (deuteragōnistḗs).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prandiālis.
From Old French saintuaire, from Late Latin and Latin sanctuārium (“sacred place, shrine”), from Latin sanctus (“holy, sacred”).
Inherited from Old French mescroire. By surface analysis, mé- + croire.

Inherited from Middle French canton, from Old French canton (from the 1240s), from Old Occitan canton (“corner; canton”) (recorded before 1218), adopted in Occitan from North Italian (Gallo-Italic, early Lombard) cantone (“edge, corner; canton”), ultimately representing Latin cant- (“rim (of a wheel)”) with the addition of the -ō (accusative -ōnem) suffix forming augmentatives in Romance.
Inherited from Middle French chevalier, from Old French chevalier, from Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus. Doublet of cavalier.
Attested in Old French as enseler, from en- + selle + -er. Compare Spanish ensillar.
From Latin irresistibilitās. By surface analysis, irrésistible + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin dissimulātiō. By surface analysis, dissimuler + -ation.
From Old French trinité, borrowed from Latin trīnitātem.
From Latin eclīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐκλειπτικός (ekleiptikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin argūmentātiōnem. By surface analysis, argumenter + -ation.
From Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), with influence of Italian corsa.

Inherited from Middle French pastoureau, from older pastourel, from Old French pastorel, from pastor + -el (diminutive suffix). Equivalent to modern pasteur + -eau. The ou is due to the pretonic position (compare douloureux vs. douleur, prouver vs. preuve).
Inherited from Old French sort, from Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Cf. also the borrowed doublet sorte.
Learned borrowing from Latin flaccidus. Displaced the inherited Old French flaistre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin incantātiōnem. By surface analysis, incanter + -ation.
From lapin + -ou, creating a hypocoristic (affectionate or diminutive) form.
From Old French agnel (whence modern French agneau) + the suffix -et.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēvāstātiōnem. By surface analysis, dévaster + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French application, from Old French aplicacion, from Latin applicātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin stōicus, from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós).
From Old French, from Latin manifestus.
From Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma).
Inherited from Old French songe, from Latin somnium. Compare Italian sogno, Spanish sueño and Portuguese sonho.
First known attestation 1314 in the French translation of Chirurgie by Henri de Mondeville. Learned borrowing from Latin incisiōnem.
Inherited from Old French areignee, extended form of araigne, from Latin arānea. Equivalent to now archaic ara(i)gne + -ée.
Learned borrowing from Latin virilitātem. By surface analysis, viril + -ité.

Inherited from Middle French tesmoing, from Old French tesmoin, from Latin testimōnium. The same Latin noun was also borrowed into Old French as testimonie, testemoigne (whence English testimony); this has been lost in modern French.
From Latin Caesariānus, from Caesar + -iānus. By surface analysis, César (“Caesar”) + -ien (“-ian”). Piecewise doublet of tsarien.
Inherited from Middle French chaire, from Old French chaiere, chaere, inherited from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra). Doublet of cathèdre and chaise.
Learned borrowing from Latin althaea, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλθαία (althaía).
From the sense "likely to be destroyed by a mine," from miner + -able.

Inherited from Middle French marteau m, from a back-formation from Old French marteaus (ca. 1140), plural of martel, from Late Latin martellus, from martulus, variant form of marculus, diminutive of Latin marcus, or from malleus.
Inherited from Old French jureor. By surface analysis, jurer + -eur. Possibly corresponds to Latin iūrātōrem.
From Old French papier, from Old Catalan paper.
Borrowed from Latin stupefactus with the latter part gallicised after fait.
Inherited from Old French chantre, from Latin cantor, via the nominative form. Compare chanteur, derived from the Latin accusative cantōrem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin amalgamātiōnem.

From cable, an Old Northern French (i.e. Old Norman or Picard) variant of chable, cheable, chaable, from Vulgar Latin *caplum, contracted form of Late Latin capulum, from Latin capiō. The Norman-Picard form, used primarily in a maritime sense, coexisted with the Francien dialect forms until replacing them by the 18th century. The Old French forms cheable and chaable were crossed with or influenced by the separate word chaable (“catapult”), from a Vulgar Latin *cadabulum.
Via Old French, from Late Latin scissiōnem, from Latin scindere.
Borrowed from Italian pecora, from Latin pecus.
Derived from Classical Persian ملا (mullā), from Arabic مَوْلًى (mawlan, “vicar, guardian”).
Inherited from Middle French mien, from Old French meon, from Latin meum, the neuter of meus.
Inherited from Old French infamie, borrowed from Latin īnfamia. By surface analysis, infâme + -ie.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin dorsum with adjective-forming suffix -al.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μασσαλιώτης (Massaliṓtēs), from Μασσαλία (Massalía) + -ώτης (-ṓtēs).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μυγαλέη (mugaléē).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ūsufrūctus.

From Middle French bastille, from Old French baastel, basstel (“fortification; fortified tower; temporary fortification constructed for attack or defence; (small) castle or fortress”) (compare Medieval Latin bastīle), from bastide (“fortification; fortress”) with the ending modified after nouns ending in -ille (from Latin -īle (suffix forming place names)). Bastide is derived from Old Occitan bastida (“fortification; (Provence) country mansion”), from bastir (“to build, construct”) + -ida (suffix forming nouns); while bastir is from Medieval Latin bastīre, the present active infinitive of *bastīre, from Frankish *bastijan (“to sew; to weave”), from Proto-West Germanic *bast (“fibre; rope”); further etymology uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰask- ~ *bʰasḱ- (“bundle, heap, load”) but this is disputed. Compare typologically Russian опло́т (oplót), плете́нь (pleténʹ) (akin to плести́ (plestí)).
Borrowed from Latin ēvāsiōnem, action noun from ēvādere.
From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon), substantivized neuter form of ἑξάγωνος (hexágōnos, “hexagonal”).
Inherited from Middle French beauté, from Old French biauté, from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fair”).
From Ancient Greek ὑποσπαδίᾱς (hupospadíās, “one who has the orifice of the urethra too low”).
Inherited from Old French mastin, inherited from Vulgar Latin *māns(u)etīnus (“tamed (animal)”), from Classical Latin mānsuētus (“tamed”). Cognate to English mastiff.
Borrowed from Italian agrume, borrowed from Latin ācrūmen.
Inherited from Middle French lors, from Old French lors, lores, from earlier lur, lor, from Vulgar Latin illā hōrā, from Latin ille + hōrā.

From Middle French senestre, from Old French senestre, from Late Latin sinextrum, from Latin sinistrum. Doublet of sinistre, a borrowing from Latin. The expected result of the Middle French senestre, pronounced approximately as /səˈnɛːtrə/, should have been senêtre in modern French (which does exist in heraldic jargon). A spelling-pronunciation, with etymologically restored /s/, came to predominate as the word became increasingly archaic, having been driven out of common usage as the word for "left" by gauche in the sixteenth century.
Inherited from Old French liquide, from Latin liquidus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin intempestīvitās. By surface analysis, intempestif + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin Areopagus, from Ancient Greek Ἄρειος Πάγος (Áreios Págos, literally “Rock of Ares”).
Borrowed from Latin azymus, from Ancient Greek ἄζυμος (ázumos).
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin īnfōrmātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin exorcista, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐξορκιστής (exorkistḗs).
From Middle French and Old French descrier.
From Old French, corresponding to diable (“devil”) + -esse (“-ess”).
Inherited from Middle French cliqueter, from Old French cliketer, equivalent to cliquer (“to click, clink”) + -eter (frequentative suffix).
From Old French exces (12th c.), a borrowing from Latin excessus.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin agnomen. Doublet of agnom.
Learned borrowing from Latin rapidus. Compare the inherited Old French rade.
From Middle French ny, from Old French ne, from Latin nec. Compare Italian né, Catalan and Spanish ni, Portuguese nem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin misericordiōsus . By surface analysis, miséricorde + -eux.
Borrowed from English ventilator, calque of Latin ventilātōrem. By surface analysis, ventiler + -ateur.
Inherited from Old French invocacion, borrowed from Latin invocātiōnem, accusative form of invocātiō.
Borrowed from Latin ferōcitātem. Equivalent to féroce + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin secūritātem. Doublet of sûreté.

Inherited from Middle French legs, latinising spelling of lais, from Old French lais, derived from laisser (“to let, leave”). The Middle French alteration is based on an etymologically unfounded association with Latin lēgātum. The -g- was originally silent, but has come to be pronounced since the 19th century by analogy with the verb léguer, a borrowing from Latin lēgāre.
Borrowed from Spanish arroba, an old weight unit.
Inherited from Old French taquehan, from Middle Dutch takehan.
Inherited from Old French safran, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin safranum, borrowed from Arabic زَعْفَرَان (zaʕfarān), from Aramaic צפר.
Learned borrowing from Latin prōvincia. Doublet of Provence.
An Anglicism, from English stim + toy.
Borrowed from Spanish palabra, from Latin parabola. Doublet of parole and parabole.
From English magnesium, from New Latin magnēsium, from Ancient Greek μαγνησία (magnēsía), after Μαγνησία (Magnēsía, “Magnesia”).
Learned borrowing from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”).
From Latin pelagicus, from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós).
Borrowed from Occitan brusc, from Italian brusco. Doublet of brusque.
Borrowed from Late Latin monumentālis, from Latin monumentum. By surface analysis, monument + -al.
Inherited from Middle French vice, from Old French vice, borrowed from Latin vitium.
Inherited from Middle French acteur, from Latin actor.
Learned borrowing from Latin irratiōnālis. By surface analysis, ir- + rationnel.
Inherited from Old French mitan (“middle, center”), from Latin medium tantum (“middle, center”).
Inherited from Middle French cuer, quer, a semi-learned adaptation or borrowing (from different stages in time) from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós). Doublet of chorus.
From Middle French agriculteur, borrowed from Latin agricultor.
Learned borrowing from Latin respirātiō. By surface analysis, respirer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French bec, from Latin beccus (“beak”), from Gaulish *beccos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos.
Inherited from Middle French chair, char, from Old French char, charn (earlier carn), from Latin carnem, carō, from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-, *(s)ker-. Doublet of carne.
Inherited from Latin vicarius. Doublet of vicaire.
Inherited from Old French horror, borrowed from Latin horror, from the verb horreo (“to shiver”). The feminine gender's origin is unclear.
Inherited from Middle French inconfusible, from Latin incōnfūsibilis. By surface analysis, in- + confusible.
Inherited from Middle French practicien. By surface analysis, pratique + -ien.
Borrowed from Late Latin sphinctēr (“the muscle of the anus”), from Ancient Greek σφῐγκτήρ (sphĭnktḗr, “lace, band; contractile muscle”).
Inherited from Old French nativité, borrowed from Latin nātīvitātem. Compare also naïveté.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin approbātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin argūmentum, from arguō (“prove, argue”).
Inherited from Old French merlus, borrowed from Old Occitan merlus, derived from Latin merula. Alternatively from Old French lus, derived from Latin lucius, under influence from merlan.
Learned borrowing from Latin aquārium. Doublet of évier.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek τεχνολογία (tekhnología, “systematic treatment (of grammar)”), from τέχνη (tékhnē, “art”) + -λογία (-logía).
Borrowed from Latin mania or Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).
Inherited from Middle French cinquiesme. Also cinq + -ième.
From continu + -ité, or borrowed from Latin continuitātem.
Inherited from Old French fret, from Middle Dutch vrecht, from Old Dutch *frēht, from Proto-West Germanic *fra- + *aihti.
Learned borrowing from New Latin elasticitās. By surface analysis, élastique + -ité.

Inherited from Middle French trophée, borrowed from Latin trophaeum, tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion, “monument of an enemy's defeat”), from neuter of τροπαῖος (tropaîos, “of defeat”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “a rout, a turning of an enemy”).
English bonus, from Latin bonus. Compare bon (“good”), a doublet inherited from the same Latin word.
Inherited from Old French liecol, from lier + col.
Inherited from Middle French abstinence, from Old French abstinence, borrowed from Latin abstinentia.
Inherited from Latin scālārium. Doublet of escalier
Borrowed from Occitan panicaut, from Vulgar Latin *panecaldus, alteration of Gaulish Latin *panecardus, from panis + cardus.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from French caravane + English -ing, formed in French as in camp/camping.
Inherited from Old French lorier, from Vulgar Latin *laurārius, suffixed from Latin laurus (whence Old French lor).
From Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós). By surface analysis, myélo- + -ome.
Borrowed from Latin sinciput (“half a head”; “smoked hog’s cheek or half-jowl”; (transferred senses): “brain”, “head”), whence English sinciput.
Inherited from Old French emplastre, borrowed from Latin emplastrum, from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron, “daub; salve”).
Inherited from Old French composicion, borrowed from Latin compositiōnem.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin necessitāre (“to oblige, compel”), from Classical Latin necessitās (“necessity, compulsion”) (whence nécessité). According to the Trésor de la langue française, attested by the 14th century.
From English humour, itself from Old French humor, humour. Doublet of humeur.
From Medieval Latin delphīnātus, from delphīnus (“dauphin”) + -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, dauphin + -at. Doublet of delphinat, dauphiné, and Dauphiné.
Borrowed from Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia).
Inherited from Middle French poinct (with orthography modified to reflect the Latin etymology), from Old French point, from Latin pūnctum.
Inherited from Middle French envenimement, from Old French envenimement.
From débiter + -eur, or borrowed from Latin debitor.
Learned borrowing from Latin nauticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós).
From Italian diana, from Latin Diana.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós).
Perhaps a calque of English absorptivity.
Inherited from Middle French chasteté, from Old French, a semi-learned adaptation of Latin castitātem. By surface analysis, chaste + -té.
From English forcing. Sense 1 is a pseudo-anglicism derived from forcing, analyzed as force + English -ing
Inherited from Old French solucion, from Latin solūtiōnem, from the verb solvō.
Formed from the root of Latin cōnstrictus, with the suffix -eur; equivalent to New Latin constrictor.
From a variant of Old French escarrer, from Vulgar Latin *exquadrāre, from Latin quadrus, quadra.
Inherited from Old French bal, deverbal of baller, from Late Latin ballare (“to dance”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τριλογία (trilogía).
Borrowed from Portuguese caldeira. Doublet of chaudière.
Inherited from Old French, from Late Latin ingrātitūdō.
Borrowed from Russian узбек (uzbek), from Uzbek oʻzbek.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Σελήνη (Selḗnē, “the Moon”) because of the white spots' resemblance to moons.
Inherited from Old French boutoner, botoner. By surface analysis, bouton (“button”) + -er.
Inherited from Old French barriere, from barre, from Vulgar Latin *barra, possibly from Frankish *bara, from Proto-Germanic *barō.
From in- + compréhensible, or from Middle French incomprehensible.
From Middle French sabort. Ultimate origin unknown.
Inherited from Old French frein, from Latin frēnum n. Cognate with Portuguese freio and Spanish freno. Cf. the borrowed freiner.
Inherited from Middle French onques, from Old French onques, from Latin umquam, unquam.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin viscerālis. By surface analysis, viscère + -al.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin elegīacus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλεγειακός (elegeiakós).
Borrowed from English rifle. First attested in 1833.
Inherited from Middle French ornement, from Old French ornement, inherited from Latin ornāmentum. By surface analysis, orner + -ment.
Inherited from Old French inventif, from Medieval Latin inventivus, from Latin inventum.
Learned borrowing from Latin receptiōnem (“the act of receiving; reception”), from recipiō (“receive”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to hold”).
Inherited from Old French demoniaque, a borrowing from Late Latin daemoniacus.
Inherited from Middle French penible, from Old French peinible. By surface analysis, peine + -ible.
From (combining form of) Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).
Inherited from Old French nois, from Latin nux.
From Middle French usage, from Old French usage. By surface analysis, user + -age. Compare Medieval Latin usagium.
From Middle French agathe, from Latin achatēs, from Ancient Greek ἀχάτης (akhátēs, “agate”).
Borrowed from Russian шама́н (šamán), from Evenki шаман (şaman). More at shaman.
From Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía, “lung disease”), from πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -ία (-ía).
Inherited from Middle French credulité, from Old French credulite, borrowed from Latin credulitātem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin spīrālis. By surface analysis, spire + -al.
Inherited from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). For the sense of "gel", compare English gel; compare gélatine.
From Latin Ptolemaicus, from Ancient Greek Πτολεμαϊκός (Ptolemaïkós).

Inherited from Old French pipie, from Vulgar Latin *pippīta, alteration of Latin pītuīta (“mucus”). The form with a geminated *-pp- also underlies the Germanic borrowings (German Pips, Dutch and English pip). Other Romance shows simple -p- (e.g. Italian pipita, Portuguese pevide) attested as Medieval Latin pipīta. Doublet of pituite.
Inherited from Old French octobre, borrowed from Latin Octōbrem. Replaced the inherited Old French uitovre. Compare also the Old French form witembre from the Vulgar Latin variant octember.
From Old French investigacion, from Latin investigātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from New Latin cremātōrium, from cremō + -tōrium.
Borrowed from Latin adōrātiōnem (“worship, adoration”), from adōrō (“beseech; adore, worship”), from ad (“to, towards”) + ōrō (“beg”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin illī, which sounded il in Old French, to which a plural -s was added. While il was the nominative form from late Latin, els, eus was the oblique form ("them") that had evolved from late Latin illōs, and is the ancestor of modern French eux. In Old French, "they", being a nominative, was il from late Latin *illi, thus it didn't have the final -s, thus it was il used both for "he" and "they". The -s was added at the end of the 13th century in some regions, at the time the declension system of Old French started to collapse. As a consequence, some oïl languages in France have retained the original Old French il-form, and in some other regions, the ils-form supplanted the older one. Some dialects have even retained both forms depending on the locals. See cognates in regional languages in France: Angevin, Champenois, Lorrain, and Orléanais is; Bourbonnais-Berrichon ils; Bourguignon âs; Franc-Comtois and Poitevin-Saintongeais és; Gallo i and iz; Norman i and is; Picard is and i; Franco-Provençal ils; Occitan els (Gascon eus); Catalan ells; Corsican elli.
Inherited from Middle French confusion, from Old French confusion, borrowed from Latin cōnfusiōnem, from verb confundo.
From Old French, from Latin humilis (“low, slight, hence mean, humble”) (compare Greek χαμαλός (khamalós, “on the ground, low, trifling”)), from humus (“the earth, ground”), humi (“on the ground”).

From Old French dromedaire, from Late Latin dromedārius (“kind of camel”), from Classical Latin dromas, from Ancient Greek δρομὰς κάμηλος (dromàs kámēlos, “running camel”), from δρόμος (drómos, “race course”).
Borrowed from English lasso, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lacs.
Borrowed from Latin catastropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ).
From Middle French total (14th c.), a borrowing from Medieval Latin tōtālis.
Borrowed from Latin archontem, accusative of archōn, from Ancient Greek ἄρχων (árkhōn).
Inherited from Old French novembre, from Latin novembrem.
Inherited from Middle French contemption, from Latin contemptio.
Inherited from Old French cardamome, from Latin cardamomum, from Ancient Greek καρδάμωμον (kardámōmon).
Borrowed from German Allergie, coinage crafted using Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”).
From Middle French confermer, from Latin cōnfirmāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia (“beast”).
Inherited from Old French richesce. By surface analysis, riche + -esse.
Borrowed from Latin implicitus, derived from plico (whence French plier).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēcollātiō. By surface analysis, décoller + -ation.
From Old French jai (“jaybird, magpie”), from Late Latin gaius (“jaybird”), which see for more. The modern spelling with ge- is influenced by the Latin etymon.
From New Latin Camoniānus [from Camonius + -ānus] or directly from Portuguese Camon- (stem of Camões) + -ien.
From Latin exterior + -iser. Compare French intérioriser.
Borrowed from Late Latin obsequiae, alteration of Latin exsequiae.
From Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis).
The original sense was "carriage", itself adapted from English curricle.
Inherited from Old French savor, savour, inherited from Latin sapōrem (“taste, flavour”).
Learned borrowing from Latin permūtātiō, from permūtāre.
From outre- + tombe. Cognate with Italian oltretomba.

Inherited from Middle French nord, nort, from Old French nort(h), borrowed from Old English norþ (“north”). The English (rather than Dutch or Norse) origin of the French compass points is evidenced by the vowel in est.
Borrowed from English bachelor. Doublet of bachelier.
Inherited from Middle French practique, from Medieval Latin prāctica.
Borrowed from Latin calamus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of the inherited chaume.
Learned borrowing from Latin caementum. Doublet of ciment.
Borrowed from Latin adoptīvus, from adoptō (“to adopt”, literally “to choose for oneself”).
Inherited from Middle French pouls (an etymologizing spelling with a silent ‹l› alongside pous, poux), from Old French pous, from earlier polz, from Latin pulsus (“beat”), from pellō (“drive, push”).
Inherited from Middle French excision, from Latin excīsiōnem.
Learned word formed from the root of Latin bucca (whence French bouche) with the suffix -al.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin correspondēre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin commentātōr (“one who interprets writings”).
From Old French afermacion, from Latin affirmare (“to assert”).

From Old French morlue, a compound of Breton mor (“sea”) + Old French lus (“pike”). Cognate with the specific name in Gadus morhua. Likewise, cognate with English milwell (an old word spelled many ways before English spelling was standardized).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin terminālis, from Latin terminus.
Learned borrowing from Latin vīvārium. Doublet of vivier.
From Old French salamandre, from Latin salamandra.
Inherited from Middle French grammatical, from Late Latin grammaticālis.
Inherited from Old French deciple, borrowed from Latin discipulus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuālis, from punctus (whence French point).
From English comfortable, from earlier Middle English comfortable, itself from Old French confortable.
Borrowed from Spanish fanfarrón; in turn perhaps related to Arabic فَرْفَار (farfār).

Pseudo-anglicism, the first sense derived from English skateboard, and the second from English skateboarding. Note that the English noun skate only refers to an instance of skateboarding, and not the activity itself.
Learned borrowing from Latin suppositus. Compare impôt from Latin impositus, prévôt from praepositus.
Borrowed from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus, verbal adjective of praebere. Compare the popular Old French provende, provendre.
From lever + -ure. Compare Spanish levadura, Medieval Latin levātūra.
Inherited from Middle French theologie, from Old French theologie, from Latin theologia, from Ancient Greek θεολογία (theología). By surface analysis, théo- + -logie.
Inherited from Middle French subiugateur, from Latin subiugātor. Compare Italian soggiogatore, Portuguese subjugador, Spanish subyugador / sojuzgador. By surface analysis, subjuguer + -ateur.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fascellus, diminutive of Latin fascis (“bundle”).
Inherited from Old French, from Latin ferventem.
Borrowed from Latin corrōsum (supine of corrōdere > corrōdō) + -if
From Latin Gaetūlus, from Ancient Greek Γαίτουλος (Gaítoulos).

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French sens, sen, san (“sense, reason, direction”), partly borrowed from Latin sēnsus (“sense, sensation, feeling, meaning”), from sentiō (“feel, perceive”); partly from Frankish *sinn (“sense, reason, mental faculty, way, direction”) (via Vulgar Latin *sennus), from Proto-West Germanic *sinn (“mind, meaning”), particularly in the sense of "direction". Both Latin and Germanic from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”). Compare also French assener (“to thrust out”), forcené (“maniac”). More at send.
Learned borrowing from Latin collēcta, from colligō. Compare cueillette, an inherited doublet.
