Learned borrowing from Late Latin irradiatio. By surface analysis, irradier + -ation.
From Latin prōpositiōnem (“statement, proposition”), from prōpōnō (“propose”), from pōnō (“place; assume”).
From Old French boistous or from boiter, from Old French botter, débotter (“dislocate”).
From Old French gruel, suffixed form of gru (“groats, grits”), from Frankish *grūt.
From Latin phyllon, from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).
Inherited from Old French inclusion, borrowed from Latin inclūsiōnem.
From Latin phallophorus, from Ancient Greek φαλλοφόρος (phallophóros). By surface analysis, phallo- + -phore.
Agent noun from Medieval Latin aperītīvus (“opening”), from aperiō (“to open”). (The Classical Latin agent noun was apertor.)
English permaculture; blend of permanent + culture.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, ultimately from Latin fortis (“strong”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omniscientem (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciēns (“knowing”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclusivus, from Latin inclusus.
Inherited from Old French heresie, borrowed from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”).
Inherited from Middle French casuel, borrowed from Latin cāsuālis.
From Middle French abayer, from Old French abaier, abayer, abaüer, probably of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Latin baubari, Italian abbaiare.
Learned borrowing from Latin ambulantem, present participle of ambulō (“to walk”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin episcopātus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin imperturbābilis.
Learned borrowing from Latin duplicator or dupliquer + -ateur.
Inherited from Middle French rançonner, from Old French raençonner. By surface analysis, rançon + -er.
Inherited from Middle French sonnet, borrowed from Italian sonetto, from Old Occitan sonet (“a song”), diminutive of son (“song, sound”), from Latin sonus (“sound”).
Borrowed from Latin pinacotheca, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).
Inherited from Middle French sapience, from Old French sapience, borrowed from Latin sapientia.
Inherited from Middle French experimental, borrowed from Latin experīmentālis.
Borrowed from English square. Doublet of équerre.

Inherited from Middle French novice, from Old French novice, borrowed from Late Latin novīcius, novīcia (“one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent”), from Latin novīcius, novītius (“new, newly arrived”), from novus (“new”).

Inherited from Old French, borrowed (according to the TLF) from Late Latin commāter, from com- (“together”) + māter (“mother”). Cognate with Italian and Catalan comare, Neapolitan cummà, Sicilian cummari, Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish comadre, Norman conméthe, Romanian cumătră.
From Ancient Greek χιλιάγωνος (khiliágōnos), from χίλιοι (khílioi, “thousand”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).
From Latin nubifer, from nūbēs (“cloud”) + ferre (“to carry”).

Inherited from Middle French polaire, from Medieval Latin polāris (“relating to poles”), from Latin polus (“pole or end of an axis”), from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “sky, pivot or axis of a sphere”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolo- (“turn around”), from *kʷel- (“to move around, to roll or wheel”).
Borrowed from Italian pedante, of uncertain origin.
From in- + visibilité or from invisible + -ité.
From Old French gibelet, from gibier.
From front + -ière. Compare Catalan and Spanish frontera; Portuguese fronteira; Italian frontiera.
Inherited from Old French statut, from Late Latin statūtum (“a statute”), neuter singular of Latin statūtus, past participle of statuō (“to set up, establish”).
Learned borrowing from Latin oppidum (“(chiefly walled or fortified) town”).
Inherited from Old French joste, from Latin iuxtā (“near, next to, close to”).
From immatériel + -ité or from im- + matérialité.

From Latin trīcennālis, from trīcennium (“30-year period”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”), from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium (“-ium: forming abstract nouns”), from trīciēs (“30 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”).
From mal (“bad”) + veuillant (archaic present participle of vouloir; unrelated to veiller). Calque of Latin malevolēns.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from a clipping of talkie-walkie, itself a pseudo-anglicism.
Inherited from Middle French scarabée, borrowed from Latin scarabaeus, from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos). Compare the inherited doublet escarbot.
Inherited from Middle French giraffe, from Italian giraffa, from Arabic زُرَافَة (zurāfa).

Inherited from Middle French lévre, from Old French levre, earlier lavras (plural) (ca. 980), from Vulgar Latin labra, originally a neuter plural of Latin labrum, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang down, droop”). An Old and Middle French variant, leffre, may have blended with Old High German leffur (“lip”).
Borrowed from Italian concerto, deverbal from concertare.
From Middle French hymen, from Latin hymēn (“hymen”), from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French pleuresie.
Inherited from Old French estanchier, of uncertain origin: possibly from a Vulgar Latin *stanticāre < *stanticus < Latin stantem. Compare Italian stanco, stancare, Spanish estancar.
Inherited from Middle French contemner, from Latin contemnere.
Learned borrowing from Latin ulcus, ulceris.
Borrowed from Latin icterus, from Ancient Greek ἴκτερος (íkteros).
From lait + -ier, possibly corresponding to Latin lactārius. Compare also laiteron, and lactaire.
From Saoud + -ite, on the model of israélite. Compare Catalan saudita, Italian saudita, Portuguese saudita, Spanish saudita.
Inherited from Middle French definition, ultimately from Latin dēfīnītiōnem.
Borrowed from English lady, from Middle English lady, from Old English hlǣfdīġe.
From Old French atente, inherited from Latin attendita.
Borrowed from Latin intercessor. Masculine counterpart to intercessrice.
Inherited from Middle French visiter, a learned borrowing from Latin vīsitāre (“to visit”). Replaced the inherited form seen in Old French visder.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mentālis (“of the mind, mental”).
From Late Latin oidium, from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”).
From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many, much”), from Proto-Indo-European *polh₁ús (“much, many”).

From Middle French, from Old French lisiere (“border on the sides of a cloth, edge”), of uncertain origin. Probably from Frankish *lisa (“rut, furrow, track”), from Proto-Germanic *lisō, *laistiz, *laista-, *laisō (“track, trace”), from Proto-Indo-European *leys- (“furrow, track”), related to Old High German lesa (“wrinkle, line”), Old English lāst (“footstep, track, trace”), Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍃𐍄𐍃 (laists, “track, trace”). Possibly influenced by Frankish *lista (“border, edge”), see liste, last.
Borrowed from Old Occitan milan, from Vulgar Latin *mīlānus, alteration of Latin mīlvinus, from mīlvus.
Borrowed from English eagle. Doublet of aigle.
From Latin Laestrȳgōn, from Ancient Greek Λαιστρῡ́γων (Laistrū́gōn).
Borrowed from Late Latin compulsāre (“push with force”), intensitive form of Latin compellere (“compel, impel”).
From Latin silūrus, in turn from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin parentēla.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin elongātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French communicacion, borrowed from Latin commūnicātiō (“sharing, communication”). By surface analysis, communiquer + -ation.
From Latin absentia, from absēns (“absent”), present active participle of absum (“to be away or absent”), from ab (“of, by, from”) + sum (“to be”).
Borrowed from Latin dictiōnem, from dictus, past participle of dicere (“to speak”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show, point out”).
From Late Latin ochra, from Ancient Greek ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “yellow”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).
Inherited from Old French fais, from Latin fascis (“bundle, burden”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰask- (“bundle, band”).
From Middle French ouvé, from Old French oevé. By surface analysis, œuf + -é.
Borrowed from Latin synchronus, from Ancient Greek σύγχρονος (súnkhronos).
Learned borrowing from Latin absentem. Compare the popular form ausent.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ossuārium (“charnel house”), from ossuārius (“of or for bones”), from Latin os (“bone”).
Learned borrowing from Latin truculentus (“fierce, savage”), from trux (“fierce, wild”).
From Ancient Greek σκοπέω (skopéō, “examine, inspect, look to or into, consider”).

From Old French Michel, from Latin Michāēl, Michāēlem, borrowed from Koine Greek Μῐχᾱήλ (Mĭkhāḗl), in turn borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mikha'él, “Michael”, literally “Who is like God?”). Cognate with English Michael, Spanish and Portuguese Miguel, Italian Michele.
Inherited from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).

Inherited from Middle French lacs, respelling (after related lacer, lacet) of older laz, las, from Old French laz, las, lais, lace, from Latin laqueus. Cognate with Old Occitan latz, Spanish lazo, whence the doublet lasso.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnitīvus, from pūniō (“to punish”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κοῖλος (koîlos, “hollow”) or κήλη (kḗlē, “hernia”).
Borrowed from New Latin stalactites, from Ancient Greek σταλακτός (stalaktós).
From Latin cholēdochus, from Ancient Greek χοληδόχος (kholēdókhos).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin interruptor, from Latin interrumpō (whence interrompre).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin corpus (“body”). Doublet of corps.

Inherited from Old French maguesin (“storeroom, storehouse”), either from a regional language (compare Medieval Latin magazenum as found in a contract allowing Marseillais merchants to build storehouses in ports of the Maghreb) or from Italian magazzino, from Arabic مَخَازِن (maḵāzin), plural of مَخْزَن (maḵzan, “storeroom, storehouse”), from خَزَنَ (ḵazana, “to store, to stock, to lay up”). First attested in 1389. Doublet of magazine.
Learned borrowing from Latin pedester. Doublet of piètre.
From micocoulier or borrowed from Occitan micocola.
Learned borrowing from Latin magicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós). By surface analysis, magie + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin zēlātōrem.
From Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía, “prophecy”).
Inherited from Middle French escuyer, from Old French escuier, inherited from Late Latin scūtārius. Doublet of scutaire.
From Old French (h)abile (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin habilis (“suitable, apt”).
Inherited from Old French trestel, inherited from Late Latin trānstellum, diminutive of Latin trānstrum beam.
Inherited from Middle French extreme, extrême, borrowed from Latin extrēmus.
From Latin immundus (“unclean”). Compare Italian immondo, Spanish inmundo and Portuguese imundo.
Borrowed from Italian squadra. Doublet of équerre and square. See also escadrille.
Borrowed from Arabic فَتْوَى (fatwā, “formal legal opinion”), the verbal noun of أَفْتَى (ʔaftā, “to deliver a formal opinion”).
Inherited from Old French soler, from Late Latin subtelāris.
Borrowed from English catamaran, from Tamil கட்டுமரம் (kaṭṭumaram).
Borrowed from English Alabama, itself likely from Alabama Albaamaha.
Borrowed from Latin frīgidus. Doublet of froid, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Late Latin accessibilis (“accessible”), from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”).
Inherited from Old French Affrique, borrowed from Latin Āfrica.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English sweatshirt.
From Middle French diabolique, fron Late Latin diabolicus, from Koine Greek διαβολικός (diabolikós, “devilish”), from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “the Devil”).
From Latin scyphus, from Ancient Greek σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).
Learned borrowing from Latin irreligiōsus. By surface analysis, ir- + religieux.
Learned borrowing from Latin agnōmen, from ad- + nōmen. By surface analysis, a- + nom. Doublet of agnomen.
Borrowed from Latin sīstrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σεῖστρον (seîstron).
Borrowed from Latin operculum. See also couvercle.

Inherited from Old French immeuble/immoble, borrowed from Latin immōbilis (“that which is immovable”) but adapted to the ending of meuble (“furniture”), inherited from the Latin antonym mōbilis (“that which is movable”). The two terms constituted a recurrent pair in juridical Latin. Doublet of immobile.
Inherited from Old French precedent, borrowed from Latin praecedentem. Attested earlier than the verb précéder, which is possibly a back-formation.
Learned borrowing from Latin Francia. Doublet of France.
From région + -al. See also Latin regiōnālis.
Inherited from Old French, inherited from Latin cippus. Doublet of cippe, cèpe, and sep.
From Latin spira, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra).
Learned borrowing from Latin inclīnātiōnem. See also inclinaison.
From Ancient Greek τετράμορφος (tetrámorphos, “having four shapes”). By surface analysis, tétra- + -morphe.
Learned borrowing from Latin Aramaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀραμαϊκός (Aramaïkós).
Learned borrowing from New Latin placenta.
From Latin portentōsus. See more at English portentous.
From Old French decoccion, decoction (“decoction; coction, completion of cooking; digestion”), from Latin decoctiōnem, form of decoquō (“to boil down”), from de- + coquō (“to cook”).
Learned borrowing from Latin provinciālis. By surface analysis, province + -ial. Compare provençal.

Inherited from Middle French homme, from Old French home, hom, hume, homme, etc, from Latin hominem (with the loss of the -in- syllable, via syncope and then assimilation of -mn- to -mm-), from Old Latin hemō, from Proto-Italic *hemō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰmṓ (“earthling”). Compare Catalan home, Italian uomo, Portuguese homem, Romanian om, Sardinian òmine, Neapolitan ommo, Spanish hombre. Also doublet of on, derived from the nominative of Latin homō. Further cognates in regional languages in France: Norman houme, Gallo honme, Picard onme, Bourguignon oume, Franco-Provençal homo, Occitan òme, Corsican omu.
Inherited from Middle French contemnement. By surface analysis, contemner + -ment.
Inherited from Middle French thore (attested 16th c.), ultimately from Latin taura.
From Old French posterne, alteration of posterle, from Late Latin posterula (“back door”), from Latin posterus (“later”).
Learned borrowing from Latin causticus (“burning”), from the Ancient Greek καυστικός (kaustikós, “burning”).
From Old French quarrefourc, from Latin quadrifurcus, from quadri- < quattuor + furca.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intimidāre (“to make afraid”), from timidus (“afraid, timid”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin hōrārius.

Inherited from Middle French effreer, from Old French esfreer, esfreder (whence also English affray), from a Vulgar Latin *exfridāre, itself of Germanic origin (with the prefix ex- added), from a Frankish *friþu (“security, peace”), from Proto-Germanic *friþuz (“peace”), from *frijōną (“to free; to love”), from Proto-Indo-European *prāy-, *prēy- (“to like, love”).
Inherited from Middle French esche, from Old French esche, from Latin ēsca.

From Middle French coy, from Old French coi, from Latin qu(i)ētus. Doublet of quiet, which was borrowed. The original feminine coie is attested until the 18th century. The modern form is analogous (e.g. with droit, droite) and/or influenced by the aforementioned doublet. Compare similar spelling inconsistencies in absous, andalou, esquimau, favori.
Borrowed from German Haubitze, from Czech houfnice (“catapult”).
Inherited from Old French universitei, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin universitātem.
Borrowed from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos). Doublet of the inherited plane, now a regional term.
Inherited from Middle French issue, from Old French issue (“exit”), from issu, past participle of issir, eissir.
Inherited from Middle French nez, from Old French nés, from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Compare Italian naso.
Inherited from Middle French chevelu, from Vulgar Latin *capillūtus. By surface analysis, cheveu (“hair”) + -u.
Borrowed from Spanish fiesta. Originally Parisian slang. Doublet of fête.
Inherited from Old French omnipotent, from. From Latin omnipotentem (“almighty”).
Inherited from Middle French sincere, borrowed from Latin sincērus.
Borrowed from Latin parallēlogrammum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παραλληλόγραμμον (parallēlógrammon).
From cul m + -otte f. Equivalent to the feminine derivative of culot m.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ūnivocus.
Inherited from Middle French montaigne, from Old French montaigne, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin mōns, montem.
From Latin systylos, from Ancient Greek σύστυλος (sústulos) composed of σύν (sún) and στῦλος (stûlos).
From Latin Athenaeum, from Ancient Greek Ἀθηναῖον (Athēnaîon), from Ἀθήνη (Athḗnē, “Athena”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bilinguis. See bi- and langue.
Learned borrowing from Latin atticismos, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ττῐκῐσμός (ăttĭkĭsmós).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin scabrōsus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παραλογισμός (paralogismós).
From Middle French desconcerter, from des- (“dis-”) + concerter (“to bring into agreement, organize”).
Borrowed from Latin scēnicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σκηνικός (skēnikós). By surface analysis, scène + -ique.
Inherited from Old French neveu, from Latin nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts.
From Late Latin impostor < impositor, agent noun of Latin impōnō (“impose”).
Inherited from Old French apostre (c. 1180), apostle (c. 1100), borrowed from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “one sent forth, apostle”).
Inherited from Middle French fust, from Old French fust, from Latin fūstis.
From Occitan esquintar, from Old Occitan esquintar, probably from Vulgar Latin *exquintare (“divide into five”), from Latin ex- + quintus.
Inherited from Latin sēmita. Compare sentier.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin rectificātiō. By surface analysis, rectifier + -ation.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin paradoxum, from Latin paradoxa (“things contrary to expectation”), from Ancient Greek παράδοξα (parádoxa).

Inherited from Old French fantosme, from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma); alternatively, according to the TLFi, it may have arrived in French through late Gallic Vulgar Latin in what is now southern France/Occitania, from an Ionian Greek dialect brought to Marseille, presumably in a form *phantagma > *phantauma. The later spelling in Old French thus reflects the influence of the spelling of phantasma, the standard Latin form.
Borrowed from Latin dētractor, from dētrahō (“to diminish”).
Inherited from Old French apointier. By surface analysis, a- + point + -er. Possibly corresponds to a Late Latin appunctāre, from Latin ad + punctum.
Inherited from Old French penil, from Vulgar Latin *pectinī̆culum, diminutive of pecten (“pubic hair, comb”).
Inherited from Old French tavernier, from Latin tabernārius. By surface analysis, taverne + -ier.
Learned borrowing from New Latin Lycium.
From Old French confirmacion, from Latin cōnfirmātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin absorptiō. By surface analysis, absorber + -tion.
Inherited from Middle French crediteur, from Old French creditor, creditour, borrowed from Latin crēditōrem. By surface analysis, créditer + -eur.
Inherited from Middle French donner, from Old French doner, from Latin dōnāre.
From Latin praestātiōnem, from the verb praestare, from prae (“in front of”) + stare (“to stand”).
From Middle French imitation, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitātiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French peur, from Old French peor, poür, from Latin pavōrem (“fear, fright”). Compare Catalan por and Italian paura.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sequentia, from Latin sequēns.
Borrowed from Italian agitato. Doublet of agité.
Borrowed from English terminus, from Latin terminus. Doublet of terme.
Borrowed from Iranian Persian آیتالله (âyatollâh), from Arabic آيَةُ اللّٰه (ʔāyatu llāh, “sign of God”, from آيَة (ʔāya, “sign”) + اللّٰه (allāh, “God”)).
Borrowed from Latin mōtor. Displaced Old French mouveur.
Inherited from Middle French Æque, from Latin Aequus.
From Latin dēficientia. Compare Catalan deficiència, Italian deficienza, Portuguese deficiência, Spanish deficiencia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rārēfactiōnem, from rarefaciō (“to rarefy”).
From Old French parastre, from Latin patrastrum.
From Middle French majeur, a borrowing from Latin maior (“larger, greater”). Doublet of maire, major, and mayeur.
Learned borrowing from Latin naumachia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ναυμαχία (naumakhía).
Inherited from Old French ciprés, from Latin cupressus, cypressus, cyparissus, from Ancient Greek κυπάρισσος (kupárissos).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impeccābilis, from peccāre (whence pécher).
From psychanalyse + -iste on the model of analyste.
Borrowed from Italian tombola, from tombolare.
Learned borrowing from Latin littorālis, alternative form of lītorālis, from lītus (“shore”).
Inherited from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).
Inherited from Middle French createur, from Old French creatur, creator, borrowed from Latin creātōrem.
From Latin fulica, probably via Occitan folca.
Inherited from Middle French argent m, from Old French argent m, from Latin argentum n, according to the TLFi etymological dictionary, a borrowing).
From Old French cordoan (“(leather) of Cordova”) + -ier. Compare English cordwainer and cordovan.
Borrowed from English thug, in turn derived from Hindustani ठग (ṭhag) / ٹھگ (ṭhag, “swindler, fraud, cheat”), further derived from Prakrit 𑀞𑀕 (ṭhaga), of uncertain origin. See there for more.
From blanchiss(ant) (stem of the present participle of blanchir) + -eur.
From Middle French illegitime, borrowed from Latin illegitimus. By surface analysis, il- + légitime.
From Middle French, from Old French abandoner, from a ban doner (“give up to banishment”), from Frankish *bann, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diversificātiōnem, from diversificātus, past participle of diversificō (“diversify”), from Latin diversus (“turned in different ways”) + faciō (“make, do”)
Learned borrowing from Latin praenōmen. By surface analysis, pré- + nom.
[1540s] From Middle French grandiloquence, from Latin grandiloquus + -ence, after éloquence.
From Middle French; originally from Latin cadaverōsus.
Borrowed from Latin digitālis. Doublet of dé. Use in electronics is a literal borrowing from English, through a misinterpretation of the English word digit.

From Middle French ost, from Old French ost, host, from Latin hostis. An archaic or literary term referring to an army from the Middle Ages, taken from Middle French (i.e. no longer reflecting a popularly inherited form). The modern pronunciation is based on the spelling, differing from the original one, which was /o/. Has survived as an inherited form in the dialects of the Picardy and Maine regions as o (“herd”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin saturātiō. By surface analysis, saturer + -ation.
Inherited from Latin sōlus. Doublet of solo, which is a borrowing from Italian.
Borrowed from Latin dēsōlātiōnem f or derived from Middle French desolation f.
Inherited from Old French pousiere, derived from pous, from Vulgar Latin *pulvus, neuter form derived from Latin pulvis m.
Borrowed from English skillet. Doublet of écuelle.
From par- + courir, based on Latin percurrere.
From Latin mythos m, from Ancient Greek μῦθος m (mûthos).

Inherited from Old French arain, from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen, derived from Latin aer-. Cognate with Catalan aram, Italian rame, Occitan aram, Portuguese arame, Romanian aramă, Sardinian arràmene, Sicilian ramu, Spanish alambre (“wire”).
Borrowed from German Formant, from Latin fōrmāns (“shaping; forming; fashioning”), present participle of fōrmō (“to shape; to form; to fashion”). Doublet of formans.
Inherited from Old French imperatif, borrowed from Latin imperātīvus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin bioticus, from Ancient Greek βιωτικός (biōtikós), from βίος (bíos, “life”).
Inherited from Old French sobre, borrowed from Latin sobrius.
Inherited from Old French cisterne, from Latin cisterna.

Borrowed from Latin vāgīna. Compare the inherited doublet gaine. Compare also gouine, which may be borrowed from Breton gouin, itself ultimately borrowed from the Latin. Also a doublet of gaine (“sheath”), which was inherited from the Latin.
Inherited from Old French essorer (whence also English soar), from Vulgar Latin *exaurare (“to rise into the air; to expose to air”), from Latin ex (“out”) + aura (“the air, a breeze”).
Borrowed from Spanish sainete, diminutive of saín.
Inherited from Middle French escremir, from Old French escremir, escermir, eschirmir, from Frankish *skirmijan, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
Borrowed from Latin prehēnsiōnem. Doublet of prison, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Italian capriccioso. By surface analysis, caprice + -eux.
Borrowed from English wallaby, from Dharug wollabi.
Learned borrowing from Latin fragilis. Doublet of frêle.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin scrūtinium (in the phrase per viam scrutinii), ultimately from Latin scrutari.
Inherited from Old French distinction (attested from the 12th century), borrowed from Latin distinctiōnem.

Inherited from Late Latin dēlīberāre, dēlīberō (“to set free”) (unrelated to the Classical Latin dēlīberō (“to weigh, to ponder”), which was borrowed in French as délibérer). By surface analysis, dé- + livrer.
Inherited from Late Latin īnsūbulum, from Latin īnsuō + -bulum, or related to sūbula.
Learned borrowing from Latin pressiō, pressiōnis.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin catēchismus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin correspondentia.
From penne + -age, from Latin penna, pinna (“wing, feather”).
Inherited from Old French pasnaie, from Latin pastinaca. Doublet of pastenague.
16th century, from Dutch klieven, of Germanic origin. More at English cleave.

Inherited from Middle French baptesme, from Old French batesme, bapteme, baptesme (earlier batesma), a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin baptisma, from Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma), and Late Latin baptismus, baptismum from Ancient Greek βαπτισμός (baptismós). Doublet of baptisme.
Inherited from Old French triste, borrowed from Latin trīstis. Old French originally had trist, inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, a variant of the same word.

Via Late Latin apophasis from Ancient Greek ἀπόφασις (apóphasis, “denial, negation”) from ἀπο- (apo-, “away, from, off”) + φάσις (phásis, “statement, proposition”) from φημί (phēmí, “to speak”) from Proto-Hellenic *pʰā́mā from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂; whence Latin fārī, cognate to English fame, fable.
Inherited from Old French formacion, borrowed from Latin fōrmātiōnem. Cf. also the archaic formaison.
Inherited from Middle French atourner, from Old French atorner.
From pou + -eux, or possibly from Vulgar Latin peduclōsus, from Latin peduculōsus.
Learned borrowing from Latin prōdigiōsus. By surface analysis, prodige + -eux.
Inherited from Old French plenier, plener, borrowed from Late Latin plēnārius, from Latin plēnus.
Inherited from Middle French restriction, from Old French restriction, borrowed from Late Latin restrictiōnem, from Latin restringō.
Learned borrowing from Latin sedentārius (“sitting”), from sedeō (“to sit, to be seated”).
Borrowed from Latin operātōrem. Cf. also ouvreur (“worker in glassmaking or papermaking”), possibly an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Latin māternus (“relating to a mother, maternal”) + -er.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek λαμπαδηδρομία (lampadēdromía).
From Old French maior, from Latin maiōrem, accusative of maior. Doublet of maire, majeur, and major.
Learned borrowing from Latin redemptiōnem. Doublet of rançon.
English budget, from Old French bougette. Doublet of bougette.
Borrowed from Latin puerīlis, from puer (“boy, child”).
Borrowed from English vitamine, older form of vitamin. First attested in 1913.
From Old French hastif. By surface analysis, hâte + -if.
From saveur + -eux or Late Latin sapōrōsus, from Latin sapor.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ψευδεπίγραφος (pseudepígraphos, “(literally) (with) false superscription”). By surface analysis, pseud- + épigraphe.
From Middle French certitude, borrowed from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus (“sure”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin arborizāre.
From Old French trons, from Vulgar Latin *trunceus, from Latin truncus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mūcilāgō.
From moquer (“to mock”) + -eur (“suffix forming agent nouns”).
Inherited from Old French moncel, from Late Latin monticellus, diminutive of Latin mōns.
Inherited from Old French creste, from Latin crista.
Inherited from Middle French fresle, from Old French fraisle, byform of fraile, inherited from Latin fragilis. Doublet of fragile.
Learned borrowing from Latin Septembrem. Compare Old French setembre, sietembre.
Borrowed from Latin obstāculum, from obstō.
From Old French difference, borrowed from Latin differentia.
From Old French amiable, from Late Latin amīcābilis.
Borrowed from Italian attaccare. Doublet of attacher.
Borrowed from Late Latin lampsana, from lapsana.
Inherited from Old French coin m, from Latin cuneus m (“wedge”) (see there for further etymology).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin catacumbae, a compound of Ancient Greek κατά (katá) and Late Latin tumba (whence French tombe).
Learned borrowing from Latin dēnotātiō. By surface analysis, dénoter + -ation.
From Middle French subsequent (14th c.), a learned borrowing from Latin subsequēns.
Borrowed from Latin successiōnem (accusative singular successiōnem).
From Old French contribuir, borrowed from Latin contribuō.

Learned borrowing from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”) (whence machine).
Borrowed from Late Latin pōtābilis, from Latin potō.
Inherited from Old French angoisse, from Latin angustia.
Inherited from Middle French visceres, vixeres m (first attested in 1478), borrowed from Latin viscera n pl.
Present participle of tenir. From Old French tenant; corresponding to Latin tenentem.
From Old French amender, from Latin ēmendāre (“to free from faults, correct, improve, remedy, amend, revise, cure”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mendum (“fault”).
From Old French chaut, from Latin cal(i)dus.
From Old French larmoiier, from Vulgar Latin *lacrimizāre. Synchronically larme (“teardrop”) + -oyer (verb-forming suffix).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin bovinus.
Inherited from Middle French unze, from Old French onze, from Latin ūndecim.
In the original sense from Occitan bòria. In the sense of shelter, a repurposing, c. 1970, of the original, obsolete term.
Learned borrowing from Latin interrogātiōnem. By surface analysis, interroger + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin hallūcinātiōnem. By surface analysis, halluciner + -ation.

Inherited from Old French loisir, from Latin licēre, infinitive of licet. The final -ir < Latin -ēre is regular and results from the palatalization of the preceding -c- to *[d͡zʲ], as in gésir, moisir, plaisir.
From Old French dancier, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre. Displaced the older Old French baller.
Inherited from Old French mesdire, corresponding to mé- + dire.

Borrowed from Late Latin idiōma (“idiomatic”), from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “the local dialect of an area that varies from the main dialect from which it came”), from Ancient Greek ἰδιούμαι (idioúmai, “to usurp, appropriate”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “mine, belonging to me”).
From English grizzly, ellipsis of grizzly bear, from 1866.
Inherited from Old French benefice (attested since 1198), borrowed from Latin beneficium.
From Old French espan with change of prefix to em-; borrowed from Frankish *spanna, from Proto-Germanic *spānnõ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to stretch”). Cognate with English span.

Inherited from Middle French feuille, from Old French fueille, from Late Latin folia, plural of folium in Classical Latin, itself probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”). Doublet of folio, which was borrowed from Latin. Compare English foil, Spanish hoja, Portuguese folha, Catalan fulla, and Italian foglia.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin crēdibilis, from crēdō (“believe”). Compare croyable.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin invasivus.
Borrowed from English manosphere; compare blogosphère.
Inherited from Middle French manumisseur, from Latin manūmissor, from manūmittō + -tor. The sense “executor” is a semantic loan from Catalan marmessor.
Inherited from Old French esclater, of Germanic origin, from Old High German skleizan or Frankish *slītan, from Proto-Germanic *slītaną (“to tear apart”).
Borrowed from Italian mancare, derived from manco (“maimed”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin propaganda.
Inherited from Old French peresce, from Latin pigritia.
Inherited from Middle French insatiable, from Old French insaciable, from Latin īnsatiābilis. by surface analysis, in- + satiable.
From Old French chesible, from Late Latin casubla, an alteration of Latin casula (“little cottage, hooded cloak”), a diminutive of casa (“house”).
From Ancient Greek μῑ́μησις (mī́mēsis, “imitation”), from μιμεῖσθαι (mimeîsthai, “to imitate”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “a mime”).

Inherited from Middle French estamper, stamper, étamper, from Old French estamper (“to crush”), from Frankish *stampôn (“to crush”) or Old High German stampfōn (modern German stampfen), from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną, from Proto-Indo-European *stembʰ- (“to trample down”).
Inherited from Old French inquisicion, itself borrowed from Latin inquisitiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French arable, from Old French arable, from Latin arābilis.
Inherited from Middle French fragilité (compare Old French fraileté), borrowed from Latin fragilitātem. By surface analysis, fragile + -ité. Compare also Old French fraileté.
Borrowed from Latin mentula (vulgar term for the penis).
From Middle French conjugaison, alteration of earlier conjugation, borrowed from Latin coniugātiōnem. Equivalent to conjuguer + -aison.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin reductiōnem.
Diminutive of Old French feuil (with -et), from Latin folia.
From Old French moustarde, from moust (“must”) (modern moût), from Latin mustum.
From tourner (“to turn”) + vis (“screw”). Compare Piedmontese tornavis.
Learned borrowing from Latin inhūmānus. By surface analysis, in- + humain.
From Middle French, from Old French servant, a substantivized present participle of servir. Cf. also Latin serviens, and French sergent.
Inherited from Old French porche, inherited from Latin porticus. Doublet of portique.
From Middle French davantaige, from Old French d'avantage, corresponding to de + avantage.
From Middle French diversité, from Old French diversité, from Latin dīversitātem.
Inherited from Middle French attestation, borrowed from Latin attestātiōnem.

Inherited from Middle French auvans, from Old French anvant (1180), from Gaulish *andebanno (“eaves, portico”) (compare Occitan ambans, Catalan envà), compound of ande (“intensive prefix”) (compare Welsh an-) + banno (“horn”) (compare Welsh ban), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *an- + *bandā.
From Middle French, from Old French cofre, from Latin cophinus (“basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “basket”). Doublet of couffin.
Learned borrowing from Latin dis-. Compare the inherited dé-.
Borrowed from Occitan arboça, from arboç, from Latin arbuteus (“of the strawberry tree”), from arbutus (“strawberry tree”).
From Ancient Greek ἐκχύμωσις (ekkhúmōsis, “bruise”), from ἐκχέω (ekkhéō, “to flow out”).
Borrowed from Italian colorito with change of suffix. By surface analysis, colorer + -is. Related to couleur.
From Middle French inhabitable, from Latin inhabitābilis (“uninhabitable”). By surface analysis, in- + habitable.
Inherited from Old French voiable. By surface analysis, voir + -able.
From Latin salmō, potentially from Gaulish salmō.
Inherited from Middle French real, from Old French reel, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”), from Latin rēs.

Inherited from Middle French dune, from Old French dune, from Middle Dutch dūne (modern Dutch duin), from Old Dutch dūn, dūno, from Proto-West Germanic *dūnā (“hill”), of uncertain origin. More at Proto-West Germanic *dūnā.
Borrowed from Latin glaucōma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek γλαύκωμα (glaúkōma).
Inherited from Old French autorité, borrowed from Latin auctoritātem.
From Middle French aster, from Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓στήρ (ăstḗr). Doublet of star.
Inherited from Latin caballīnus. By surface analysis, cheval + -in.
From émerveiller (“to amaze; to marvel at”) + -ment.
Borrowed from Occitan flaunharda, from flaunhar (“flatter, fawn, spoil”).
Borrowed from English gay, itself a borrowing from French gai. Doublet of gai.
Inherited from Old French vocation, borrowed from Latin vocātiōnem.
Feminine of the Old French adjective cras, from Latin crassus. Doublet of gras.
Inherited from Middle French college, from Old French college, borrowed from Latin collēgium.
From Latin Aemilianus, a derivative of Aemilius.
Inherited from Old French avarice, borrowed from Latin avaritia. Cognate with Italian avarizia, Portuguese avareza, Spanish avaricia.
Inherited from Middle French significatif, borrowed from Latin significātivus.
From English sprinter, reanalyzed in French as sprinter (verb) + -eur.
From Ancient Greek λάτρις (látris, “servant”). The circumflex is by influence of unrelated -âtre.
Borrowed from Latin famōsus, from fama; cf. Old French fame.
From Latin esse, the infinitive of sum.
Borrowed from Late Latin quiētūdō, from Latin quiētus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀντι- (anti-), from ᾰ̓ντῐ́ (ăntĭ́), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti, from *h₂énts + *-i.
From Latin cardinālātus, from cardinālis (“cardinal”), itself the noun use of the adjective derived from cardō (“hinge, main point”) + -ālis (“-al”).
Borrowed from Latin subtīlitātem. Displaced Old French sotileté.

A semi-learned term borrowed from Latin innātus (“inborn”), perfect active participle of innāscor (“be born in, grow up in”), from in (“in, at on”) + nāscor (“be born”). Replaced the inherited Old French form enné.
Inherited from Middle French personne, from Old French persone, presonne, from Latin persona, of unknown, perhaps Etruscan, origin.
Inherited from Old French chancel, from Latin cancellus.
From the Old French boscage, from Vulgar Latin *boscāticum, from Late Latin boscus, from Frankish *busk (compare Middle Dutch busch), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“forest, woods”).
Borrowed from Latin nausea, nausia, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “seasickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
Inherited from Old French palefreid, from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin palefredus, variant of Late Latin paraveredus.
Inherited from Old French inspiration, borrowed from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem (nominative: īnspīrātiō), from Latin īnspīrātus (past participle of inspīrō).
Learned borrowing from Latin affectuōsus. Doublet of affettuoso
Learned borrowing from Late Latin distorsiō, from Latin distortiō.
Inherited from Old French huche, from Late Latin hutica.
Inherited from Middle French astronomie, from Old French astronomie, borrowed from Latin astronomia (“astronomy”), from Ancient Greek ἀστρονομία (astronomía). By surface analysis, astro- + -nomie.
Semi-learned term resulting from a modification, under the influence of the Latin etymology, of Old French treble, itself from Latin triplus.
Learned borrowing from Latin singulāris. Doublet of sanglier.
Inherited from Old French chievrefeuil, from Late Latin caprifolium, from Latin caper + folium. Superficially it looks like a compound chèvre + feuille, but the gender is different.

Borrowed from German Genom, coined by German botanist Hans Winkler in 1920 as a blend of Gen (“gene”) + Chromosom (“chromosome”). By surface analysis, blend of gène + chromosome. Spelling altered by association with the surface analysis.
Inherited from Old French jarzeu, jardeau, jargerie.
Learned borrowing from Latin lītigium, from līs.
Borrowed from German Akkordeon, from Akkord (“harmony”), itself from French accord, from Old French acorder, based on Italian accordare (“to tune”).
Inherited from Old French jusque, from Latin inde + ūsque.
From Middle French bastardise. The variant bastardie disappeared, but survives in English as bastardy.
Inherited from Middle French obscur, from Old French oscur, from Latin obscurus. The -b- through learned relatinisation in Middle French.
Borrowed from Latin visibilitātem, from visibilis (“visible”). By surface analysis, visible + -ité.
From Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “the bearer of light”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”).
Learned borrowing from Latin metoecus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nūtrītiō.
From Old French automne, a borrowing from Latin autumnus. The inherited equivalent was après août (literally “after August”).

Inherited from Middle French resver, from Old French resver (“to consider, reflect, be delirious”), of uncertain origin. The Trésor de la langue française informatisé links it back either to an unattested *esver (“to wander”) or to Latin *reexvadō, from re- + ex- + evadō. The Französisches Etymologisches Wörterbuch links it back to *reexvagus, hence the same as the first proposal by the Trésor de la langue française informatisé. Compare Old English rǣswan (“to consider, suspect, conjecture”), of similar form and meaning.
Borrowed from Latin tenebrositas. By surface analysis, ténébreux + -ité.
From Ancient Greek μεγαλογραφία (megalographía). Morphologically mégalo- + -graphie.
Inherited from Middle French ypocrisye, from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “acting on the stage, pretense”).
From Middle French quintuple, from Latin quīntuplus, from quīntus (“fifth”) + -plus (“-ple”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin myrtillus.
From joie + -eux. cf. also Late Latin gaudiōsus.
Inherited from Old French incube, borrowed from Latin incubus.
Learned borrowing from Latin testāmentārius (“of or belonging to wills”). By surface analysis, testament + -aire.
Borrowed from Latin injūstus. Equivalent to in- + juste.
From Latin ethicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós).

From Occitan Bearn, from Medieval Latin Beneharnum, corruption of Benarni, Vernarni, Gaulish pronunciation of an Aquitanian/Basque tribe in southwest France. The municipality in Québec is named after the Béarn Regiment.
Borrowed from Latin syzygia, from Ancient Greek συζυγία (suzugía).
From Middle French instrument, from Old French instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin paronymon. By surface analysis, para- + -onyme.
From Old French, from Latin capācitātem. By surface analysis, capace (“capacious”) + -ité (“-ity”).

Inherited from Old French compaignon, from Late Latin compāniōnem (literally “he with whom one shares one's bread”) (compare Italian compagnone, Spanish compañón), from com- (“with”) + pānis (“bread”), first attested in the Frankish Lex Salica as a calque of a Germanic word represented by Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌱𐌰 (gahlaiba, “messmate”) from 𐌲𐌰- (ga-, “with”) + 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍃 (hlaifs, “bread”), Old High German galeipo, itself from Proto-Germanic *ga- (“togetherness”) + *hlaibaz (“loaf, bread”). Compare with the etymologically related terms copain and compagnie. More at co-, loaf.
From the stem of the Latin paternus and the suffix -el.
Inherited from Old French solaz, solas, from Latin solācium.
Inherited from Old French indigence, from Latin indigentia.
Learned borrowing from Latin anxietātem. By surface analysis, anxieux + -té.
English gravitation, itself borrowed from New Latin gravitātiō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin productīvus, or formed from Latin productus with the suffix -if.
Inherited from Old French matrice, borrowed from Latin mātrīcem. Supplanted the older inherited forms marriz, marris.
Borrowed from Late Latin evictiōnem, from Latin evincō.
Borrowed from Latin catēna. Doublet of chaîne, which was inherited, as well as cadène, a borrowing from Old Italian.
Learned borrowing from Latin rhythmus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós).
Borrowed from English goal. The sense "goalkeeper" is a pseudo-anglicism.
Borrowed from Portuguese selva, cognate with the Old French word below.
Borrowed from Latin catenāria, nominalised feminine of catenārius, from Latin catena (whence French chaîne).
Inherited from Middle French cadence, borrowed from Italian cadenza. Doublet of chance.
Derived from Old French cocodril, inherited from Latin crocodīlus with metathesis, later respelled to match the Latin form. Compare English crocodile, itself respelled from Middle English cocodrill.
Inherited from Middle French cognom, from Latin cōgnōmen, from con- + nōmen. By surface analysis, con- + nom. Doublet of cognomen.

Inherited from Middle French veoir, from Old French veoir, veir, from earlier vedeir, from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-. Unrelated to voie and its derivatives and to voirie or avoir. See cognates in regional languages in France : Norman veî or veir, Gallo vair, Picard vir, Bourguignon voi, Franco-Provençal vêre, Occitan veire, véder, véser, Corsican vedè, Catalan veure. See cognates in Romance languages outside France : Aromanian ved, Galician ver, Italian vedere, Lombard vedè, véet, Portuguese ver, Romanian vedea, Sardinian bidere, Sicilian vìdiri, Spanish ver.
Inherited from Middle French requerir, from Old French requerre (with a conjugation change as with quérir), from Latin requirere.

From Middle French mesiraigne (16th c.), merisengne (15th c.), from Latin mūsarāneus, from Latin mūs (“mouse”) + arāneus (“spider-like”). So called because the bite of many shrews (e.g. Neomys fodiens) is venomous. According to the Trésor informatisé, the word is a borrowing from Latin, but the Middle French forms look by no means learned and could well be inherited. The modern -u- may be a Latinate alteration, however.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prosaicus, from Latin prosa.
Learned borrowing from Latin cōnsōlātiō. Morphologically, from consoler + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin sanguinārius, from sanguis (whence French sang).
Inherited from Old French ample, inherited from Latin amplus.
Inherited from Middle French couardise, from Old French cuardise. By surface analysis, couard + -ise.
From Old French cinabre, from Latin cinnabaris, from Ancient Greek κιννάβαρι (kinnábari).
Inherited from Middle French beate, from Latin beatus (“happy, blessed”).
Inherited from Middle French imagerie. By surface analysis, image + -erie.
Borrowed from the legal Latin dētentor, from dētineō (whence détenir) + -tor (whence -teur).
From Middle French fascinacion, from Latin fascinātiō.
From Middle French offechinne, offecine, offichine, officine, borrowed from Latin officīna. Doublet of usine.
Borrowed from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).

Alteration (based on the Latin source) of Old French chetel, itself an alteration (after chef (“important”)) of chatel, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin capitāle (in the sense of “head of cattle”), substantivization of Latin capitālis. Doublet of capital. Cognate with English cattle (from Old Northern French) and chattel (from common Old French).
Borrowed from Occitan ubac, from Latin opācus. Doublet of opaque.
Inherited from Middle French fusion, from Old French fusion, a borrowing from Latin fūsiōnem. Doublet of foison.
From Late Latin effigiāre. By surface analysis, effigie + -er.

Coined with Latin septem (“seven”) and Ancient Greek ἑπτᾰ́ (heptắ, “seven”) in mind, for the seventh order of 10³. The consonants pt are reduced to tt; the initial z was chosen instead of s to avoid confusion with s (“second”, symbol)
Inherited from Middle French nuque, nuche, borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).
From Medieval Latin petroleum, from petra (“rock”) + oleum (“oil”).
Borrowed from Italian babbola. The suffix is influenced by frequent forms such as bestiole, cabriole.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obiectum.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σῐδηρουργῐ́ᾱ (sĭdērourgĭ́ā). By surface analysis, sidéro- + -urgie. Compare Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish siderurgia, Catalan siderúrgia.
Inherited from Old French rescusse, nominalised past participle of rescourre, from Latin excutere (“to shake off, drive out”).
From Late Latin basaltes, a misspelling of Latin basanites, from Ancient Greek βασανίτης (basanítēs), from βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”), from Egyptian.
Inherited from Middle French balance, from Old French balance, from Vulgar Latin *bilancia, from Latin bilanx, from bi- (see Latin bis) and lanx.
Inherited from Middle French tel, from Old French tel, tal, from Latin tālis. Compare Spanish tal.
From calme + -er, or possibly from Italian calmare.
Borrowed from New Latin urticaria, formed from Latin urtica (“stinging nettle”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin quā̆tuor, a variant spelling of quattuor.
Learned borrowing from Latin concha. Doublet of conche.
Inherited from Old French delit, borrowed from Latin dēlīctum.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pūrgātōrium (“cleansing”). By surface analysis, purger + -atoire.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French entreprendre (“to begin something, undertake”). By surface analysis, entre + prendre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēclārātīvus.
Inherited from Middle French, from Ancient Greek λιθοτόμον (lithotómon), neuter of λιθοτόμος (lithotómos, “stone-cutting”).
Inherited from Old French diffamacion, borrowed from Latin diffāmātiōnem, from diffāmō (“to spread an unfavorable report; to defame, malign, decry”), from dis- + fāma (“report, opinion, reputation”).
Borrowed from German Handball (“handball”), from Hand (“hand”) + Ball (“ball”), literally “hand ball”.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin retrocessiō.
From sauce + -ière. Cognate with Italian salsiera.
Clipping of soutien-gorge with an otherwise unknown suffix.
Inherited from Old French effimere, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros).
From parer + brise. Compare Spanish parabrisas, Italian parabrezza, Portuguese para-brisa.
Learned borrowing from Latin ineluctābilis. By surface analysis, in- + éluctable.
Borrowed from English iceberg, from Dutch ijsberg (literally “ice mountain”).
Borrowed from English vote. Doublet of vœu.
Inherited from Middle French visqueux, from Old French viscous, borrowed from Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum.
From Latin concupiscentia, from concupīscō (“to desire strongly, to desire eagerly; to covet”).
From Late Latin cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), ultimately from Hebrew כְּרוּב (kerúv).
Borrowed from Moroccan Arabic حبس (ḥabs), from Arabic حَبْس (ḥabs).
Borrowed from Latin macula. Doublet of maille, which was inherited.
Learned borrowing from Latin prīvātiō. Morphologically, from priver + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin āsiāticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιατικός (Asiatikós).
Borrowed from Latin sirēna, from Latin Sīrēn, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). Cf. also Old French sereine. Doublet of serin.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κύανος (kúanos).

Inherited from Middle French prestre, from Old French prestre (nominative form, compare provoire), from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Doublet of praire and presbytre, a recent borrowing.
Probably borrowed from Italian bravo. Compare Spanish, Portuguese bravo. Doublet of bravo.
Inherited from Middle French croix, from Old French croix, crois, from the Latin crucem. Doublet of crux, croiseur, and cruiser.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀρθός (orthós).
From Old French chancelier, cancelier, from inherited from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancellus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin peremptiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēflōrātiōnem. By surface analysis, déflorer + -ation.
From Latin catachrēsis, from Ancient Greek κατάχρησις (katákhrēsis).
From Middle French partial, borrowed from Late Latin partiālis (“relating to a part”), from Latin pars (“part”). Doublet of partiel.
Inherited from Old French circonference, borrowed from Latin circumferentia.
Inherited from Old French tisun, from Latin tītiō. Cognate with Spanish tizón and Catalan tió.
Inherited from Old French assaut, asalt, from Vulgar Latin *assaltus, modification of Latin assultus.
From Old French pastoral, from Latin pastorālis, from pāstor (“shepherd”) (whence pâtre).

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French draper (“to drape", also, "to full cloth”), from drap (“cloth, drabcloth”), from Late Latin drappus, drapus (“drabcloth, kerchief”), a word first recorded in the Capitularies of Charlemagne, probably from Old Low Frankish *drap, *drāp- (“that which is fulled, drabcloth”) from Proto-Germanic *drap-, *drēp- (“something beaten”), from *drepaną (“to beat, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreb- (“to beat, crush, make or become thick”). Cognate with English drub (“to beat”), Low German drapen, dräpen (“to strike”). More at drape.
Borrowed from Latin īnfatīgābilis; morphologically, from in- + fatiguer + -able.
From Latin burra, nominative feminine singular of burrus.
Inherited from Old French bargaignier, from Frankish *borganjan. Compare English bargain and Portuguese barganhar.

From Middle French chapitre, from Old French chapitre (also capitre, chapitle), an early borrowing from Late Latin capitulum (literally “little head”), diminutive of Latin caput (whence French chef). If inherited through Vulgar Latin, it would have yielded *cheveil. Doublet of capitule, a modern borrowing.
From Old French fillastre, from Latin fīliaster m, fīliastra f.
From vert (“green”) + -ure (noun-forming suffix), or from Vulgar Latin *virdūra.
From Old French esturnel, from Late Latin sturnellus, from Latin sturnus.
Inherited from Old French charité, carité, a borrowing from Latin cāritātem (“love, regard”), which see for more. Doublet of cherté.
Inherited from Middle French vanité, from Old French, borrowed from Latin vānitātem.
Inherited from Old French voiage, viage, veiage, from Latin viāticum. Doublet of viatique.
From Middle French hyver, from Old French iver, from Late Latin hībernum.
Inherited from Middle French chiffe, from Old French chippe (“cloth, rag”), from Middle English chippe, from Old English ċipp (“chip, wooden shaving”).
Inherited from Middle French armature, borrowed from Latin armātūra. Doublet of armure, which was inherited through Old French.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō.
From Latin typicus (“typical”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vitriolum.
Inherited from Old French salut, salu, from Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).
Borrowed from Latin inventiōnem, from invenio.
Inherited from Old French jeudi, jusdi, from Latin Jovis diēs or Iovis diēs, variant of diēs Iovis (“day of Jupiter”).
Borrowed from English neurotypical. Analysed as neuro- + typique.
From Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion, companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, ally”).

Inherited from Old French setante, from Latin septuāgintā, from *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥dḱomt (“seven-ten”). The ⟨p⟩ was restored under influence of its Latin etymon.
Learned borrowing from Latin epithalamium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”).
From English girl. Doublet of gow.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin fomentāre.
Inherited from Old French estreine, inherited from Latin strēna (“good omen, New Year's gift”). Compare Portuguese estreia and Spanish estrena.
Inherited from Old French reaume, realme, a derivative of real, or from an alteration (with influence from royal) of Old French reiame, from Latin regimine. Compare régime.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ērūctātiō. By surface analysis, éructer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin confrontātiō.
From Old French statue, from Latin statua.
Borrowed from Latin trepidātiōnem (“agitation, trepidation”). Equivalent to trépider + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin verbālis. By surface analysis, verbe + -al.
Inherited from Middle French paradoxal (first attested in 1588). By surface analysis, paradoxe + -al.
From mal- + poli. The noun is the adjective used substantively.
From Portuguese palanquim (“palanquin, palanquin-bearer”), from Odia ପାଲଙ୍କି (pālaṅki, “litter”), ultimately from Sanskrit पल्यङ्क (palyaṅka), variant of पर्यङ्क (paryaṅka, “bed, couch, litter”).
Inherited from Old French pertinent (first attested circa 1300), borrowed from Latin pertinēns, pertinentem.
Learned borrowing from Latin astronomicus. By surface analysis, astronomie + -ique.
Borrowed from Latin orgia, a neuter plural reinterpreted as a feminine singular; itself from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia).
Borrowed from Late Latin isoscelēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἰσοσκελής (isoskelḗs), from ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + σκέλος (skélos, “leg”).
Borrowed from Spanish escabeche, which see for more.
Inherited from Old French enfance, borrowed from Latin īnfāntia, from īnfāns (“unable to speak”).
Inherited from Old French ru, riu, from Vulgar Latin *rius, from Latin rīvus (“brook, small stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós (from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move, set in motion”) + *-wós).
Inherited from Middle French, from Italian balaustro, from Latin balaustĭum. See English baluster for more.
Inherited from Middle French ancien, from Old French anciien, from Vulgar Latin *anteānus.
Inherited from Middle French accomplir, from Old French acomplir, from Vulgar Latin *(ac)complīre, from Latin complēre.
Inherited from Old French sajette, a Latinizing modification of earlier saete, inherited from Latin sagitta.
Inherited from Middle French mainlevee, from the univerbation of main + levee, literally “raised hand, lifted hand”. By surface analysis, main + levée.
From Middle French magister, borrowed from Latin magister. Doublet of maestro, maître, and master.
From Italian fresco. Doublet of frais.
Inherited from Middle French debvoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (to owe; ought, must).

From Latin ōdēum, from Ancient Greek ᾠδεῖον (ōideîon), from ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”). By surface analysis, ode (“ode”) + -ée m (“-eum”).
Learned borrowing from Latin persevērantia. By surface analysis, persévérer + -ance.

* (daughter): From Middle French fille, from Old French fille, from Latin fīlia. * (slang, prostitute): By ellipsis of the euphemisms fille des rues (“girl of the streets”), fille de joie (“girl of joy”), fille publique (“public girl”), and others like them that signify "prostitute".
Borrowed from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement, ordering”).
Learned borrowing from Latin magistrālis, itself from magister. Doublet of mistral.
Learned borrowing from Latin chēlē, from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ).
Inherited from Old French dixme, from Latin decima (pars) (“tenth (part)”). Compare the borrowed doublet décime.
Inherited from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir; equivalent to entre + tenir.
From re- + épandre. Compare Romanian răspândire.
From Middle French difficil(e) (14th c.), a borrowing from Latin difficilis.
Learned borrowing from Latin complēmentum. Doublet of compliment.
Inherited from Middle French jupon. By surface analysis, jupe + -on.
Borrowed from Late Latin antipodes, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀντίποδες (antípodes), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + πόδες (pódes), nominative plural of πούς (poús, “foot”).
Alteration of earlier brocat, from Italian broccato.
Borrowed from Italian soperchieria, obsolete form of soverchieria (“abuse; bullying”).
From Middle French directrice, from Latin dīrēctrīx. By surface analysis, directer + -trice.
Inherited from Old French archangle, borrowed from Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos) from ἀρχ- (arkh-) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”).
From Old French necessité (12th c.), a borrowing form Latin necessitās.
Univerbation of au + près. Compare au loin.
Inherited from Middle French morsure, from Old French morsure, from Early Medieval Latin morsūra; equivalent to mors + -ure.
Inherited from Old French amener, from a- + mener (“to lead”), ultimately from Latin minārī (“to threaten”) (infinitive minārī).
From Latin piscis + culture, modelled after agriculture.
Borrowed from Latin commiserātiōnem, from misereo.

Borrowed from Late Latin patriarcha, from Medieval Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “-arch”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin vannāre, from Latin vannere, vannō.
Inherited from Middle French probleme, a borrowing from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”).
[1315] Inherited from Old French casenier (“Italian userer”), from Italian casana, casaniere; the sense of "homebody" is similar to the Occitan casanier, casernier. See also caserne and quartier.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios). Cognate to Old French ypidime.
Borrowed from Italian modiglione. Doublet of moellon.
19th century: chromo- + -some, from German Chromosom, ultimately from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”) (because they are stained under the microscope).
From Old French mantel from the Latin mantus.
Inherited from Old French inocence, a borrowing from Latin innocentia.
Borrowed from Latin maledictiōnem. See mal and bénédiction. Supplanted the inherited Old French form maleiçon. Compare also maudition.
Inherited from Middle French syringe, from Latin sȳringem, accusative of sȳrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx). Cognate with Italian siringe, Portuguese siringe, Spanish siringe.

Formed from juste + -esse; cf. also Latin iūstitia. Compare Italian giustezza, Spanish and Portuguese justeza, Catalan and Occitan justesa, Galician and Asturian xusteza, Friulian justece. Doublet of justice.
Inherited from Old French covercle, from Latin cooperculum.
From Latin -phila, from Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).
Learned borrowing from Latin leōnīnus, from leō (whence French lion).
From remuer + ménage. Compare Walloon rimowe-manaedje.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs).
From Middle French inquietude (15th c.), a borrowing from Latin inquiētūdō. Earlier was the verb inquiéter (12th c.).
Inherited from Old French macrocosme, from Medieval Latin macrocosmus, formed from Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós, “great, long”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”); macro- + -cosme.
Learned borrowing from Latin hereditārius. Doublet of héritier.
Learned borrowing from New Latin acīnacifōrmis.
Learned borrowing from Latin rarefacere. By surface analysis, rare + -fier.
Borrowed from Latin strictus, perfect participle of stringere (“to draw tight, bind, contract”). Doublet of étroit.
Inherited from Old French damoisel, from Vulgar Latin *domnicellus, diminutive of Classical Latin dominus (“master, lord”).
Inherited from Middle French franc (“noble”), from Old French franc, from Latin Francus, from Frankish *Franko (“a Frank”), from Proto-Germanic *frankô (“javelin”).
Inherited from Middle French Florentin, from Latin Flōrentīnus, from Flōrentia (“Florence”) + -īnus.
Inherited from Middle French rose, from Old French rose, borrowed from Latin rosa (the expected form if it was inherited would be *reuse).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μασσαλιώτης (Massaliṓtēs), from Μασσαλία (Massalía) + -ώτης (-ṓtēs).
From Latin Tusculānus, from Tusculum + -ānus. By surface analysis, Tuscule + -an.

Inherited from Middle French pasteur, from Old French pastur, pastor, an accusative form corresponding originally to nominative pastre (whence modern pâtre), from Latin pastor, pastōrem. Early on was there a tendency towards functional split, the original accusative being influenced by the Latin etymon and used particularly in religious context. This influence also explains the survival of the /s/ (instead of *pâteur). A strict division between inherited form and learned use is hardly possible, however, as the word is continuously attested and would have been spelt pasteur in Middle French in any case. Compare the diminutive pastoureau (also pâtoureau), which is clearly inherited from Old French pastorel.

Inherited from Middle French beurre (16th c.), from a regional (eastern or western) variant of burre, from Old French burre, bure, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron, “butter”, literally “cow-cheese”).
Inherited from Old French marchié, marchiet, from Latin mercātus. Doublet of mercato.
Inherited from Middle French mur, from Old French mur, from Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Italic *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).
Inherited from Middle French delicat, borrowed from Latin dēlicātus. Doublet of délié.
Inherited from Middle French Hernique, from Latin Hernicus.
Borrowed from Spanish maíz, from Taíno mahís.
Inherited from Middle French sceur, from Old French seür, inherited from Latin sēcūrus.
From Latin Iūstīniānus. By surface analysis, Justin + -ien.
From Medieval Latin delphīnātus, from delphīnus (“dauphin”) + -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns). Doublet of dauphinat and delphinat. By surface analysis, dauphin + -é (abstract noun suffix).
Borrowed from Latin ïambus, from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos).
From Latin Chananaeus, from Ancient Greek Χαναναῖος (Khananaîos).

Inherited from Middle French patois (“local dialect”), from Old French patois (“incomprehensible speech, rude language”), alteration (due to influence of the suffix -ois in words relating to nationalities and languages) of earlier *patoi, a deverbal of patoier (“to gesticulate, handle clumsily, paw”), from pate (“paw”), from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”), from Frankish *patta (“paw, sole of the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *pat-, *paþa- (“to walk, tread, go, step”), of uncertain origin and relation. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pent-/*(s)pat- (“path; to walk”), a variant of *pent-/*pat- (“path; to go”). Cognate with Dutch pat, Low German pedden (“to step, tread”). Related to pad, path.
From Old French peluchier (“to peel; pluck”).
Inherited from Old French clou, from Latin clāvus, from Proto-Italic *klāwos, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u-.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from auto- (relating to cars) + stop (hitchiking).
From Old French contrerollour, contreroulour. By surface analysis, contrôler + -eur.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French marchier, from Frankish *markōn, from Proto-Germanic *markōną. Compare also marquer.
From ciné- + -aste, coined by Louis Delluc circa 1920.
From Latin messis (“harvest”) + Ancient Greek δῶρον (dôron, “gift”).
Borrowed from Latin palmārēs, plural of palmāris (“that deserves the palmary or prize, superior, excellent”).
Inherited from Middle French aimable, amable, from Old French amable, from Latin amābilis. By surface analysis, aimer + -able. Doublet of amabile.
From brume + -eux, or possibly borrowed from Latin brumōsus.
First attested in the 17th century. From Italian bamboccio.
Inherited from Old French onguent, a borrowing from Latin unguentum (“ointment, unguent”).
Inherited from Middle French fustet, from Old Occitan fustet, from Arabic فُسْتَق (fustaq) with Occitanized ending.

From Medieval Latin theosophus (“a theologian”, noun), from Koine Greek θεόσοφος (theósophos, “wise in things concerning god”, adjective), from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”) + σοφός (sophós, “wise”). Cognate to Spanish teósofo (noun).
Inherited from Old French enveie (with /ei̯/ modified to /i/ to match the verb envier), from Latin invidia.
Borrowed from Latin provocātōrem. See provoquer, -ateur.
Inherited from Middle French merde, from Old French merde, from Latin merda.

From Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's table”), from Old High German bank, banch, banc (“counter, bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”).

Inherited from Middle French espaule, from Old French espalle, from Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spathula (“flat, broad piece”), itself the diminutive of Latin spatha (“straight sword”) (whence French épée (“sword”)). Doublet of spatule, a learned borrowing.
From Old French cuiracer, from cuirace + -er. More at English cuirass, French cuirasse.

From cholestérine, from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “gall, bile”) + στερεός (stereós, “firm, solid”); coined in 1816 by Michel Eugène Chevreul. From originally being discovered by François Poulletier de la Salle in 1769, as a solid in gallstones.

From Old French cramail + -ière, from Latin cramalius, cramalium, cramaculus, cramaculum (“trammel”), alteration of cremasculus, cremasculum (“trammel”), diminutive of cremaster from Ancient Greek κρεμαστήρ (kremastḗr).

Inherited from Middle French chez, from Old French chies, from Latin casa (“house”). Doublet of case. The lack of final -e may be due to contraction in unstressed position; however, it has also been explained as the continuation of a Proto-Romance dative-genitive form case (from Latin casae).
From Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “movement”) + -graphe. Coined by the Lumière brothers in the 1890s.
From clair + voyance, from roots indicating clearsightedness and extended figuratively to precognition; compare also clairvoyant.
Inherited from Middle French couleur, from Old French color, from Latin colōrem m.
Inherited from Old French mole, muele, from Latin mola, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Borrowed from Latin rēbus, ablative plural of rēs (“thing”); cf. English rebus for further discussion.
From Middle French vicontesse, viscontesse; equivalent to vicomte (“viscount”) + -esse (“-ess”).
Inherited from Old French chevruel, chevrol, from Latin capreolus.
17th century, borrowed from Latin praecox. Doublet of abricot.
From Middle French real (“actual”) + -iser, from Old French reel, from Latin reālis, from rēs (“thing, event, deed, fact”).
Inherited from Old French descente, from descendre.
Inherited from Old French toile, earlier teile, from Latin tēla.
From sage + -esse, equivalent to Latin sapientia (“wisdom, science”).
First attested in Old French as blesseüre, corresponding to blesser + -ure.
From Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) + -ine, because xanthine is yellowish-white.
Borrowed from New Latin gastricus, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ, γαστρός (gastḗr, gastrós, “stomach”).
From parfiler (“to unravel, to weave with gold or silver thread”) + -age (“noun-forming suffix”).
Inherited from Old French banlieue, from Medieval Latin banleuca. Compare Middle High German banmile, modern German Bannmeile.
Inherited from Middle French bouche, from Old French boche, buche, from Latin bucca. Doublet of bouque.
Inherited from Old French ligne, from Latin līnea.
From the present participle of mendier, corresponding to Latin mendīcantem. Compare English mendicant, Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese mendicante.
From contre- + temps, by calque of Italian contrattempo.

Inherited from Middle French terre, from Old French terre, from Latin terra (“earth”), from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”). See cognates in regional languages in France: Norman terre; Gallo tèrr or terre; Picard tère; Bourguignon târre; Franco-Provençal and Occitan tèrra; Corsican terra.

Deverbal from éclater (“to burst”), from Middle French esclater (“to break, break violently”), from Old French esclater (“to separate from, sunder out”) (deverbal also in Old French esclat), from Frankish *slaitan (“to split, break”), from Proto-Germanic *slaitijaną, causative of Proto-Germanic *slītaną (“to cut up, split”). Akin to Old High German sleizan (“to tear”), Old English slītan (“to split”). More at slice, slit, slate, slat.
Learned borrowing from Latin prōtotypus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos).
First attested in 1881. A portmanteau/Blend of théâtre + -o + -phone.
Inherited from Middle French pareil, from Old French, from Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Compare Occitan parelh, Spanish parejo.

Inherited from Middle French cauchemare, from Old French cauquemare. By surface analysis, cauque + mar. Compare Walloon tchôcmwår. * First element from Old French cauche, from the verb chauchier (“to press”), from Latin calcare (“to trample, tread on”), from calx (“heel”), of uncertain origin. * Second element from Frankish *marā (“evil spirit”), from Proto-West Germanic *marā, from Proto-Germanic *marǭ (“nightmare, incubus”), from Proto-Indo-European *mor- (“malicious female spirit”), from *mer- (“to die”); related to the homograph English mare. More at mare.
From Vulgar Latin *viriola, diminutive of viria (“bracelet”).
From viole + -on (diminutive suffix). Compare Italian violino.
Inherited from Old French pris, from Latin pretium (“price, reward”), from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”). Compare précieux.
From Middle French saulcisson (“large sausage”), from Italian salsiccione (“large sausage”). By surface analysis, saucisse + -on.

From Old French muguete, muguede (as in nois muguete (“nutmeg”)), from Latin muscāta, feminine of muscātus (“musky”), from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian mwšk' (/⁠*mušk⁠/, “musk”), ultimately from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle”), the shape of the gland being similar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin iterativus, from Latin iteratus.
Inherited from Old French bastonet. By surface analysis, bâton + -et.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin indūbitābilis.
Inherited from Middle French brigade, from Italian brigata.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēplōrābilis. By surface analysis, déplorer + -able.
Borrowed from Latin quadrimestris, or formed on the model of trimestre.
From Renaissance Latin allantoidēs, from Ancient Greek ἀλλαντοειδής (allantoeidḗs, “sausage-shaped”).
Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Latin gurdus.
Deverbal from afficher (“to put up, display”).

Inherited from Middle French fourneau, from Old French fornel, a diminutive of Old French forn (“oven”) (Modern French four) with suffix -eau, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare Italian fornello, Occitan fornèl, Catalan fornell, Spanish hornillo, Walloon fornea, etc.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin beneficiārius. By surface analysis, bénéfice + -aire.
Inherited from Middle French écran, from Old French escran, escren, borrowed from Middle Dutch scherm, from Old Dutch *skirm, from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi, from Proto-Germanic *skirmiz.
Inherited from Old French mortier, inherited from Latin mortārium.
Borrowed from Latin chrōmaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χρωματικός (khrōmatikós).

Inherited from Old French clapier (“brothel”), from Old Occitan clapier (“rabbit hutch”), from clap (“heap of stones”), from Medieval Latin claperius, possibly of Pre-Roman or Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klappo, *klapf-, considered to either be from a Pre-Indo-European substrate or instead derived from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ- (“to cleave, split”). Compare Occitan clapàs, Catalan claper.
Inherited from Old French cercel, from Latin circellus.
Formed from radio(actif) + -ium; cf. New Latin radium.

Inherited from Old French amelette, derived by metathesis from older alemette, itself an alteration of alemelle (“blade”), probably rebracketed from la (definite article, "the") lemelle (“blade”), diminutive of lame or directly derived from Latin lamella.
Ultimately from Latin caput (“head”), with the diminutive French suffix -ote. Piecewise doublet of capot.
Inherited from Middle French responsable, corresponding to response (Modern French réponse) + -able.

Inherited from Old French, from Medieval Latin terrārius (“of earth”) from Latin terra (“earth”); or equivalent to terre + -ier. Most terrier breeds were developed to hunt vermin both over and under the ground.
From Latin nāvis (“ship”) + -ette (referring to the boat-like shape of a shuttle).
Inherited from Old French puree; feminine past participle of verb purer (“to make pure”), from Late Latin purare (same sense), from Classical Latin pūrus (“pure”).

Inherited from Middle French desrober, from Old French desrober, from des- + rober (“to steal”), the latter from Late Latin raubāre, from Frankish *raubōn, from Proto-Germanic *raubōną (“to rob; steal”).
From Middle French détail, from Old French detail, from detaillier, from de- + taillier (“to cut”).
Borrowed from German Karbatsche, from Polish karbacz, karabacz, korbacz, from Ottoman Turkish قرباچ (kırbaç).
Inherited from Old French reschignier, from Frankish *kīnan (“to split open”).

Inherited from Old French mite, miste (“playful name for cat”) + -aine. See also minet (“cat”) and Provençal mino (“female cat”), both of expressive origin. Sense 3 is borrowed from English meeting; cf. the sound change in domplaine (“dumpling”).
From vandale + -isme, coined by Henri Grégoire in 1794.
Inherited from Old French esposicion, borrowed from Latin expositiōnem.
Coined by Paul Gervais in 1850 from Ancient Greek ὅλος (hólos, “entire”) + καινός (kainós, “new”).
Learned borrowing from Latin praecīsus (“cut off”), perfect passive participle of praecīdō (“shorten”), from prae (“before”) + caedō (“cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- (“to strike”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mōbilis. Doublet of meuble.
Inherited from Old French coverture, from Late Latin coopertūra, from Latin coopertus. By surface analysis, couvrir + -ture.

Inherited from Old French putain, originally the oblique case of pute (“dirty woman”) formed with the suffix -ain, from Vulgar Latin pūtta, from Latin pūta (“girl”). Compare with salope, Italian puttana, Spanish puta.
From grogner (“to snarl, grunt, growl, grumble”) + -ard.
From lampas + -é. The word is first attested with the meaning "having lampas (an inflammation of the palate)".
From Old French non, from Latin nōn.

Inherited from Middle French main, Old French main, mein, man, from Latin manus (“hand”), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry). Compare Spanish mano and Italian mano.
Inherited from Middle French soleil, from Old French soleil, from Vulgar Latin *sōliculus, diminutive of Latin sōl (“sun”), from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.
Inherited from Old French boucle, bocle, from Latin buccula (“the cheek strap of a helmet”), diminutive of bucca.

From Middle French favori, favorit (16th c.), from Italian favorito, past participle of favorire (“to favour”). The form in -it was borrowed directly from the Italian participle, while that in -i (feminine accordingly favorie) is in line with the Middle French verb favorir (now replaced with favoriser). Inconsistent standardization led to the modern hybrid forms (compare also absous, andalou, coi, esquimau).
