Inherited from Middle French savate (“old shoe”), from Old French chavate, çavate, of unknown origin shared with Spanish zapato. Possibly from Tatar чабата (çabata, “overshoes”), ultimately either from Ottoman Turkish چاپوت (çaput, çapıt, “patchwork, tatters”), from Ottoman Turkish چاپمق (çapmak, “to slap on”), or of Iranian origin, cognate with modern Persian چپت (čapat, “a kind of traditional leather shoe”). Doublet of sabot.
From Latin exemptus, past participle of eximō.
Inherited from Old French mol, inherited from Latin mollem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin alcohol, from Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).

Inherited from Old French liere, formed by rebracketing of the elided article l' and iere m, itself from Latin hedera f, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to seize, grasp, take”). The change in gender can be explained as assimilating the more common masculine form for trees and shrubs in French.
From bannière + -et, see bannière, English banner.
Inherited from Old French convive, from Latin convīva. Compare Friulian, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish convivio.
Inherited from Old French soverain, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super. Compare Italian sovrano; Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish soberano.
From Ancient Greek ξυλοθήκη (xulothḗkē). Morphologically xylo- + -thèque.
Inherited from Old French mont, from Latin montem.
Inherited from Old French materiel, from Late Latin māteriālis (“material, made of matter”), from Latin māteria (“wood, material, substance”) from māter (“mother”).

Inherited from Middle French trouveur. By surface analysis, trouver (“to find, invent”) + -eur. Or from Old French troveor (objective/accusative case), itself from the verb trover + -eor, or possibly corresponding to a Gallo-Vulgar Latin *tropatōre(m), accusative of *tropātor, from the verb *tropō, tropāre, from Latin tropus. Cognate to Occitan trobador. See also French troubadour, which was taken from Old Occitan.
Metathesis of Old French tiule, from Latin tēgula. Doublet of tégule, a borrowing. Compare Italian tegola. Compare also Middle French teille, the Champenois form inherited from Vulgar Latin *tegla.
Borrowed from Occitan mesclum (“mixture”), from Early Medieval Latin misculāre.
Learned borrowing from New Latin cuneifōrmis, from Classical Latin cuneus (“wedge”) (whence French coin) + fōrma.
Inherited from Late Latin *frīctiōnem, from Latin frīgeō (“to be cold”). Unrelated to the Classical Latin frictiō, borrowed as French friction.
Inherited from Old French coutel, from Latin cultellus, diminutive of culter (“knife, plough blade”); cognate with Italian coltello. Not related to couper.
From Middle French merveilleux, from Old French merveillos, merveillus, equivalent to merveille + -eux.
Borrowed from Latin gnōmōn, from Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn, “indicator”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mōtīvus.
From rille (“dialectal form of reille (“small plank”)”) + -ette.
Borrowed from Italian duo. Doublet of deux.
Inherited from Middle French croistre, from Old French croistre, creistre, from Latin crēscere.
Inherited from Old French duchesse. By surface analysis, duc (“duke”) + -esse (“-ess”).
Borrowed from Latin quadratus (possibly through the intermediate of Italian quadrato). Compare the inherited doublet carré.
Inherited from Middle French suprême, borrowed from Latin suprēmus.
Inherited from Old French jambe, from Late Latin gamba.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēcapitātiō. By surface analysis, décapiter + -ation.
Borrowed from Latin equitātiōnem, from equitō (“to ride a horse”).
Inherited from Old French audience, borrowed from Latin audientia, from present participle audiēns (“hearing”), from verb audiō (“to hear”).
Early Modern French crouston, corresponding to croûte + -on.
Inherited from Late Latin puncta, from the feminine form of Latin punctus, perfect passive participle of pungō (“to prick”).
From Old French chançonete, from chanson + -ette.
From Late Latin clīnicus, from Ancient Greek κλῑνικός (klīnikós).
From Ancient Greek πρωτεῖος (prōteîos, “of the first quality”) + -ine. Coined 1838 by Dutch chemist Gerardus Johannes Mulder.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Norvegia.
Borrowed from Latin angelicus, from angelus (“angel”).
Inherited from Middle French rosette. By surface analysis, rose + -ette.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin secrētārius, from Latin secrētus.

Inherited from Old French langouste, languste, borrowed from Old Occitan langosta, from Vulgar Latin lacusta, from Latin locusta, of uncertain origin. Cf. also the Old French laöste, laüste, laouste, which was inherited from the Latin, as well as locuste, which was a learned borrowing.
From Louis + -iane. Named for king Louis XIV of France.
Compound of Old French char ("flesh", Modern French chair) + cuit (“cooked”) + -erie (suffix denoting a shop or vendor).
Inherited from Middle French ventouse, from Old French ventuse, ellipsis of Medieval Latin [cucurbita] ventōsa. Doublet of venteux and ventôse.
Possibly “going below the base” from Medieval Latin gamma ut, the note below the tonic in Guido D'Arezzo's six-note scale.
From collaborer (“to collaborate”) + -ateur. Ultimately from Latin col- (“with, together”) + labor (“work”).
Inherited from Middle French peché, from Old French pechié, from Latin peccātum.
Learned borrowing from Latin litterārius, from littera (whence lettre).
From Latin betōnica or ve(t)tōnica, from Vettones, a people in Lusitania. Compare Italian betonica.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōmptitūdō. By surface analysis, prompt + -itude.
Inherited from Old French rençon, raençon, inherited from Latin redemptiōnem. Doublet of rédemption.
From gâter (“to spoil (by soiling oneself with feces)”) + -eux.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”).
Learned borrowing from Latin galacticus (“milky”), from Ancient Greek γαλακτικός (galaktikós).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin pilula, apparently first attested in the fourteenth century, in turn inherited from the Classical Latin, attested in the medical sense in Pliny. Note that Italian pillola and Spanish píldora are widely regarded as inheritances, not borrowings.
Borrowed from Latin pubis, the genitive of pubes (“pubic hair”). The noun was generalized from medical Latin expressions such as os pubis, the pubic bone.
Borrowed from Latin aemulātōrem. Morphologically, from émuler + -ateur.
Inherited from Old French article, borrowed from Latin articulus. Compare the inherited doublet orteil.
Borrowed from Latin hibernālis or derived from hiver (“winter”).
From Old French frenesie, from Latin phrenesis, from Ancient Greek *φρένησις (*phrénēsis), a later equivalent of φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”).
From coumarou + -ine, coined by French pharmacist Nicolas Jean-Baptiste Gaston Guibourt.
Learned borrowing from Latin grabātus, from Ancient Greek κράββατος (krábbatos).
Inherited from Middle French dieu, from Old French deu, from Latin deus, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós.
Borrowed from English bitch, from Middle English biche, bicche, from Old English biċċe, from Proto-Germanic *bikjǭ.
Learned borrowing from Latin extenuātiō, extenuātiōnem.

Inherited from Middle French sucre, borrowed from Old French çucre, borrowed from Old Italian zucchero, borrowed from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), borrowed from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar), borrowed from Gandhari 𐨭𐨐𐨪 (śakara), from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorkeh₂ (“gravel”).
Inherited from Old French mievre, esmievre.
Learned borrowing from Latin vindicta. Doublet of vendetta.
Learned borrowing from Latin cōnfigūrātiō. By surface analysis, configurer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French juge, from Latin iūdicem, jūdicem, accusative singular of iūdex.
From Ancient Greek τετράγωνος (tetrágōnos, “quadrilateral, square”). By surface analysis, tétra- + -gone.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin vesperālis.
From Latin Alcaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκαϊκός (Alkaïkós), from Ἀλκαῖος (Alkaîos, “Alcaeus”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”). By surface analysis, Alcée + -ique.

Inherited from Old French geuse, josier, from Vulgar Latin *gusia or *gausia (compare Italian gozzo (“gizzard”), Friulan gose, Romanian guşă (“maw, gullet”)), from Late Latin geusiae, from Gaulish geusiae (compare Welsh gewai (“glutton”)).

Inherited from Middle French havir, from Old French havir (“to desire ardently”), either from Old French have ("pale; dull"; > French hâve) or from Frankish *haiju (“heat, burning”), akin to Old High German heiēn (“to dry; scorch; desiccate; singe”).
Borrowed from Latin oculāris, from oculus (whence œil).
Inherited from Old French chrestien or Christian, from Latin Christiānus, ultimately from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós). Doublet of crétin and Christian.
Borrowed from Latin quadriceps, from quadri- + -ceps.
Inherited from Middle French aristocratie, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā, “the rule of the best”).
From Old French heir, inherited from Latin hērēs.
Inherited from Late Latin astella, from astla, from Latin assula (“splinter”).
From Old French empoise (“weight”), from Latin impēnsa.
From Latin cōnīventia. Compare Italian connivenza, Spanish connivencia.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek νάρκωσις (nárkōsis). By surface analysis, narco- + -ose.

Possibly from Italian vogare, itself perhaps from Latin vocāre, possibly related to Ancient Greek βαυκάλη (baukálē, “crib”), or alternatively possibly of Germanic origin (related to vogue), from Proto-Germanic *wagōną (“to sway, fluctuate”).
Borrowed from Late Latin tractiōnem, from trahō.
From Middle French scelette, a learned borrowing from Latin sceletus, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós, “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”).
From Middle French arquebusier, hacquebousier, equivalent to arquebuse + -ier.
Learned borrowing from Latin dithyrambus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek διθύραμβος (dithúrambos).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἄτονος (átonos).
Borrowed from Occitan degun, from Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”). Compare Catalan degú, Spanish ninguno, Portuguese nenhum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin abōminābilis (“abominable, detestable”).
Inherited from Middle French impudent, from Latin impudentem.
Borrowed from Latin comprehēnsiōnem, from comprehendere (“to grasp”), from the prefix com- + prehendere (“to seize”).
Borrowed from Italian festino. Doublet of fête.
Learned borrowing from Latin temperantia. By surface analysis, tempéré + -ance.
Inherited from Old French interjection, borrowed from Latin interiectiōnem.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin simplex.
From Ancient Greek βάρος (báros, “weight”), from βαρύς (barús, “heavy”).
Plural of Old French bestial. The rare singular form bestiau is a back-formation from the plural.
Learned borrowing from Latin līberātor, from līberō (“to set free”). By surface analysis, libérer + -ateur.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek άλεξητήριος (álexētḗrios, “remedy”). The noun is attested since the late sixteenth century.
From Vulgar Latin *margella, from Latin margō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin tonitruō, from tonitrus (“thunder”) (whence tonnerre).
From Latin spectaculum, from spectare (“to look”).
Borrowed from Latin vulvāria, from vulva (because the plant was used in gynaecology).
Inherited from Old French rasseürer, from re- + asseürer. By surface analysis, r- + assurer.
Ultimately from Latin addictiōnem; probably through English addiction.
From épice (“spice”) + -erie, literally “spice shop”, as they originally sold spices.

Inherited from Middle French soeur, from Old French suer (nominative), from Latin soror (cf. also the Old French oblique form seror from the Latin accusative sorōrem), from Proto-Italic *swezōr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
From Late Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma, “anointing”, “unction”), from χρίω (khríō, “anoint”).
Inherited from Old French giguer, from gigue (“fiddle”).
Inherited from Middle French sablon, from Old French sablon, sablun, from Late Latin sablō, sablōnem, from Latin sabulōnem.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inguinem, a masculine form of the Classical Latin neuter noun inguen.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum. Doublet of esclandre.
From mil + -et; a diminutive of mil, from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French mitte (“kind of insect which gnaws on cloth or cheese”), from Middle Dutch mīte (“moth, mite”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mītǭ (“biting insect”, literally “cutter”), from *maitaną (“to cut”). Akin to Old English mīte (“mite, tiny insect”), Old High German mīza (“mite”), Danish mide (“mite”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολιορκητικός (poliorkētikós), from πολιορκέω (poliorkéō, “to lay siege”).
Inherited from Middle French hune, from Old French hune, a borrowing from Old Norse húnn, from Proto-Germanic *hūnaz. Cognate with English hune, hound (“foretop”).
Coined by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard in 1808, from the same root but independently of English boron.
Inherited from Latin tinea, sense from genus name Tinea for the moth.
Learned borrowing from Latin fēcunditātem. By surface analysis, fécond + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin inchoātīvus.
Learned borrowing from Latin conversiō, from convertō.
Inherited from Old French lent, from Latin lentus. Doublet of lento, taken from Italian.
Inherited from Middle French psalterion, from Old French salterion, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion), probably through Latin psalterium. Compare English psalterion.
Borrowed from Spanish puma, from Quechuan.
Pseudo-anglicism; clipping of pull-over, from English pullover.
From Late Latin pericope, from Greek περικοπή (perikopḗ, “section”).
Borrowed from Latin vivacitātem. Equivalent to vivace + -ité.
Borrowed from Latin theōricus, from Ancient Greek θεωρικός (theōrikós). By surface analysis, théorie + -ique.
Borrowed from English jogging. The sense "jogging pants" is a pseudo-anglicism.
Borrowed from German ambivalent, from Latin ambi- + Latin valēns, the latter from the verb valeō.
From Middle French houer, from Old French hoer. Synchronically houe + -er.
From Middle French estudier, from Old French estudier.

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French sergeant, sergent, serjant, sergient, sergant (“sergeant, servant”), from Medieval Latin or Late Latin servientem (“a servant, vassal, soldier, apparitor”), from Classical Latin servientem (“serving”), present participle of serviō, servīre (“serve, be a slave to”). See also servant.
From Latin octosyllabus, morphologically octo- + syllabe.
Inherited from Old French escolier, escoler, an early borrowing from Late Latin scholāris (equivalent to école + -ier), from Latin schola. Compare also the doublet scolaire, a later borrowing.
Inherited from Old French nain, from Latin nānus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin itinerans.
Borrowed from New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis).
Inherited from Middle French cors, from Old French cors, inherited from Latin corpus (“body”). The p was added back to reflect the Latin etymology. Doublet of corpus.
Borrowed from English flirt. Forms with -eu- may have arisen by influence of fleur (“flower”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ultrā. Doublet of outre.
From Old French regeneracion, from Latin regenerātiōnem.
Borrowed from English abalone, borrowed in the mid-20th century.
Borrowed from Latin prōmōtiōnem, from prōmoveō (whence French promouvoir).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”).
Borrowed from Italian biscotto. Doublet of biscotto and biscuit.
From Middle French symmetrie, from Latin symmetria, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).
From Latin Ephthalītēs, from Ancient Greek Ἐφθαλίτης (Ephthalítēs).
Inherited from Middle French chilindre, cylindre, that borrowed from Latin cylindrus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros). Doublet of calandre.
Learned borrowing from Latin scincos, from Ancient Greek σκίγκος (skínkos).
From New Latin isometria, from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to iso- + -métrie.
Inherited from Old French voisin, veisin, from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.
Inherited from Middle French prouesse, from Old French proece, proeche, proesce. See preux and -esse.
Calque of English defragment, or dé- + fragmenter
Inherited from Middle French Castelan, borrowed from Spanish castellano, from Latin castellanus. Doublet of châtelain, the native French word, and castellan.
Inherited from Old French discret, borrowed from Latin discretus (“separate”).
From Latin mūtus + -ité, on the model of surdité and cécité; see also Medieval Latin mūtitātem.
Inherited from Middle French densité, from Old French dempsité, borrowed from Latin dēnsitātem.
Borrowed from Late Latin cōnstructor (“builder”), from Latin cōnstruere (“to build, pile together”).
Inherited from Old French sauge, from Latin salvia.
Borrowed from Latin corrēctor, from corrigō (“to straighten (out), rectify, correct”).
Borrowed from English palace, itself from Old French palais. Doublet of palais.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἰσόπλευρος (isópleuros), from ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + πλευρά (pleurá, “side”).
Learned borrowing from Latin decemvirālis. By surface analysis, décemvir + -al.
Inherited from Old French joie, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin *gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium.
Borrowed from Latin refractārius (“obstinate”), from refractus (“broken up”).
From Latin hebdomadārius, from Latin hebdomas (English hebdomad), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “seven, group of seven”).
Inherited from Old French quelesquunques, a borrowing of Latin qualiscumque, matched to the Old French quel (“which”) + que (“what”) + onques (“ever”). See Italian qualunque, a similar formation.
Inherited from Old French sanc, from Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”).
Inherited from Old French alechier, probably from a Vulgar Latin root *allecticāre, from Latin allectāre.
Influenced by professeur, from Latin profiteor.
Learned borrowing from Latin pectorālis. Doublet of poitrail.
From Middle French subterfuge m, borrowed from Medieval Latin subterfugium n, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugio (“to flee”).
From Latin suffix -phagus, from Ancient Greek φάγος (phágos, “glutton”), from Ancient Greek φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”).
From Italian dogale, from Late Latin ducalis (“ducal”). Doublet of ducal.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin quadrangulāris. See quatre and angle.

Probably borrowed from German Entropie, from Ancient Greek ἐντροπῐ́ᾱ (entropĭ́ā); literally "turning over" but taken in the sense of "transforming". A term proposed in 1850 by the German physicist R. J. Clausius by analogy with German Energie.
Learned borrowing from Latin iūbilātiōnem (“a shouting for joy”). By surface analysis, jubiler + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French Volsque, from Latin Volscus.
From Latin collum. Doublet of col. Cognate with Italian collo, Galician and Portuguese colo, Spanish cuello.
Borrowed from English hall. Doublet of halle.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀέρος (aéros), the genitive singular of ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”).

Inherited from Middle French estriquer, borrowed from Middle Dutch striken (“to stroke, smooth”), from Old Dutch *strīcan. Cognate with English strike. Compare also Old French estrikier, estriquer (“to strike”).
Inherited from Middle French bataille, from Old French bataille, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō, of Gaulish origin.
Inherited from Old French antartique, from Latin antarcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós).

Inherited from Middle French immun (“acquitted, exempt”), from Latin immūnis (literally “dutyless”). The use of the word to refer to medical, rather than judicial, immunity is due to the influence of English immune.
Inherited from Middle French preferer, from Old French preferer, borrowed from Latin praeferre.
Borrowed from Latin dēmentia, from dēmēns.
Learned borrowing from Latin cōpulātiōnem. By surface analysis, copuler + -ation.

Learned borrowing from Latin abyssus, whence also the doublet abîme. Isolated uses can already be found of Middle French abys, Old French abis, but the word did not really enter the language before the 19th century. The adjective abyssal is older, however.

Inherited from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Compare Catalan ple; Italian pieno; Portuguese cheio; Romanian plin; Sardinian prenu; Spanish lleno; English plene, full.

Inherited from Middle French fesser, derived from Old French faisse, fece ( compare Old French faisser), derived from Latin fascia. The spelling and sense (originally "to strike with a rod") influenced by unrelated fesse (“buttock”)). Compare also Late Latin fasciāre.
Inherited from Middle French subiection, from Latin subiectiōnem, accusative of subiectiō.

Inherited from Middle French déguerpir, deswerpir (“to leave”), from Old French deguerpir (“to abandon”), from de- + guerpir (“to give up, abandon”), from Frankish *wurpijan (“to throw, cast off”), from Proto-Germanic *werpaną (“to throw”), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to turn, twist”). Compare Walloon diwerpi, Occitan degurpir, Middle French gurpir (“to give up, abandon”). Cognate with Old High German werfan (“to throw”), Old English weorpan (“to throw, cast, cast away”). More at warp.
From Latin oleum (“oil”) + dūcō (“to guide”), on the model of aqueduc.
Learned borrowing from Latin dīxit (“he or she has said”).
Inherited from Old French teie, inherited from Latin thēca, itself from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē). Doublet of thèque and -thèque.
Borrowed from Spanish cacahuete, from cacahuate (“peanut”), from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl (“cocoa bean”).
Inherited from Old French santé, from Latin sānitātem.

From Old French faramineux (“verminous”), referring to a "bête faramine", a wondrous beast of Breton legend, from faramine (“vermine,harmful animal”), from Vulgar Latin feramen, ultimately from Latin fera (“beast, wild animal”).
Inherited from Latin tormenta, plural of tormentum.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin meditativus. By surface analysis, méditer + -atif.
Calque of English overtourism. Also sur- + tourisme.
Learned borrowing from Latin īnfidēlis. By surface analysis, in- + fidèle.
Inherited from Old French proportion, borrowed from Latin prōportiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin comestibilis, from Latin comedō (“to eat”).
Inherited from Middle French presteur. By surface analysis, prêter + -eur.
Learned borrowing from Latin ignifer. By surface analysis, igni- + -fère.
From Italian and Maltese Malta, from Arabic مالطا, from Latin Melita.

Inherited from Middle French huyle, from Old French oile, from Latin oleum, from olea (“olive”), from Ancient Greek ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”). The h was added in Middle French to indicate that the u was a vowel, as in typography u and v were used interchangeably at the time. Compare huit (“eight”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνδροκτόνος (androktónos), from ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”) + κτείνω (kteínō, “slay”).
Inherited from Old French sermoner, sermuner. By surface analysis, sermon + -er.
From monter + charge. Compare Spanish montacargas and Portuguese monta-cargas.
From Latin indicātiōnem. By surface analysis, indiquer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French turquois, from turc + -ois.
Inherited from Old French martire, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).
From Latin Tusculānus, from Tusculum + -ānus. By surface analysis, Tuscule + -an.
Borrowed from Latin dioecēsis (“district under a governor”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek διοίκησις (dioíkēsis).
From Old Occitan bigorna, from Latin bicornis. Doublet of bicorne.
From Middle French vieillesse. By surface analysis, vieil + -esse. Compare Catalan vellesa, Spanish vejez, Italian vecchiaia.

Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French vipre, directly borrowed from Latin vīpera. Displaced an earlier Old French doublet guivre (cf. also French vouivre) and its Old Northern French equivalent wivre.

Inherited from Middle French verge (“rod or wand of office”), hence "scope, territory dominated", from Old French verge, virge, from Latin virga (“shoot, rod stick”), of uncertain origin, but probably from a Proto-Indo-European *wisgeh₂ (“flexible rod or stick”). Doublet of vergue.
Borrowed from Latin lāmella (“small, thin plate”), the diminutive of lāmina (“thin plate, knife blade”). This is the etymon of French omelette, English omelet.
From Old French chamel (whence French chameau) + -et.
From Latin polemarchus, from Ancient Greek πολέμαρχος (polémarkhos).
From Old French chamel (whence French chameau) + -on.
Inherited from Old French empeechier, inherited from Latin impedicāre. Cognate with English impeach. Doublet of empiéger.
Borrowed from Late Latin praeteritiōnem, from praetereō (“to pass by”).
From Latin Atropatēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτροπατηνός (Atropatēnós). By surface analysis, Atropatès + -ène.
Learned borrowing from Latin pugnācitās. By surface analysis, pugnace + -ité.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄσπερμος (áspermos). By surface analysis, a- + -sperme.
Inherited from Middle French particulier, from Old French particulier, borrowed from Latin particularis.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥοία (rhoía, “flow, flux”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσθένεια (asthéneia), from ἀσθενής (asthenḗs, “sick, weak”), from ἀ- (a-, “not, un-”) + σθένος (sthénos, “strength”).

Inherited from Old French soif, from earlier seif, seit, from Latin sitis. The unetymological -f seems to have been inserted, following cases such as Old French noif (“snow”), possibly to avoid homophony with soit (“[may] it be”) and soi (“-self”).
From in- + puissance (or possibly from impuissant + -ance).
From mitrailleuse, with substitution of suffix (mitrailler + -ette).
Inherited from Middle French Cynosure, from Latin Cynosura, from Ancient Greek Κυνοσούρα (Kunosoúra).
Borrowed from Latin stupidus (“struck senseless, amazed”), from stupeō (“be amazed or confounded, be struck senseless”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin devolutiōnem, from Latin devolvō.
Inherited from Old French champestre, from Latin campestrem.

From Middle French tribut (15th c.), learned alteration of Old French treü (12th c.), itself either inherited or early borrowed from Latin tribūtus. Forms such as trebu (14th c.) show that the relatinization was a gradual process.
Inherited from Middle French incarnation, from Old French incarnacion, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French embleme, from Latin emblēma, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma).

From Middle French, from Medieval Latin īnstallāre (“to install, put in place, establish”), from in- + stallum (“stall”), from Frankish *stall (“stall, position, place”), from Proto-Germanic *stallaz (“place, position”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to place, put, post, stand, be rigid”). Cognate with Old High German stal (“location, stall”), Old English steall (“position, stall”), Old English onstellan (“to institute, create, originate, establish, give the example of”), Middle High German anstalt (“institute”), German anstellen (“to conduct, employ”), German einstellen (“to set, adjust, position”), Dutch aanstellen (“to appoint, commission, institute”), Dutch instellen (“to set up, establish”). More at on, stall.
Borrowed from German Dreifuß, an older name for Trèves, from Latin Augusta Trēverōrum.
Borrowed from English pudding. Doublet of boudin.
Inherited from Old French acolyt, from Ecclesiastical Latin acolytus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).
Inherited from Middle French toi, tei, from Old French tei, te, from Latin tē.
From Old French beve (altered based on baver), from Vulgar Latin root *baba, of imitative origin. Compare Spanish baba, Portuguese baba.
Borrowed from Latin bracchiālis, from bracchium (“arm”).
From Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis). Doublet of dot.

Inherited from Middle French marinier, from Old French mariner. By surface analysis, marin + -ier. Compare Catalan mariner, Italian marinaio, Spanish marinero, Portuguese marinheiro. Cf. also Vulgar Latin marinarius.
From Medieval Latin dentālis, from Latin dēns (“a tooth”). By surface analysis, dent + -al.

Borrowed from Arabic فُنْدُق (funduq), borrowed from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon), from πᾰν- (păn-, “all, every”) + δοκ- (dok-, o-grade of the stem of δέχομαι (dékhomai, “to receive”)) + -εῖον (-eîon).
Borrowed from Latin amiantus, from Ancient Greek ἀμίαντος (amíantos).

From Middle French navigation, from Old French [Term?], from Latin nāvigātiōnem (“sailing, navigation”), from nāvigātus, perfect passive participle of nāvigō (“sail”). By surface analysis, naviguer + -tion.
From prime (adjective) + -eur (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns from adjectives).

PIE word  *ḱóm From Old French contraction, borrowed from Latin contractiōnem, the accusative singular of contractiō (“a drawing together, contraction; abridgement, shortening; dejection, despondency”), from contrahō (“to draw things together, assemble, collect, gather; to enter into a contract”) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to actions or their results); contrahō is derived from con- (prefix denoting a bringing together of objects) + trahō (“to drag, pull”) (probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to drag, pull; to run”)).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin susceptibilis.
Borrowed from English yacht, from Dutch jacht.
Learned borrowing of Latin cadmīa, from Ancient Greek καδμεία (kadmeía). Compare calamine.
By surface analysis, télécharger + -ment or télé- + chargement
Borrowed from Latin asyndeton, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδετον (asúndeton).
Inherited from Latin cornūtus. Equivalent to corne + -u.
From sous- + fifre (“pipe (instrument)”). Compare second fiddle.
Borrowed from New Latin trājectōria f (“trajectory”) (used by Newton).
Inherited from Middle French miroir m, Old French mireor m. Equivalent to mirer + -oir.

Inherited from Middle French suave, borrowed from Latin suāvis (“sweet, pleasant”), replacing the inherited form souef (in use until the 17th century), from Old French soef, suef (“sweet, mild, agreeable, tranquil, peaceful”), descendants of which live on in other Oïl languages.
Borrowed from Middle French bulle, from Old French bulle, borrowed from Latin bulla. Doublet of the inherited boule.
From Latin anabaptismus, from Ancient Greek ἀνα (ana) "thorough" + Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma) "baptism".
Inherited from Old French tonsure, borrowed from Latin tōnsūra (“a clipping, trimming”), from tondeō (“shear, clip, trim”).
From Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + κάμπτω (kámptō, “to bend”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Trōglodytae (“cave-dwelling people”), from Ancient Greek τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs, “one who dwells in holes”).
Inherited from Old French liberal, from Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”).
Learned borrowing from Latin apostasia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía, “withdrawl, defection”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin itinerārium, from Late Latin itinerārius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Scientific Latin iugulāris, from Latin iugulum.
Borrowed from English paddy, from Malay padi.
Inherited from Middle French nonchaloir, from Old French chaloir (“to heat”), from non + chaloir.
Learned borrowing from Latin inattingibilis. By surface analysis, in- + attingible.
Inherited from Old French semer, from Latin sēmināre.
Ultimately from Latin brāca (“breeches”), itself from Transalpine Gaulish *brāca, from Proto-Germanic *brāks, *brōks (“breeches, pants”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre, from Latin in- + clāvis + -āre.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Late Latin dēfēnsa, from Latin dēfendō.
Inherited from Latin ventōsus, or coined in French from vent + -eux. See also ventouse.
Learned borrowing from Latin implicātiō. By surface analysis, impliquer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin auriculāris. Doublet of oreiller.
From Latin lenifiantem, present participle of lenifaciō (“make smooth”), from lenis (“smooth”) + faciō (“to do, to make”).
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin roborētum. Analyzable as rouvre + -aie. Cognate with Italian rovereto, Occitan roveda.
Inherited from Old French espice, an old (12th century) borrowing from Latin speciēs, which in Late Latin meant "spice", "foodstuff", "commodity", "drug". Doublet of espèce.
Inherited from Old French poindre, puindre, from Latin pungere.
Inherited from Old French rural, a borrowing from Latin rūrālis (“rural”), from rūs (“countryside”) + -ālis.

Inherited from Middle French houblon, houbelon (15th c.), from a confluence of two words: * Middle French hoppe, houppe (“hopped beer”, 14th c.), from Middle Dutch hoppe (“hops”), from Old Dutch *hoppo, from Frankish *hoppō (“hops”), of uncertain further origin. See English hop for more. * Old French homlon (“hops”, 11th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *humilō (“hops”), also of uncertain origin, but assumed to be of Finnic/Uralic origin, as the Finno-Ugric tribes were the first to use hops for beer. Cognate with Old English hymele, Middle Low German hōmel, and probably Proto-Slavic *xъmeľь.
Learned borrowing from Latin aestuārium. Doublet of étier.
From Latin pharetra, from Ancient Greek φαρέτρα (pharétra).
Learned borrowing from Latin metaphora, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).

Inherited from Middle French aubin, hobin, hobi, from Old French hobi, *haubi, haubby, hobin (“a nag, hobby”), from Old French hober, ober (“to stir, move”), from Old Dutch *hobbon (“to toss, move up and down”) (Modern Dutch hobben (“to bob, wear oneself out”)); or from North Germanic origin related to Danish hoppe (“a mare”), Old Swedish hoppa (“a young mare”), North Frisian hoppe (“horse”); both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *huppōną (“to hop”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewb- (“to bend; a bend, joint”). More at hobby, hop, hobble.
Clipping of restaurant. The original spelling restau has been altered to resto under the influence of other colloquial nouns in -o.
Inherited from Middle French million, from Italian milione.
Borrowed from Latin captūra (“catching, capture”), from captus, perfect passive participle of capiō (“capture, seize, take”).
Borrowed from Latin condēnsātiōnem. Equivalent to condenser + -ation.
Unadapted borrowing from Late Latin ūvula (“small grape”), diminutive of Latin ūva. Doublet of uvule, another borrowing.
Based on the verb contrefaire. Composed of contre- + façon (the latter taken as a noun counterpart to faire).
Borrowing from Italian don or older dom, from Latin dominus (“master”). Cognate with English don.
Borrowed from Russian во́дка (vódka), diminutive of вода́ (vodá, “water”).
Inherited from Old French geu, gieu, giu, from Latin iocus, jocus.
From Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā).
Inherited from Old French gesir, from Latin iacēre. The final -ir < Latin -ēre is regular and results from the palatalization of the preceding -c- to *[d͡zʲ], as in loisir, moisir, plaisir.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin abbreviātiōnem. See also abréger and -ation.

Inherited from Middle French dialogue, from Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos, “conversation, discourse”), from διά (diá, “through, inter”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, discourse”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to converse”), from διά (diá) + λέγειν (légein, “to speak”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin tyrannia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τυραννία (turannía). By surface analysis, tyran + -ie.

From Old French berçuel (diminutive of bers) from Vulgar Latin berciolum diminutive of *bertium, from Gaulish *berta, from Proto-Celtic *bertā, variant of *bereti (“to carry”). Compare Old Irish bert (“bundle”). Cognate with Catalan bressol, Portuguese berço and Galician berce.
Inherited from Middle French aronde, from Old French aronde, from Latin hirundō (cf. harundo), possibly a borrowing, according to the TLFi.

Borrowed from Latin astrologia (“astronomy”) (equivalent to astro- + -logie), from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογία (astrología, “telling of the stars”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin īnsufflātiō. By surface analysis, insuffler + -ation.
Inherited from Old French proie, preie, from Latin praeda (probably via a Late Latin variant proeda or *prēda; the expected outcome of praeda would be *priée).
Learned borrowing from Latin nomotheta /nomothetēs, from Ancient Greek νομοθέτης (nomothétēs).
Borrowing from Latin dēbitum (“debt”). Doublet of dette
Inherited from Middle French crepuscule m, from Old French crepuscule m (first attested in the late 13th c.), borrowed from Latin crepusculum n.
Adjective - from Latin generalissimus; see général + -issime Noun - from Italian generalissimo
Borrowed from Late Latin coriāceus (“leathery”), a derivative of corium (→ French cuir (“leather”)). Doublet of cuirasse.
From Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus.
Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”).
From légal + -ité, or borrowed from Medieval Latin legalitātem, from Latin legalis. Compare also loyauté.
Inherited from Old French remetre, inherited from Latin remittō. By surface analysis, re- + mettre.

Inherited from Middle French voluntaire, from late Old French voluntaire, borrowed from Latin voluntārius (“voluntary; volunteer”), from voluntās (“free will”), from volō, velle (“wish, intend”). Compare volontiers, inherited from a related word.

Inherited from Middle French machine, borrowed from Latin machina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), itself a borrowing from Doric Ancient Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́). Not to be confused with machin, which means "thing".
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χρυσελεφάντινος (khruselephántinos, “gold”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin adhērentem.
From re- + pousser, or from Late Latin repulsāre.
From Spanish noria, from Arabic نَاعُورَة (nāʕūra), from Classical Syriac ܢܥܘܪܬܐ (nāʿōrtāʾ, “water wheel; growler”), from ܢܥܪ (nʿar, “to roar, growl, bray”).
Learned borrowing from Latin līmitātiōnem. By surface analysis, limiter + -ation.
Borrowed from German Harmonika; compare harmonique.
Inherited from Old French atisier, from Vulgar Latin *attītiāre, derived from Latin tītiō (“firebrand”).
Borrowed from Late Latin mandibula, from Latin mandō.

Learned borrowing from Latin polyōnymos (adjective), from Ancient Greek πολυώνυμος (poluṓnumos, adjective), from πολυ- (polu-, “poly-”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”) + -ος (-os, suffix forming compound adjectives). By surface analysis, poly- + -onyme (adjective-forming suffix).
Learned borrowing from Latin viāticum. Doublet of voyage.
First known attestation 1314, borrowed from Latin compressiōnem.
From an alteration, through the influence of conduire, of Old French escondire, itself from a Vulgar Latin *excondīcere, from Latin ex- + condīcere.

Inherited from Middle French arrimer, from Old French arimer (“to dispose of goods in the appropriate manner, store goods in the hold of a ship”), from Middle English rimen (“to make room for, clear away”), from Old English rȳman (“to make roomy, extend, widen, spread, enlarge, amplify, prolong, clear, open up, make clear by removing obstructions, to clear a way”), from Proto-Germanic *rūmijaną (“to make roomy, give room, remove”), from Proto-Indo-European *rewh₁- (“free space”). Cognate with Old Norse rýma (“to make room for, clear away, break up”). More at ream.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek δεικτικός (deiktikós, “capable of proof”).
From Old French cohabitacion, from Late Latin cohabitātiō. By surface analysis, co- + habitation.
Inherited from Old French diminucion, borrowed from Latin dīminūtiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin pulpōsus, from Latin pulpa. By surface analysis, pulpe + -eux. Cf. the older form poulpeux.

From Latin decēnārius, with unetymological doubling of the ⟨n⟩ under the influence of décennal and décennie. Compare sénaire / sexénaire, septénaire, novénaire, dénaire / décénaire, which are regularly derived.
Borrowed from Late Latin volūminōsus, from volūmen (whence volume).
From New Latin appendiculāris, from Latin appendicem.
Borrowed from Late Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós).
Inherited from Middle French moral, from Old French moral, borrowed from Latin morālis.
Inherited from Middle French vessie, from Old French vessie, from Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca.
Borrowed from Latin calceolārius, via the feminine.
Borrowed from Latin silentiōsus (adjective). Documented since 1527.
Inherited from Old French genest, earlier geneste f, from Latin genesta.
Learned borrowing from New Latin analgēsia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀναλγησίᾱ (analgēsíā, “want of feeling, insensibility”).
Learned borrowing from Latin barbula (“little beard”).
Borrowed from Late Latin metathesis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετάθεσις (metáthesis).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos).
Borrowed from Latin inertia (“want of art or skill; inactivity”), from iners (“inept, slow”), itself from in- (“not”) + ars (“art, skill”).
Inherited from Middle French clergié, from Old French, from Late Latin clēricātus, from clēricus. Compare Italian chiericato.
Learned borrowing from Latin perfidia. By surface analysis, perfide + -ie.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin captiōsus.
From in- + convénient, or from Middle French inconvenient, borrowed from Latin inconvenientem.

Inherited from Middle French prognostic, borrowed from Medieval Latin prognōsticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from προ- (pro-, “before”) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “relating to knowledge”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to be aware of, perceive, observe, know, learn”).
Inherited from Middle French pire, from Old French pire, from Latin peior, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yōs (“to the ground, downward”). Related to pis.
Borrowed from Latin ligāmentum, from ligō (“tie, bind”). Cf. also liement, possibly an inherited doublet.

From Middle French pluvieux, from Old French pluviex (13th c.), from Latin pluviōsus. The regular descendant of this is Old French plujos, which would have yielded modern *plugeux; compare Catalan plujós. By analogy with pluie, there was also a byform pluios (Middle French pluyeux), in which /v/ may have been inserted after plovoir; compare the Middle French variants plouvieux, pleuvieux. However, the form may also be of learned origin and was, at any rate, reinforced by its Latinate shape.
Learned borrowing from Latin poēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós).
From Middle French ravoir: equivalent to re- + avoir.
Borrowed from Spanish cacao, ultimately from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl.
Inherited from Middle French errone, from Latin errōneus (“vagrant, wrong”), from errō (“to go astray”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περικάρδιον (perikárdion).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure; hoard”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse; treasure”). See also the doublet trésor.

Inherited from Old French [Term?] (compare 11th-century Judeo-French jencives, 12th-century Walloon genchives), from Latin gingīva (with dissimilation of the second -g-), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
Borrowed from Latin merīdiōnālis, from merīdiēs (“noon; south”).
From Latin Tāprobana, from Ancient Greek Ταπροβάνη (Taprobánē).

Inherited from Middle French moufle, from Old French mofle (“thick glove”), from Medieval Latin muffula (817, Carolingian), a Germanic borrowing from Frankish *molfell (“soft garment made of hide”), from *mol (“softened, forworn”) + *fell (“hide, skin”), from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz (“tender, soft”) + *fellą (“skin, film, fleece”). Compare modern Dutch moffel.
Inherited from Middle French ruyne, from Old French ruine, borrowed from Latin ruīna.
From Latin prōvideō (“to foresee; to provide”) (supine stem prōvīs-) + -oire (suffix forming adjectives).
Inherited from Middle French formeus, from Latin fōrmōsus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin claustrālis.
Inherited from Middle French gaster, from Old French gaster, guaster, which see for more.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἕδρα (hédra, “seat, base”).
From émett(ant) (stem of the present participle of émettre) + -eur.

Borrowed from Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talent”).
Inherited from Middle French hostilité (attested from 1353), borrowed from Latin hostilitātem.

Inherited from Middle French athletique, a learned borrowing from Latin āthlēticus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾱ̓θλητῐκός (āthlētĭkós), from ἀθλητής (athlētḗs, “athlete”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjective suffix). By surface analysis, athlète + -ique.
From capter (“to capture; to sense”) + -eur (suffix forming agent nouns from verbs).
Learned borrowing from New Latin indium.
From Latin clīmactēricus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek κλιμακτηρικός (klimaktērikós).
Inherited from Old French pestilence, borrowed from Latin pestilentia.
Inherited from Middle French jaune, iaune, from Old French jaune, jalne, from Latin galbinus.
Learned borrowing from Latin stratēgus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós, “general”).
Inherited from Middle French departir, from Old French departir, from Late Latin departīre, from Latin de + partiō. Or from dé- + partir.
Borrowed from Latin cōnsortium, from consors, consortis.
Ca. 1600, borrowed from Latin castrāre. Doublet of inherited châtrer.
From servir + -eur. Cf. also Old French serveor, Late Latin servitor.
Inherited from Middle French respondre, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēpositārius.

Borrowed from Portuguese casta, if of Germanic origin, possibly from Gothic *𐌺𐌰𐍃𐍄𐍃 (*kasts), from Proto-Germanic *kastuz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ǵ-es- (“to throw”), similar to English cast. Or, alternatively from a derivative of Latin castus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χορηγός (khorēgós).
Calque of English superpower, from super- + pouvoir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sempiternālis.
Borrowed from Latin immātūritātem. By surface analysis, immature + -ité or im- + maturité.

Borrowed from Italian trempellino, from trempellare, from an unidentified Germanic form. Compare Middle Low German, Middle High German trampeln, Middle English trample. Attested since 1680 while Italian trampolino is only attested since early 19th century.
Inherited from Middle French toutesfoys, from the plurals toutes and fois. In Old French, the adverb was totesvoies (from voie (“way”)), closer to Italian tuttavia and Portuguese todavia.
Inherited from Middle French lectionnaire, borrowed from Medieval Latin lēctiōnārium (“lectionary”), derived from Latin lēctiō (“lesson”) + -ārium.
From Old French anet (ca. 1300), a borrowing from Latin anēthum, from Ancient Greek ἄνηθον (ánēthon).
From ré- + organisation. Compare with the verb réorganiser.
Inherited from Middle French fer, from Old French fer, from Latin ferrum.
Borrowed from Dutch sering, from Medieval Latin sȳringa, from Classical Latin sȳrinx. Doublet of seringue.
From Medieval Latin gabulum, of Celtic origin, from Gaulish gabalos, from Proto-Celtic *gablā (“fork”). Closely related to Old Norse gafl (English gable).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin zerumbet, zurumbet, zurumbeth, from Arabic زُرُنْبَاد (zurunbād), from Persian زرنباد (zoronbâd).
Learned borrowing from Latin vēnālitās. By surface analysis, vénal + -ité.
Inherited from Old French taille, deverbal of Old French taillier (“to cut”). Compare Italian taglia, Catalan talla.
From Occitan embrum, from embruma (“to drizzle”).
Inherited from Old French fraternité, borrowed from Latin frāternitātem, from frāter (“brother”). * Cognate with Italian fraternità, Spanish fraternidad
Inherited from Middle French pontife m, learned borrowing from Latin pontifex m.
Learned borrowing from Latin catēchēsis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin prioritātem, derived from Latin prior.
Borrowed from New Latin grāvitāre, from Latin grāvitās.
Inherited from Middle French cervoise, from Old French cervoise, from Latin cervēs(i)a.
Inherited from Middle French deité, from Latin deitātem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pediluvium.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōdigālitās.
From Old French matiere, borrowed from Latin materia.
Borrowed from Latin occlūsiōnem (“occluding", "obstruction”), from the Classical Latin occlūdō (“to shut up or close up”, “to restrain”), from ob + claudō (“to shut or close”).
Inherited from Old French desparer. By surface analysis, dé- + parer.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mictiōnem, from the verb mingō.
Inherited from Middle French queste, from Old French queste, from Latin quaesta, noun use of quaesita, feminine of quaesitus, past participle of quaerō.
Learned borrowing from Latin energīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).
Learned borrowing from Latin exhortātiōnem. By surface analysis, exhorter + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پری (peri), from Persian پری (pari).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek διήγησις (diḗgēsis).
Learned borrowing from Latin pilōsus. Doublet of pelouse, a borrowing from Provençal or Occitan.
Inherited from Middle French farde, from Old French farde (“load, package, bundle”), a borrowing from Arabic فَرْدَة (farda, from فَرْد (fard, “a spread, an unfolding”)).
Learned borrowing from Latin formālis, from forma (“form”) (whence forme).
From Ancient Greek ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company, later a people, nation”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin virtuālis.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin exterminātiōnem. By surface analysis, exterminer + -ation.
From English subsection. By surface analysis, sous- + section.
From terrasse + -er. First attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Italian maggiordomo, from Late Latin maior domūs (“steward”), from Latin maior (“main, principal”) + genitive singular of domus (“household”).
Learned borrowing from Latin quadrāgēsima. Doublet of carême.
Middle French chicquenode, from Occitan chicanaudo.
Inherited from Old French consideracion, from Latin cōnsīderātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φώνημα (phṓnēma).
Inherited from Old French espineus, espinus, from Latin spīnōsus. By surface analysis, épine + -eux.
From Old French averer, from Early Medieval Latin advērō, derived from Latin vērus (“true”).
Borrowed from Italian carezzare. Morphologically, from caresse + -er.
Inherited from Old French sec, from Latin siccus (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.
Alteration of Old French hante, influenced by Latin hasta.
Learned borrowing from Latin rigiditās. By surface analysis, rigide + -ité.
Borrowed from Latin portionem (accusative singular of portio).
Inherited from Old French cruel, from Latin crūdēlis; either remade based on the Latin or evolved from the Old French form crual, possibly from a Vulgar Latin form *crūdālis.
Inherited from Middle French perfection, from Latin perfectiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French fracture, from late Old French fracture, borrowed from Latin fractūra. Compare the inherited Old French fraiture, and the frainture (influenced by fraindre).
Learned borrowing from Latin multiplicātiō. By surface analysis, multiplier + -ation.
Borrowed from Latin acanthus, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos).
From marin, from Latin marīnus, derived from mare (“sea”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin incorruptibilitātem.
Borrowed from Latin diaeta, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin deambulātōrium.

Inherited from Middle French Escosse, from Old French Escoce, Escouce, from Latin Scōtia. The Old French variant with ou is the expected one. However, it seems unlikely that the word was inherited through Vulgar Latin in either form.
Inherited from Old French estanc, from estanchier (modern: étancher).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prosēlytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”).
Learned borrowing from Latin hyacinthus. Doublet of jacinthe.
Inherited from Old French com(m)unalté, alteration after comunal (see communal) of communité, itself borrowed from Latin communitātem.
Borrowed from Breton boued, from Middle Breton boet, from Old Breton boit-ol-ion, from Proto-Brythonic *buɨd, from Proto-Celtic *beitom, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃tom, from *gʷeyh₃-.
From Latin rādīx, rādīcis (“root”) + -ande, on the model of multiplicande, dividende.
From Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French savourer, from savour. Compare with the noun saveur.
Inherited from Middle French miel, from Old French miel, Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.
From Middle French pacification, from Old French pacification, from Latin pācificātiō.
Inherited from Middle French eschapper, from Old French eschaper, from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”). Doublet of escaper.
Inherited from Old French ordre, ordene, borrowed from Latin ōrdinem (accusative of ōrdo). Doublet of the inherited orne, now a regional term with a specialized agricultural sense.
Inherited from Old French mahustre (“shoulder”) (12th c.).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin paritātem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nephriticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek νεφριτικός (nephritikós).
Inherited from Middle French numerateur, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin numerātōr.
Borrowed from Latin cicātrīcula, diminutive of cicātrīx (“scar”).
From Old French espars, past participle of espardre.
Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek συστολή (sustolḗ), from συστέλλω (sustéllō, “to contract”), from σύν (sún, “together”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to send”).
Inherited from Middle French tremblay. Also tremble + -aie.
Inherited from Old French solstice, a learned borrowing from Latin sōlstitium, from sōl + sistō + -ium.
Inherited from Middle French cheveu, from Old French cheveu, from Latin capillus. See there for more details.
Inherited from Old French violette, from viole + -ette, from Latin viola.
Borrowed from Spanish caudillo, from Late Latin capitellum. Doublet of cadeau, cadet, and chapiteau.
Borrowed from Occitan pechaire (the Vivaro-Alpine form of pecaire, used in Provençal too as an interjection), from Latin peccātor (“sinner”). Doublet of pécaïre.
Borrowed from Old Occitan sorba, from Vulgar Latin *sorba, feminine singular formed from the plural of Latin sorbum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *classum, from Latin classicum (“trumpet signal”).
From Latin hilaris (“cheerful, merry”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful”).
Learned borrowing from Latin nūllitātem; morphologically, from nul + -ité.

PIE word  *h₂éd From Old French ascendant, borrowed from Latin ascendentem, the accusative singular of ascendēns (“ascending, rising”), the present participle of ascendō, adscendō (“to climb up, go up, move upwards; to rise; to spring up”), from ad- (prefix meaning ‘(up) to’) + scandō (“to ascend, climb, mount; to clamber”) (from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to climb, scale; to dart; to jump; to scan (poetry)”)).
Inherited from Middle French nosocome, from Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon).
Inherited from Old French pais, paiz, from Latin pāx (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to join, to attach”).
From Ancient Greek μύρμηξ (múrmēx, “ant”) + χωρέω (khōréō, “to carry, transport”). By surface analysis, myrméco- + -chore.
Borrowed from Latin sinister, whence also French senestre, an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from English alien (“stranger, foreigner”), from Middle English alien, from Old French alien, from Latin aliēnus.
Inherited from Old French ametiste, from Latin amethystus.
Inherited from Middle French sembler, from Old French sembler, from Late Latin similāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). Doublet of simuler.
Inherited from Old French trot, troter, from Medieval Latin trottare, of Germanic origin.
From Old French columbin, from Latin columbinus.
Learned borrowing from Latin mētropolītānus. By surface analysis, métropolite + -ain.

Inherited from Middle French amuser (“to amuse, divert, babble”), from Old French amuser (“to stupefy, waste time, be lost in thought”), from a- + muser (“to stare stupidly at, gape, wander, waste time, loiter, think carefully about, attend to”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Cognate with Occitan musa (“idle waiting”), Italian musare (“to gape idly about”). Possibly from Old French *mus (“snout”) from Vulgar Latin *mūsa (“snout”) (compare Medieval Latin mūsum (“muzzle, snout”)), from Proto-Germanic *mū- (“muzzle, snout”), from Proto-Indo-European *mū- (“lips, muzzle”). Compare German Maul (“muzzle, snout”). An alternative etymology connects Old French muser and Occitan musa with Old High German muoza (“careful attention, leisure, idleness”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtǭ (“leave, permission”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to acquire, possess, control”). Compare also Old High German muozōn (“to be idle, have leisure or opportunity”), German Muße (“leisure”). More at empty.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin incūrābilis. By surface analysis, in- + curable.
Borrowed from Italian porcospino, from Vulgar Latin *porcospinus, calque of Ancient Greek ἀκανθόχοιρος (akanthókhoiros), from ἄκανθα (ákantha, “spine”) + χοῖρος (khoîros, “pig”).
Borrowed from Latin dēplētiōnem, from dēpleō.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin occidentem.
Learned borrowing from Latin dissēminātor. By surface analysis, disséminer + -ateur.
Inherited from Middle French valee, from Old French valee, from val + -ée, from Latin vallis. Cf. also Medieval Latin valleta.
Inherited from Old French narine, from Vulgar Latin *narina, from Latin nāris.
Borrowed from Late Latin subtractiōnem, and based on soustraire.
Inherited from Old French crocefis, crucefix, borrowed from Latin crucifixus.
Inherited from Old French parchemin, from Vulgar Latin *pergamīnus, from Late Latin pergamēna.
Borrowed from the Ancient Greek μαιευτική (maieutikḗ).
Inherited from Middle French achever, from Old French achever, from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. Compare English achieve.

Borrowed from Latin ingestionem, accusative of ingestio (“a pouring in”), noun of action from the perfect passive participle of ingerere (“pour in”), from in- (“in, into”) + gero (“to carry, to bear”).
From bijou (“piece of jewelry”) + -ier, with intrusive -t-.
Borrowed from Spanish hacienda. Doublet of fazenda.
Inherited from Middle French serpent, from Old French serpent, from Latin serpentem, accusative form of serpēns.
Inherited from Old French passerel, from Latin passer + French suffix -eau. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *p(e)t-tro- (“who flies, bird”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”).

Inherited from Middle French vingt, from Old French vint, from Latin vīgintī, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wih₁ḱm̥ti, *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti. The Latin -g- was regularly lost in Old French, but was added back to the spelling in Middle French (now placed after the -n- in order to maintain the pronunciation).
Borrowed from Late Latin anacolūthon, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνακόλουθον (anakólouthon).
Inherited from Latin forum; doublet of fur and forum. Unrelated to French fort.

Inherited from Middle French esmoy, from Old French esmai (“confusion, agitation caused by fear”), from esmaier (“to worry, scare, vex, dismay”), from Vulgar Latin *exmagare (“to deprive (someone) of strength, to disable”), from ex- + *magare (“to enable, empower”), from Proto-Germanic *maginą, *maganą (“might, power”), from Proto-Indo-European *mēgh- (“to be able”). Akin to Old High German magan, megin (“power, might, main”), Old English mæġen (“might, main”), Old English magan (“to be able to”). More at main, may.
Unadapted borrowing from English leprechaun, from Irish leipreachán.
Borrowed from Latin viā, the ablative of via (“road, way”), of uncertain origin, plausibly cognate with vehō (“convey”).
From Middle French zephire, from Latin zephyrus.
Learned borrowing from Latin oleārius, from oleum + -ārius. Doublet of huilier.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk, used in manuscripts to mark passages”), diminutive of ἀστήρ (astḗr, “a star”); see Latin aster.
From Italian mandorla. Doublet of amande and amygdale.
Borrowed from Italian cipollino (“a little onion”), from cipolla (“onion”). (compare French ciboule) So called because its veins consist, like onions, of different strata, one lying upon another.
Inherited from Middle French manumettre, from Latin manūmittere.
From Middle French trope, troupe, from Old French trope, trupe, of unknown origin, though likely related to Early Medieval Latin troppus (“herd”).
From trans- + percer. Displaced French trespercier.
Learned borrowing from Latin variātiō. By surface analysis, varier + -ation. See also véraison.
Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French ermitage. Equivalent to ermite + -age.
Inherited from Old French espi, from Latin spīcum, one of the variants of spīca. Doublet of aspic.
Inherited from Late Latin scrīptōrium, or possibly formed in French, from écrit + -oire.
Learned borrowing from Latin ellīpticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin papālis. By surface analysis, pape + -al.
From jouiss(ant) (stem of the present participle of jouir) + -ance.
Inherited from Middle French nègre, from Spanish negro or Portuguese negro, itself from Latin niger. Doublet of noir (“black”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin optātīvus.
Inherited from Old French servise, borrowed from Latin servitium (compare Portuguese serviço, Italian servizio, Norman sèrvice, Spanish servicio), from servus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πλουτοκρατία (ploutokratía).
Inherited from Old French bourjon, burjon, from Vulgar Latin *burriōnem, from Late Latin burra.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.
Inherited from Old French pont, from Latin pontem.
Borrowed from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Doublet of épée, which was inherited.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French noble, borrowed from Latin nōbilis according to the TLFi dictionary.
Learned borrowing from Latin tenāx. Compare inherited Old French tenais.
Inherited from Middle French [Term?], learned borrowing from Latin lētālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin ciborium. Doublet of ciborium.

Inherited from Old French deschauz, from Vulgar Latin *discalceus, itself either from a shortening of Late Latin discalceātus, from discalceō, or from Latin dis- + calceus. Cognate with Occitan descauç, Catalan descalç, Spanish descalzo, Portuguese descalço, Italian scalzo, Walloon dischås, and Romanian desculț.

Inherited from Old French maintenir, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). Equivalent to main + tenir. Compare Spanish mantener, Portuguese manter, Italian mantenere.
From Old French saumastre, from Vulgar Latin *salmaster, alteration of Latin salmacidus (“salty and bitter”), from salgama (“salted pickle”) + acidus (“bitter”). Doublet of saumache.
Borrowed from Late Latin stater, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στατήρ (statḗr).
Inherited from Middle French, from Latin stimulātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía), or maybe formed in French from orthodoxe + -ie.
From Latin antinomia, from Ancient Greek ἀντινομία (antinomía).
From investiss(ant) (stem of the present participle of investir) + -eur.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin litanīa, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía).
Borrowed from Latin longitūdō (“length, a measured length”), from longus (“long”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin logarithmicus. By surface analysis, logarithme + -ique.
Borrowed from Latin reliqua, neuter plural of reliquus.
From Russian совхо́з (sovxóz), abbreviation of советское хозяйство (sovetskoje xozjajstvo, “soviet farm”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mātrimōniālis.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κλαστός (klastós, “broken”), verbal adjective of κλάω (kláō, “to break”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin reflexiōnem. By surface analysis, refléter + -xion.
Inherited from Middle French pavillon, from Old French paveilun, inherited from Latin pāpiliōnem. Doublet of papillon.
From intense + -ité. Cf. also Medieval Latin intensitas.
Inherited from Middle French defun(c)t, from Old French defunz (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin (de vita) defunctus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lacōnicus (“laconic”), from Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós).
Inherited from Middle French paradis, from Old French paradis, borrowed from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. Doublet of parvis.
Inherited from Old French rumeur, rimur, from Latin rūmōrem.
Learned borrowing from Latin adolēscentem, present participle of adolēscō.
From salive + -er, based on Latin salīvāre.
Inherited from Middle French latte, from Old French latte, late, from a Germanic source, probably Frankish *lattu. See also German Latte, Dutch lat, and English lath and lattice.
Borrowed from English clan, from Scottish Gaelic clann (“progeny, race”), from Old Irish cland, from Old Welsh plant, from Latin planta (“shoot, offspring”), and therefore a doublet of plante.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin superficiālis. By surface analysis, superficie + -el.
Learned borrowing from Latin instabilitās, from instabilis (whence instable).
From spirite + -isme. Term coined by the French writer and educator Allan Kardec in 1857.

Inherited from Middle French enterrer, from Old French enterrer, from Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put into earth”), from Latin terra. Equivalent to en- (“into”) + terre (“earth”) + -er (infinitive marker). Cognate with English inter.
Borrowed from Latin exōtericus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερικός (exōterikós, “external”), from ἐξωτέρω (exōtérō, “outside”) + -ικός (-ikós).
Ultimately, a borrowing from Spanish tornado.
Borrowed from Late Latin proclāmātiōnem, from Latin proclāmō.
Borrowed from Latin cubus, from Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos).
Inherited from Old French moinel, equivalent to moine (because of its plumage) + -eau.

Inherited from Middle French eglise, from Old French eglise, esglise, from Vulgar Latin *eclesia, from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “gathering”). * Cognate with Catalan església, Italian chiesa, Portuguese igreja, Spanish iglesia
From Old French tialz (“awning, tent on a ship”), borrowed from Old Norse tjald (“tent”), from Proto-Germanic *teldą (“drape, tent”).
Inherited from Old French parement, from Medieval Latin parāmentum, from parō (“adorn”) + -mentum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praesūmptuōsus, from Latin praesūmō (whence présumer).
From Middle French Chaldee, from Latin chaldaeus, from Ancient Greek Χαλδαῖος (Khaldaîos).
Inherited from Middle French maritime, borrowed from Latin maritimus (“of the sea”), from mare (“sea”). Doublet of Maremme.
Inherited from Middle French mesler, from Old French mesler, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin miscēre.
Borrowed from Spanish arroba, an old-fashioned weight unit.
Learned borrowing from Latin quīncunx (“by five”).

Inherited from Middle French mettre, from Old French metre, from Latin mittere, probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with Occitan metre. Portuguese meter, Spanish meter and Italian mettere.
Inherited from Old French courre, corre (modified under the influence of -ir verbs), from Latin currere (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).
Inherited from Old French val, from Latin vallem.
From dés- + espérer (“to hope”); cf. also Old French desperer.
From Old French cimitiere, a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion, “sleeping chamber”).
From in- + fertilité or from infertile + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin vēlum (“veil, sail”).
Inherited from Old French controver (whence also English contrive). Equivalent to con- + trouver.
17th century, borrowed from Dutch kajuit. Doublet of cahute, which see for more.
Inherited from Old French manace, from Latin minācia (“threat”), a noun based on mināx (“threatening”).
From Occitan berigola, from Latin maurucula, from Maurus (literally “Moorish”).
Inherited from Old French destrucion, borrowed from Latin dēstrūctiōnem.
Borrowed from German Aspirin, from acetylierte Spirsäure (“acetylated salicylic acid”). The second word comes from the name of the plant genus Spiraea.

Inherited from Old French perilleus, inherited from Latin perīculōsus (probably through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *periclosu(s)). By surface analysis, péril + -eux. Doublet of périculeux, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Italian cittadino. Doublet of citoyen.
Inherited from Old French erratique, borrowed from Latin erraticus.
Learned borrowing from Latin incendiārius. By surface analysis, incendie + -aire.
From sou- + lever, or Latin sublevāre. Compare Spanish solevar.
Inherited from Old French bas, from Late Latin bassus.
Inherited from Old French enterin (“entire, whole”). Compare French entier, from the same root.
Learned borrowing from Latin munificentia (“generosity”), from munus (“gift”).
From an alteration of the suffix of Old French feeil, fëel, fedel, inherited from Latin fidēlis. Doublet of fidèle.
Unadapted borrowing from German Ersatz (“replacement, substitute”).
Borrowed from Latin dēclārātiōnem (accusative singular dēclārātiōnem).
From Middle French cirage. By surface analysis, cirer + age.
Learned borrowing from Latin abductiō(n) (“robbing; abduction”), from abdūcō (“take or lead away”) + -tiō(n) (suffix forming nouns relating to actions or their results).
Borrowed from English crux. Doublet of croix, croiseur, and cruiser.
From Portuguese cacatua, from Malay kakaktua.

Inherited from Middle French tavaiolle, from Italian tovagliola (“napkin”), diminutive of tovaglia (“tablecloth”), from Medieval Latin toallia, toacula, duvahila, toacla (“towel”), from Frankish *þwahilu (“cloth”). Doublet of touaille.
From Spanish bernia, possibly as a shortening from Latin Hibernia (“Ireland”) where this fabric was made.
Borrowed from Late Latin excretiōnem, from Latin excernō.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek εὐδαίμων (eudaímōn, “having a good genius, happy, fortunate”).
Borrowed from Late Latin diūrēticus, from Ancient Greek διουρητικός (diourētikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin apoplexia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (apoplēxía).
Borrowed from Latin contrārius. See contre and -aire.
Borrowed from Latin deicīda, from deus (“god”).
From Latin māternus, from māter (“mother”) with the suffix -el or from Medieval Latin māternālis.

Inherited from Middle French solennel, from Old French sollempnel, sollempnal, borrowed from Latin sollemnis, with Old French -el added under the influence of the Old French equivalents of annuel, éternel, spirituel, etc.
Borrowed from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).
From the stem of Medieval Latin sirupus + -eux.
Borrowed from Arabic حَشِيش (ḥašīš, “hay, dried herb”).
Learned borrowing from Latin procreātiō. By surface analysis, procréer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French chastelain, castelain, from Latin castellānus. By surface analysis, château + -ain. Doublet of castillan, a borrowing from Spanish.
Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Latin anxius.
Inherited from Old French demande, from the verb demander.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós).
Unadapted borrowing from New Latin myosōtis, from Ancient Greek μυοσωτίς (muosōtís, “mouse's ear; forget-me-not”). It is so named because the shape of the petals resembles that of a mouse's ear.
Inherited from Old French foene (“harpoon, trident”), from Latin fuscina (“trident”).
Learned borrowing from Latin circumscriptiōnem. Compare Italian circoscrizione.
Inherited from Old French sain, from Latin sānus, from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”).
Borrowed from Latin ephēbus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔφηβος (éphēbos).
Learned borrowing from Latin ruptūra. Doublet of roture.
From Russian хрущоба (xruščoba), blend of хрущёвка (xruščovka, “khrushchevka”) and трущоба (truščoba, “hovel, shack”).
Calque of English shrinkflation, from réduction + inflation.
Inherited from Latin cornicula (“small crow”), variant of cornīcula, diminutive of cornīx. Compare Spanish corneja.
Learned borrowing from Latin līneāris, from līnea (whence French ligne).
Borrowed from Latin nōtiōnem (accusative singular nōtiōnem).
Borrowed from Italian lento. Doublet of lent.
Borrowed from German Plexiglas, a trademark.
Learned borrowing from Latin medicīnālis. Displaced Old French mecinnel.

Inherited from Middle French and Old French vescu, derived from the preterite vesqui, itself from a metathesis of Latin vixi, likely influenced by nasqui (“I was born”). See the same development in Occitan and Catalan viscut. Compare also Italian vissuto.

From Old French rosel (“reed”), a derivative of Old French ros (“reed, tooth of a weaver's comb”), from Frankish *rausa (“reed”), from Proto-Germanic *rausą, *rauzą (“pipe, reed, shaft, tube”), from Proto-Indo-European *er- (“to move, excite, grow”). The base word survives as the obsolete ros (“weaver's comb”). Cognate with Old High German rōr (“pipe”) (German Rohr (“tube”)), Old Norse reyrr (“reed”) (Danish rør (“reed, pipe, tube”)), Old English rysc (“reed, rush”). More at rush.
Borrowed from English tabloid. Analyzable within French as table + -oïde.
From Latin Syriarcha, from Ancient Greek Συριάρχης (Suriárkhēs).
From a modification of the older popular form aver after the original etymology, Latin avarus.
From Latin Thēbaicus, from Ancient Greek Θηϐαϊκός (Thēbaïkós).
From Latin stylobata, from Ancient Greek στυλοβάτης (stulobátēs). By surface analysis, style + -bate.
Borrowed from Latin rigidus. Compare the inherited doublets roide and raide.
Borrowed from Latin astrum, from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron).
Inherited from Old French confeccion, borrowed from Latin cōnfectiōnem.
From Latin fēllātrīcem, accusative of fēllātrīx.
Inherited from Old French servage. By surface analysis, serf + -age.
Inherited from Middle French admirable, borrowed from Latin admirābilis.
Learned borrowing from Latin indistīnctus. By surface analysis, in- + distinct.
Learned borrowing from Latin vitrum. Doublet of verre. Compare Spanish vidrio and Catalan vidre.
Borrowed or adapted from Latin restrictus, modeled after étreint.

From Spanish español or from Middle French espaignol, from Old French espagneul or espaigneul, borrowed from Old Occitan espaignol, espainol, from a Vulgar Latin *Hispaniolus, from Latin Hispānus, from Hispania. Doublet of épagneul and Pagnol.
From Latin synchysis, from Ancient Greek σύγχυσις (súnkhusis).
Borrowed from English tholin, from Ancient Greek θολός (tholós, “muddy”).
Learned borrowing from Latin perversitās. Morphologically, from pervers + -ité.
Borrowed from Latin cathedra, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra). Doublet of chaire and chaise.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ξενηλασία (xenēlasía).
Inherited from Old French fomentation, borrowed from Late Latin fōmentātiōnem.

Borrowed from Spanish mosquito, diminutive of mosca, from Latin musca, whence also the French doublet mouche (“a fly”). The metathesis of /k/ and /t/ might have been due to influence of tique (“a tick”).
From Middle French hanse, from Old French hanse (13th c.), from Middle Low German hanse. Compare German Hanse, English hansa.
Borrowed from Latin circumspectiōnem (“looking around, circumspection”), from circumspiciō (“to look around”). By surface analysis, circonspect + -tion.
Learned borrowing from Latin circumlocūtiōnem. By surface analysis, circon- + locution.
Inherited from Old French caution, borrowed from Latin cautiōnem, from cautus, past participle of caveō, cavēre (“be on one's guard”).
Learned borrowing from Latin thesis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θέσις (thésis).
Learned borrowing from Latin mediātōrem. Doublet of médiator.
Borrowed from Italian oratorio. Doublet of oratoire.
Inherited from Middle French offensif, from offendre + -if, by analogy with défensif and parallel to Medieval Latin offēnsīvus. By surface analysis, offenser + -if. First attested in 1417.
Borrowed from Italian flemma, from Latin phlegma (“phlegm”), one of the four bodily humours, thought to cause a sluggish and unemotional nature. First attested in the late 1700s. Doublet of flegme.
From Old French targier, from targe + -er.
Borrowed from Latin pēnsum. Doublet of poids, which was inherited.
Borrowed from English subpage. By surface analysis, sous- + page.
From Old French legende, from Medieval Latin legenda, feminine of Latin legendus, gerundive of legēre.
Learned borrowing from Latin sperma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma).
From Old French violet, a back-formation from violette (“violet (flower)”), from viole + -ette, from Latin viola.
Inherited from Old French tribu, from Latin tribus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin restaurātiōnem. By surface analysis, restaurer + -ation.
First attested in Old French as telier, from toile + -ier.
Inherited from Middle French monstre, from Old French monstre, borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.
Inherited from Old French chaume, from Latin calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of the borrowed calame.
Inherited from Old French *meienel, from Vulgar Latin *medianellus, from Latin mediānus (“middle, central”). Cognate with Catalan mainell.
Learned borrowing from Latin apertus (“open”). Doublet of ouvert.
Inherited from Middle French grenier, from Old French grenier, gernier, guernier, from Latin grānārium.
From Middle French grammaire, from Old French gramaire, itself from Latin grammatica.
Borrowed from English escalator. Genericized trademark.
Learned borrowing from Latin scrība. Doublet of écrivain.
Inherited from Old French ramifier, borrowed from Medieval Latin ramificāre, from Latin ramus (“branch”) + facio (“to do”).
Calque of English barometer, using baro- + -mètre.
Inherited from Middle French albastre, from Old French alabastre, aubastre, from Latin alabaster, alabastrum, from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος (alábastros).
Borrowed from Latin rēsīnōsus. Also résine + -eux.
