Inherited from Old French cisne, cine, from Late Latin cicinus, from Latin cycnus (“swan”), from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos). The modern spelling is in imitation of the Latin variant form cygnus, and the modern pronunciation is a spelling-pronunciation based on that.
Ultimately from Latin helcium (“collar harness”), altered by association with hausser
Learned borrowing from Latin fertilitās. By surface analysis, fertile + -ité.
From Old French aigrun, from Medieval Latin acrumen.
Inherited from Middle French lyon, from Old French lion, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin leōnem, from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn).
Inherited from Middle French vocatif, borrowed from grammatical Latin vocātīvus.
Inherited from Middle French instruire, from Old French enstruire~estruire (with latinization of the prefix), from Latin īnstruō. Compare Jersey Norman înstruithe.
Inherited from Old French celier, from Late Latin cellārium (“pantry”), from Latin cella.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin īrāscibilitās. By surface analysis, irascible + -ité.
From Italian palanco, variant of paranco (“hoist”), from Vulgar Latin palanca, alteration of Latin phalanga. See also palanque, planche, palanche.
Inherited from Old French geneivre, from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus.
Borrowed from Occitan ; ultimately from Latin posterula.
Inherited from Old French tumour, from Latin tumor.
From Ancient Greek ἱερο- (hiero-), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred, holy”).
Inherited from Middle French honneur, from Old French enor, eneur, onor, honor, from Latin honor, honōrem.
Inherited from Old French violent, borrowed from Latin violentus.
Inherited from Middle French charnel, from Old French charnel, inherited from Latin carnālis. Also analysable as a derivative of Old French charn (→ Modern French chair) + -el.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀξύς οὐρά (oxús ourá, literally “sharp tail”).
Calque of English creativity, from créatif + -ité.

A combination of Latin ballare and a family of Middle French words beginning in *brimb-, esp. brimber (“to beg”), which give the sense of "wandering to and fro". Likely influenced by Middle French trinqueballer (“to chime a bell”), itself from Middle French triballer (“to wander”) (modern French trimbaler).
From Latin pannucia, a diminutive of pannus (“cloth, rag”).
Borrowed from Italian tessitura. Doublet of texture.
Learned borrowing from Latin zōophorus, from Ancient Greek ζωοφόρος (zōophóros).
From Old French consuetude, a learned borrowing from Latin cōnsuētūdō (“custom”). Doublet of coutume, which was inherited, and costume, a borrowing from Italian.
Inherited from Middle French moine, metathesis from Old French monie, from Late Latin monicus, variant of monachus.
Inherited from Old French concave, borrowed from Latin concavus.
From re- + sembler. Compare Italian rassomigliare.
Inherited from Middle French pierre, from Old French pierre, from Latin petra.
From Yiddish ישיבה (yeshive), from Hebrew יְשִׁיבָה (y'shivá, “sitting”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Rōmānitās. Morphologically, from romain + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin bipedem. By surface analysis, bi- + -pède.
From jeune + -esse; found in Old French as juenesce. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *juvenitia. Compare Italian giovinezza.
From Medieval Latin barbarinus (“Berber, pagan, Saracen, barbarian”), from Latin barbaria (“foreign country”).
Deliberately humorous spelling of English English.
From temple + -ier; cf. the Medieval Latin templarius.
Borrowed from Latin arborēscentem, present active participle of arborēscō (“to become a tree”).
Inherited from Middle French Syrie, from Latin Syria, from Ancient Greek Συρία (Suría).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra). The word was feminine (like its etymon) until the 18th century.
Inherited from Old French estencele, from Vulgar Latin *stincilla, a metathesis of Latin scintilla.
Borrowed from Latin negligentia, variant of neglegentia.
Alteration of German Vielliebchen, influenced by Philippe.
Inherited from Latin lānōsus. Equivalent to laine + -eux.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin extravagantem.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French nimphe, borrowed from Latin nympha or nymphē (“nymph”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “young woman, nymph”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin epanalēpsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπανάληψις (epanálēpsis).
Borrowed from English jeep. Genericized trademark.

Inherited from Old French rifler (“to scrape, scratch”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīfilōn via either Frankish *rīffilōn or Old High German riffilōn (“to tear by rubbing”), akin to rip, ripple. Compare Old English geriflian (“to wrinkle”), Old Norse rifa (“to tear, break”).
ultimately from Latin flagrāre (“to burn, urge”)
Borrowed from Moroccan Arabic جديد (jdīd), from Arabic جَدِيد (jadīd).
Inherited from Old French, inherited from Latin verrūca.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin substantiālis. By surface analysis, substance + -iel.
From Middle French myrobolan, from Old French mirabolan, from Latin myrobalanum, myrobalanus, from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos).
From Latin phlegmaticus, from Ancient Greek φλεγματικός (phlegmatikós), from φλέγμα (phlégma).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cāritātīvus, from Latin caritas (“charity, dearness”).
Inherited from Old French somet, sommette, diminutive derivation of som (“highest part, top of a hill”) from Latin summum.
From signer + -ture; cf. Medieval Latin signatura.
From Vulgar Latin *vermicellus, alteration of vermiculus (“small worm”), from vermis (“worm”). Doublet of vermicelle.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin verticālis.
Inherited from Old French encoragier. By surface analysis, en- + courage + -er.
Borrowed from Latin remediāre. See also remède.

Inherited from Middle French loyaulte, from Old French loiauté (whence English loyalty), leialté, possibly corresponding to Medieval Latin lēgālitās, lēgālitātem, from Latin lēgālis. Compare Spanish lealtad, Portuguese lealdade, Italian lealtà.
Learned borrowing from Latin sentina (“bilge water, hold of a ship, dregs”).
Borrowed from English rember, deliberate misspelling of remember.
From Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “box or chest”).
Originally written isle; from Middle French isle, from Old French isle, from Vulgar Latin *īsula, from Classical Latin īnsula.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin fictiōnem (accusative of fictiō).
Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Latin circinus (“pair of compasses”). Compare Romanian cearcăn.
Learned borrowing from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnem. By surface analysis, occuper + -ation.
From Latin hierophanta, from Ancient Greek ἱεροφάντης (hierophántēs).
Inherited from Old French repos. Compare Catalan repòs, Italian riposo, Spanish reposo, Portuguese repouso, Romanian repaus.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement, ordering”).
Learned borrowing from Latin prōcessus. Doublet of processus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin palpebrālis, from palpebra (whence paupière).
From Old French eschevinage [1219]. By surface analysis, échevin + -age.
Learned borrowing from Latin archīvum (with a change in gender), from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon).
Learned borrowing from Latin meditātiō. By surface analysis, méditer + -ation.
See αποτροπαϊκός (apotropaïkós), from Ancient Greek ἀποτροπή (apotropḗ, “dissuasion”).
From Latin arbor + -cole, on the model of agricole.
Learned borrowing from Latin collēctiō. Cf. also Old French quieuçon, which may be inherited from the same source, and the modern cueillaison, which was probably formed analogically.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin indīviduālis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin magnesia.
Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French [Term?], from Latin prōlixus.
Inherited from Old French evesque, inherited from Late Latin episcopus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).
From Middle French matutinal, itself borrowed from Late Latin mātūtīnālis.
From dû (past participle of devoir) + -ment. Spelled with circumflex accented û as a mark of the e elided from the older spelling duement.
Back-formation from endurcir, based on Latin dūrēscere.
Inherited from Middle French espace, from Old French espace, borrowed from Latin spatium.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin obsequiae, alteration of Latin exsequiae.
Borrowed from Latin Ptolemaeus, itself from Ancient Greek Πτολεμαῖος (Ptolemaîos).
From casser (“to break”) + cou (“neck”), literally “neck breaker”.
Borrowed from English panel, itself borrowed from Old French panel. Doublet of panneau.
From cheminer (“to walk on; to keep walking”) + -ment.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παροξῠ́τονος (paroxŭ́tonos, “paroxytone”).
Borrowed from English cocktail, which is of unclear origin.
Inherited from Old French veel, vedel, inherited from Latin vitellus. Doublet of vitellus.
Borrowed from Latin īlicō (“on the spot”), from in + ablative of locus (“place”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cōnsummātiō. By surface analysis, consommer + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French mémorable, itself borrowed from Latin memorābilis.
Borrowed from English coroner. First attested in 1624.
The sense in Middle French was "slightly yellow," from jaune + -et.

Borrowed from Latin abscōnsus. First attested in a translation dated to 1478 of a medical book in Latin written in 1363 (Guy de Chauliac's Inventarium sive chirurgia magna). Related to Old French abscondre, which it eclipsed in usage while being its participle, and Old French escondre.
Learned borrowing from Latin notātiō. By surface analysis, noter + -ation.
From Middle French commentaire, from Latin commentārium.
Inherited from Old French prescripcion, itself borrowed from Latin praescrīptiō.
From croix + -er. Compare Spanish and Portuguese cruzar.
Learned borrowing from Latin geōmētrēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs).
Inherited from Old French piestre, peestre, paëstre, inherited from Latin pedestrem. Doublet of pédestre and perhaps pitre.
Inherited from Middle French odeur, from Old French odor, from Latin odōrem m.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin brūtālis (“savage, stupid”), from brūtus (“dull, stupid”). See brut and -al.
Learned borrowing from Latin fidēlitās. By surface analysis, fidèle + -ité.
Inherited from Old French narcotique, borrowed from Medieval Latin narcōticus.
Borrowed from Late Latin spīnālis, from Latin spīna.
Learned borrowing from Latin decēnārius. Compare sénaire / sexénaire, septénaire, novénaire, dénaire.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin interrogator. By surface analysis, interroger + -ateur.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin subornatio. By surface analysis, suborner + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin frīgidārium. Doublet of frigidaire.
Inherited from Old French existence, from Late Latin existentia (“existence”).
Inherited from Old French ramel, from Vulgar Latin *ramellus, from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).
From Middle French aultrement, from Old French autrement, from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente. Synchronically autre + -ment.
Inherited from Middle French voix, from Old French voiz, from Latin vōcem, accusative of vōx (“voice”), from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs.
Learned borrowing from Latin mōrālitātem. By surface analysis, moral + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin rigōrōsus. By surface analysis, rigueur + -eux.
Inherited from Middle French initiation, borrowed from Latin initiātiō. Morphologically, from initier + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin, Medieval Latin herēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós).
Inherited from Middle French despense, from Late Latin dīspēnsa, feminine past participle of dīspendō, from Latin dis- + pendō.
From Ancient Greek μισάνθρωπος (misánthrōpos), from μισέω (miséō, “to hate”) and ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man; human”).
Inherited from Middle French rire, from Old French rire, from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre. The past participle's root-final S was lost.
Inherited from Middle French manumis, from Latin manūmissus.
Borrowed into Middle French from Italian sbirro, from birro, from Latin birrus (“hooded coat”), related to burrus (“reddish; red-headed”).
From Middle French plustost, see plus + tôt. Compare Italian piuttosto and Catalan més aviat. Compare the etymology of English rather.
Inherited from Middle French and Old French question (12th c.), borrowed from Latin quaestiō. At first a learned word, therefore retaining preconsonantal -s- (compare related quête).
From Middle French verbosité, borrowed from Late Latin verbōsitās. By surface analysis, verbeux + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French and Old French vache, from Latin vacca.
From sur- + doué. Compare Spanish superdotado.
From Latin vermis (“worm”) + fugāre (“to cause to flee”).
Inherited from Middle French firmament, from Old French firmament, borrowed from Latin firmāmentum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praedecessor.
Borrowed from Italian ciurma, from Late Latin celeusma, from Ancient Greek κέλευσμα (kéleusma).
Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superanus, from Latin super. Doublet of the inherited souverain.
Inherited from Middle French elysee, from Latin Elysius (“Elysian”).
Borrowed from Latin caudālis, from cauda. See also queue.
From Latin vātēs (“prophet, poet”). Compare Italian vate, Spanish vate, Portuguese vate, Catalan vate, English vates. Doublet of ovate and vaticiner.
Inherited from Late Latin fastuosus, from Latin fastosus (“superb, disdainful, magnificent”) [from 1537]. By surface analysis, faste + -ueux.
Formed from the root of Latin mīca, with the suffix -elle, or borrowed from New Latin micella.
Inherited from Middle French expression, borrowed from Latin expressiōnem (“a pressing out”).
From porte + -ier. From Old French portier, from Late Latin portārius (“porter, gatekeeper”), from Latin porta.
Learned borrowing from Latin synecdochē, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”).
From Middle French glorification, from Latin glōrificātiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangō.
Inherited from Middle French tourment, torment, from Old French torment, from Latin tormentum. Related to tordre.

Inherited from Middle French vous, from Old French vos, vous, from Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs. See cognates in regional languages in France: Angevin, Bourbonnais-Berrichon, Bourguignon, Champenois, Lorrain, Orléanais, and Poitevin-Saintongeais vous; Franc-Comtois vôs; Gallo vouz; Norman and Franco-Provençal vos; Picard os; Occitan vosautres (Provençal vousautes); Catalan vosaltres; Corsican voi. Other cognates with the same usage are voi in Italian as well as вы (vy) in Russian.
Inherited from Old French vuz, inherited from Latin vōtum. Doublet of vote, a borrowing from English.
Inherited from Middle French sumptueusement. By surface analysis, somptueux + -ment.

From Middle French, from Old French gaber (“to tell jokes”), from Old Norse gabba (“to mock”), from Proto-Germanic *gabbōną (“to mock, jest”), from Proto-Indo-European *ghabh- (“to be split, be forked, gape”). Cognate with Old English gabban (“to scoff, mock, delude, jest”), Old Frisian gabbia (“to accuse”), Middle Dutch gabben (“to mock”), Middle Low German gabben (“to have fun, jest”). More at gab.
From a modification, based on signe, of Old French seignier, itself from Latin signāre.
Inherited from Old French treuil, from Vulgar Latin *troculum, from Latin torculum.
Inherited from Old French messon, meissun, from Latin messiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin immarcēscibilis.

Inherited from Middle French macis, from Old French macis, from late Medieval Latin macis, possibly a corruption of Latin macir (denoting a different red spice from India), from Ancient Greek μάκιρ (mákir, “macir”), an eastern loanword of unknown further origin.
From Middle French labile, borrowed from Latin lābilis (“apt to slip, transient”), from lābor, lābī (“slip; glide, flow”).
From en- + dur + -ir, based on Latin indūrēscere, dūrēscere.
Inherited from Latin cōnflāre. Compare Italian gonfiare.
From Latin licentiōsus, from licentia (“license, freedom”).
Inherited from Middle French cure, from Old French cure, from Latin cūra, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sicārius, derived from sica.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin renālis, from Latin ren (whence rein).

Inherited from Old French suvent, sovent, from Latin subinde, morphologically sub + inde. The original meaning of subinde was “immediately after”, which then evolved to “repeatedly” and then to “often”.
Borrowed from Latin productor, from productus.
Inherited from Middle French naistre, from Old French naistre, from Latin nascere.

Inherited from Old French inspeccion, borrowed from Latin īnspectiōnem (“examination, inspection”), from the verb īnspectō (“to inspect”), from spectō (“to observe, to watch”), frequentative of speciō (“to look at”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”).
Inherited from Old French glose, from Medieval Latin glossa (“explanation of a difficult word”). See also English gloze (“to make a comment”).
Learned borrowing from Latin iterātiōnem. By surface analysis, itérer + -ation.
Borrowed from Latin dictātūra, from dictō.
Inherited from Middle French trahir < Old French traïr, itself from Latin trādō 'betray'.

Inherited from Middle French arrester (“to stop”), from Old French arester (“to stay, stop”), from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“stop, remain behind, stay back”). Compare English arrest.
Learned borrowing from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “a return home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain, suffering”) as a calque of German Heimweh.
From Late Latin glenare, a Celtic borrowing from Gaulish, possibly from Proto-Celtic *glanos.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin ascēticus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀσκητικός (askētikós). By surface analysis, ascète + -ique.
Inherited from Middle French dormir, from Old French dormir, from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.
Inherited from Middle French quantité, from Old French quantite, from Latin quantitātem, possibly borrowed or semi-learned.

Inherited from Middle French eloquent, from Old French eloquent, borrowed from Latin ēloquentem (“speaking, having the faculty of speech, eloquent”), present participle of ēloquī (“to speak out”), from ē- (“out”) + loquī (“to speak”).
Learned borrowing from Latin inter. Doublet of entre-.
Borrowed from Latin diesis (“quarter-tone”), from Ancient Greek δίεσις (díesis).
From chevalier (“knight”) + -ière (“-ess”, feminine noun-forming suffix). In the sense “signet ring”, an ellipsis of bague à la chevalière (“ring in knightly style”), first attested in 1821.
Learned borrowing from Latin angulāris. Compare Old French angler.

From Middle French psaulme, from Old French psalme, salme, borrowed from Latin psalmus, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós). The p- was silent well into Modern French, but later came to be pronounced by analogy with learned words with ps- which had since been borrowed from Greek.
Unadapted borrowing from English antidumping, analyzed as anti- + dumping.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin agnella, possibly borrowed.
Learned borrowing from Latin spontāneitās. By surface analysis, spontané + -ité.
From Ancient Greek βλέννα (blénna, “mucus”) and ῥαγή (rhagḗ, “a breaking”).
Inherited from Old French gré, from Latin grātum, from grātus (“agreeable”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese grado.
A Frenchification (see carré) of Italian bequadro, itself derived from Medieval Latin b quadrātum (“B natural”, literally “square B”).
Borrowed from Occitan garopa, also Medieval Latin garropa in the 11ᵗʰ century, ultimately a substrate.
Inherited from Old French cohourge, ultimately from Latin cucurbita, perhaps via Vulgar Latin *cucurbica. Doublet of gourde (from the form cohourde).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nōtōrius.

Borrowed from Arabic لَاطُون (lāṭūn, “copper, copper alloy”), itself from Proto-Common Turkic *altun (“gold”). See Turkish altın, Old Turkic 𐰞𐱃𐰆𐰣 (altun, “gold”), Karakhanid اَلْتُونْ (altūn, “gold”).
Learned borrowing from Latin alterātiō. By surface analysis, altérer + -ation.
From désintégrer + -ation or from dés- + intégration.
Inherited from Old French feve, from Latin faba, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”). Cognate with Spanish haba, Italian fava.
Substantivization of Old French lange (“woollen”), from Latin laneus.
Inherited from Old French melon, from Late Latin mēlōnem, shortening of Latin mēlopepō, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, “melon”). More at English melon.
Learned borrowing from Latin psȳchopompus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ψῡχοπομπός (psūkhopompós).
Learned borrowing from Latin principālitās. Morphologically, from principal + -té. Doublet of principalité.
Inherited from Old French rebelle, borrowed from Latin rebellis.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολύγραφος (polúgraphos). By surface analysis, poly- + graphe.
Calque of English autocomplete, auto- + compléter.
Borrowed from Spanish alguazil (now alguacil), from Arabic اَلْوَزِير (al-wazīr, “minister, vizier”).
Borrowed from Latin aegrōtantem, present participle of aegrōtō (“to be sick”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χιλιασμός (khiliasmós), from χῑ́λῐοι (khī́lĭoi, “thousand”). Doublet of chiasme.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin frontispicium.

From Old Occitan rossinhol (cf. Catalan rossinyol), from Vulgar Latin *lusciniolus, masculine diminutive of Latin luscinia (“nightingale”). According to De Vaan, "might be explained with haplology from *lusci-cania (“singing in the night; blind singer”), but this is conjecture.
Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis. Doublet of loyal.
Inherited from Middle French theme, from Old French teme, tesme, a learned borrowing from Latin thema, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).
Learned borrowing from Latin adūlātōrem. By surface analysis, aduler + -ateur.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin vulnerābilis.
Borrowed from English interview. Doublet of entrevue.
From Old French romancier (“to narrate in the vernacular”), from romanz.
From Old French avantageus. By surface analysis, avantage + -eux.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin delphīnālis, from delphīnus + -ālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).
Borrowed from English electrocute, equivalent to a blend of électro- + exécuter.
Inherited from Old French vespre, from Latin vesper, vespera.
Borrowed from Late Latin discretiōnem, from Latin discernō.
Borrowed from Latin unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”), so-called because of its transparency and its shape, reminiscent of a fingernail.
Learned borrowing from Latin patriarchātus. By surface analysis, patriarche + -at.
Inherited from Old French grumiel, from Vulgar Latin *grimellus or *grumellus, variant of Latin grumulus, diminutive of grumus, from Proto-Indo-European *gar-, *ger- (“to tie, bind together”).
From Middle French espinocher (compare Jèrriais êpinnotchi), from espinoche (“morsel”).
Inherited from Old French peticiun, borrowed from Latin petitiōnem.
Inherited from Old French inflation, borrowed from Latin inflātiō. Cf. also the dialectal enflaison, which may be of popular origin.
From Latin emphyteoticus. By surface analysis, emphytéose + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin mulsiōnem.
Borrowed from Spanish bolívar. Named after Venezuelan statesman and military officer Simón Bolívar (1783–1830).

Inherited from Old French superlatif, borrowed from Late Latin superlātīvus, from Latin superlātus (“extravagant, of hyperbole”), past participle of superfero (“carry over”), from super (“above”) + fero (“bear, carry”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mediānus. Doublet of moyen and misaine.
Inherited from Latin terrōsus, from terra.
Inherited from Middle French corage, from Old French corage, from Vulgar Latin *corāticum, from Latin cor. Cognate with Catalan coratge, Italian coraggio, Occitan coratge, Spanish coraje.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin iūrista.
Borrowed from Late Latin ventilātiōnem, from Latin ventilō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin aequivocus.
Borrowed from English audit. Doublet of ouï.
Borrowed from English Texas, from Spanish Texas, Tejas.
Borrowed from Italian mercato. Doublet of marché and mercado.
Borrowed from Italian lesina. Doublet of alêne.
Learned borrowing from Latin trāns. Doublet of très.
From Old French, from Latin iam. Cognate with Portuguese já, Spanish ya, Italian già.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lenticulāris.
Learned borrowing from Latin magisterium, from magister (whence French maître).
Learned borrowing from Latin precārius. Doublet of prière.

Inherited from Middle French biche, from Old French biche (“doe, female deer”) and bisse (“wild animal”), of uncertain origin and relation. The form bisse is almost certainly from Vulgar Latin bīstia, variant of Latin bēstia (compare bête); however, the contemporary biche is an enigma, and possibly unrelated. It may be the Picard or Norman form of bisse, (compare chent for cent) or may share origin with Middle French bique (“nanny-goat”), believed to be derived from Frankish *bik (“goat”) or perhaps related to Icelandic bikkja (“old mare, nag”). More at bouc.
Inherited from Old French raucus, borrowed from Latin raucus. Compare also enrouer.
Borrowed from Italian chianti, after Chianti, its area of production. Through Latin from the Etruscan 𐌂𐌋𐌀𐌍𐌕𐌄 (clante).
From Latin cognōscō. Compare with modern French connaître and connaitre.
Borrowed from Russian бри́чка (bríčka), from Polish bryczka.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin soliloquium.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin complex.
Inherited from Latin turturellus (or turturillus), both diminutives of turtur (“turtle (archaic), turtle dove, turtledove”).
From Latin acquisītīvus, from acquīrō (“to acquire”).
Inherited from Middle French jonc, from Old French jonc, from Latin iuncus (“bulrush; cane made from a bulrush”).
From Ancient Greek οἰκουμένη (oikouménē, “inhabited world”), from οἰκέω (oikéō, “to inhabit, dwell”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “residence”).
Borrowed from Latin palpātiōnem, or from palper + -ation.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rotātōrius, from Classical Latin rotō. Cognate to Catalan rotatori, Italian and Spanish rotatorio, Portuguese rotatório.
Inherited from Middle French pæan, from Latin paean, from Ancient Greek παιάν (paián).
From dés- + agréable. Compare Catalan and Spanish desagradable, Italian sgradevole and Portuguese desagradável.
Inherited from Old French denominacion, borrowed from Latin dēnōminātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin genesis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis, “origin, source, beginning, nativity, generation, production, creation”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sincēritās. By surface analysis, sincère + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).
Learned borrowing from Latin centrālis. By surface analysis, centre + -al.
Borrowed from Late Latin ūvula (“small grape”), diminutive of Latin ūva. Doublet of uvula.
Inherited from Middle French caduc, itself a learned borrowing from Latin cadūcus (“falling; transitory”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin competentia.
From Middle French quand, from Old French quant, from Latin quandō (“when”).
Inherited from Middle French milliesme, from Old French millesme, from Latin mīllēsimus. Doublet of millésime. By surface analysis, mille + -ième.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin apothecārius. Compare French boutiquier.
Inherited from Middle French quel, from Old French quel, from Latin quālis.
Inherited from Old French artere, artaire, borrowed from Latin artēria, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría).
Borrowed from German Brezel. Doublet of brèchetelle.
Borrowed from Latin ēlabōrāre. Cognate with Italian elaborare, Spanish elaborar.
Borrowed from English sponsor, from Latin spōnsor.
From Latin Eleutherius, from Ancient Greek Ἐλευθέριος (Eleuthérios, literally “liberating”).
Inherited from Old French marastre, from Late Latin mātrastra (“stepmother”), from Latin māter (“mother”).
Inherited from Old French vermine, from verm + -ine, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *verminum, from Latin vermis (“worm”).
From Latin index (“pointer, indicator”), from indicō (“point out, show”).
Learned borrowing from Latin pācificus (“peace making”).

Inherited from Middle French holocauste, from Old French olocauste, learned borrowing from Late Latin holocaustum, from the neuter form of Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos), from ὅλος (hólos, “whole”) + καυστός (kaustós, “burnt”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”).
Modification, based on the Latin source, of Old French plurer, plurier (cf. also plurel), borrowed from Latin plūrālis.

Borrowed from Late Latin monētārius (“monetary, of or related to coinage or money”), from earlier Latin monētārius (“of or related to mints or minting”), from monēta (“mint, coinage”) (whence monnaie).
Borrowed from Occitan cap, from Latin caput. Doublet of chef.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).
Inherited from Middle French rein, from Old French rein, from the plural reins, from Latin rēnes < rēn.
Inherited from Old French torche, from Vulgar Latin *torca, from torqua, Classical Latin torques, from the verb torqueō (“to twist; to turn”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nūditās, from nūdus (whence nu).
Borrowed from Late Latin invāsiōnem, nominative of invāsiō.
Inherited from Old French Lombard, Lombart, from Late Latin langobardus, longobardus, from Germanic, derived from the Proto-Germanic *langabardaz (literally “long beard”). Doublet of Langobard.
Learned borrowing from Latin symphōnia, from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). Doublet of chifonie.
Inherited from Middle French terreur f, from Old French terreur f, itself borrowed from Latin terror m.
Borrowed from Italian golfo, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). Doublet of gouffre.
Learned borrowing from Latin līberātiōnem. See also livraison.
Deverbal from violer, from Latin violō (“to violate”).
Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin pelegrīnus m, a dissimilated form of Classical Latin peregrīnus m. Doublet of pérégrin m, a borrowing.
Inherited from Middle French empeschement. Morphologically, from empêcher (“to impede”) + -ment.
From Latin testiculātus. By surface analysis, testicule + -é.

From Middle French mediterrané, mediterranee, a learned borrowing from Latin mediterrāneus, itself from medius + terra + -āneus (the last element from -ānus + -eus). In modern French, only words descending from Latin borrowings of Greek origin ending in the suffixes -ēus/-ēum, -aeus/-aeum (and exceptionally -ius/-ium, as in élysée/Élysée) are written with -ée in the masculine. Words descending from Latin words in -āneus (a different suffix, from -ānus + -eus), are now written with the ending -ané (as seen, for example, in momentané, spontané). The first four editions of the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française spelled these words with -anée before adopting the current spelling in the fifth edition.
Borrowed from Latin umbella, and adapted partially to ombre. See also ombrelle.

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French atirer, atirier (“to draw to oneself”), from a- + tirer (“to draw, pull out with great effort, snatch violently, tear away”), from Gothic *𐍄𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌽 (*tiran, “to tear away, remove”), from Proto-Germanic *teraną (“to tear, tear apart”), from Proto-Indo-European *derə- (“to tear, tear apart”). By surface analysis, a- + tirer. More at tirer.

From beuveur (“a drinker”) + -erie, with the first part being an antiquated form of current buveur. A more regular form buverie was created in the sixteenth century but dropped from usage in the nineteenth.
Learned borrowing from Latin cessātiō. Morphologically, from cesser + -ation.
From Ancient Greek τεχνο- (tekhno-), from Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē, “skill”).
From Old French devise (“division, separation; heraldic band, emblem”), from deviser. The financial sense is a semantic loan from German Devise. Compare divisa in the other Romance languages.
Learned borrowing from Latin delphīnātus, from delphīnus (“dauphin”) + -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns). Doublet of dauphinat and dauphiné.
From Middle French heure, from Old French houre, from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time, season, year”), from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”).
From politique + -ien, calque of English politician.
Learned borrowing from Latin cancer. Doublet of chancre and cancer.
Borrowed from Italian gradino. Related to grade.
Inherited from Old French long, from longe, longue, feminine of lonc, lunc, from Latin longus. Cognate with English long, origin of German Chaiselongue.
Borrowed from Italian amabile. Doublet of aimable.
Inherited from Middle French hospital, from Old French hospital (12th c.), a borrowing from Late Latin hospitāle (“hospital, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Doublet of hôtel.
Borrowed from Latin anapaestus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπαιστος (anápaistos, “reversed; anapest”).
Learned borrowing from Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “play, drama”, noun).
From Old French patrimoine (13th c.), patremoine (12th c.), a borrowing from Latin pātrimōnium.
From Middle French jour, from Old French jor(n), from Late Latin diurnum. Doublet of diurne, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin prosperus, prosper. Cf. also the Anglo-Norman form prospre.
Inherited from Old French larcin~larrecin, inherited from Latin latrōcinium.
Borrowed from English raid, from Scots raid. Doublet of rade from Middle English.
Borrowed from Latin sēparātiōnem. Cf. also inherited Old French sevraison.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin thuriferarius, from Latin thurifer.
From os + -eux, or Late Latin ossuōsus, from Latin os.
From Latin inexplicābilis. By surface analysis, in- + explicable.

Inherited from Middle French bramer, from Old Occitan bramar, from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐌼𐌼𐍉𐌽 (*brammōn), *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (*bramjan), from Proto-Germanic *bramjaną (“to bellow, roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrem-. Compare Middle Low German brammen (“to roar”), Dutch brommen (“to bellow”), English brim. More at brim.
Formed from the root of Latin camera with the suffix -al, or borrowed from a Late Latin, Medieval Latin camerālis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obituārius.
From Latin praesentia. By surface analysis, présent (adjective) + -ence.
Borrowed from Old Occitan bancal, from Medieval Latin bancālis, from the base of Proto-Germanic *bankiz + -alis.
Borrowed from Latin inclūsus. Doublet of the inherited enclos.
Inherited from Old French plainte, pleinte (from the feminine past participle of plaindre, pleindre), corresponding to a Medieval Latin plancta, from Latin planctus.
From Arabic سُعُودِيّ (suʕūdiyy). By surface analysis, Saoud + -i.
From Middle French ingredient, from Latin ingredientem, present participle of ingredior (“to go or enter into or onto”).
Inherited from Middle French estimable, from estimer + -able. By surface analysis, estimer + -able.
Borrowed from Latin rhīnocerōs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ῥινόκερως (rhinókerōs).
Inherited from Middle French compte, from Old French conte (with ⟨mp⟩ added back to reflect Latin computus). Cf. also the form conte.
Inherited from Late Latin villūtus, derived from Latin villus (“tuft, hair”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lumbāgō.
Inherited from Middle French climat, borrowed from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma).
From Middle French opinion, from Latin opīniōnem.
From Ancient Greek δενδρίτης (dendrítēs, “relating to trees”), from δένδρον (déndron, “tree”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsiōnem, from Latin propulsus.
Borrowed from Spanish adobe. Doublet of toub.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πρωτᾰγωνῐστής (prōtăgōnĭstḗs).
Inherited from Old French horrible, orrible, orible, borrowed from Latin horribilis.
Borrowed from Latin congratulātiōnem, from congratulor.
From re- + habiller, with the initial e elided before the silent h.
Learned borrowing from Latin narrātiōnem. By surface analysis, narrer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin frūgālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá).
Unadapted borrowing from English coach. Doublet of coche.
Inherited from Old French priere, preiere, from Early Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem.
Borrowed from Italian numero. Doublet of nombre.
Inherited from Middle French texture, borrowed from Latin textūra (“a weaving, web, texture, structure”), from textus, past participle of texere (“to weave”). See text.
Learned borrowing from Latin polygōnum, from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon).
Borrowed from Late Latin compūnctiōnem (“prick [of conscience]”).
From an alteration of Old French meure, from Vulgar Latin *mōra, from Latin mōrum, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
Inherited from Old French sodein, from Vulgar Latin *subitānus, from Latin subitāneus (“sudden”), from subitus.
Inherited from Old French meshui. Equivalent to mais + hui.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūxuriōsus, by surface analysis, luxure + -eux.
Borrowed from Italian radice, from Latin rādīx (“root”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mīca. Doublet of mie and miche.
Borrowed from Latin hūmidus, variant of ūmidus.

Inherited from Old French conoistre, from Late Latin conōscere, from Latin cognōscere. One of few examples where ⟨oi⟩ had been turned into ⟨ai⟩ /ɛ/ instead of /wa/ (alongside adjectival -ais and imperfect tense endings).

Inherited from Old French recete (also reçoite, receite, recepte), from Latin recepta, derived from recipere (“to receive”). The Old French form is phonetically regular (cf. dete < Vulgar Latin *depta), but was probably not inherited, but borrowed from Latin.
Inherited from Middle French criquet, from Old French criket, from Old French criquer (“to crack, creak”), of Germanic origin. Compare Dutch kriek, krekel (“cricket”), English creak.
Learned borrowing from Latin lapidārius (“stony”). The terse sense is from inscription lapidaire, short inscriptions carved in stone.
From envie + -eux, or from Old French envious, envieus, from Latin invidiōsus.
From Latin clēmatis, from Ancient Greek κληματίς (klēmatís), from κλῆμα (klêma, “vine, branch with vines”).
Inherited from Middle French joug, from Old French jug, jou, jof, from Latin jugum, iugum, from Proto-Italic *jugom, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin metonymia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”).
From Ancient Greek ἐπιγαμία (epigamía), equivalent to épi- + -gamie.
From Latin chōrepiscopus, from Ancient Greek χωρεπίσκοπος (khōrepískopos).
From Ancient Greek ἄκαρπος (ákarpos). Morphologically a- + -carpe.
From Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Hebrew ישוע (y'hoshúa).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολύγαμος (polúgamos).
Learned borrowing from Latin mīllēsimus (“thousandth”). Doublet of millième.
Borrowed from Latin eunūchus, itself from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διάκονος (diákonos, “servant, minister”).
Learned borrowing from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos).
Inherited from Old French archiere, likely from the feminine of Latin arcuārius (“bow-related”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin extortiō.
Inherited from Old French posicion, borrowed from Latin positiōnem.
Inherited from Old French revendre, from Latin revēndere, from re- (“re-: again, back”) + vēndere (“to sell”). Equivalent to re- + vendre.
Inherited from Old French arc, from Latin arcus (“bow, arch”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo-.
Inherited from Middle French accointer, from Old French acointier, from Early Medieval Latin accognitāre, from Late Latin accognitus, past participle of accognōscere, from Latin cognōscere.
Learned borrowing from Latin sēlēctiō (“the act of choosing out, selection”), from sēligō (“to choose out, select”), from sē- (“apart”) + legō (“gather, select”).
Inherited from Middle French rite, rit m (first attested in 1479), borrowed from Latin ritus m (“rite”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin comminatorius.
Learned borrowing from Latin zīzania (“tares, cockle”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cymbalum (“cymbal”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κύμβαλον (kúmbalon).
Learned borrowing from Latin perennitās. By surface analysis, pérenne + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French publicateur, from Latin publicātor. By surface analysis, publier + -ateur.
From Middle French pacte, earlier also pa(c)t (14th c.), a borrowing from Latin pactum.
From Old French ancre, from Latin ancora (“anchor”).
Inherited from Old French amer, from Latin amārus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃mós (“bitter, raw”).
Learned borrowing from Latin etymologus, from Ancient Greek ἐτῠμόλογος (etŭmólogos). By surface analysis, étymo- + -logue.
Borrowed from Italian bravo. Doublet of brave.
Inherited from Old French tous, tos, from Latin tussem, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).
Borrowed from Italian forzato. Doublet of forcé. By surface analysis, forcer + -at.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin coenobita, from Latin coenobium.
Learned borrowing from Latin abaculus, a diminutive of abacus (“panel”).
Borrowed from Latin clepsydra, from Ancient Greek κλεψύδρα (klepsúdra).
Inherited from Middle French dolent, from Old French dolent, borrowed from Latin dolentem (“hurting, suffering”).
Inherited from Middle French magnanimité, from Old French [Term?], borrowed from Latin magnanimitātem.
From Latin papāver. Doublet of papaver.
From brin + -ille, with -d- of obscure origin.
Borrowed from Arabic زَاوِيَة (zāwiya, “corner, prayer room”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek αἰσθητής (aisthētḗs).
Inherited from Middle French appetit, from Old French apetit, loaned from Latin appetītus.
Borrowed from English charter. Doublet of charte.
Inherited from Late Latin veruina (“long javelin”), from Latin veru (“javelin”).
From Latin majorare (“to augment”), derived from Latin maiōrem.
Inherited from Middle French lacer, from Old French lacier, from Latin laqueare.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin palpābilis.
Borrowed from Old Occitan maestral (whence Occitan mistral) from Late Latin magistrālis, from Latin magister. Doublet of magistral.
From Latin fortūnātus. By surface analysis, fortune + -é in the form of a past participle.
Inherited from Middle French cire, from Old French cire, chiere, ciere, from Latin cēra.
Inherited from Middle French angle, from Old French angle, from Latin angulus, anglus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin resultātum, the substantivized neuter singular of resultātus (perfect passive participle of resultō). By surface analysis, résulter + -at.
Learned borrowing from Latin Baiae f pl.
Inherited from Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, a borrowing from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon).
Borrowed from Old Occitan rodar, from Latin rotāre. Doublet of rouer.
From Middle French, from Old French nen (preceding vowel sounds) or ne (preceding consonant sounds), from Latin nōn (“not”).
Inherited from Old French nice, inherited from Latin nescius.
Borrowed from English bowling. The sense "bowling alley" is a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English bowling alley.
Inherited from Middle French train, from Old French train, from the verb trahiner (“to pull, drag”) (whence traîner).
From profit + -erole, i.e. "benefit" + diminutive suffix, a small treat given as a reward.
Inherited from Middle French flascon, from Late Latin flascō. Doublet of fiasco and flasque.
Inherited from Old French peril, from Vulgar Latin *periclu(m), syncopated form of Latin perīculum.
Most likely from a- + long + -er, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from ad + Late Latin longāre, from Latin longus.
Borrowed from Occitan mascaret (“steer with a mottled face”). The appearance of the tidal bore was thought to resemble a herd of stampeding cattle.
From Wallon + -ie, coined by Honoré Chavée in 1842.
Borrowed from Italian complimento, itself a borrowing from Spanish cumplimiento, from Latin complēmentum. Doublet of complément.
Inherited from Middle French sympathic, from sympathie, from Late Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia), from συν- (sun-, “with, together”) + πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek λεξικογράφος (lexikográphos); cognate with English lexicographer, Dutch lexicograaf, German Lexikograf.
Learned borrowing from Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós).
Inherited from Old French dos, from Latin dorsum (through Vulgar Latin dossum). Compare Romansh dies, Catalan dors, Italian dosso, and Romanian dos.
Borrowed from Russian кумы́с (kumýs), itself from a Turkic source. Compare Tatar кымыз (qımız), Kazakh қымыз (qımız), Kyrgyz кымыз (kımız), Turkish kımız, Azerbaijani qımız.
Borrowed from Latin Phaëtōn, from the Ancient Greek Φᾰέθων (Phăéthōn).
Inherited from Middle French trés, from Old French trés, inherited from Latin trāns, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of trans-, trans, and tré-.
Inherited from Old French entier, inherited from Latin integrum (although modified with the -ier suffix analogically). Compare the borrowed doublet intègre.
From Ancient Greek τᾰ́ξῐς (tắxĭs, “arrangement”, “order”) + δέρμᾰ (dérmă, “skin”). First attested in 1803.
Inherited from Middle French alibi (14th c.), borrowed from Latin alibī.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek καρωτίς (karōtís), from κάρος (káros, “stupor”).

Inherited from Middle French langue, from Old French langue, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”). See cognates in regional languages in France: Champenois laingue, Norman laungue, Gallo lenghe, Picard lingue, Bourguignon laingue, Franco-Provençal lengoua, Occitan lenga, Corsican lingua.
Originally berlinguaux (“kind of pastry”), most probably from Italian berlingozzo (“kind of pastry”), itself from berlingo, a borrowing from Old French brelenc: brelan in modern French.
Inherited from Middle French nef, from Old French nef, from Latin nāvem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Displaced by bateau and navire in the sense of "boat".
Inherited from Old French, from Latin parāre, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”).
Inherited from Old French quatorze, from Latin quattuordecim.
Probably borrowed from Medieval Latin retorta, from Latin retortus.
From Middle French adorateur, borrowed from Latin adōrātor. By surface analysis, adorer + -ateur.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνώδυνος (anṓdunos, “free from pain”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain”).

Inherited from Old French mestier, inherited from Vulgar Latin *misterium, a syncopated form of ministerium (whence French ministère). Compare Portuguese mister, also mester, Italian mestiere, Spanish and Catalan menester.
From commissaire + -at. Compare Medieval Latin commissāriātus [1352].

Inherited from Old French menton, mentun, from Vulgar Latin *mentō (accusative *mentōnem), from Classical Latin mentum. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to project”). Compare Occitan menton, Catalan mentó, Romansh mintun.
Coined by French chemist François Stanislas Cloëz in 1870, from a blend of eucalyptus + -ol.

Inherited from Middle French puy, from Old French puy (“hill, height”), pui, from Latin podium. Its current use as a regionalism referring to certain geographic features may be taken at least in part from Franco-Provençal; cf. also Occitan puèg and Catalan puig. In Old French, it had a somewhat different or more varied set of meanings (cf. also the feminine puie, puye, poye (“balustrade”), whence English pew through Anglo-Norman), later coming to be applied to mountains and hills especially in the Auvergne region and Massif Central, the remains of extinct volcanoes. Doublet of the later borrowing podium.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin habitāculum.

Inherited from Middle French avec, avecques (“with”), from Old French avoc, avoec, avuec (“with”), from an assumed Vulgar Latin *aboc, *abhoc, *apud hŏque, from Latin apud (“with, near, close to”) + hoc (“this”) + -que. First used as a replacement for Latin cum (“with”) in Merovingian and Carolingian documents from France. Gradually supplanted Old French od (“with”), itself from apud (od however survives in some dialects in Western France under the form d'od, especially in Normandy). Cognate with Picard avuc, Norman aveuc, Walloon avou and, more distantly, with Franco-Provençal avoi (from *ab hoc and not *abhocque).
* lagon + -ite Named after the word "lagon" because it is found as an incrustation at Tuscan lagoons.

From Old French piscine, pecine (12th c.), a borrowing from Latin piscīna (“pool, basin, fishpond”), derived from piscis (“fish”). Originally used in French in the context of religious ablutions; the sense “swimming pool” is first attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Latin quīnus (“fivefold; five by five”).
Inherited from Middle French boufon, from Italian buffone.
From bouillir + -otte. The card game is so-called due to an analogy being drawn between the high temperature of a boiler and the high speed at which the game is played.
From Old French gelee; from the feminine past participle of geler (compare Latin gelāta). Compare Italian gelata, Spanish helada, Portuguese geada, Catalan gelada.
Inherited from Latin dēsūrsum, from dē and sūrsum.
From goitre + -eux, or possibly from Latin gutturōsus, from guttur.
Inherited from Old French escuele, from Latin scutella (in Vulgar Latin influenced by scūtum), diminutive of Latin scutra. Doublet of esquilette.
Inherited from Middle French armateur, probably from an unattested sense of Medieval Latin armātōrem.
From Old French destrait, past participle of destraire (modern distraire), from Latin distrahō (“to distract”).
From Latin mimus, from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos).

From ballet + -mane. Although the spelling balletomane is the most common nowadays, the spelling ballettomane may be justified by analogy with other derivatives of nouns ending in the diminutive suffix -et, which commonly insert an additional t before vowel-initial suffixes (for example, sonnettiste, motettiste, juillettiste, cornettiste, flageolettiste, galoubettiste). Indeed, ballet derives from Italian balletto, a diminutive of ballo, formed with the Italian suffix -etto, which is a cognate of the French suffix -et (both deriving from the Late Latin suffixe -ittus or -ettus).
Learned borrowing from Latin mediocris, from medius (“middle, central”).
From Old French rondel, diminutive of ront.
Inherited from Old French cogole, from Latin cucūlla.

Inherited from Old French reoïlle, from Vulgar Latin *robicla, from syncopation of Latin *robicula, a diminutive of Latin rōbīgō (“rust”) + -cula (from -culus (suffix forming diminutives)). Rōbīgō is derived from rōbus (a variant of rūfus (“red, reddish”)) + -īgō (suffix forming nouns usually denoting diseased conditions). Compare Catalan rovell, Occitan rovilh, Spanish robín.

Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from aborder, from Old French aborder (“to hit a ship in order to board it”), from bord (“side of a ship, edge”), from Frankish *bord (“side of a ship or vessel”), from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“edge, border, side”), from Proto-Indo-European *bheredh- (“to cut”). Cognate with Old High German bort (“edge, rim, rand”), Old English bord (“ship, side of a ship”), Old Norse borð (“edge, side of a vessel”). More at board.
From caille (“quail”) + -ette, because of the color of certain varieties of the bird.

Inherited from Old French giste, past participle of gesir, modern French gésir (“to lie, to be in a horizontal position (especially dead people); later by extension, to be located (as in "here lies"”). Compare regional jas (“sheepfold”).
From earlier garbe, borrowed from Italian garbo, from Italian garbare, from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐍂𐍅𐍉𐌽 (*garwōn). Alternatively from Middle High German walbe (“slope”).
Learned borrowing from Latin accelerātiō. By surface analysis, accélérer + -ation.
From Old French patron (“patron, protector”), from Latin patrōnus, from pater (“father”).
Inherited from Old French dame, from Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina.
Coined by physicist Joseph Sauveur, from Latin acousticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός (akoustikós), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “hear”).

From Old French conopé, conope (later altered in form and meaning based on Medieval Latin canāpēum, alteration of canōpēum (“mosquito net”)), itself from Latin cōnōpēum (“seat with a canopy”), from Ancient Greek κωνωπεῖον (kōnōpeîon), from κώνωψ (kṓnōps, “mosquito”). Cognate with English canopy.
Present participle of the verb croître (“to increase, to grow”). From Old French croisant, from earlier creissant, from Latin crēscentem, present active participle of crēscō (“to augment”).
Inherited from Old French marne, variant of marle, from Gaulish *margila, a diminutive of marga, attested in Pliny.
1611, alternative spelling charabine late 16th century, from carabin. The meaning "mistress of one of the carabins" is recorded in the dictionary of Guérin (1892).
Inherited from Old French messagier, from message.
From artiller + -eur, itself from a Vulgar Latin *apticlāre, *apticulāre, from Latin aptāre (“to make capable”).

Inherited from Middle French bignet, from Old French bignet (“fried dough enveloping a food substance”), a diminutive of bigne, bugne, buyne (“lump, swelling”), from Frankish *bungjō (“lump, bump, swelling”), from Proto-Germanic *bungô, *bunkô (“lump, heap, crowd”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰenǵʰ- (“thick, dense, fat”). Alternatively, from Gaulish *bunia. Cognate with Old High German bungo (“swelling, tuber”) (German Bunge), Dutch bonk (“lump, clump”), Scottish Gaelic bonnach (“cake, biscuit”). Also related to English bun, bunk, bunch, bunion. Equivalent to beigne + -et.
Inherited from Middle French paltoke, paletoc, from Middle English paltok; first element related to Latin pallium (“cloak”), second element of uncertain origin.
From quitter (“to make quits”) + -ance, from quitte (“quits”).
Inherited from Latin Garumna, Garonna, probably from Gaulish *garunda (“shallows, riverbank”).

Inherited from Middle French corbeau m, from Old French corbel m, itself either a diminutive of corp m (“raven”), or from a Late Latin corbellus, corvellus m, from Latin corvus m (Vulgar Latin variant *corbus m).
From Latin simia, simius (whence French singe) + -esque.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin lūmināre, from Latin lūmen. Doublet of lumière, which was inherited.
From muscardin (“musk-scented lozenge, hazel mouse”), from muscade (“nutmeg”), from Latin muscus (“musk”).
Deverbal from employer. Akin to Italian impiego, Occitan emplec, and Spanish empleo.
From in- (“not”) + tolérance or borrowed from Latin intolerantia (“insolence, insufferableness; (very rare) intolerance”).
Inherited from Middle French chercher, cercher, altered from Old French cerchier through assimilation, from Late Latin circāre, from Latin circa, circus.
Inherited from Middle French corporéité (first attested in 1482), borrowed from Medieval Latin corporeitātem.
Inherited from Middle French commerce, borrowed from Latin commercium (“commerce, trade”), from com- (“together”) + merx (“good, wares, merchandise”).
Inherited from Middle French champ, from Old French champ m, inherited from Latin campus m (“field”). Doublet of camp m and campus m.
Borrowed from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”).
Cognate with or borrowed from Spanish caparazón. Possibly related to carapace (with metathesis) + the suffix -on.
Inherited from Old French verille, ve(d)ille, from Vulgar Latin *vĭtīcula, from Late Latin vītīcula, from Classical Latin vītĭcula.
Inherited from Old French eschevin, from Early Medieval Latin scabīnus from Frankish *skapin, related to *skappjan.
Inherited from Old French cumble, inherited through a Vulgar Latin form *cumlu(s) from Latin cumulus. Doublet of cumulus, a borrowing.
Inherited from Old French eschale, inherited from Latin scāla. Doublet of escale.
Borrowed from Russian ю́рта (júrta, “yurt”), from a Turkic language, from Proto-Turkic *yūrt (“dwelling place”).
From craie (“chalk”) + -on (diminutive suffix), derived from Latin crēta (“chalk, clay”).
From mono- + lithique or from monolithe + -ique.
From thym + -ol, coined by French chemist Alexandre Lallemand in 1853.
Inherited from Middle French beau, from Old French biau, bel, from Latin bellus.
Inherited from Old French neutre, from Latin neuter.
Borrowed from Latin aenigmaticus, from Ancient Greek αἰνιγματικός (ainigmatikós). By surface analysis, énigme + -(at)ique.
From Latin indolentem, accusative singular masculine and feminine of indolēns, from in- (“not”) + dolēns (“pain”).
Inherited from Middle French quinze, from Old French, from Latin quīndecim.
Learned borrowing from Latin chrysalis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χρυσαλλίς (khrusallís).

Inherited from Old French chanteor (oblique form), from Latin cantōrem. By surface analysis, chanter + -eur. Compare also chantre, derived from the Latin nominative. Alternatively, from a Latin cantator, cantatorem.
Diminutive of canne (“reed”); from Old French canele, kanele
Inherited from Middle French cassette, from Old Northern French casse (“case”) + -ette (diminutive). By surface analysis, *casse + -ette. Compare Italian cassetta.
Inherited from Old French ovrier, inherited from Latin operārius. Cf. also the doublet opéraire, a very rare and jargony term borrowed from the same Latin term.
Inherited from Old French cuisse, from Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂.
From convenir + -ance (compare convenant); possibly corresponds to Latin convenientia.
Inherited from Middle French claret (compare English claret), from Medieval Latin clārātum, from Latin clārus (“clear”).
From coiffer (“to cover the head, to give a haircut, style the hair”) + -ure.
Inherited from Middle French gouster, from Old French goster, inherited from Latin gustāre. Compare the borrowed prefixed verb déguster.
From Latin lympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē).

Usually derived from Middle French eiguenot, eyguenotz (“Swiss confederate; kind of soldier”), from German Eidgenosse (“confederate; Swiss person”), from Eid (“oath”) + Genosse (“companion”). It would then appear that the singular in -t is a French backformation from the plural, although it has also been compared to the Dutch eedgenoot (eed + genoot). An alternate theory considers it a diminutive of Hugues (“Hugh”). The theory states that the term was originally used by Savoyard Roman Catholic supporters of the ruling Savoy dynasty as a derogatory designation (later embraced by Geneva republicans and by French Calvinists), with a meaning similar to "little Hughey", after the surname of Geneva burgomaster Besançon Hugues, who (though a Catholic himself) supported and participated in the rebellion against the rule of the Savoy dynasty, which led to the independence of Geneva in 1526. See Huguenot on Wikipedia for more.
Inherited from Middle French teinture, from Old French tainture, from Latin tinctūra, from tinctus the perfect passive participle of tingō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin numerārius, from numerus (whence French nombre).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dispōnibilis.

From Latin Capharnaūm, the Biblical town Capernaum in Galilee. The sense derives from the Biblical story of the healing of a paralytic (Luke 5:17–26; Mark 2:1–12), in which a crowd of people assembles when Jesus visits Capernaum.
Borrowed from Latin crotalum, from Ancient Greek κρόταλον (krótalon).
From Late Latin astrologicus, from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, astrologie + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Latin redactiō, from redigō (whence rédiger).
From German Nihilismus, itself from Latin nihil (“nil, nothing”) + German -ismus '-ism', coined in 1817 by German philosopher Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi, but repeatedly 'reinvented'.
Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Latin cēnsus.
From being shaped like a trumpet. Inherited from Middle French, borrowed from Italian tromba. Doublet of trompe.
Inherited from Middle French nation, from Old French nacion, borrowed from Latin nātiōnem.

From Middle French bider (“to trot”), of unknown ultimate origin, + -et. Possibly related to Medieval Italian bidetto (“small horse”), itself probably related to Proto-West Germanic *biti (“bite; horse's bit”); or, possibly from a lost Middle French rabider (“go quickly, violently”), a descendant of Latin rabidus (“furious, fierce”), with loss of the initial prefix. Modern sense derives from analogy with the straddling of a bidet and the straddling of a small horse.
Inherited from Old French enceinte, from Latin incīncta, feminine past participle of incingō. Compare Italian incinta, Spanish and Catalan encinta.
From Old French vis + à + vis, vis m being an obsolete word for “face”, replaced in Modern French by visage m.
Borrowed from Portuguese chicote, probably borrowed from French chicot.

Inherited from Middle French corbeille, from Old French corbeille, corbeil, corbele, curbeyle, from Late Latin corbicula, diminutive of Latin corbis (“basket”), probably from Frankish *korb, from Proto-Germanic *kurbaz, *krebô (“basket”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ- (“bundle”).
Inherited from Middle French dictionnaire, borrowed from Medieval Latin dictiōnārium (“dictionary”), derived from Latin dictiō (“saying, speaking”) + -ārium.
Inherited from Middle French entituler, ultimately from Latin titulus (“title”).

Inherited from Middle French gascher (“to waste, ruin; row (with oars)”), from Old French gaschier, gacher, gasser (“to soil, spoil, waste”) and Old French gaschier, guaschier, waschier (“to wash, soak”), both from Old Dutch *wascon, *wascan (“to wash, bathe”), from Frankish *waskan (“to wash”), from Proto-Germanic *waskaną (“to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *wod- (“wet”). Compare related Italian guazzare (“to splash, wallow”), from the same Germanic root. Cognate with Old English wasċan (“to wash”). More at wash.
Borrowed from Italian altezza or, less convincingly, from Spanish alteza. Doublet of hautesse, the inherited French equivalent.
From cape + -uche, or borrowed from Italian cappuccio. Compare capuce.
From œil + -ade, perhaps an adaptation of Italian occhiata or some other descendant of Vulgar Latin *oculāta. First attested ca. 1480.
Inherited from Old French Macedoine, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin Macedonia, from Ancient Greek Μακεδονία (Makedonía, “Macedonia”), which see for more.
Pseudo-Latinism, literally, “pulled by the hair”, from Latin capillus (“hair”) + tractus (“pulled”), a humorous Latinization of tiré par les cheveux.
From Latin Libanus, from Ancient Greek Λίβανος (Líbanos), from a Semitic source.
Inherited from Old French farmacie, borrowed from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).
Inherited from Middle French inexcusable, from Latin inexcusabilis.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Medieval Latin sigillata (terra), from the past participle of sigillō (cf. French sceller).

Inherited from Old French lïesce or liesse, from earlier ledece, inherited from Latin laetitia. The first syllable shifted under influence from Old French lié, liet, itself from related Latin laetus. Doublet of Liesse, Léticie, and Laetitia.
Borrowed from Latin sanguinolentus. See also sanglant.
Learned borrowing from Latin aegis, aegidis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís).
From earlier jouvencel, Old French jovenenciel, from Vulgar Latin *iuvencellus, from Latin iuvenculus.
From the gerund form zapping of English zap.
From actif, both from Latin activus.
Borrowed from Latin opportūnitātem. Morphologically, from opportun + -ité.
Inherited from Old French estension, borrowed from Latin extentiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin tripodem, from Ancient Greek τρίπους (trípous). By surface analysis, tri- + -pode.
Inherited from Middle French reste, from Old French reste, equivalent to the stem of rester.
Inherited from Middle French elegie, a borrowing from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεία (elegeía).
From Ancient Greek ἀνθρωπολόγος (anthrōpológos), which comes from ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”) and λόγος (lógos). Essentially anthropo- + -logie.
Borrowed from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl, of uncertain origin; see that entry for more information.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin correlātiō.
Learned borrowing from Latin reconciliātiō. By surface analysis, réconcilier + -ation.

Inherited from Middle French roustir, from Old French rostir, from Frankish *rōstjan (“to roast”), from Proto-Germanic *raustijaną (“to roast”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hrews- (“to crackle, roast”). Germanic cognates include Old High German rōsten. Compare Italian arrostire and Spanish rostir.
From Ancient Greek λειπογγράμμα (leipongrámma), λείπω (leípō, “leaving out”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”), 18th c..
From quarante + -aine, the medical sense a calque of Italian quarantena.
From président + -ence, or a borrowing from Medieval Latin praesidentia. See also préséance.
Learned borrowing from Latin factīcius. Compare the inherited Old French form faitis as well as the doublet fétiche, borrowed from Portuguese.
Inherited from Middle French barque, probably borrowed from Italian barca or a Medieval Latin equivalent, from Late Latin barca. Doublet of barge.
Inherited from Middle French procuration, from Old French procuracion, from Latin prōcūrātiōnem; by surface analysis, procurer + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French computation, from Latin computātiō.
From déchoir + -ance, possibly corresponding to Late Latin decadentia, from decadēns, present participle of decadō, from Latin de + cadō. Doublet of décadence, borrowed from Latin.
Borrowed from Latin etymologicus. By surface analysis, étymo- + -logique.
After a German term coined by Ferdinand Christian Baur in an 1831 issue of the Tübinger Zeitschrift für Theologie. Also judéo- + christianisme.
Learned borrowing from Latin adaequātiō, or formed in French from adéquat + -tion.

Inherited from Middle French avoir, from Old French avoir, aveir, aver, from Latin habēre (“have, hold, possess”), probably from a Proto-Italic *habēō or *haβēō, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰh₁bʰ- (“to grab, to take”). Influenced and reinforced by similar (yet etymologically unrelated) verbs in Germanic; compare Frankish *habbjan (“to have”), Old High German habēn (“to have”), Old Norse hafa (“to have”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (haban, “to have”). See closer cognates in regional languages in France: Angevin avouèr, Bourbonnais-Berrichon avoér, Bourguignon aivoi, Champenois aouâr, Corsican avè, Franco-Provençal avêr, Franc-Comtois aivoi, Gallo avair, Lorrain ahoir, Norman avaer, Occitan aver, Picard avoèr. Further cognates include: Italian avere, Portuguese haver, Romanian avea, avere, and Sardinian (Campidanese airi, Logudorese àere), Sicilian aviri, Spanish haber, and English aver (borrowed via Old French).
Borrowed from Late Latin nigella. Doublet of nielle, which was inherited.

Inherited from Old French prés (“closely”), from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”) and pressus (“concise”), from premō (“to press, push, condense”). Cognate with Italian presso and Sicilian pressu.
Inherited from Middle French debatre, from Old French debatre. Equivalent to dé- + battre.
Learned borrowing from Latin rusticitās. By surface analysis, rustique + -ité.
Inherited from Old French ignorance, borrowed from Latin ignōrantia.
From Latin subscrīptor; related to souscrit.

Inherited from Middle French amoureux, from Old French amoreus, amereus, from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, derived from Latin amōrem (“love”, noun). Compare English amorous, borrowed from Middle French. Doublet of amoroso, borrowed from Italian.
Inherited from Middle French cendre, from Old French cendre, from Latin cinerem, from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”).
Inherited from Middle French, borrowed from Latin compositus. Doublet of compote and compost.
Inherited from Middle French fortune, from Old French fortune, borrowed from Latin fortūna.
Inherited from Old French moiste, muste, from a cross between Vulgar Latin *mucidus (from Latin mūcidus) with forms of mustum; cf. *mustidus.
From Medieval Latin graduālis, from Latin gradus (“step”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰradʰ-, *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”).
Learned borrowing from Latin facultās. Doublet of facilité.
Learned borrowing from Latin apertūra (“opening”). Doublet of ouverture.
From Middle French garnement, from Old French garnement (“garrison soldier”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin ischaemia, itself derived from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”).
Borrowed from Italian nocchiero, from Latin nauclērus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).
Inherited from Old French literal, borrowed from Late Latin litterālis.
From Ancient Greek λακωνίζω (lakōnízō). By surface analysis, Laconien + -iser.
Of Germanic naval origin, from Old Norse þilja, thilia, from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ (“plank, board”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Syriacus, from Ancient Greek Συριακός (Suriakós), from Συρία (Suría).
From Spanish listón. By surface analysis, liste + -on.
Inherited from Middle French contempteur, from Latin contemptor.
From Latin praenominatio, from praenominare + -tio. By surface analysis, prénommer + -ation.
Inherited from Latin con-, from cum (“with”).

Learned borrowing from Latin fētus. This spelling is originally a hypercorrection (which already arises in Latin, where foetus is also found), but is today almost the only one in use. The spelling fétus, though etymologically more correct (and thus promoted by some grammarians), is of very limited usage.
Inherited from Middle French, from Ancient Greek λοβός (lobós).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grāna, neuter plural of grānum reanalysed as a feminine. Compare grain.
Inherited from Middle French irregulier, a borrowing from Late Latin irrēgulāris.
From English kidnapper, reanalyzed in French as kidnapper (verb) + -eur (suffix forming agent nouns).
From Ancient Greek ἀλλο- (allo-), combining form of ἄλλος (állos, “other”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin pāgānismus. See païen and -isme.
Inherited from Latin concurrentem, present active participle of concurrō (“happen at the same time”), from con- (“with”) + currō (“run”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin gehenna, from Aramaic ܓܗܢܐ (gēhannā) from Hebrew גֵּיהִנּוֹם (ge'henom, “hell”, literally “valley of Hinnom”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περῐσπώμενος (perĭspṓmenos).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nāsālis, from Latin nāsus (“nose”).
Inherited from Old French bourrache, from Medieval Latin borāgō or borrago, either from Latin borra (“short wool, rough hair”) or Arabic أَبُو العَرَق (ʔabū l-ʕaraq, literally “father of sweat”).
Borrowed from Latin breviārium, from brevis (“short”). Doublet of brimborion.
Learned borrowing from New Latin coronilla.
From Late Latin astrālis, from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).
From Old French mondain, from Late Latin mundānus. Compare Italian mondano.
Inherited from Middle French nombre, from Old French nombre, nonbre, from Latin numerus. Doublet of numéro.

From Middle French major, from Spanish mayor, from Latin maior. Doublet of maire, majeur, and mayeur. The use for a non-commissioned officer in the French army (since 1972) is a short form of adjudant-major or sergent-major.
From Spanish navajo, from Tewa navahúuˀu.
From Old French ebaine (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin ebenus, which see.
Inherited from Old French vital, from Latin vītālis (“of life, life-giving”).
Inherited from Middle French esponge, from Old French espoinge (cf. also variant espoigne), from Vulgar Latin *sponga, from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).
Learned borrowing from Latin canālis. Doublet of chenal.
Borrowed from translingual Gammarus, from Latin gammarus.
From Ancient Greek ψίλωσις (psílōsis, “[the act of] stripping bare”), from ψιλόω (psilóō, “I strip bare, I denude”).
From Middle French pus (16th c.), a borrowing from Latin pus (“pus”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin abdicātīvus.
Inherited from Middle French stupéfaction, borrowed from Late Latin stupefactiōnem, from Latin stupefaciōnem, from stupeō (“to be stunned, speechless”) + faciō (“to do, make”).
Coined by Ferdinand de Saussure, from synchrone + -ie.

Inherited from Middle French ours, from Old French urs, from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *orsos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos. The Early Modern French pronunciation was /uʁ/ before consonants, /uʁz/ before vowels, and /uʁs/ in pausa. For the most part, the pausal pronunciations were eventually lost, but in some cases they were re-established as the basic form (reinforced in part by the spelling, in part by related words; in this case perhaps the feminine ourse).
Inherited from Middle French piege, from Old French piege, from Vulgar Latin *pedicus, from Latin pedica, from pēs, pedis (“foot”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τετραλογία (tetralogía).
Learned borrowing from New Latin frutescens.
Inherited from Middle French lampe, from Old French lampe, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp, flambeau”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin coxālis, from Latin coxa.
Inherited from Middle French, from Latin mīlitia (“military, military service”), from mīles (“soldier”).
Borrowed from Latin sīderālis, from sīdus.
Borrowed from Italian affettuoso. Doublet of affectueux.
Learned borrowing from Latin hūmānitās. By surface analysis, humain + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French and Old French signe, a borrowing from Latin signum. Doublet of seing, which was inherited through Vulgar Latin.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek δίπους (dípous). By surface analysis, di- + -pode.

Inherited from Old French certifier, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin or Medieval Latin certificāre, from Latin certus (“resolved, certain”), a modified form of the perfect passive participle of cernō.
Inherited from Middle French scholastique, borrowed from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολαστικός (skholastikós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin excentricus, from ex- (“away”) + centrum (“the centre”) + -icus. By surface analysis, ex- + centre + -ique.
From Old French enseignement. By surface analysis, enseigner (“to educate; to teach”) + -ment.

Most likely from Old French beguer, from Middle Dutch beggen (“to chat”) (related to beggaert (“one who rattles off prayers”)). This word itself is of uncertain origin, but could possibly be related to spreken (“to speak, tell”), lacking the initial s and r due to some substrate influence. Rejected or unlikely sources of the Middle Dutch word include beige (“wool color”), but the phonetics don’t fit, and French always had /g/ pronunciation instead of /d͡ʒ/ as in Dutch; Medieval Latin Albigenses (“heretic”), but no real phonological or semantic match; and finally the proper name Begga, borne by several pious women, now abandoned as a mere guess.
From Middle French paucité, apparently borrowed in the mid 14th century from Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”).
Inherited from Old French ver, verm (“worm”), from Latin vermem (“worm”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.
Learned borrowing from Latin cremātiōnem. By surface analysis, crémer (“to cremate”) + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of premier.
Learned borrowing from Latin cippus (“stake”). Doublet of cep.

Inherited from Middle French escot, from Old French escot, escoz (“payment”), from Old Frankish *skot (“tax”, literally “that which is thrown in”), from Proto-Germanic *skutą (“that which is thrown, shot, projectile, bullet, missile”). Cognate with Old High German scoz (“bullet, missile, projectile, javelin, shot”), Old English scot, sceot (“shot, lot, payment”). More at scot.
Inherited from Old French besistre, Late Latin bisextus (“intercalary day”); so called because intercalary days were seen as portending misery.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin rectilineus altered by association with ligne (“line”).
Borrowed from Dutch drossen, though this could instead be a reverse borrowing; both are probably ultimately from Italian trozza (“gooseneck”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin phallus. Doublet of phalle.
Learned borrowing from New Latin āpetalus. By surface analysis, a- + pétale.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōnōminālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin pulverulentus, from pulvis, pulveris (“dust, powder”) (whence French poudre).
From Latin bombyx, from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux).
Learned borrowing from Latin disparātus, past participle of disparō (“to divide”), from dis- (“apart”) + parō (“to make equal”), from par (“equal”).
Inherited from Old French garlande, probably derived from Frankish *weron (“bedeck, adorn”), from or related to Proto-Germanic *wīraz; compare Old High German wieren, English wire.
From offense + -er, from Latin offēnsāre (“to strike against”), replacing previous Middle French offendre.
Inherited from Middle French Argive, from Latin Argīvus.
Borrowed from Occitan castanhòla, diminutive of castanha (“chestnut”).
Inherited from Old French los, from Latin laus, probably via the nominative singular form.
From Old French grifer, either deverbal from griffe, which see, or from Old High German grīfan, from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną. Doublet of gripper.
Learned borrowing from Latin vertebrālis. By surface analysis, vertèbre + -al.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek γλυπτικός (gluptikós, “fit for engraving, carving”), from γλυπτός (gluptós) + -ικός (-ikós).

Unadapted borrowing from English bacon, from Middle English bacon (“meat from the back and sides of a pig”), from Old French bacon, bacun (“ham, strip of lard”), from Frankish *bakkō, from Proto-Germanic *bakō, *baką, *bakaz (“back”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“back, buttocks; to vault, arch”). Attested since 1899.
Borrowed from Spanish pecadillo, with change of gender.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cutina, from Latin cutis.
Borrowed from Latin satellitem (accusative singular of satelles).
Learned borrowing from Latin patriarchālis. By surface analysis, patriarche + -al.
From English cam, a shortening of camera.
Borrowed from Late Latin illuminātiōnem, from Latin illuminō.
Inherited from Old French es-, from Latin ex-, ē-.
Borrowed from English eusocial. By surface analysis, eu- + social. First used in 1966.
Inherited from Middle French lippe, from Old French lipe, lepe (“underlip”), from Middle Dutch lippe (“lip”), from Frankish *lippjō (“lip”).
Inherited from Middle French foison, from Old French foison, inherited from Latin fūsiōnem. Doublet of fusion, a borrowing.
From Middle French Aust(e)riche, Ost(e)riche, from Old French Ostriche (ca. 1200), from Middle High German Ōsterīche, from Old High German Ōstarrīhhi (literally “eastern realm”).
From Old French galatas (“housing in the upper part of a building”), from the tower of Galata, in Constantinople.
First attested in the 19th century. Calque of German Übermensch. Also sur- + homme.
Learned borrowing from Latin helix, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).
