Coined based on Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”).
From Middle French flammant (16th c.), from Occitan flamenc.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin syringa, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, syrinx”).
Borrowed from Latin opācitātem (accusative of opācitās).
Borrowed from Spanish negro, first attested in 1845. Doublet of nègre, borrowed earlier from Spanish.
Learned borrowing from Latin turbidus. See also trouble.
Learned borrowing from Latin mediocritās. By surface analysis, médiocre + -ité.
Borrowed from Latin scēptrum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek σκῆπτρον (skêptron).
Borrowed from German Eulenspiegel, based on the folklore character Till Eulenspiegel; from Middle Low German Ūlenspēgel.
Inherited from Middle French collet. By surface analysis, col + -et.
Learned borrowing from Latin pūbertātem. By surface analysis, pubère + -té.
From Latin Chananaeus, from Ancient Greek Χαναναῖος (Khananaîos).
From Occitan cagòla, feminine of cacou.
Inherited from Middle French ébaudir, from Old French esbaudir, esbaldir. By surface analysis, é- + baudir.

Inherited from Middle French prophete, from Old French prophete, from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”).
Inherited from Old French somier, from Late Latin saumārius, sagmārius, from Latin sagma.

Inherited from Old French lie, from Early Medieval Latin lias (“lees, dregs”) (descent via winemaking common in monasteries), from Gaulish *ligyā, *legyā (“silt, sediment”) (compare Welsh llai, Old Breton leh (“deposit, silt”)), from Proto-Celtic *legyā (“layer”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).
First attested in Old French, borrowed from Latin prohibitiōnem.
From Latin Allobrogem, accusative of Allobrox.
Borrowed from Latin censōrem, accusative of censōr.
From Latin agaricum, from Ancient Greek ἀγαρικόν (agarikón, “a tree fungus (Phellinus pomaceus”)), from the country of Agaria, in Sarmatia.
Inherited from Old French ier, from Latin heri.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin argumentātor.
Inherited from Middle French escrire, from Old French escrire, escrivre, from Latin scrībere.
Inherited from Old French fener, from Vulgar Latin *fenāre, from Latin fenum. Compare Occitan fenar.
Inherited from Middle French registre, from Medieval Latin registrum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin īrōnicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). By surface analysis, ironie + -ique.
From English magazine. Doublet of magasin.
Borrowed from Italian credito, from Latin crēditum.
Inherited from Middle French mi (“middle”), from Old French mi, mie (“middle”), from earlier *miei (compare lit, liet < *lieit), from Latin medius (adjective), medium (noun).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ubīquitās (“ubiquity, omnipresence”).
Borrowed from Spanish adive, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic ذِئْب (ḏiʔb).
From Latin etēsius (“annual”), from Ancient Greek ἐτήσιος (etḗsios, “annual”), from ἔτος (étos, “year”).

Probably a derivative of chippe (compare chiffe (“old cloth, rag”)) in the sense of "to hide something of little value", from Middle English chip, chippe (“fragment, worthless thing”) from Old English ċipp (“splinter, beam”) from Proto-Germanic *kippaz, *kipaz (“beam, log”). More at chip.
Learned borrowing from Latin aedīlitās. By surface analysis, édile + -ité.
Borrowed from Italian vibrato m, past participle of vibrare (“to vibrate”), cognate with vibré m.

From Middle French stucq (“a coating imitating marble”) from Italian stucco (“coating made of pulverised gypsum, plaster, stucco”) from Old Italian stucco, from Lombardic stucki, *stucchi (“crust, fragment, piece”) from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją (“stick, beam, stump”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“shock, impact”). Akin to German stukki (“crust, fragment, piece”) (German Stück (“piece”)), Old Saxon stukki (“piece, fragment”), Old English stycce. More at stucco.
From New Latin Lycosa, from Latin lycos, from Ancient Greek λύκος (lúkos).
Inherited from Middle French stratageme, from Old French stratageme, a borrowing from Latin strategema, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma).
Inherited from Middle French engin m, from Old French engin m, from Latin ingenium n.
Inherited from Old French criminal, borrowed from Late Latin or Juridical Latin criminālis, from Latin crīmen.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin incommēnsūrābilis.
Deverbal from flairer, from Latin flagrare (“to blow”). Cognate to Portuguese cheiro.
Learned borrowing from Latin sōlāris, from sōl (“sun”).
From Latin coeliacus, from Ancient Greek κοιλιακός (koiliakós), from κοιλία (koilía, “belly”).
Learned borrowing from Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).
Inherited from Old French comparatif, borrowed from Latin comparātīvus, from comparō (“to compare”) + -īvus.
Inherited from Old French insensible, from Late Latin īnsēnsibilis.
Learned borrowing from Latin paenultimus (“almost last”), with change of ending by analogy with the ordinal numerals (troisième, quatrième, etc.).
Inherited from Old French chape, from Late Latin cappa. Doublet of cape.
From Middle French cacapulte, catapulte, cathapulte, borrowed from Latin catapulta.

Inherited from Old French archevesque, from Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “first, chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”), from ἐπισκοπέω (episkopéō, “to watch over”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”), + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to examine”).
Inherited from Old French estole, borrowed from Latin stola.
Inherited from Old French bonté, bunté, from Latin bonitātem. By surface analysis, bon + -té. Doublet of bounty.
Learned borrowing from Latin harmonicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἁρμονικός (harmonikós), from ἁρμονία (harmonía, “harmony”). By surface analysis, harmonie + -ique.
From Middle French guerison, from Old French guarisun (“healing”, ca. 1100). By surface analysis, guérir + -ison.
Inherited from Old French alienacion, itself borrowed from Latin aliēnātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin āthlēta, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs), from ᾱ̓θλέω (āthléō, “to contend”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).
Inherited from Old French liberté, itself borrowed from Latin lībertātem.
Inherited from Middle French phoque f, focque m, borrowed from Latin phōca, from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē). Cognate with Italian foca f and Spanish foca f.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin rōmānus.
Inherited from Middle French bordel, from Old French bordel, from Medieval Latin bordellum (“brothel, small hut”).
From Latin cosmos, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos).
Borrowed from Latin captīvus. Cf. the inherited doublet chétif.
From Latin renūntiātiōnem. Compare English renunciation.
Learned borrowing from Latin immēnsitās. By surface analysis, immense + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin alternativus, from alternatus, perfect participle of alterno, from Classical Latin alter (“other”).
Borrowed from Late Latin Christiānismus, from Ancient Greek Χριστιανός (Khristianós), from Χριστός (Khristós, “Christ, anointed one”).
From Latin corōnālis, from corōna (“a crown”).
From Old French acorcier (“to shorten”); morphologically, from a- + court + -ir.
From Old French monarchie, learned from Late Latin monarchia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía).
Borrowed from Late Latin dēceptiōnem, from dēcipiō, whence French décevoir.

Borrowed from Italian grandissimo, itself inherited from grandissimus, the superlative of grandis (“big, large”). Old French had grandisme inherited from the same Latin word, which would have given grandîme if it had survived until Modern French.
From Ancient Greek νηματώδης (nēmatṓdēs, “fibrous, in filaments”), from νῆμα (nêma, “thread, yarn”) + -ώδης (-ṓdēs, “-like”).
Learned borrowing from Latin augurium. Doublet of heur.
From Old French influence, borrowed from Medieval Latin īnfluentia, from Latin īnfluēns (“flowing in”), present active participle of īnfluō (“flow into”), from in- (“in-”) + fluō (“flow”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vīperīnus. By surface analysis, vipère + -in.
A learned derivation from quantité or Latin quantitātīvus.

Borrowed from Italian arrivederci (“goodbye”), from a (“to”) with rivederci (“to see each other again”), from the infinitive rivedersi (“to see each other again, to meet again”), from ri- (“re-”) with the infinitive vedersi (“to see each other”), from vedere (“to see”) with the variable pronoun si (“oneself; one another”). Cognate with French au revoir.
Inherited from Old French particion, from Latin partītiōnem. By surface analysis, partir + -tion.
Inherited from Middle French halle, from Old French hale, from Frankish *hallu, from Proto-Germanic *hallō. Doublet of hall. More at English hall.
Inherited from Middle French fondement, from Old French fondement, from Latin fundamentum.
Inherited from Middle French volunté, from Old French volunté, from Latin voluntās.
Inherited from Middle French puissance, derived from Old French puissant.
From Middle French zetha, borrowed from Latin zēta, from Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta). Doublet of zède.
From Middle French and Old French cene, an ecclesiastical borrowing from Latin cēna, from Proto-Italic *kert(e)snā, from Proto-Indo-European *kert-sna, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-, *sker-.
Borrowed from English electronic. By surface analysis, electron + -ique.
Inherited from Old French devers, either from de + vers or directly borrowed from Latin deversus.
From Middle French togue, from Latin toga.
From Latin umbra, influenced in form by Old French umble from Latin humilis.
Learned borrowing from Latin factiō. Doublet of façon.

Inherited from Middle French surprendre, from Old French sorprendre. By surface analysis, sur- + prendre. In Old French sorprendre (“to overtake”, formed from sor- (“over”)); cf. modern French sur-) was distinguished from sousprendre (“to surprise, catch unaware (from beneath)”, formed from sous- (“under”)); the two verbs later became one over time.
From Middle French conformité, from Latin cōnfōrmitās. By surface analysis, conforme + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin olibanum.
From English presbyterian. By surface analysis, presbytère + -ien.

Inherited from Middle French, derivative of abri, from Old French abri (“a place where one is sheltered from the elements or harm”), from abrier (“to cover”). Displaced synonymous abrier from Old French, which is uncommon today.
From partage + -er. Displaced partir in the sense of "to share, to divide".
Inherited from Middle French utile, borrowed from Latin ūtilis.
Inherited from Old French execrable, a borrowing from Latin execrābilis. By surface analysis, exécrer + -able.
Borrowed from Spanish bibliodiversidad (1990s). By surface analysis, biblio- + diversité.
From Ancient Greek μισολογία (misología), from μισόλογος (misólogos), from μισέω (miséō, “to hate”) + λόγος (lógos, “account, reason”).

From Medieval Latin accessorius, as in the phrase accessorium sequitur principale (“the accessory follows the principal”). Possibly influenced by accidens (“falling down, something unfortunate happening”).
Inherited from Middle French lot, from Old French loz, los, from Frankish *lot, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą. Cognate with English lot.
Learned borrowing from Latin mediātōrem. Doublet of médiateur.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin persōnālitās.
From Old French sus, from Latin sūsum.
Inherited from Middle French prince, from Old French prince, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin prī̆nceps.
Inherited from Old French loial (with various alternative forms: leial, leal, loyel) from Latin lēgālis. Equivalent to loi + -al. Doublet of légal.
From Ancient Greek γύψ (gúps, “bird of prey”) + ἀετός (aetós, “eagle”).

Inherited from Middle French anneau, from Old French anel, from Latin ānellus, diminutive of ānus (“ring”). Cognates in regional French languages: Franco-Provençal anèu, Gallo anè, aniao, anot Norman anné, Occitan anèl, Picard èniau. Cognates with Catalan anell, Corsican anellu, Galician anel, Italian anello, Portuguese anel, Romanian inel, Sicilian aneḍḍu, Spanish anillo.
Learned borrowing from New Latin amblyōpia.
From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar), from Proto-Indo-European *néḱtr̥h₂, derived from the roots *neḱ- (“to perish, disappear”) and *terh₂- (“to overcome”).
From New Latin cētācea, from Latin cētus (“whale”).
From earlier enquent, from Middle French inquant, from Medieval Latin inquantum (“in as much as”).
Learned borrowing from Latin perpetrator, analyzed as perpétrer + -ateur.
From vertu + -eux. Cf. also Late Latin virtuōsus. Piecewise doublet of virtuose.
Borrowed from Portuguese chicotear or chicotar, which itself is from the noun chicote, probably borrowed from either French chicot or Nahuatl xicohtli, equivalent to chicotte + -er.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin morātōrium, nominalised neuter of morātōrius, from moror (“to delay”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dīrēctor. By surface analysis, directer + -eur.
Inherited from Old French porte, from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”). Compare English portal.

Inherited from Old French letuaire, respelled to more closely match Late Latin ēlectuārium, from Ancient Greek ἐκλείκτον (ekleíkton, “medicine which is licked away”), from ἐκλείχω (ekleíkhō, “to lick up”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”).
From Old French talon (“heel, spur”). Cognate with Italian tallone.
From re- + connecter, perhaps a calque of English to reconnect.
First attested circa 1350, borrowed from Late Latin speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor.
From Italian scimitarra, ultimately from Persian شمشیر (šamšir, “sword”).
Inherited from Old French epistre, epistle, from Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ). Doublet of épistule / épistole.
Learned borrowing from Latin monōdia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μονῳδία (monōidía).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἑτερόδοξος (heteródoxos).
Inherited from Middle French commercer. By surface analysis, commerce + -er.
Inherited from Old French armaire, aumaire, borrowed from Latin armārium, from arma (“weapons, tools”).
Borrowed from Latin tympanum. Doublet of timbre, which was inherited.
Inherited from Middle French peau, from Old French pel, from Latin pellem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin expiātōrius.
From Ancient Greek συνίζησις (sunízēsis, “a sitting together”).
Middle French pilori, from Old French pilori, of uncertain origin, probably via Old Occitan espilori and/or Old Catalan from Latin pīla.
Formed from Latin repulsus with the French suffix -if, or borrowed from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus.
Borrowed from translingual Magnolia, from New Latin magnolia, from. From French Magnol + Latin -ia.
Inherited from Old French sacrement, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentum. Doublet of serment.
Learned borrowing from Latin arbustīvus. By surface analysis, arbuste + -if.
Borrowed from English tunnel, itself a borrowing from French tonnelle; hence a reborrowing. Doublet of tonnelle.
Inherited from Middle French colomne, colonne, from Old French columne, colonne, from Latin columna. Doublet of colombe.
Inherited from Middle French abrogation, from Latin abrogātiōnem (“repealed”), from Latin abrogō, from ab (“from”) + rogo (“ask, inquire”).
Borrowed from Portuguese cobra, from Latin colubra. Doublet of couleuvre.
Borrowed from Latin branchia, from Ancient Greek βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”).
Inherited from Middle French finicion, itself borrowed from Latin fīnītiō.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin cursus m. Doublet of cours m and course f.
Inherited from Middle French souventefois. By surface analysis, souvent (“often”, inflected as an adjective) + fois (“time”). Compare English oftentime, German oftmals.
Borrowed from Latin paragraphus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos). Doublet of paraphe.
Borrowed from English star. Doublet of aster.
Learned borrowing from Latin ciborium. Doublet of ciboire.
From Middle French sintaxe, borrowed from Late Latin syntaxis, from Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”).
From Latin chōrographus, from Ancient Greek χωρογράφος (khōrográphos). By surface analysis, choro- + -graphe.
Inherited from Old French cortois, from Old French cort (whence Modern French cour) and -ois. Compare Czech zdvořilý, German höflich.
Borrowed from Latin impatientem. Morphologically analyzable as im- + patient.
Learned borrowing from Latin dūrābilis. Morphologically, from durer + -able.
Inherited from Middle French Merovinge, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Merovingus, from Proto-West Germanic *Mārīwīg or *-ing. By surface analysis, Mérovée + -inge.
Inherited from Middle French continuation, from Old French continuation, borrowed from Latin continuātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin verbum. Doublet of verve.
Learned borrowing from Latin solidus. Doublet of sou.
Inherited from Old French chenu, inherited from Late Latin cānūtus, from Latin cānus.
Borrowed from English oleoresin. Doublet of huile + résine.
Borrowed from Italian maestro, from Latin magistrum. Doublet of magister, borrowed from Latin, maître, inherited from Latin, and master, borrowed from English.
Inherited from Old French chevestre, inherited from Latin capistrum.
From Middle High German bleichvar (“pale-coloured”), from bleich (“pale”) + var (“colour”) (compare German Farbe).
Borrowed from Latin ōminōsus, derived from ōmen (“omen”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin sānctificātōrem. Compare Old French saintefieur.
Inherited from Old French decré, decret, borrowed from Latin dēcrētum.
Inherited from Middle French sceptique, borrowed from Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikós) or possibly intermediately borrowed from New Latin scepticus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ῐ̓δῐοσῠγκρᾱσῐ́ᾱ (ĭdĭosŭnkrāsĭ́ā).
Borrowed from Latin apnoea, from Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐραστής (erastḗs).
Learned borrowing from Latin convocātiō. Morphologically, from convoquer + -ation.
Borrowed from Dutch batik, from Javanese bathik.
Inherited from Middle French blason, from Old French blason.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin paternitātem (“paternity, fatherhood”), from paternus (“relating to a father, paternal”) + -itās, from pater (“father”).
Learned borrowing from Latin comitia, plural of comitium.
Borrowed from Late Latin reservātiōnem, reservātiōnem, from Classical Latin reservātus, perfect passive participle of reservō.
Alteration of Middle French espinocher, from espinoche (“morsel”).
Borrowed from New Latin commemorātīvus, from commemorō. By surface analysis, commémorer + -atif.

From Middle French, from Old French lastage (“ballast”), from Medieval Latin lestagium (“tax imposed on a ship's lading”), from Old English hlæst (“load, freight”), from Proto-Germanic *hlastą, *hlastuz (“load, burden”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”). Cognate with Old High German hlast, hlesti (“load”) (German Last). More at lade.
Borrowed from Latin sēsquipedālis. By surface analysis, sesqui- + pédal.
From Middle French enchantement, from Old French enchantement.
Inherited from Middle French aspre, from Old French aspre, from Latin asper, according to the TLFi, an early borrowing. Compare Italian aspro, Spanish and Portuguese áspero.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin simultaneus, from simultim (“at the same time, extended”), from simul (“together, at the same time”).
Borrowed from Latin acūtus. Doublet of aigu, an earlier loan, with the obsolete inherited form being eu.
Inherited from Old French ajoster, from Vulgar Latin *adiuxtāre, *adjuxtāre, from Latin ad + iuxta. Compare also ajuster.

Inherited from Middle French quitte, from Old French quite (11th c.), borrowed from Latin quiētus (pronounced in Medieval Latin as quíetus > quitus). Doublet of inherited coi and the later borrowing quiet.
From Dutch bakboord (from bak (“rear”) + boord (“board”)), because the pilot was formerly located on the starboard and turned his back to the other side.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀμφίς (amphís), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi (“round about, around”), possibly from *h₂énts, from *h₂ent- (“face, forehead; front”) + *-s.
Learned borrowing from New Latin Agrostis.
Modelled after or borrowed from English responsibility, corresponding to responsable + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French (compare the form buxine), borrowed from Latin buccinum, variant of bucinum. Compare buse and buisine, inherited from a related root.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentem (“transparent”), present participle of transpareō, from Latin trāns + pareō.
Borrowed from English arena. Doublet of arène.
Inherited from Middle French couster, from Old French coster, inherited from Latin cōnstāre. See also constat, constater.
From bienfait + -eur, modeled on Late Latin benefactōrem (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”).
Inherited from Old French creveüre, perhaps inherited from Late Latin crepātūra; morphologically, from crever + -ure.
Borrowed from English listing, equivalent to lister + -ing.
Inherited from Middle French torsion, borrowed from Late Latin torsiōnem, from Latin tortiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin exonerātiōnem. Morphologically, from exonérer + -ation.
From Italian serraglio, from Ottoman Turkish سرای (seray, saray).
Alteration of Middle French pantine, from pan (“piece of fabric”) + suffix -ine.
Inherited from Middle French asseoir, from Old French asseoir, from Vulgar Latin *assedēre, re-formed from Latin assidēre, on the basis of sedeō.
Borrowed from English femme, fem (with the rarer spelling borrowed to avoid ambiguity with French femme (“woman”)). English fem is itself from French femme.
Inherited from Old French bercal, from Vulgar Latin *berbicale, from *berbīx, from Latin vervex (“wether; castrated ram”).
From Italian fantaccino, from fante, short form of infante (“child; young soldier”).
From Middle French issir, yssir, from Old French issir, eissir, from Latin exeō, exīre.
Clipping of Christenaux (now Knistenaux), from Cree Kenisteniwuik (the name of a Cree village).
Inherited from Middle French amande, from Old French amande (also alemande), from Late Latin amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē). Doublet of amygdale and mandorle.
Borrowed from Latin megaricus, from Ancient Greek Μεγαρικός (Megarikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin vāticinātiōnem. By surface analysis, vaticiner + -ation.

Inherited from Middle French escallier, borrowed (through written form) from Occitan escalier, from Late Latin scālārium (attested in some inscriptions), neuter nominalization of *scālārius (“pertaining to a flight of stairs”), or from scālāris, from Latin scāla (“ladder”). Replaced the older French degrés and montée in this sense. Doublet of échalier.
Borrowed from Latin cutīcula, diminutive of cutis (“skin”).
Learned borrowing from Latin indigēns, present participle of indigeō (“to need”).
Borrowed from Late Latin perceptibilis (from Latin percipiō).

Learned modification of the inherited Old French enemisté, enemistié (whence also English enmity), itself from a Vulgar Latin *inīmicitātem, based on Latin inīmicitia, and modeled on the French amitié.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀταραξία (ataraxía).
Learned borrowing from Latin attenuātiōnem (“a diminishing”).
From Old French abaubir with change of prefix.
Learned formation from the root of Latin receptus with the suffix -if. Compare Medieval Latin receptivus.
Inherited from Middle French notable, from Latin notābilis.
From Late Latin dynastēs, from Ancient Greek δυνάστης (dunástēs, “lord, ruler”), from δύνασθαι (dúnasthai, “to be powerful”).
Inherited from Old French atifer. More at tiff.
Inherited from Late Latin festucum, from Latin festūca. Compare fétuque.
Learned borrowing from Latin eparchus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔπαρχος (éparkhos).
Inherited from Middle French avecques, from Old French avuec, from Latin apud *hoque (“near this”), which became *apu-hoque, then *apoque.
Learned borrowing from Latin scandalōsus. By surface analysis, scandale + -eux.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin larynx, from Ancient Greek λάρυγξ (lárunx).
Learned borrowing from Latin māchinātiō. By surface analysis, machiner + -ation.
From re- + vente. Compare with the verbe revendre.
Inherited from Middle French hanneton, from Old French haneton, from Frankish *hanō (“rooster”), from Proto-Germanic *hanô; + -et + -on.
From English pogo (“corndog”) genericized from the trademark Pogo.
Borrowed from English speaker. The sense "announcer" is a pseudo-anglicism.
Inherited from Middle French adjective insceu (“unknown”), corresponding to in- + su.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trānspirātiō. By surface analysis, transpirer + -ation.
From assainir (“to heal; to clean up”) + -ment.

Inherited from Middle French and Old French escriture, inherited from Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”), from scrīptum, the supine of scrībō (“to write”). Compare Middle French scripture, a borrowing from Latin.
From Latin Dionȳsiacus, from Ancient Greek Διονυσιακός (Dionusiakós), from Δῐόνῡσος (Dĭónūsos, “Dionysus”) + -ακός (-akós).
From Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).
Learned formation from the root of Latin perceptus and the suffix -if. Cf. also Medieval Latin perceptivus.
Learned borrowing from Latin phallicus, from Ancient Greek φαλλικός (phallikós), from φαλλός (phallós) + -ικός (-ikós). By surface analysis, phalle + -ique or phall(us) + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Latin harmonia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δικαστήριον (dikastḗrion).
Borrowed from Latin saeculāris, from saeculum (“generation; century”). Doublet of séculier.
Borrowed from Latin crātēr, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κρατήρ (kratḗr).
Borrowed from Latin -archia, from Ancient Greek ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).
Inherited from Old French interrupcion, borrowed from Latin interruptiō.
Learned borrowing from Latin quid. Doublet of que and quoi.
From Old French deslacer, deslacier, corresponding to Modern French dé- + lacer.
Inherited from Old French res, from Latin rāsus (“scraped”). Doublet of ras.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin audibilis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin metōnymicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μετωνυμικός (metōnumikós). By surface analysis, métonymie + -ique.

From Old French pichier, bichier (compare English pitcher), from Late Latin pīcārium, bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos). Compare Italian bicchiere, German Becher.
Learned borrowing from Latin pītuīta. Doublet of pépie.
Learned borrowing from Latin remūnerātiō. By surface analysis, rémunérer + -ation.
From Middle French Ottoman, from Italian Ottomano, from Arabic عُثْمَان (ʕuṯmān). Doublet of Osman.
Inherited from Old French mesaventure. By surface analysis, més- + aventure.
Inherited from Middle French pain, from Old French pain, from Latin pānem.

Inherited from Middle French chappon, from Old French chapon, chiapun, from Vulgar Latin *cappōnem, from Latin cāpō. Compare Catalan capó, English capon, Italian cappone, Occitan capon, Portuguese capão, Spanish capón.
Inherited from Middle French eschardre, from Old French escharde, escherde, from Frankish *skarda, from Proto-Germanic *skardō, *skardą. More at shard.
Learned borrowing from Latin oeconomicus. By surface analysis, économie + -ique.
Inherited from Middle French grand, from Old French grant, from Latin grandem.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek διηγητικός (diēgētikós).
Borrowed from English sinecure, an ellipsis of Latin beneficium sine cūrā, from Latin sine (“without”) + cūra (“worry”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin partītīvus, from Latin partītus + -īvus.
Inherited from Middle French chose, from Old French chose, from Latin causa. Compare Italian cosa, Portuguese coisa, Spanish cosa among many others. Compare cause, a borrowed doublet.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin timōrātus.
Inherited from Middle French maistre, from Old French maistre, from Latin magistrum. Doublet of maestro, borrowed from Italian, magister, borrowed from Latin, and master, borrowed from English.
Borrowed from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (/⁠qanû⁠/, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na).
Learned borrowing from Latin cremāre. Doublet of cramer.
From Latin mumia, from Arabic مُومْيَاء (mūmyāʔ).
From Middle French hoyau, höel, hoel, from Old French hoel, diminutive from Old French hoe (whence French houe (“hoe”)).
Inherited from Old French estat, borrowed from Latin status (whence also the past participle été).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin augmentātiōnem.
Inherited from Latin exāmen. Doublet of examen.
Inherited from Old French vain, from Latin vānus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty”).
Inherited from Latin ātrium. Doublet of atrium.
Borrowed from Latin stropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ).
Inherited from Middle French, Old French ferir, from Latin ferīre.
Borrowed from Italian disinvolto, from Spanish desenvuelto.
From Middle French organiser, borrowed from Medieval Latin organizāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin mātriculārius. See also matriculaire.
Either from charpenter, or directly from Old French charpent (itself from Latin carpentum) [from 13th century].
From laver + -eur. Cf. also Latin lavator. Compare Spanish lavador, Italian lavatore.
From Old French jurement, from Latin iuramentum. By surface analysis, jurer + -ment.

Inherited from Middle French trinquer (ca. 1400), from Middle High German trinken, from Old High German trinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną. Cognate with English drink.
Inherited from Old French plume, from Latin plūma.
Inherited from Old French laver, from Latin lavāre, from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin patrimōniālis.
Inherited from Old French force, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”).

Inherited from Middle French bras, from Old French bras, from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn). Displaced Old French feminine noun brace, ultimately from the same Latin and Ancient Greek roots.
Borrowed from Old Occitan muscada, from musc. See also muguet and muscat.
Borrowed from Old Occitan calar, from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō).
From Old French sidre, from Latin sicera, from Ancient Greek σῑ́κερᾰ (sī́keră), from Hebrew שֵׁכָר (šēḵār), from Proto-Semitic *šikar- (“alcoholic drink”).
Borrowed from Spanish peón. Doublet of pion.
Learned borrowing from Latin haesitātiōnem. By surface analysis, hésiter + -ation.
Inherited from Old French barbel (“barbel fish”), from Vulgar Latin *barbellus, from Late Latin barbulus, diminutive of Latin barbus (“a type of fish”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek αὐτοκέφαλος (autoképhalos).
Borrowed, through Latin agoranomus, from Ancient Greek ἀγορανόμος (agoranómos, “clerk of the market”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vitrōsus (“glassy, transparent”), from vitrum (“glass”).

From Old French leitrun, from Medieval Latin lectrinum, from Late Latin lectrum, from lēctus, perfect passive participle of legō (“to read”). The noun was influenced by lu, past participle of lire, from a similar root.
Borrowed from Latin submersus (past participle of submergo) with the suffix -ible.
Inherited from Middle French haste, from Old French haste, from Frankish *hai(f)st (compare Old High German heisti).
From guerre + -ier. From Old French guerrer, guerreier.
From Ancient Greek via Latin Graecus.
Inherited from Old French cage, from Latin cavea. This form did not undergo the palatalization of c before a.
From Old French, from Late Latin glūtem, from Latin glūten.
From Latin threnus, itself from Ancient Greek θρῆνος (thrênos), θρέομαι (thréomai).
From Latin obscūritātem. By surface analysis, obscur (“dark”) + -ité (“-ity”).
From Old French, borrowed from Latin errōrem.
Inherited from Middle French hestre, from Old French hestre, from Frankish *haistr. Displaced native fau, from Latin fagus, which can still be found in faîne (“beechnut”).
Borrowed from Italian scenario, from scena + -ario.
Inherited from Middle French initial, from Latin initiālis, from initium (“a going in, entrance”).
Inherited from Old French chapelain, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappellānus. Doublet of capelan.
Inherited from Old French raisin, from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus. Doublet of racème, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Russian белу́га (belúga), from бе́лый (bélyj, “white”).
Inherited from Old French predicament, from Late Latin praedicāmentum.
From Latin prōlēs (“offspring”) + Latin ferre (“to bear, carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *bher- (“to carry, to bear children”).
Inherited from Old French justise, justice, borrowed from Latin jūstitia. Doublet of justesse.
Inherited from Old French propre, borrowed from Latin proprius.

From Middle French distance, from Old French destance, destaunce, distaunce (“debate; difference, distinction; discord, quarrel; dispute; space between two points; time interval”), borrowed from Latin distantia (“difference, diversity; distance, remoteness; space between two points”).
Unadapted borrowing from Spanish quetzal, from Classical Nahuatl quetzalli.
Inherited from Old French a! (“oh! ah! woe!”), of expressive origin.
Borrowed from Late Latin praeventiōnem, from Latin praeventus, from praevenio.
Borrowed from Spanish aficionado. Doublet of affectionné.
Learned borrowing from Latin -logus, from Ancient Greek -λόγος (-lógos).
Inherited from Old French barbu, from Vulgar Latin *barbūtus (“bearded”). By surface analysis, barbe (“beard”) + -u.
Inherited from Middle French parallèle, borrowed from Latin parallēlus.
Learned borrowing from Latin peripherīa, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek περιφέρεια (periphéreia).
Borrowed from Latin metopa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετόπη (metópē).
From Medieval Latin santalum, sandalum, from Medieval Greek σάνταλον (sántalon), from Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal).
From noir + -eur. The ⟨c⟩ is from the verb noircir.
From Old French mortel, from Latin mortālis.
Inherited from Middle French terrible, from Old French terrible, from Latin terribilis.
Learned borrowing from Latin prōvīsor (“provider, foreseer”).
Borrowed from Latin compati, and adapted as a fourth-conjugation French verb, as with the related pâtir.
From Old French vit, from Latin vectis (“rod, lever”).
From sur- + réalisme. The word first appeared in the preface to Guillaume Apollinaire's play Les Mamelles de Tirésias, first performed in 1917.
Inherited from Old French pité, pitet, inherited from Latin pietātem. Doublet of piété.
Inherited from Middle French accroistre, from Old French acroistre, acreistre, inherited from Latin accrēscere. By surface analysis, a- + croître.
Inherited from Middle French prepuce, borrowed from Latin praeputium.
Inherited from Old French plovoir, from earlier pluveir, from Vulgar Latin *plovere (with a change in conjugation to *plovēre), from Classical Latin pluere.
Learned borrowing from Latin absurditās. By surface analysis, absurde + -ité.
Borrowed from Late Latin legatārius. See léguer and -aire.
Learned borrowing from Latin pollūtiō. By surface analysis, polluer + -tion.
From Middle French il, from Old French il, from Late Latin illī.
Inherited from Middle French Hernique, from Latin Hernicus.
From the stem of Ancient Greek φρέαρ (phréar, “well, spring”) + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Latin orans, orantis, noun use of the present participle of orare (“pray”).
Borrowed from Italian bambino, from onomatopoeic bambo for the first stammerings of children.
Inherited from Old French saül, saol, inherited from Latin satullus, diminutive of satur (“full”).

Inherited from Middle French sot, from Old French sot, from Medieval Latin sottus (“foolish”), of uncertain ultimate origin. Possibly an expressive interjection, similar to modern zut! (“damn it!”). This Latin word was borrowed into Germanic languages such as Dutch zot, Old English sott (modern English sot).
Borrowed from Late Latin carentia, from Latin careō (“to lack”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sāl petrae, from sāl (“salt”) and petra (“rock, stone”).
Borrowed from Latin psalmōdia, a borrowing from Koine Greek ψαλμῳδία (psalmōidía). From psalmus.

Inherited from Middle French joly (“considerable, ingenious, agreeable, pretty”), from Old French joli, jolif (“pretty, smart, joyful, merry”), possibly from Old Norse jól (midwinter festival), from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą, *jeulō (“Yule, Yule month, December”) (more at yule); alternatively from Vulgar Latin *gaudivus (from Latin gaudeō, more at joy).
Learned borrowing from New Latin bactērium,
Borrowed from Italian bagno. Doublet of bain.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek εὐφορία (euphoría).
Inherited from Old French taxacion, borrowed from Latin taxātiōnem. By surface analysis, taxer + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French difficulté, from Old French difficulté, a borrowing from Latin difficultās.

Learned borrowing from Latin mōmentāneus. In modern French, only words descending from Latin borrowings of Greek origin ending in the suffixes -ēus/-ēum, -aeus/-aeum (and exceptionally -ius/-ium, as in élysée/Élysée) are written with -ée in the masculine. Words descending from Latin words in -āneus (a different suffix, from -ānus + -eus), are now written with the ending -ané (as seen, for example, in méditerrané, spontané). The first four editions of the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française spelled these words with -anée before adopting the current spelling in the fifth edition.
From Caló caló, self-designated Romani slang.
Borrowed from Algerian Arabic زبل (zbal), from Arabic زِبْل (zibl).
Inherited from Middle French destruire, from Old French destruire, from Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).
From Middle French permanant, permanent, from Latin permanentem (accusative of permanēns).
From Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “to swell”).
Borrowed from Portuguese cornaca, from Sinhalese කූරුව-නායක (kūruwa-nāyaka, “elephant trainer”), from කූරුව (kūruwa, “elephant department”) + Sanskrit नायक (nāyaka, “guide, leader”).
From Latin vacuitātem (“empty space, vacancy, vacuity”).
From réguler + -ation. Compare with English regulation and Spanish regulación.

From Middle French dague, from Old French (13th century), from either Old Occitan or Italian daga. The Catholicum Armoricum glosses Breton dac as French dague, Latin pugio, adding “ou c'est badelaire” (Du Cange).
Learned borrowing from Latin cōpulātōrem. By surface analysis, copuler + -ateur.
From chrono- + -logie, from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) and λόγος (lógos, “word”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φλύκταινα (phlúktaina).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin communia, neuter plural of communis.
Inherited from Middle French athéiste. By surface analysis, athée + -iste.
Inherited from Middle French (g)renouille, from Old French (g)renoille, from Vulgar Latin *rānucula, diminutive from Latin rāna (“frog”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin praedicātōrem.
From Old French assignacion, from Latin assīgnātiō.
From Latin epicoenus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκοινος (epíkoinos).
Inherited from Old French cil, from Latin cilium.
Borrowed from Latin Amphictyones, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀμφικτύονες (Amphiktúones), both of which are only attested in the plural.
Essentially borrowed from German Morphologie in using parallel elements morpho- + -logie.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin intellēctuālis. Morphologically, from intellect + -uel. Cognate to English intellectual.
From Old French pochier (“enclose in a bag”), from poche (“pocket, bag”).
From Latin exterminātōrem. By surface analysis, exterminer + -ateur.
From Middle French tranquille (15th c.), a borrowing from Latin tranquillis.
From Latin orthographia, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek ὀρθογραφία (orthographía), from ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) and γράφω (gráphō, “write”). By surface analysis, ortho- + -graphie.
Learned borrowing from Latin rapīna. Doublet of ravine.
Inherited from Old French circonstance, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin circumstāntia.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin medulla. Doublet of moelle, inherited from the same source.
From Old French, from Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ineditus. Cognate to Italian inedito, English inedita.
From Old French astuce (first attested in 1267/68), a semi-learned borrowing from Latin astūtia.
Clipping of récréation. Compare Spanish recreo and Italian ricreazione.
Inherited from Old French coupable, from Ecclesiastical Latin culpābilis (“culpable”), derived from culpa.

Inherited from Middle French crouste, from Old French croste, cruste, from Latin crusta (“hard outer covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).
Inherited from Middle French throne, from Old French trone, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “a seat, chair”).
From Latin bisextilis, from bis + sextus.
Inherited from Middle French parementier, from parement + -ier, from parer+-ment, from Latin parare, from paro.
Borrowed from New Latin, from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos).
Inherited from Old French poudre, poldre, from Late Latin pulvera, neuter plural based on Latin pulvis m, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”).
From Old French pelican, from Latin pelecānus.
Borrowed from Late Latin peritonaeum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion).
Learned borrowing from Latin dētēctiōnem. By surface analysis, détecter + -tion.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin praeiūdicium (“previous judgment or damage”), from prae- (“before”) + iūdicium (“judgment”).
Inherited from Old French gogue (“joke, fun”), of unknown origin. Compare gogo and goguenard.
Inherited from Old French amistiet, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Gorgō, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ).
Inherited from Middle French détestable, from Old French detestable (14th c.), from Latin detestābilis (“abominable, execrable”).
Calque of English to smash, from smash + -er.
Borrowed from Latin negligentem, variant of neglegens.
Learned borrowing from Latin ūnanimitātem. By surface analysis, unanime + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin cōnfīdentia. Doublet of confiance.
Learned borrowing from Latin vīnārius, from vīnum + -ārius. By surface analysis, vin + -aire.
From haut + parleur, a calque of English loudspeaker.
Inherited from Old French prolongation, borrowed from Late Latin prōlongātiō. By surface analysis, prolonger + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin caprīnus. Compare chèvre.
Borrowed from Italian ricolta (modern Italian raccolta).
Borrowed from Late Latin spatula. Doublet of épaule, which was inherited.
From merveilleuse + -ment, compare Old French merveillusement.
From German Hase, from Middle High German hase, from Old High German haso, from Proto-Germanic *hesô (“hare”). More at hare.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from tramway, from Middle Dutch trame, ultimately from a lost West Germanic (Ingvaeonic) word.
Learned borrowing from Latin volūbilitās. By surface analysis, volubile + -ité.
From Middle French modulation, a learned borrowing from Latin modulātiō. By surface analysis, moduler + -ation.
From Latin flaccus. Originally a feminine form corresponding to a masculine flac. Doublet of flaque and flasque.
Learned borrowing from Latin invitātiō. By surface analysis, inviter + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin certificātum.

Inherited from Middle French grappin, from Old French grapin (“hook”) (compare Old French grappil (“a ship's grapple”)), from grape, grappe, crape (“hook”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *krappō (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *grep- (“hook”), *gremb- (“crooked, uneven”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend, twist”). More at grapple.
Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French quaille.
From New Latin rhachis/rachis, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis).
Learned borrowing from Latin cumulus. Doublet of comble.
Borrowed from Late Latin fulīginōsus, from fulīgō (“soot”).
Learned borrowing from Latin racēmus. Doublet of raisin.
Borrowed from New Latin interlocūtor, from Latin interloquor.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin febrilis, from Latin febris (whence fièvre).
Inherited from Middle French agacement, agassement. By surface analysis, agacer (“to irritate”) + -ment.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin beātitūdō.
Inherited from Old French minute, borrowed from Latin minūta. Compare menu, an inherited doublet.

Inherited from Middle French geole, from Old French jaiole, from Late Latin caveola (later attested in Medieval Latin as gabiola), a diminutive of Latin cavea. The long vowel (indicated by the circumflex) is due to the elision of the first syllable.
From re- (“a repetition, a turn back”) + voilà (“there”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dēlīrium. Not related to Turkish delirmek.
From Latin satisfecit (“he/she has satisfied”), the third person singular perfect tense of satisfacio (“satisfy”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin persecutiōnem, from Latin persecutus.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin umbrōsus; by surface analysis, ombre (“shadow”) + -eux.
Inherited from Old French chevez, from Latin capitium.
Borrowed from Algerian Arabic زلابية (zlābiyya), from Arabic زَلَابِيَّة (zalābiyya).
Learned borrowing from Latin pleonasmus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós).
Inherited from Old French toit, teit, from Latin tēctum.
From modern Latin Jasione after ancient Latin īăsĭōnē.
Inherited from Old French temps and its variants, from Latin tempus.
From Old French, a borrowing from Latin palaestra.

From Middle French protocolle, protocole (“document, record”), from Medieval Latin prōtocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Medieval Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).
From Italian castrato, from Latin castrō (“to castrate”), likely from caedō (“to cut”).
Borrowed from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermit's cell”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”). Doublet of moutier (Old French mostier).
Learned borrowing from Latin tībia. Compare the inherited doublet tige.
Inherited from Middle French ignoble, borrowed from Latin ignōbilis, from in- (“not”) + gnōbilis, later nōbilis (“noble”).
Inherited from Middle French dévot, inherited from Old French devot, Ecclesiastical Latin dēvōtus.
Inherited from Old French estation, estacion, borrowed from Latin stātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French governail, from Latin gubernāculum. By surface analysis, gouverner + -ail.
Learned borrowing from Latin contribūtiō. By surface analysis, contribuer + -tion.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin āctīvitās. By surface analysis, actif + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French faconde, from Latin fācundia.
Formed from Latin convolutus, with the suffix -tion.
Inherited from Middle French prestresse. By surface analysis, prêtre (“priest”) + -esse (“-ess”).
Inherited from Old French lancete (diminutive of lance). By surface analysis, lance + -ette.

Inherited from Middle French gascon, from Old French gascon, Guascuinz, gascoign, gascun, from Latin vascōnem. The initial -g- is likely due to influence from Germanic (Visigothic) pronunciation. Doublet of basque.
Inherited from Old French fillol, filiol, from Latin fīliolus (“young son”) (compare glaïeul, tilleul), from fīlius.
Learned borrowing from Latin sollicitātiōnem. By surface analysis, solliciter + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin ignōminiōsus (“disgraceful”). By surface analysis, ignominie + -eux.
Borrowed from Latin proxenēta, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek προξενητής (proxenētḗs).

Inherited from Middle French vivre, from Old French vivre, from Latin vīvere. Forms in véc- originate from Latin irregular perfect stem vīx- (vīxī, vīxistī, ...) undergoing metathesis and shortening to vĭsc-.
Inherited from Old French sur-, sour-, from syncopation of Latin super-. Doublet of super-.
From dés- + orientation or from désorienter + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin vagābundus.
Borrowed from Latin hypallage, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπαλλαγή (hupallagḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin efficācem (“efficacious, effectual, powerful, efficient”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin energumenos, from Ancient Greek ἐνεργούμενος (energoúmenos).
Borrowed from Arabic حَشُومَة (ḥašūma). Compare Dutch hsjoema.
Inherited from Old French esperon (also Middle French), from Frankish *spurō (compare German Sporn).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θωρακικός (thōrakikós), from θώραξ (thṓrax) (whence thorax).
Inherited from Old French buisine, from Latin būcina.
Inherited from Old French berbis, berbiz, from Vulgar Latin *berbicem, from Late Latin berbēcem, from Latin vervēx (“wether”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin linguālis.
From lin + -otte (from its fondness for flaxseed).
Learned borrowing from Latin ministerium, from minister (whence French ministre). See also métier.
Learned borrowing from Latin antecessor. Doublet of ancêtre.
From Latin Astypalaea, from Ancient Greek Ἀστυπάλαια (Astupálaia).
Borrowed from Latin modestia. Morphologically, from modeste + -ie.
Inherited from Middle French fondateur, from Latin fundātōrem. Compare fondeur.
Learned borrowing from Latin apotheōsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις (apothéōsis).
From Old French inundacion, from Latin inundātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin vicārius. Doublet of voyer.
From the Ancient Greek στοιχεῖον (stoikheîon, “element”) with -métrie (“-metry”), -μετρία (-metría, “measurement”).
From Russian борщ (boršč) and Ukrainian борщ (boršč).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dislocātiōnem.

Inherited from Middle French moytié, from Old French meitié, from Late Latin medietātem (“half”), from Latin medius (“middle, half”). Compare the borrowed doublet médiété. Cognate with English moiety.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin digestibilis.
From Middle French bastir, from Old French bastir, from Vulgar Latin *bastīre (“to build, construct; weave, sew”), borrowed from Frankish *bastijan (“to sew, weave”).
Borrowed from Latin reformātiōnem. Equivalent to réformer + -ation or ré- + formation.

Inherited from Middle French hypothese, a learned borrowing from Late Latin hypothesis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”, literally “a placing under”).
Inherited from Old French exercice (first attested in the early thirteenth century), borrowed from Latin exercitium.
Inherited from Old French profit, from Latin prōfectus.
Inherited from Middle French traictement. By surface analysis, traiter + -ment.
Inherited from Middle French fievre, from Old French fievre, from Latin febris.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin propitiātōrius.
Inherited from Old French incorporacion, from Latin incorporātiōnem. By surface analysis, incorporer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin distribūtor. By surface analysis, Latin distribūtum (supine of distribuō) + -eur.
Inherited from Old French corone, inherited from Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē).

Borrowed from Spanish remontada. Popularized in France in 2017 following FC Barcelona's 6-1 victory over Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League. FC Barcelona overcame a four-goal deficit in the second leg of their 2016–17 UEFA Champions League round of 16 tie against Paris Saint-Germain to win 6–5 on aggregate, making it the largest comeback in UEFA Champions League history.
Inherited from Old French secunt, second, segont, borrowed as a semi-learned term from Latin secundus (“second”); related to sequi (“follow”). Doublet of son (“bran”), which was inherited.

From Old French siege, sege, seige, from Vulgar Latin *sedicum, from sediculum, diminutive of Latin sedem. Alternatively, derived from a lost verb Old French *siegier (cf. assegier), corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *assedicāre.
Borrowed from Latin praeoccupātiōnem, composed of prae- and occupātiō.
Learned borrowing from Latin irrevocābilis. By surface analysis, in- + révocable.
From New Latin chiasma, from Ancient Greek χῑ́ασμα (khī́asma), from χῑάζω (khīázō, “to mark with an X”).
From Latin conchylium. Doublet of escargot.
Inherited from Old French vitaille, from Latin victualia. It was partially readapted to its Latin etymon, hence the /k/ and /ɥ/.
Inherited from Middle French plom, from Old French plom, from Latin plumbum.
Learned borrowing from Latin clandestīnus (“secret, concealed”).
From Ancient Greek κινητικός (kinētikós). First attested in 1877.
From New Latin chōrographicus, from Ancient Greek χωρογραφικός (khōrographikós). By surface analysis, choro- + -graphique. * IPA⁽ᵏᵉʸ⁾: /kɔ.ʁɔ.ɡʁa.fik/
Learned borrowing from Latin chamaeleōn, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χᾰμαιλέων (khămailéōn).
From Spanish copal, from Classical Nahuatl copalli (“incense”).
Borrowed from English jazz. The compound jazband is attested in a 1918 copy of Le Matin.
Inherited from Middle French poesie, from Late Latin poēsia, from earlier poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis).
Borrowed from Middle French Thuringe, a learned borrowing from Latin Thuringus.
Inherited from Old French pasture, from Latin pastūra, from pastus.
From Old French, borrowed from Latin minister.
Altered as a semi-learned form, based on exil, from Old French essillier, from Late Latin exiliāre, from Latin exsiliō.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin īnfūsiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin approbātīvus.
From Late Latin truella, from Latin trulla.
From Old French, from Latin qualitātem.
Borrowed from Latin calendārius < calendārium. Doublet of calendrier.

Ca. 1600, borrowed from Latin incendium. Perhaps influenced by Occitan incendi (in the 16th c. also encende), from Old Occitan encendi (11th c.), which may be inherited or is at least a much earlier borrowing.
Inherited from Old French image, borrowed from Latin imaginem (“a copy, likeness, image”).
Learned borrowing from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “organ, instrument, tool”). Doublet of orgue, an older borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin inopportūnus. By surface analysis, in- + opportun.
From Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma).
Learned borrowing from Latin dēvastātōrem. By surface analysis, dévaster + -ateur.
Borrowed from Latin recentem. Replaced the inherited Old French roisant, roisent, resant.
Inherited from Old French bufle, from Italian bufalo, from Vulgar Latin *būfalus, variant form of Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos).
First attested in Old French, corresponding to cruel + -té. Possibly from an unattested Vulgar Latin *crūdālitās, crūdālitātem (from Latin crūdēlitātem).
Learned borrowing from Latin gravidus, from gravis (“heavy”).
Inherited from Middle French douloureux. By surface analysis, douleur + -eux.
Borrowed from Latin scrīptōrem. By surface analysis, scripter + -eur.
Inherited from Middle French bibliotheque, borrowed from Latin bibliothēca (“library”), originally from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “book-room”). Morphologically biblio- + -thèque.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin adgnātus, past participle of variant form of agnāscor (“to be born in addition; to develop, to grow later”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin marginālis, from Latin margō (whence marge).
From Latin Nereis, from Ancient Greek Νηρηΐς (Nērēḯs). By surface analysis, Nérée + -ide.
Borrowed from Spanish alcázar, from Arabic قَصْر (qaṣr). Doublet of château.
From média, itself from the Latin media, the nominative plural of medium.
From affoler (“to frighten; to drive insane”) + -ment.
Learned borrowing from Latin gradus. Compare degré. Doublet of gradus.
From globe (“globe”) + -al, from Latin globus (“globe, sphere”).
Inherited from Middle French moust, from Old French moust, from Latin mustum, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ēligibilis.
Inherited from Old French chastaigne, from Latin castanea, from Ancient Greek κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă). Doublet of castagne.
Inherited from Middle French and Old French fraude (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin fraus, fraudem.
Inherited from Old French ambitios, borrowed from Latin ambitiōsus.
From collectif (“collective”), from Latin collectus, the past participle of colligere (“to collect”), from col- (a form of co- (“together”)) + legere (“to lay, place”).
Re-latinization of Old French segnal, from Medieval Latin signale, from Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum.
Borrowed from Latin hypocaustum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπόκαυστον (hupókauston).
Inherited from Old French nagier, inherited from a reduced form of Latin navigāre. Doublet of naviguer, a later borrowing. Displaced Old French noer, from Latin natāre, natō (“to swim”).
From Old French escharbot, from Latin scarabaeus (with the suffix -ot added), from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle, crayfish”).
Inherited from Old French crimne, borrowed from Latin crīmen, from Proto-Italic *kreimen, from Proto-Indo-European *kréymn̥, from *krey- (“sieve”) + *-mn̥.
Diminutive of Old French bouge (“pouch”), probably of Celtic origin. Doublet of budget.

From Old French comedie, from Latin cōmoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía), from κῶμος (kômos, “revel, carousing”) + either ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) or ἀοιδός (aoidós, “singer, bard”), both from ἀείδω (aeídō, “to sing”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek αὐτάρκεια (autárkeia).
From négocier + -ateur, or borrowed from Latin negōtiātōrem (“merchant, banker”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀξῠ́τονος (oxŭ́tonos).
Borrowed from Late Latin territoriālis, from Latin territorium. By surface analysis, territoire + -al.
From Middle French housser, from Old French houcier, houchier, from Frankish *hulfti (“cover, blanket, saddle-cloth”), equivalent to housse + -er.
Inherited from Middle French Parthe, from Latin Parthus, from Ancient Greek Πάρθος (Párthos).
From Old French idiot (cf. also the older form idiote), borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

Inherited from Middle French encombrer, from Old French encombrer (“to hinder, burden, encumber”), from Early Medieval Latin incombrāre (“to hinder, inconvenience, burden”), from combrus (“barricade of felled trees”), possibly from Gaulish *komberū (cf. Breton kember, Irish comar, cumar, Welsh cymmer), from Proto-Celtic *kombereti (“to bring together”) (compare Old Irish conbeir (“brings together, bears”)), from *kom- + *bereti (“to bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to be carrying”). Alternatively from Latin cumulus (“heap, pile”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“to swell”).

Inherited from Old French fantaisie, fantasie (“imagination”), from Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía), of φαντάζεσθαι (phantázesthai), from φαντός (phantós, “visible”), from φαίνεσθαι (phaínesthai, “appear”). Doublet of fantasy.

As a French word, coined by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1802. Possibly formed as bio- + -logie. Possibly borrowed from German Biologie or New Latin biologia. In any case, derived from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “bio-, life”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study, to speak”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin incarcerāre, incarcerō.

Inherited from Old French motion, mocion, borrowed from Latin mōtiōnem, noun of action from perfect passive participle mōtus (“having been moved”), from verb movēre (“move”), + noun of action suffix -iō.
From compter (“to count”) + -eur (“-er”). Piecewise doublet of computeur and conteur. Compare comptoir.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπαναστροφή (epanastrophḗ, “return”).
From Latin claustrum (“a shut in place”) + -phobe.
From New Latin coccus, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”).
From Occitan cavilhòt attested in Languedoc and Gascon, derived from cavilha cognate with French cheville.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek εὐεργέτης (euergétēs).
Inherited from Middle French patient, from Old French patient, borrowed from Latin patientem.
Inherited from Middle French escorce, from Old French escorce, from Latin scortea, feminine noun form of scorteus (“made of skin or leather”). Compare Italian scorza.
Inherited from Old French sermon, from Latin sermōnem.
Borrowed from Latin juniorem; Doublet of geindre. Cf. also the inherited Old French oblique case gignor.
Inherited from Old French cedre, from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros).
Borrowed from Spanish merengue, itself borrowed from French meringue.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek φιλογυνία (philogunía), from φίλος (phílos) + γυνή (gunḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin imperiālis, from imperium (whence French empire).
Inherited from Middle French turbulent, from Old French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus.
Inherited from Old French malice, borrowed from Latin malitia.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós, “of or relating to life or the soul”).

Inherited from Old French pro (“profit”), from Late Latin prōde (“profitable, useful”), from Latin prōdest (“is useful”), third-person singular of prōsum (“be useful”), after being reanalyzed as prōde est. Compare Catalan prou, where the form is widely used.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin longanimitātem.
Learned borrowing from Latin scrūpulōsus. By surface analysis, scrupule + -eux.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀντίλογος (antílogos, “contradictory, reverse”), from ἀντιλέγω (antilégō, “speak against, gainsay, contradict”).
Inherited from Middle French phalle, from Latin phallus, from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós).

Inherited from Middle French fauve, from Old French falve, from Late Latin falvus, a borrowing from Frankish *falu, *falw- (compare Dutch vaal, English fallow and German falb), from Proto-Germanic *falwaz (“pale, grey”). The adjectival sense of "savage, fierce" comes from the noun sense "wild animal," which is in turn a shortening of bête au pelage fauve (“animal with tawny fur”).

Inherited from Middle French beste, from Old French beste, probably partially borrowed from Classical Latin bēstia (“beast”), or less likely from an alternative Vulgar Latin bēsta (“animal”). Compare biche (probably from Old French bisse, itself from Vulgar Latin bīstia; compare Italian biscia).
Borrowed from Spanish armada. Doublet of armée.
From Latin cunnus and lingō (“to lick”).

Inherited from Middle French égarer, esgarer, from Old French esgarer, esguarer (“to lose one's way; be troubled or worried”), from Old French es- + Frankish *warōn (“to heed, pay attention to”). By surface analysis, é- + garer.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin tribulātiō, from Latin tribulō.
From Middle French coignat (14th c.), a borrowing from Latin cognatus.
Learned borrowing from Latin pȳgargus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πῡ́γᾰργος (pū́gărgos).
Borrowed from Italian eminentissimo. Morphologically, from éminent + -issime.
From Old French errer, from Latin errāre.
Borrowed from Russian икона (ikona, “(Eastern Orthodox) religious image”) [1859]; in the GUI sense from English icon, ultimately from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “figure, image, etc.”).
Inherited from Old French afistoler, from a- + fistuler.
Borrowed from Latin obvius, from ob- (“against”) + via (“way”).
From Late Latin int(h)ronizāre, from Ancient Greek ἐνθρονίζειν (enthronízein), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θρόνος (thrónos, “throne”).
Adapted borrowing of English toast (verb) + -er. By surface analysis, toast + -er.
Inherited from Middle French pauvre, relatinisation of earlier povre, from Old French povre, inherited from Latin pauper, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”).
Inherited from Middle French soldat, borrowed from Italian soldato, past participle of soldare, from soldo (“money, military pay”). Replaced soudard.
Inherited from Old French alaitier, from Late Latin allactāre, derived from Latin lac (“milk”, noun). By surface analysis, a- + lait + -er.
Inherited from Middle French serf, from Old French serf, from Latin servus (“slave, serf, servant”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser-wo- (“guardian”), or perhaps of Etruscan origin.
Inherited from Middle French arriver, from Old French ariver, from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre. Synchronically a- + rive + -er.
Unadapted borrowing from English fantasy. Doublet of fantaisie.
Inherited from Middle French pelle, from Old French pele, from Latin pāla (“shovel, spade”). Doublet of pale, which is of either dialectal or Occitan origin.
From Old French estier, inherited from Latin aestuārium. Doublet of estuaire.
From Middle French glosaire, borrowed from Latin glōssārium, from glōssa (“obsolete or foreign word that requires explanation”), from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”) (compare glose).
From Middle French conscientieux. By surface analysis, conscience + -eux.
Inherited from Old French terrestre, borrowed from Latin terrestris.
Inherited from Middle French messe, from Old French messe, from Late Latin missa, from Latin missum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monachālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus.
Inherited from Old French plantain, from Latin plantāginem.
Learned borrowing from Latin debilis. The original sense of "weak" was lost to faible.
Borrowed from Latin trānsmissiōnem, from transmittere.
Borrowed from Occitan brossa, of the same pre-Roman origin as brocciu.
Learned borrowing from Latin penetrātiō. Synchronically, from pénétrer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Late Latin justificationem < iustificatio, from iustifico, from Latin iustus.
Inherited from Old French confession, from Latin cōnfessiōnem (“confession, acknowledgment, creed or avowal of one's faith”).
From Ancient Greek κεραμικός (keramikós, “of clay”), from κέραμος (kéramos, “vase of clay”).
Learned borrowing from Latin prōnōmen. By surface analysis, pro- + nom.

Inherited from Middle French happer, haper, from Old French happer, haper (“to seize, snap up”), of obscure origin. Possibly onomatopoeic. Alternatively, of Germanic origin, either from Proto-West Germanic *happā (“hook, clasp”), or related to Middle Dutch happen (“to snap, bite”) (whence modern Dutch happen), Middle Dutch haperen (“to stammer, quarrel”) (whence modern Dutch haperen), German Low German happen (“to snatch something up, grab”), German Happen (“morsel, snack”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ambidexter (literally “right-handed on both sides”), from ambi- + dexter (whence French dextre).
Learned borrowing from Latin haruspicīnus. By surface analysis, haruspice + -in.
From Ancient Greek φθορά (phthorá, “deterioration”) on account of the corrosive nature of hydrofluoric acid.
From Middle French suavité, borrowed from Latin suāvitātem.
Inherited from Middle French coeur, from Old French cuer, from Proto-Romance *corem m, from Latin cor n (“heart”).
Borrowed from Latin benedictiōnem. Cf. the inherited Old French beneïson.
Inherited from Middle French grave, borrowed from Latin gravis. Doublet of grief.

From Middle French resipiscence (“act of recovering one’s senses or coming back to a more acceptable view; repentance”), a learned borrowing from Late Latin resipīscentia (“regaining of a clear state of mind, repentance”).
Learned borrowing from Latin elementarius. By surface analysis, élément + -aire.
From Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía).
Inherited from Middle French scabel, escabel, borrowed from Latin scabellum. Compare the inherited doublet écheveau.
From Breton kaoteriad, which comes from kaoter (“pot”) + -ad.
Inherited from Middle French puisné (literally “born after”), from puis né.
Borrowed from Italian cavalleria. Compare Old French chevalerie.
Borrowed from Latin obligātiōnem, from the verb obligō (“tie together”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin lapsus. Doublet of laps, another borrowing.
From Middle French and Old French digne (11th c.), a borrowing from Latin dignus.
Inherited from Old French lunatique, borrowed from Late Latin lūnāticus (“moonstruck”), derived from Latin lūna (“moon”). Replaced the older lunage.
From Russian морж (morž), from Northern Sami.
Learned borrowing from Latin nomenclatūra (“a calling by name, list of names”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ūrēthra, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek οὐρήθρα (ourḗthra).
Borrowed from English spleen in the 19th century.
From pince + -ette, as diminutive of pince. Compare Italian pinzetta.
According to the TLFi, from Old French farinier, a borrowing from Medieval Latin farīnārius, from Latin farīna (“flour”). Equivalent to farine + -ier
From Middle French verifficacion, veriffication, verificacion, vérificacion, verification, borrowed from Latin vērificātiō.
From fossoyer + -eur. For the figurative sense, compare Russian моги́льщик (mogílʹščik).
From Latin semestris (“six months”), from sex (“six”) + mensis (“month”).
From écologie + -iste, probably modeled on English ecologist.
Inherited from Old French gofre, with metathesis from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, culfus, variants of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos).
Borrowed from Swahili askari (“soldier”), from Arabic عَسْكَرِيّ (ʕaskariyy).
Inherited from Middle French pedagoge, pedagogue, borrowed from Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδᾰγωγός (paidăgōgós).
Borrowed from Latin propolis, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πρόπολις (própolis, “suburb; propolis”), from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “pro-”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).
Learned borrowing from Latin porticus. Doublet of porche.
Learned borrowing from Latin fornicātiō. By surface analysis, forniquer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French seu, sieu (with -f added by analogy with other words), from Latin sēbum, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”). Doublet of the borrowed sébum.
From Old French repast, from the verb repaistre, from Latin repascere.
From Latin epigramma, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγραμμα (epígramma).
Back-formation from réussite (“success”), a borrowing from Italian riuscita (“result, outcome; success”), past participle of riuscire.
From nation + -al. Compare New Latin nātiōnālis.
Inherited from Middle French medicine, from Old French medecine, borrowed from Latin medicīna. Replaced the inherited Old French form mecine.
Inherited from Middle French couard, from Old French cuard, from cüe, coue (“tail”); equivalent to queue + -ard.
Inherited from Middle French seigneur, from Old French seignor (oblique form), from Latin seniōrem (compare sire, derived from the nominative form). Doublet of senior.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin fraudulōsus.
Inherited from Old French ascension, borrowed from Latin ascēnsiōnem.
Borrowed from classical Latin doctus, past participle of docere.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin neomēnia.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek αὐτοψία (autopsía, “seeing with one's own eyes”). By surface analysis, auto- + -opsie.
Inherited from Old French serrer, from Vulgar Latin *serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, crossbar”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin fruticulosus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μισογυνία (misogunía), from μισέω (miséō, “to hate”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”).
Inherited from Old French protection, itself borrowed from Late Latin prōtectiō, prōtectiōnis (“a covering over”), from prōtegere (“to protect, cover in front”).
From Latin Scytha, from Ancient Greek Σκύθης (Skúthēs).
Inherited from Middle French lamentation, from Latin lāmentātiōnem (“wailing, moaning, weeping”).
Borrowed from Latin voluptuōsus. See volupté and -eux.
From Old French cresp + -u; ultimately from Latin crispus (“curly; crimped”) (→ crêpe).
Inherited from Old French abateiz. By surface analysis, abattre (“to cut down”) + -is.
Borrowed from translingual Rumex, from Latin rumex (“sorrel”).
Inherited from Middle French, from late Old French, borrowed from Italian ducato, from Medieval Latin ducātus, from dux (“duke; leader”). Doublet of duché and dogat.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θεραπευτικός (therapeutikós, “attentive, helpful, obliging, curative”). By surface analysis, thérapeute + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἡγεμονία (hēgemonía).
Inherited from Middle French pleurer, from Old French plourer, plorer, from Latin plōrāre (“cry out”). Cognate with Catalan plorar, Spanish llorar.
Inherited from Old French charpenterie, from charpentier (“carpenter”).
From Renaissance Latin sorōritās, from Latin soror (“sister”), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. Akin to Spanish sororidad, Portuguese sororidade, English sorority.
Inherited from Old French session, borrowed from Latin sessiōnem.
From Ancient Greek ᾠδεῖον (ōideîon), from ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”).
From Middle French explicateur, from Latin explicātōrem.
Inherited from Middle French cuilleree. By surface analysis, cuiller + -ée.
Inherited from Middle French réparable, from Latin reparābilis.
Inherited from Middle French and Old French emir, from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr).

Borrowed from English bagel, from Yiddish בייגל (beygl); ultimately from Middle High German bouc, boug- (“ring, bracelet”), from Old High German boug (“ring”), from Proto-Germanic *baug- (“ring”) plus *-il (noun suffix).
Inherited from Old French cause, borrowed from Classical Latin causa. Compare chose, an inherited doublet.
Inherited from Old French norriture, from Latin nūtrītūra (“act of feeding or nourishing”) and remade after the verb nourrir.
From règle + -er, or borrowed from Latin rēgulāre. See also réguler.
Borrowed from Italian biscotto (“cookie, biscuit”) (in a figurative sense). Doublet of biscuit and biscotte.
Inherited from Middle French cité, from Old French citet, from older ciptet, from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”).
Inherited from Middle French aiseement. By surface analysis, aisé + -ment.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coincidentia.
Inherited from Middle French qualification, from Medieval Latin quālificātiō.
Inherited from Middle French recevoir, from Old French recevoir, from Vulgar Latin *recipēre, from Latin recipiō. Cognate with English receive through borrowing, see there for more.
Borrowed from Old Occitan pastenago, pastenaga (“parsnip”), from Latin pastinaca. Doublet of panais.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin cōnsubstantiālis.
From Latin gynaecēum, from Ancient Greek γυναικεῖον (gunaikeîon).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trepanum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “auger, drill”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mansiō. Doublet of maison.

From an alteration of Old French tribaler (perhaps with influence from brimbaler or trimer), itself an expressive word probably formed on the basis of baller and tribo(u)ler; cf. also Latin tribulō, tribulāre.
From Ancient Greek ἱππικός (hippikós), compare ἵππος (híppos) and -ique.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ξυλοφάγος (xulophágos), from ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”) and φάγος (phágos, “one who eats”). By surface analysis, xylo- + -phage.
From Middle French dominion, from Latin dominium, with the ending reinterpreted as French -on.
Inherited from Middle French reduire, from Old French reduire, an alteration or Gallicization of Latin redūcere (“reduce”), after conduire.
Inherited from Middle French soufre, from Old French sulfre, soffre, from Latin sulfur, sulphur, sulphure, from Proto-Indo-European *swelplos, from the root *swel- (“to burn, smoulder”).
Inherited from Old French proche, derived from prochain.
From Latin gerundīvum (“gerundive”), from gerundium (“gerund”), from gerundus (“which is to be carried out”), future passive participle (gerundive) of gerō (“carry, bear”).

Borrowed from Latin ōrdinātōrem (“one who orders”), from ōrdinō (“to order, organize”). In its application to computing, it was coined by the professor of philology Jacques Perret in a letter dated 16 April 1955, in response to a request from IBM France, who believed the word calculateur was too restrictive in light of the possibilities of these machines.
Borrowed from Latin retractiōnem, from retractus.
Borrowed from Latin quadrātūra. Doublet of carrure.
Inherited from Middle French insult m, probably borrowed from Medieval Latin insultus (“attack, assault”). By surface analysis, deverbal from insulter.
Inherited from Old French faim, fain, from Latin famēs (“hunger”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, Portuguese fome, Italian fame and Romanian foame.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin persuāsīvus. Morphologically, from persuasion + -if.
From Old French mescreant, present participle of mescroire. See mécroire. Cognate with English miscreant.
From Old French succinct, from Latin succīnctus.
Borrowed from New Latin latex (“clear fluid which is part of a humour or bodily fluid”), a later use of Latin latex (“water; liquid, fluid”).
Learned borrowing from Latin gracilis. Doublet of grêle.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τακτικός (taktikós).
From pâle (“pale”, adjective) + -eur (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns from adjectives). modelled after Latin pallor.
Borrowed from English shunt, from Middle English schonten (“to evade”), of disputed origin.
Learned borrowing from Latin sēditiōnem (“sedition, discord”).
Inherited from Middle French recouvrer, from Old French recovrer, inherited from Latin recuperāre. Doublet of récupérer, which was borrowed from Latin.
Ultimately from Late Latin iūsānus (“lower”, adjective).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin īnsurrēctiō.
Inherited from Old French rut, ruit, inherited from Latin rugītus. Doublet of rugi, past participle of rugir.
Learned borrowing from Latin caruncula, diminutive of carō (“flesh”), whence chair.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μισογύνης (misogúnēs).
From Latin dīvulgātor (“publisher, publicizer”). Morphologically divulguer (to divulge, publicize) + -teur (masculine agent noun forming suffix).
Inherited from Middle French and Old French détestation, from Latin detestātiō. By surface analysis, détester + -ation.
Borrowed from Latin podium. Doublet of puy.
Inherited from Old French universal, from Latin ūniversālis, from ūniversus + -ālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin permeābilis.
From Old Occitan escarcella, from Italian scarsella (“purse”).
Inherited from Middle French adversité, from Old French adversité, from Latin adversitātem.
Borrowed from Italian coda. Doublet of queue.
Inherited from Old French guivre (whence also vouivre), from Latin vīpera. Related to English wyvern.
From Old French presentation, from Latin praesentātiōnem (“representation, exhibition”).
Borrowed from Italian moschea, ultimately from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, literally “place of prostration”).
Inherited from Middle French fondamental, from Latin fundāmentālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin taciturnitās. By surface analysis, taciturne + -ité.
From mérite, or borrowed from Latin meritāre, from meritus. Replaced inherited Old French merir, from merere.
