Inherited from Old French survivre, from Latin supervīvō, from super + vīvō. Equivalent to sur- + vivre.
Borrowed from Italian camorra, from a Neapolitan word supposedly from Spanish camorra (“dispute, quarrel”).
Borrowed from Latin folium. Cf. also feuille.
Inherited from Old French couple, from Vulgar Latin *cōpla, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copule.
Learned borrowing from Latin facilitās (“ease, easiness”). By surface analysis, facile + -ité. Doublet of faculté.
Borrowed from Late Latin gonorrhoea, from Ancient Greek γονόρροια (gonórrhoia), from γόνος (gónos) + ῥοία (rhoía).
Learned borrowing from Latin prosopopoeia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek προσωποποιΐα (prosōpopoiḯa).
Learned borrowing from Latin abstrūsus, perfect passive participle of abstrūdō.
From Latin octō (“eight”) or Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”).
From Middle French seullement, from Old French solement, from Early Medieval Latin sōlā mente. Synchronically derivable from seule + -ment.
From Old French gesier, ultimately from Latin gigēria.

From Middle French hanter, from Old French hanter (“to frequent, abide in one place”), from Old English hāmettan (“to bring home; provide a home for; house”) or/and Old Norse heimta (“to bring home”); both from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną (“to bring home, house”). More at haunt.
Inherited from Old French neu, from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”). Doublet of knout.
Borrowed from English predictive, from Latin praedictīvus.
Inherited from Old French concile, borrowed from Latin concilium.
Learned borrowing from Latin suffrāgium (“support, vote, right of voting”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin perclūsus (“obstructed”), past participle of perclūdō (“to seal shut”) (infinitive perclūdere).
Inherited from Middle French baron, from Old French baron, from Latin barōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin vocābulārium, from Latin vocabulum.
From paresse + -eux. Cognate with Italian pigrizioso, Portuguese preguiçoso and Spanish perezoso.
Inherited from Old French broutille, from brost (“sprout”).
Learned borrowing from Latin irrigātiō. By surface analysis, irriguer + -ation.
From Spanish epazote, from Classical Nahuatl epazōtl.
From fretter, or Old French freit, from Latin frīgidus (“cold”).
Inherited from Middle French naval, from nāvālis (“of ships”), from nāvis (“ship”) (whence nef).
Learned borrowing from Latin lapidātiōnem. Morphologically, from lapider + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin locūtiō (“speech”), from loquor (“to speak”).
Borrowed from the Late Latin excommūnicātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin perpetrātiō. By surface analysis, perpétrer + -ation.

Inherited from Middle French nombril, from Old French nonbril, from Vulgar Latin *umbilīculus (compare Occitan embonilh), from Latin umbilīcus. The initial n is probably due to an interference from possessive determiners: Old French mun onbril (“my navel”) → mun nonbril (i.e. a rebracketing). Compare the development of Catalan llombrígol, Romanian buric. Doublet of ombilic, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem (accusative of occāsiō). Compare the inherited Old French ochoison, achaison (the latter being influenced by Latin accūsātiō).
Borrowed from Latin odorifer (+ French -ant), from odōr + ferō.
Inherited from Middle French punir, from Old French punir, from Latin pūnīre. May have been borrowed due to its late appearance.
Diminutive of Old French cervel (“brain”), whence also cerveau
Inherited from Middle French rubrique, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rubrīca (“red ochre”) the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”).
From Latin īnfectus, perfect passive participle of inficiō (“dye, taint”).
Inherited from Old French arctique, borrowed from Latin arcticus.
Inherited from Middle French profond, from Old French profont, relatinization of inherited parfont, parfunt, from Latin profundus.
Inherited from Middle French architecte, from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”).
Borrowed from Latin synaeresis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek συναίρεσις (sunaíresis).
Originally dialectal, ultimately from Latin lōtium (“urine”).
English festival, from Old French festival.
Inherited from Middle French grange, from Old French grange, from Vulgar Latin *grānica, from Latin grānum (“grain”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin calumniōsus. By surface analysis, calomnie + -eux.
From Middle French desarmer, from Old French desarmer. By surface analysis, dés- + armer.
From Latin īnsolitus (“unaccustomed”). Compare Portuguese and Spanish insólito, Italian insolito.
Deverbal from soupirer (Old French sopir, sospir), or possibly from Latin suspirium.
Inherited from Middle French epilogue, itself a learned borrowing from Latin epilogus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos).
Borrowed from Old Occitan cardon, from Medieval Latin cardō, from Latin carduus (“thistle”). Doublet of chardon and carde.
Inherited from Old French arbrissel, from Vulgar Latin *arbuscellum, a diminutive ultimately based on Latin arbor (“tree”).
Inherited from Old French gaiant, jaiant, jaianz, from Vulgar Latin *gagantem, through assimilation from Latin gigantem, from Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin resolūbilis, from Latin resolvō.
Learned borrowing from Latin diffusiōnem. By surface analysis, diffuser + -ion.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin fēlīcitās.
Backformation from Middle French verroux, from the nominative-singular/accusative-plural of Old French veroil, from Vulgar Latin *verruculum, from Latin vericulum, diminutive of verū.
Learned borrowing from Latin dēlīberāre, dēlīberō (“to ponder”). Cognate with Italian deliberare and Spanish deliberar. Unrelated to French libérer.
Inherited from Old French replicacion, borrowed from Latin replicātiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French pole, from Old French pole, from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos).
Learned borrowing from Latin sculptor. By surface analysis, sculpter + -eur.
Inherited from Old French divin, from Latin dīvīnus. Doublet of devin.

Inherited from Middle French librairie, from Old French librairie, from Latin librāria (“library”), from liber (“book”). Sense “bookseller, bookshop” is from 16th century, and displaced “library” sense. The sense “software library” is a semantic loan from English library.

From Middle French [Term?], a semi-learned term based on Latin ingeniōsus (“endowed with good natural capacity, gifted with genius”), from ingenium (“innate or natural quality, natural capacity, genius”), from in (“in”) + gignere (“to produce”), Old Latin genere. Old French [Term?] had engignos (1160) and engenious (early 13c.), also from Latin.
Inherited from Old French dortour, from Latin dormītōrium (“dormitory”). Doublet of dormitoire, a borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κωνικός (kōnikós). By surface analysis, cône + -ique.
From lutter + -eur. Cf. also Latin luctātōrem.
From Latin arrha (“wages”), truncation of arrhabō (“down payment”), from Ancient Greek ἀρραβών (arrhabṓn, “down payment, guarantee”), from Hebrew ערבון (erabon, “guarantee”).
Inherited from Middle French recuperation, recuperacion, borrowed from Latin recuperātiō. Morphologically, from récupérer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin malignitās. By surface analysis, malin + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin pyrēum, from Ancient Greek πυρεῖον (pureîon).
Inherited from Middle French esplucher, from Old French espeluchier, from Vulgar Latin *expiluc(i)cāre, ultimately from Latin pilāre (“remove hair”). Compare Occitan espelucar, Catalan espellucar.

Inherited from Middle French cerveau, cervel, from Old French cervel, from Latin cerebellum, diminutive of cerebrum, from Proto-Italic *kerazrom, from a Proto-Indo-European form *ḱerh₂-s-ro, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head”).
Inherited from Latin cunnus, probably ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare Persian کون (kun, “anus”).
Inherited from Old French andoillee, antoillier. Cognate of English antler.

Inherited from Middle French charte, chartre, from Old French chartre, charte, from Latin chartula, diminutive of charta, with loss of the second -r- by dissimilation (or alternatively through influence from Latin charta). Ultimately from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Cognate with French carte. Doublet of charter.
Inherited from Middle French landgrave, from German Landgraf.
Inherited from Middle French antenne, from Old French antaine, borrowed from Latin antemna or antenna.
From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”).
Borrowed from Latin aloe, Ancient Greek ἀλόη (alóē).
Borrowed from Late Latin epilēpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληπτικός (epilēptikós).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin prōcessus (“process, progression”). Doublet of procès, another borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Latin prosperitās. By surface analysis, prospère + -ité.

Inherited from Middle French systeme (first attested 1552), from Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
Combining form of Ancient Greek μῑσέω (mīséō, “to hate”), from μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”).
Learned borrowing from Latin nāvigātor. By surface analysis, naviguer + -ateur.
Inherited from Old French tenor, tenëor, derived from the verb tenir, or from Latin tenor. Doublet of ténor.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin commūnicātīvus. By surface analysis, communiquer + -atif.
Inherited from Middle French penser, from Old French penser, from Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet peser, as well as panser, originally an alternative spelling which acquired a special sense.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin compassiō, from Latin compatior (“to suffer with”).
Borrowed from Latin chorus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós). Doublet of chœur.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin euchologium, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek εὐχολόγιον (eukhológion).
Inherited from Middle French clarissime, borrowed from Latin clarissimus, from clarus and superlative -issimus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin chartulārium.
From r- + éveiller, or from Old French resveillier.
Borrowed from English napalm. First attested in 1953.
From English claymore, from Scottish Gaelic claidheamh-mòr.
Inherited from Middle French onereux, from Old French onereus, from Latin onerōsus.
From Ancient Greek γαλακτοφάγος (galaktophágos, “milk-fed”). Found in the works of Voltaire.
Inherited from Old French vengeor, vengeour, vengedur. By surface analysis, venger + -eur. Possibly corresponding to Late Latin vindicātōrem, from Latin vindicō. Compare Spanish vengador.
Inherited from Middle French nature, Old French nature, borrowed from Latin nātūra.
Inherited from Middle French bassin, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinus /*baccinum, probably from Gaulish.

From Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, parocisme, paroxime, from Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”), from Late Latin paroxismus, paroxysmus (“a fit; onset of a disease; violent impulse or sadness”), from Ancient Greek πᾰροξῠσμός (păroxŭsmós, “exasperation, irritation; severe fit of a disease”), from πᾰροξῡ́νω (păroxū́nō, “to irritate, provoke”) (from παρα- (para-, prefix meaning ‘parallel to but separate from or going beyond, beside’) + ὀξῡ́νω (oxū́nō, “to provoke; to sharpen”) (from ὀξῠ́ς (oxŭ́s, “sharp”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”))) + -μός (-mós, suffix forming abstract nouns).
Inherited from Middle French genereux, from Latin generōsus.
Inherited from Old French encens, borrowed from Late Latin incēnsum, from Latin incendō.
Learned borrowing from Latin austēritās. By surface analysis, austère + -ité.
Borrowed into Middle French from Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ́λλᾰξῐς (părắllăxĭs).
From Cajun French chaudin (“stuffed and baked pig's stomach; pig's large intestine”), from Poitevin-Saintongeais chàudin, from Old French chaudun, from Medieval Latin caldūmen.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπίκλησις (epíklēsis, “invocation”).
Inherited from Old French masculin, borrowed from Latin masculīnus.
Inherited from Middle French scene (1486), borrowed from Latin sc(a)ena, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).
Borrowed from Latin indicium, from indicō (“point out, indicate, show”).
Inherited from Old French tribun, tribune, from Latin tribunus.
Inherited from Middle French effusion, borrowed from Latin effusiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin calvitiēs, from calvus (whence chauve).
From Latin Symplēgas, from Ancient Greek Συμπληγάς (Sumplēgás).
Alteration of Old French purté, inherited from Late Latin pūritātem, from Latin pūrus (“pure”) + -tās (noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, pur + -eté.
Inherited from Old French desmembrer. Morphologically, from dé- + membre (“limb”) + -er.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ileum, ileon, itself a derivative of Ancient Greek εἰλέω (eiléō).
Ultimately from Latin stupula, variant of stipula. Doublet of stipule.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin exsistentiālis, from Latin existentia (“existence”).
Borrowed from Latin candēlābrum, from candēla (“candle”). Doublet of chandelier.
First attested in Old French as precïus. Borrowed from Latin pretiōsus (“precious, of great value”).
From an alteration of Old French jogler, from Latin ioculārī, and influenced by Old French jangler (“to entertain”), itself from Frankish *jangalon.
Borrowed from Latin circumspectus, from circum (“around”) and specio (“to look”).
Learned borrowing from Latin docilitās. By surface analysis, docile + -ité.
Borrowed from Latin radius. Doublet of rai, which was inherited.
From Turkish humus or Arabic حُمُّص (ḥummuṣ).
Borrowed from Latin opācus (“shaded, shady, dark”), itself of unknown origin. Doublet of ubac.
Borrowed from Latin mēnsa. Compare the inherited doublet moise, which acquired a technical sense.
Learned borrowing from Latin tūtēlāris, from tūtēla. By surface analysis, tutelle + -aire.
Learned borrowing from Latin substrātum. Doublet of substrat.
Learned borrowing from Latin aquōsus. Compare the inherited Old French éveux.
Borrowed from Late Latin metempsychōsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετεμψύχωσις (metempsúkhōsis).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin subversiō.
Previously flame, from Middle French flame, whence English flame, from Latin flamma.
Inherited from Old French tachier, techier, from Vulgar Latin *tagicare, from Latin taxāre (“to feel, touch”). Doublet of taxer.
Borrowed from Portuguese Cantão, from Mandarin 廣東 /广东 (Guǎngdōng).
From Old French forestier, from forest + -ier.
Borrowed from Spanish Granada (city, region; island), from Arabic غَرْنَاطَة (ḡarnāṭa, initially a suburb of the city, then city, region).
Inherited from Old French mesure, from Latin mēnsūra (“measure”).
Inherited from Old French ruee, from earlier rode, from Latin rota. The current form may have been influenced by rouer and rouelle. Doublet of rote, a borrowing from Medieval Latin.
Name of a fifth century French saint, Latin Germanus, "a German", also from germanus "brother, sibling".
Inherited from Middle French anglois, from Old French anglois. By surface analysis, Angle (“Angle”) + -ais (“-ese”).
Inherited from Middle French chausse, from Old French chauce, from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).
Inherited from Middle French Romain, from Old French Romain, from Latin romānus.
Inherited from Middle French email, from Old French esmal, from Early Medieval Latin smaltum.
Inherited from Old French doble, from Latin duplus.

From Middle French pale (14th c.), ultimately from Latin pāla (“shovel, spade”). Doublet of pelle, which is the regular French descendant. The form pale is either from a western dialect or from Old Occitan pala.
From Old French cheance (“accident, chance, luck”), inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadentia (“falling”). Doublet of cadence, a borrowing from Italian.

Inherited from Middle French hault, from Old French haut, halt (“high, tall, elevated”), a conflation of Frankish *hauh, *hōh (“high, tall, elevated”) and Latin altus (“high, raised, profound”). Akin to Old High German hōh (“high, tall, elevated”). More at high, haughty.
Inherited from Middle French Bordeaulx, from Occitan Bordèu, from Old Occitan Bordel, from Latin Burdigala, from a Proto-Celtic root.
Inherited from Middle French dossier. By surface analysis, dos (“back(side)”) + -ier.

From Middle French garantie, from Old French garantie, guarantie (“protection, defense”), from Old French garantir, guarantir (“to warrant, vouch for something”), from Old French garant, guarant, warant (“a warrant; warranter, supporter, defender, protector”), from Frankish *warand (“a warrant”), from Frankish *warjan (“to fend for, designate something as true, vouch for”), from Proto-Germanic *warjaną (“to defend, protect”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to close, cover, protect, save, defend”). Cognate with Middle Low German warent, warend (“a warrant”), German gewähren (“to grant”). More at warrant.
Inherited from Middle French massacre, from the verb massacrer.
Inherited from Middle French grille, grisle, from Old French greille, graïlle, from earlier gradilie (end of 10th century), from Latin crāticula (or a Vulgar Latin graticula).

From Old French mitaille (“small coins; hence scrap iron, old iron; then grapeshot”); originally diminutive of mite (“small coin”), from Old Dutch mite (“something small”), from Proto-Germanic *mītǭ (“biting insect”, literally “cutter”), from *maitaną (“to cut”).
Inherited from Middle French quarré, from Old French quarré, from Latin quadrātus. Compare the borrowed doublet cadrat.

Inherited from Old French farse, from Medieval Latin farsa, from the feminine perfect passive participle from Latin farciō (“to stuff”). Doublet of far. The theatre sense alludes to the pleasant and varied character of certain stuffed food items.
From Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul, mind, spirit”), via Latin psyche.
Inherited from Old French Tamise, from Middle English Tamese, variant of Temse, from Old English Temese, from Latin Tamesis, potentially from Proto-Celtic *tamesās.
From Old French forfait, past participle of forfaire, from for(t) (variant of Old French fuer, fur) and faire.

Inherited from Old French broche, from Vulgar Latin brocca (“spike”), feminine substantive of Classical Latin broccus (“pointy-toothed or prominent-toothed”), ultimately from Gaulish, compare Old Irish brog (“awl”).

Inherited from Old French harpon, from Latin harpaga, a rare variant of Latin harpagō, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spiritus.
Inherited from Old French domaine, demaine, from Latin dominium or dominicus.
From Middle French cyclique, a learned borrowing from Classical Latin cyclicus. By surface analysis, cycle + -ique.
From chasser + -eur; found in Old French as chaceür, chaceor. Compare Italian cacciatore, Spanish cazador.
From Middle French attraper, from Old French atraper (compare also Old French antraper), equivalent to a- + trapper.
Learned borrowing from Latin stupiditās. By surface analysis, stupide + -ité.

Inherited from Old French flur, flour, flor, from Latin flōrem (“flower; the finest part of something”), from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃-s (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰleh₃- (“to bloom”). In some senses, from Middle French fleur (“surface, upper side, top layer”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *flōraz (“floor”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin commissiōnārius, from Latin commissiō.
Borrowed from Italian stramazzone, from stramazzare, from mazza.

Inherited from Middle French entendre, from Old French entendre, from Latin intendere (“to turn one’s attention, to strain”). Cognate with Catalan entendre (“understand”), Spanish entender (“understand”), English intend, Italian intendere (“mean”), Romanian întinde (“stretch, spread, extend”).

Inherited from Old French basoche, besoiche, from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ). The phonetic evolution was special in this case, as the expected result would be *baseuche (cf. the place name La Bazeuge). Doublet of the borrowing basilique.

Altered from Middle French françois, from Old French françois, franceis, from France + -ois, corresponding to Early Medieval Latin francēnsis, from Late Latin Francus (“a Frank”). By surface analysis, France + -ais.

From Middle French fouller (“to trample, mill, fordo, mistreat”), from Old French foler (“to crush, act wickedly”), from Vulgar Latin *fullāre (“to trample, to full”), from Latin fullō (“fuller”). More at full.
Inherited from Middle French cler, from Old French cler, from Latin clārus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call”, “to shout”).
Inherited from Middle French œuf, from Old French oef, from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum. Compare Occitan uòu.
Learned borrowing from Latin ratiō. Doublet of raison, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Basque oreinak, plural of orein (“deer”). First attested in the texts of Samuel de Champlain as orignac.
From bouche + -ée, possibly Vulgar Latin *buccata, from Latin bucca. Compare Italian boccata, Romanian bucată; cf. also Portuguese and Spanish bocado.
From dragon (“dragon (mythological creature); type of cavalry soldier, dragoon”, noun) + -er (suffix forming infinitives of first-conjugation verbs).
From Lamartine + -ien, after Alphonse de Lamartine.
From Old French trespasser (“to traverse”), equivalent to tré- + passer.
Inherited from Old French closture (see also closure), from Late Latin clausūra, from Latin clausus.
Inherited from Old French [Term?] (cf. the form limaz), from Vulgar Latin *limacea, ultimately from Latin limax (“slug, snail”).
Borrowed from Italian grotta, from Latin crypta. Doublet of crypte.
Inherited from Old French journal (“daily”), from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus (“of the day”), from diēs (“day”).
Learned borrowing from Latin quadrupedem. By surface analysis, quadru- + -pède.
Inherited from Old French trousse, trosse, torse. Equivalent to deverbal formation from trousser.
From Old French Breton, from Latin Brittō.
From Middle French soubs, from Old French soz, from Latin subtus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stagiārius, from stagium + -ārius. By surface analysis, stage + -aire.

From Provençal and Occitan petanca, pèd tanco (“foot fixed (to the ground)”), a contraction of pè (“foot”) and tancar (“to attach, close”), together meaning "feet together" in reference to the position that players are supposed to adopt when throwing the ball (in contrast to that of the Provençal version).
From vélo + -drome, after the model of hippodrome (“hippodrome”).
From caduc + -ité. Compare Medieval Latin cadūcitās.
Formed as Ypres + -ite, so named because the gas was first used at Ypres in 1917 during the First World War.
Learned borrowing from Latin cautērium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek καυτήριον (kautḗrion).

Inherited from Middle French verd, vert, from Old French vert, from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Compare Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish verde. The Old French -t is due to regular final devoicing. The feminine was originally also vert and was extended with -e only during Middle French times, thus keeping the devoiced sound.

Inherited from Middle French riz, ris, from Old French ris, from Old Italian riso, risi, from Medieval Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), ὄρυζον (óruzon). The spelling in -z after the Greek and Latin oryza, adopted in order to distinguish from ris (several senses).
Inherited from Old French saison, seson, seison, inherited from Latin satiō, satiōnem (“act of sowing, planting”).

Inherited from Middle French moy, from Old French mei, moi, mi (“me”), tonic form of me, from Latin mē (“me”), from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)me-, *(h₁)me-n- (“me”). More at me. See cognates in regional languages in France: Norman mei, Gallo mai, Picard moè and Bourguignon moi from Old French; Corsican and Franco-Provençal mè.
Inherited from Old French pance, from Latin panticem.
Inherited from Old French nacele (“small boat”), from Late Latin navicella, diminutive of Latin navis (“boat”). Doublet of navicelle.
Learned borrowing from New Latin aesthēticus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek αἰσθητικός (aisthētikós).
From voiture + -ette. Genericization of brand name "Voiturette". Coined by Léon Bollée in 1895 to name his new motor tricycle, «Voiturette».
Learned borrowing from Late Latin cachexia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek καχεξία (kakhexía).
From poil + -u; compare Spanish peludo. The figurative sense entered the language through French military slang.
From poly- + technique. See also Ancient Greek πολύτεχνος (polútekhnos).
Inherited from Middle French philosophe, from Latin philosophus, from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos).
Borrowed from Italian rotonda, from Latin rotunda, feminine of rotundus. Doublet of rond.
Borrowed from Late Latin virulentus. The second sense is probably a semantic loan from English.

Inherited from Middle French desgringueler, from Old French gringoller, of Germanic origin, from Middle Dutch crinkelen, from kring (“circle”), from Old Dutch *kring, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz. The sense would refer to someone tumbling in successive circles.
Inherited from Old French carvi, borrowed from Medieval Latin carvi, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā). Doublet of chervis.
Inherited from Middle French equippe, from Middle French equipper, esquiper. More at French équiper.

Inherited from Middle French bufet (1150), from Old French bufet, of uncertain origin; possibly a Celtic borrowing. Compare Scottish Gaelic biadh (“food, sustenance”), buadha (“valuable, precious”). Or, according to the Digitized Treasury of the French Language, from an imitative source akin to bouffer (“to eat (in excess)”).
Inherited from Old French, from Late Latin campānia (in full Campānia Rēmēnsis), from campāneus, from Latin campus. Doublet of campagne; compare also champagne.
From constat, borrowed from Latin cōnstat, the third-person singular present active indicative of cōnstō. Compare also coûter.
From Old French relaier (Modern French: relayer).
Learned borrowing from Latin inactīvus. By surface analysis, in- + actif.
Inherited from Middle French combustible, from combust (past participle of comburir) + -ible.
Inherited from Old French surveillier. By surface analysis, sur- + veiller, corresponding to Latin super (“on top of”) + vigilō (“to watch”). Cognate with English surveil.
Inherited from Old French roeler (“to roll”), from Medieval Latin rotulāre, from Latin rotula.
From chinois (“Chinese”) + -erie (suffix forming nouns that describe qualities or properties).
Inherited from Middle French vermeil, from Old French vermeil, syncopated form of Latin vermiculus (“little worm”).

Inherited from Old French bacheler, bachelier, from Medieval Latin baccalaureus, a variant of baccalārius influenced by a folk etymology from bacca (“berry”), laurea (“laurel”), i.e. “crowned with berried laurels”, in reference to the fact that graduate students were crowned with those in the Middle Ages. See baccalārius for other senses.
Borrowed from Turkish nargile, from Classical Persian نَارْگیله (nārgēla), from Sanskrit नारिकेल (nārikela, “coconut”).
Borrowed from Occitan garriga, perhaps from a pre-Roman *carra (“stone”).

From Middle French fouet, diminutive in -et of Old French fou (“beech”), from Latin fagus. Since the morpheme boundary was no longer felt in Middle French, [u.ɛ] was contracted to [wɛ] and this later developed regularly to [wa] (as it did in oi, oe). The contemporary pronunciation was reinforced by the spelling and the desire to distinguish from foi, foie and fois.
Inherited from Old French cours, inherited from Latin cursus. Doublet of course and cursus. Compare Italian corso.
From Latin libellus, diminutive of liber (“book”).
Coined by Aimé Césaire in 1935, from nègre (“Negro”) + -itude.
Inherited from Old French anguille (12th c.), from Latin anguīlla. The ⟨ll⟩ was originally pronounced /l/ (still found, alongside /ʎ/, until the 17th century).
Borrowed from Italian scrocco, from Old High German *scurgo (attested in Old High German fiurscurgo (“fire-maker, stoker”); modern German Schurke, schüren), from Old High German scurgen.
Inherited from Middle French ville, from Old French ville, vile, inherited from Latin vīlla (“country house”). Doublet of villa.
Probably borrowed from Spanish pacotilla, although the relatively recent attestation of the Spanish term makes this problematic.
From Latin cōmicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós).
Coined by René Just Haüy in 1801, Traité de minéralogie vol. 3 p. 114, after Ancient Greek σφήν (sphḗn, “wedge”).
Inherited from Middle French religieux, from Old French religieus, from Latin religiōsus.
Learned borrowing from Latin lacūna. Doublet of lagune.
Inherited from Middle French keutil, from Old French coilte (“quilt, cushion”). See also couette (“duvet”).
From naïf + -eté. Compare nativité, cf. also Latin nātīvitās.
From Old French treille + -age, from Latin trichila (“arbor, bower”). Equivalent to treille + -age.
Inherited from Middle French bon, from Old French bon, from Latin bonus (“good”), from Old Latin duenos, later duonus, from Proto-Italic *dwenos.
Borrowed from Old Occitan badau, from badar, from Medieval Latin badare (“to gape, yawn”), probably ultimately imitative of yawning or gaping. Related to English abash.
From Middle French militaire, borrowed from Latin mīlitāris.
Inherited from Old French title, a semi-learned term borrowed from Latin titulus.
Borrowed from Italian maschera. More at English mask.

Inherited from Middle French croisade (15th century), as it were crois + the suffix -ade. The change in suffix from Old French croisement, croiserie, croisée, is influenced by Old Occitan crozada (13th century) and Old Spanish cruzada (14th century), both reflecting Latin cruciāta.
From Latin quid; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís. Cognate to English what, which differs due to changing under Grimm’s law.
Inherited from Middle French jus, from Old French jus, from Latin iūs (“gravy, broth, sauce”).
From Medieval Latin sacristānus, from Late Latin sacrista, from Latin sacer (“sacred”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēteriōrātiōnem. By surface analysis, détériorer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French quatre, qatre, catre, from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Compare Catalan quatre, Italian quattro, Portuguese quatro, Spanish cuatro.
From Boulanger + -isme, after Georges Ernest Boulanger.
From syndic (“syndic, representative”) + -at. First attested in 1409.
Inherited from Middle French nouveau, from Old French novel, from Latin novellus.
From porte (“carry”, third person singular indicative) + feuille (“sheet, paper”). Cognate with Italian portafoglio (whence French portfolio).
Either from bon + -ifier or from Latin bonificare

Inherited from Old French evangile, evangeile, euvangile, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”). Cognate with Italian vangelo, Portuguese evangelho, Spanish evangelio.
Inherited from Late Latin tōnsiōnem, from Latin tondeō (“shave, cut hair”).
From froid + -eur. Compare Catalan fredor, Spanish frior.
Learned borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis).
Literally, “coffee-pusher”, from pousse (“push”, 2nd person singular imperative of pousser) + café (“coffee”). Compare Italian ammazzacaffè (literally “coffee-killer”).
From livrer + -aison, or possibly corresponding to Latin līberātiōnem. Doublet of libération, a borrowing from Latin.

Inherited from Middle French parfum, from parfumer (“to scent”), borrowed from Old Occitan perfumar or another language around the Mediterranean coast, cf. Italian profumare, themselves from Latin per (“through, thoroughly”) + fumāre (“to smoke”).

Inherited from Old French acier, acer, from Late Latin aciārium, from Latin acies, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”). Compare Catalan acer, Galician aceiro, Italian acciaio, Occitan acièr, Portuguese aço, Spanish acero.
From Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina).
Borrowed from Latin mūnitiōnem, from mūniō.
From virus + Ancient Greek -ιον (-ion, diminutive suffix).
Inherited from Old French aguille, from Late Latin acūcula, diminutive of Latin acus (“needle”). Perhaps influenced phonetically by aiguiser. Compare Occitan agulha.

Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὁμόφωνος (homóphōnos, “speaking the same language, making the same sound, in agreement, in unison”), from ὁμο- (homo-, “same”) + -φωνος (-phōnos, “with respect to language or sound”), a suffix derived from φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound, language”), in the linguistic sense coined by French philologist Jean-François Champollion 1822 (for the adjective) and 1824 (for the noun).
Inherited from Middle French bien, from Old French bien, from Latin bene (“well”).
From Ancient Greek στέαρ, στέατος (stéar, stéatos, “fat”) + πυγή (pugḗ, “buttocks”), on the model of callipyge.
Inherited from Middle French boisselier, from boissel (a Middle French form of boisseau) + -ier.
Learned borrowing from Latin octāgintā. Doublet of huitante.
Borrowed from Spanish alazán, from Andalusian Arabic أَصْهَب, from Classical Arabic أَصْهَب (ʔaṣhab).
Borrowed from Latin cubicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κυβικός (kubikós). Morphologically, from cube + -ique.
Inherited from Old French estupe, from Latin stuppa, from Ancient Greek στύππη (stúppē).
Borrowed from Italian assai. Doublet of assez.
Inherited from Middle French Perse, from Latin Persēs/Persa, from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠pārsa⁠/).
Borrowed from Spanish hablar. Doublet of fabuler.
Borrowed from Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίσις (krísis).
Borrowed from Latin theōrēticus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós). By surface analysis, théorie + -(et)ique.
From Ancient Greek θρηνῳδία (thrēnōidía, “lamentation”). Compare English threnody.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin problēmaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”) (whence problème).
Borrowed from Occitan comtat. Doublet of comté.
Learned borrowing from Latin callōsitātem. By surface analysis, calleux + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin refectōrium.
From Old French, from Latin abortivus. Cognate with Italian abortivo.

Inherited from Middle French baptiser, from Old French baptisier, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτῑ́ζω (baptī́zō, “to immerse, to baptize”). Replaced the inherited Old French baptoier, batoyer.
Inherited from Old French litiere, from Late Latin lectuāria (“bedding”), derived from Latin lectus (“bed”). By surface analysis, lit + -ière.
Learned borrowing from Latin triangulum. By surface analysis, tri- + angle.
Re-Latinized from Old French (es)chamous based on its origin, Latin squāmōsus.
Inherited from Middle French tunique, from Old French tunique, borrowed from Latin tunica.
Inherited from Middle French fugitif, a borrowing from Latin fugitīvus. Supplanted the earlier Old French form fuitif.
Borrowed from Latin dēscendentem, the present participle of dēscendere, itself from dē + scandere (“climb, ascend”).
From Latin Nīcaea, from Ancient Greek Νίκαια (Níkaia), from νίκη (níkē, “victory”). Doublet of Nicée.
Inherited from Old French lard, from Latin lārdum, lāridum (“bacon fat”).
Learned borrowing from Latin candēla. Doublet of chandelle.
From Latin trilinguis (“who speaks three languages”).
From Old French seve, from Latin sapa.
Borrowed from English gadget, itself of French origin.
From égal + -ité, or borrowed from Latin aequālitātem. Cf. also the variant forms equalité, esgalité (Middle French), igauté, and the inherited Old French form oelté.
Inherited from Middle French pieux, from Old French piu(s) (later changed on the basis of adjectives ending in -eux), from Latin pius.
Learned borrowing from Latin sūtūra (“suture”). Compare couture.

Inherited from Middle French ramper, from Old French ramper (“to crawl up, climb”), from Frankish *rampōn, *hrampōn, from *rampa, *hrampa (“hook, claw, talon”), from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to shrink up, shrivel”).
From Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).
Learned borrowing from New Latin ontologia. By surface analysis, onto- + -logie.
Borrowed from English lakh, from Hindi लाख (lākh), from Sanskrit लक्ष (lakṣa).
Learned borrowing from Latin rīvālis (literally “person using the same stream as another”), from rīvus (“small stream, brook”). Unrelated to rive.
Learned borrowing from Latin immortālis. By surface analysis, im- + mortel.
From énerver (“to get on one's nerves”) + -ment.
Inherited from Middle French coureur. By surface analysis, courir + -eur.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin īnsinuātiōnem.
From Latin sphingem f, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ f (Sphínx). Cognate with Italian sfinge f, Portuguese esfinge f, Spanish esfinge f.
Inherited from Middle French valoir, from Old French valoir, valeir, from Latin valēre, from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl̥h₁éh₁yeti, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule, be strong”).
Inherited from Old French ancestre, ancessor, from nominative case of Latin antecessor. Doublet of antécesseur.
Inherited from Old French olive, from Latin olīva.
Borrowed from Late Latin circumvallātiōnem, from Latin circumvallō (“circumvallate; surround, encompass”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dīvulgātiō. Morphologically, from divulguer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin diplōma, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma).

From Middle French rosse, from Old French roche, *rosse (“bad horse”), from Old Frankish *hross (“horse”), from Proto-Germanic *hrussą (“horse, steed”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). Cognate with Old High German hros, ros (“horse, steed”), Old English hors (“horse”). More at horse.
From Latin illustris (“bright, shining, brilliant, lustrous; clear, lucid; illustrious, distinguished, famous”), from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).
Borrowed from Latin cumulāre (“to heap together”). Doublet of the inherited combler.
Borrowed from New Latin occipitālis, from Latin occiput (whence occiput).
From Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).
Inherited from Old French devin, inherited from Latin dīvīnus (“prophetic”). Doublet of divin.
Borrowed from Latin speciēs. Doublet of épice, an older borrowing.
Learned borrowing from New Latin hypochondria.
From course + -ier. Appeared in Old French as corsier, and in Medieval Latin cursārius.
Learned borrowing from Latin complētīvus. By surface analysis, compléter + -if.
Back formation from trekking, or from English trekker
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μαρασμός (marasmós).
Inherited from Old French soissante, seixante, from Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).
Inherited from Middle French thyrse, borrowed from Latin thyrsus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of torse, a borrowing from Italian.

Literally, “well come”, from Old French bienvenu, from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“comer, welcome guest”), from which many modern Germanic forms, as in English welcome. Eclipsed Middle French willecomme, from Old French wilecome (“welcome”), borrowed from Middle Dutch willecome or Middle English welcome. Many cognates in other Romance languages, such as Spanish bienvenido, Italian benvenuto and Portuguese bem-vindo.
Inherited from Middle French embrion, from Medieval Latin embryon, embrion, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, swell”).
From Latin maenas (“bacchant”), from Ancient Greek μαινάς (mainás, “raving, frantic”), from Ancient Greek μαίνεσθαι (maínesthai, “be furious”).
Inherited from Old French paroi, parei, pareit, from Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem m.
Diminutive of meule, from Old French meulon.
From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion). Compare Catalan gimnàs, Italian ginnasio, Portuguese ginásio, Spanish gimnasio.
From Late Latin diptycha pl, from Ancient Greek δίπτυχα (díptukha), neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”).
From Middle French eslargir. By surface analysis, é- + large + -ir.

From Old French, from Latin essentia. Sense 2 very likely from Latin edō (“eat”), in the sense of 'what is eaten, fuel'. Many forms of the latter are indistinguishable from the former, and so the confusion with essence is very understandable.
Inherited from Old French venimos. Effectively a doublet of vénéneux, which was borrowed from Latin.
Learned borrowing from Latin exaltātiō. By surface analysis, exalter + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French tyran, borrowed from Latin tyrannus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos). Replaced Old French tirant.
From Middle French colonie (14th c.), from Latin colōnia (“colony”), which see. Doublet of Cologne.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one who stands before”).
From entonner (“to put in a barrel”) + -oir.
Borrowed from Italian saccoccia, from sacco.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lēgista.
Learned borrowing from Latin vacans. See also vaquant, which it could be seen as a respelling of (compare provoquant ~ provocant).
Inherited from Middle French oyseux, from Old French oisos (“idle”), from Latin ōtiōsus (“idle”), derived from ōtium.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin annuālis, from Latin annus (“year”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dactylus. Doublet of datte.
Borrowed from German Hamster and ultimately of Balto-Slavic origin.
From Latin topographia, from Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). By surface analysis, topo- + -graphie.
Borrowed from Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vīcīnālis. Displaced Middle French voisinal.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin luxātiōnem. By surface analysis, luxer + -ation.
Borrowed from Latin mandragorān. Displaced inherited mandegloire.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πυλών, πυλῶνος (pulṓn, pulônos).
Inherited from Middle French commandeur, from Old French comandeor. By surface analysis, commander + -eur.
From Middle French gloire, from Old French gloire, glorie, borrowed from Latin glōria.
Inherited from Old French venison, from Latin vēnātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French vilain, vilein, villein, from Late Latin vīllānus (“farm worker”), from Latin vīlla. Not related to vil.

Inherited from Middle French guespe, from Old French guespe, wespe, wapce (“hornet, wasp”), from a conflation of Latin vespa (“wasp”), and Frankish *wapsu; both from Proto-Indo-European *wóbʰseh₂ (“wasp”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin ūnisonus.
Learned borrowing from Latin contrītiō. By surface analysis, contrit + -ion.
Borrowed from Dutch schrijfbank, corresponding to schrijven + bank (“bench, desk, table, work area”).
From English antediluvian. By surface analysis, anté- + diluvien.
Learned borrowing from Latin lānūginōsus; compare English lanuginose, Italian lanuginoso, and Spanish lanuginoso.

Inherited from Middle French estranger, from Old French estrangier, from estrange + -ier, equivalent to modern French étrange + -er. Cf. also Vulgar Latin *extraneārius, Italian straniero, Portuguese estrangeiro.
Inherited from Old French vasselage, from Early Medieval Latin vassallāticum. By surface analysis, vassal + -age.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin immanēns.
From Latin sylva (“forest”) + culture, on the model of agriculture, horticulture, etc.
Borrowed from Late Latin urgentem, present participle of urgeō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin rectangulum.

Inherited from Middle French aise, from Old French aise, eise, probably derived from the nominative form of Latin adiacēns, present participle of adiaceō (compare Medieval Latin in aiace). If so, then cognate with Old Occitan aize; compare also Catalan eina, Italian agio, a borrowing from Occitan, doublet of adjacent, a learned borrowing. Compare also Frankish *ansiju (“loop, handle, arms akimbo, elbow room”).
Borrowed from Italian lagone, augmentative of lago (cognate with French lac).
Inherited from Old French voie, veie, inherited from Latin via. Doublet of via. Unrelated to voir and voirie, despite influencing the latter.
Inherited from Middle French lycanthropie, from Ancient Greek λυκανθρωπία (lukanthrōpía). By surface analysis, lycanthrope + -ie.
From Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign, of a stranger”).
Inherited from Old French furieus, borrowed from Latin furiōsus.
Learned borrowing from Latin retrō. Compare arrière.
Borrowed from Latin territōrium. Compare the inherited doublet terroir.
Inherited from Middle French advancer, from Old French avancier, from Vulgar Latin *abanteāre, from Late Latin ab ante, from Latin ab + ante.

Inherited from Middle French aigle, from Old French aigle, itself either borrowed from Old Occitan aigla or taken from Latin aquila, though not as a popular term. Cf. the Old French and regional form aille, which may be popularly inherited. Cognate with Italian aquila, Portuguese águia, Spanish águila, Romanian aceră. Doublet of eagle.
Borrowed from Late Latin reprehēnsibilis, from Latin reprehendō.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin sophisticāre (“to trick, falsify, corrupt”). The sense "to make more complex" is probably due to later developments in sophistiqué, influenced by changes in sense in English sophisticated.
From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion), neuter form of στάδιος (stádios, “stable, firm”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to be standing”).
From général + -iste, on the model of spécialiste.
Inherited from Old French amasser. By surface analysis, a- + masse + -er.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.
Learned borrowing from Latin placēbō (“I will please”), the first-person singular future active indicative of placeō (“to please”).
Inherited from Old French almosne, from Vulgar Latin *alēmosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεέω (eleéō, “to have mercy”).
Inherited from Middle French lien, from Old French lien, liem, from Latin ligāmen (“bond”), from ligō.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French imaginacion, borrowed from Latin imāginātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin attribūtiō. By surface analysis, attribuer + -tion.
Inherited from Old French chastiement, from the verb chastier (whence Modern French châtier), from Latin castīgō.
Inherited from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō.
Inherited from Old French grace, from an early borrowing from Latin grātia, from grātus (“as a favour”). The lengthening of the vowel, which is indicated with the circumflex, is irregular.
Learned borrowing from Latin āleātōrius (“relating to a gamester”).
From Latin presbyterālis, from Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old”).
Learned borrowing from Latin donātor. Compare donneur.
From Italian amoroso. Doublet of amoureux.
Inherited from Middle French cerf, from Latin cervus.
Inherited from Old French poiree, from a variant of which also French poireau (“leek”).
Learned borrowing from Latin fistula. Doublet of felle.
Learned borrowing from Latin gladiātōrem (“gladiator, swordsman, swordman (uncommon)”).
Borrowed from Italian marzapane, with influence of masse.
Inherited from Middle French enfleure, see enfler + -ure.
From Old French charitable, from charité.
Inherited from Middle French venger, vengier, from Old French vengier, from Latin vindicāre.
Inherited from Old French facilement. By surface analysis, facile + -ment.
From Italian colonnello. Compare Middle French coronnel, borrowed earlier from the same source. See English colonel for more.
Learned borrowing from Latin senātōrem. By surface analysis, sénat + -eur.

Inherited from Middle French < Old French tisique. Respelled in Middle French to more closely match the Latin phthisicus (with the pronunciation changing to reflect the spelling). By surface analysis, phtisie + -ique.
Inherited from Late Latin *nūtrītiōnem (distinct from the abstract noun nūtrītiō), from nūtrītus, past participle of nūtriō.

Inherited from Middle French escaille, from Old French escaille (“scale”), from Frankish *skallija (“scale, shell”), from Proto-Germanic *skaljō (“scale, shell, husk”) ( > English shell), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut, part, sunder, split, divide”). Compare Italian scaglia. Doublet of écale.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin catēchūmenus, from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos).
Inherited from Old French penne f, from Latin pinna f, penna f, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”). Doublet of panne. See also pinacle–panache.
From Latin intestātus, from in- (“not”) + testātus (“testate”).
Inherited from Middle French meur, from Old French meur, from Latin mātūrus. Doublet of mature.
Borrowed from Italian loggia, from Old French loge.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen.
Borrowed from Italian ortolano, from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortelain, found in regional usage.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin fortificātiō. By surface analysis, fortifier + -ation.
Inherited from the Middle French obnubilation.
From Middle French requeste, from Old French requeste, from Vulgar Latin *requaesita, from Latin requīsīta.
Borrowed from New Latin temporālis, from tempus (“temple”) (whence tempe).
Inherited from Old French preambule, borrowed from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from Late Latin praeambulō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin fūnerārius, from Latin funus.
Borrowed from English setlist. The Office québécois de la langue française recommends the term programme de concert as its replacement.
Borrowed from Latin diapason, from Ancient Greek διαπασῶν (diapasôn), that is διά (diá, “through”) + πασῶν (pasôn, “all”) (χορδῶν (khordôn, “notes”)), “through all (notes)”.
Borrowed from Latin integritātem (“soundness, integrity”), from integer. Doublet of entièreté
Inherited from Old French last, lest, from Old Dutch last, from Frankish *hlasti, from Proto-Germanic *hlastuz.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē). Doublet of taie, which was inherited from Latin thēca.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γνῶσις (gnôsis, “knowledge”).
From Middle French musel (“snout”) (whence French museau) + -ière.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin hypostasis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis). Compare substance.

Inherited from Old French fraye (“fry, spawn”), related to frayer. Cognate to Italian frega, fregolo, fregola (“fry, spawn”), Spanish freza (“fry, spawn”). The similarity to English fry and its Germanic family is a coincidence.
From Latin lamia, from Ancient Greek Λάμια (Lámia).
Borrowed from Latin pecūniārius, from pecūnia (“money”).
From Latin scaenographia, from Ancient Greek σκηνογραφία (skēnographía).

From Middle French prosne (“homily”), from Old French prodne (“grating around the altar, in front of which the priest stood during homily”), from Vulgar Latin *protinum, dissimilation of protirum, from Classical Latin prothyra, from Ancient Greek πρόθυρα (próthura, “vestibule”).
From Old French obtus (14th c.), a borrowing from Latin obtūsus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐμφατικός (emphatikós).
Borrowed from Latin museum. Later replaced by musée.
Learned borrowing from Latin rīsibilis, from rīdeō (“to laugh”).
From Latin Eleutheria, from Ancient Greek Ἐλευθέρια (Eleuthéria).
From Ancient Greek δημοτικός (dēmotikós, “common”), from δημότης (dēmótēs, “commoner”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “the common people”).
Derived from Latin ātrāmentum with the suffix -aire.
Inherited from Old French chenel, chanel, from Latin canālis (“channel; canal”). The suffix was later modified from inherited -el to learned -al after the Latin etymon. Doublet of canal.
From Latin ātrabīlārius (“characterized by black bile”). By surface analysis, atrabile + -aire.
Inherited from Old French anis, from Latin anīsum, from Ancient Greek ἄνισον (ánison).
Inherited from Middle French declinaison, from Latin dēclīnātiōnem. By surface analysis, décliner + -aison.
From déclencher (“to trigger; to set off”) + -ment.
Inherited from Old French pavement, from the verb paver + -ment, based on Latin pavimentum (“a hard surface, a pounded surface”).
Borrowed from Spanish real. Doublet of royal.
From Latin similitūdinem (“likeness, similitude”); from similis.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνάκλιτος (anáklitos, “for reclining”), from ἀνακλίνω (anaklínō).
Clipping of handball; pseudo-anglicism. Compare foot from football.
Learned borrowing from New Latin vanadium

Inherited from Middle French bonet, from Old French bonet (“material from which hats are made”), from Frankish *bunni (“that which is bound”), from Proto-Germanic *bundiją (“bundle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”). Compare also Late Latin abbonis, obbonis (“ribbon of a headdress”), also of Germanic origin, from Frankish *obbunni, from *ob- (“above, over”) + *bunni. Cognates: see above, English bonnet. More at over, bundle.
From Old French -ville, from Latin vīlla.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēducātor. By surface analysis, éduquer + -ateur.

From Middle French cabestant, of uncertain origin. Either from Old Occitan cabestran (“instrument to coil cords”), a noun use of present participle of verb cabestrar, from cabestre (“pulley rope”) ; or from Spanish cabestrante, cabrestante, from cabestrar (“to bind with a halter”), from cabestro (“halter”), from Latin capistrum (“halter”), from capere (“to hold”) (see capacious); or perhaps the Spanish is from Latin caper (“goat”) + -stans, present participle of stare (“to stand”); compare French chèvre (“she-goat”), also a machine for raising heavy weights.
From Late Latin hebdomadārius, from hebdomas (“week”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥῆμα (rhêma, “word, phrase, verb”).

Inherited from Middle French tresor, from Old French tresor, from Vulgar Latin *tresaurus, a Gallo-Roman variant of Latin thēsaurus, from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse, treasure”). Eclipsed Old French escat (“treasure”), from Frankish *skatt. See also the doublet thésaurus.
Inherited from Old French rancor, from Latin rancōrem. Spelling influenced by cœur (“heart”).
Inherited from Middle French roy, from Old French roi, rei, from Latin rēgem.
Borrowed from German Quarz, from a West Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *tvьrdъ (“hard”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dissonantia.
From légitime, or borrowed from Medieval Latin legitimāre, from Latin legitimus.
Borrowed from Italian arcipelago, from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + πέλαγος (pélagos).
Inherited from Middle French omelie, from Ecclesiastical Latin homilia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὁμιλία (homilía).
From Old French soudre, from Latin solvere.
From Ancient Greek ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + Ancient Greek παιδεία (paideía, “upbringing; training”).
A verb based on Latin bifurcus (“two-pronged”).
From Latin cyta, from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “vessel”).
From Latin enargīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνάργεια (enárgeia).
Inherited from Middle French parc m, from Old French parc m, from Early Medieval Latin parricus m, possibly borrowed from Frankish *parrik m.
Borrowed from Latin tonus. Doublet of ton, an earlier borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”).
Inherited from Old French rosier. Equivalent to rose + -ier.
Inherited from Old French espurge, from espurgier (“to purge”); compare English spurge.
Borrowed from ecclesiastical Latin primitiae, with change of first vowel after praemissa.
Taken from the Old French ferrier, from Latin ferrārius, from ferrum (“iron”); alternatively, fer + -ier. Only used in historical contexts in modern French.
Borrowed from Russian подзо́л (podzól), consisting of под (pod) "under" and зола́ (zolá) "ash".
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin prior.
Borrowed from Latin agenda, substantive use of the neuter plural of agendus (“which ought to be done”), future passive participle (gerundive) of agō (“to do, act, make”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin cognomen. Doublet of cognom.
Inherited from Old French principe, from Latin prīncipium.
Inherited from Old French aventuros, or aventure + -eux.
Inherited from Middle French estable, from Old French estable, from Latin stab(u)la pl.
From Latin colurus, ultimately from Ancient Greek κόλουρος (kólouros, “truncated, dock-tailed”). Compare English colure.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek καλλίπυγος (kallípugos).
From Latin piscis (“fish”) + -cole, on the model of agricole.
From Ancient Greek μορφο- (morpho-), the combining form of μορφή (morphḗ, “form”).
Inherited from Old French valur, valeur, valor, from Late Latin valōrem, accusative singular form of valor, from Latin valeō.
Borrowed from Spanish pasionaria (“passionate one”), nickname (La Pasionaria) of Spanish anti-fascist activist Dolores Ibárruri (1895-1989)
From Middle French analogie, from Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογία (analogía), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).
Inherited from Middle French piegier, from Old French piegier. By surface analysis, piège + -er.
Learned borrowing from Latin arōmatem (“spice, herb”), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma).
Learned borrowing from Latin anadiplosis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀναδίπλωσις (anadíplōsis).
From Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”) possibly via New Latin.

From Old French escarlate (“scarlet cloth”), from Medieval Latin scarlatum (“scarlet cloth”), via Persian سقرلاط (saqerlât, “a warm woollen cloth”), a variant of سقلاط (seqellât, “scarlet cloth”) from Medieval Greek σιγιλλᾶτος (sigillâtos), ultimately from Latin (textum) sigillātum.
From révéler + -ateur. The adjectival sense is the attributive form of the noun.
From Late Latin dynastia, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía, “power, dominion”).
Learned borrowing from Latin -vorus, from Latin vorare (“to devour”).

Inherited from Old French hom, om (nominative form), from Latin homō (“human being”) (compare homme from the Old French oblique form home, from the Latin accusative form hominem). Its pronominal use is of Germanic origin. Compare Old English man (“one, they, people”), reduced form of Old English mann (“person”); Catalan hom; German man (“one, they, people”); Dutch men (“one, they, people”).
From Latin nauclērus, from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).
Inherited from Old French ydropique, from Latin hydropicus.
Representing the combining form of Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).
From parasite, from Latin parasitus 'parasite', ultimately from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin barytŏnus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek βαρύτονος (barútonos).
Learned borrowing from Latin cynicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós).
From Middle French hyperbole, yperbole, a learned borrowing from Latin hyperbolē, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”).
Inherited from Middle French and Old French face, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face, shape”). Doublet of faciès.
Borrowed from Latin sēbum; doublet of the inherited suif.
From Ancient Greek ψευδο- (pseudo-, “false”), from Ancient Greek ψευδής (pseudḗs, “false, lying”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κάθετος (káthetos).

From Old French pale, palle, from Latin pallidus (“pale, pallid”). In Old French one would expect a syncopated *paut, *paude; the form pal(l)e requires a lack of syncope. According to Trésor de la langue française it is a borrowing, though it might also reflect a regional development. Doublet of pallide.

From Southeastern Occitan amelanca, rebracketing with the article from melanco, containing an Ancient Ligurian suffix attached to a word for black cognate to Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “black”) and Latvian melns (“black”), calling the fruits by their colour.
Borrowed from Italian fallita, influenced by failli, faillir. Doublet of faute.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin amidum, from Latin amylum, from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon). Compare Spanish almidón, Greek άμυλο (ámylo), Hebrew עמילן (amilan).
Borrowed from Spanish gitano, itself derived from apheresis of older egiptano (“Egyptian”), from the mistaken belief that gypsies originated from Egypt.
Borrowed from Late Latin dīcibilis, from dīcō (“say”) + -(i)bilis (“-able”). In French, it could almost be surface-analyzed as dis + -ible, except that this would result in *disible, with /z/.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from a clipping of volleyball.
Inherited from Middle French fusible, from Latin fusibilis, from fundō + -bilis. By surface analysis, fondre + -ible.
Learned borrowing from Latin opus. Doublet of œuvre and opéra.
Inherited from Old French ramoner, ramon (“broom”) + -er.
Inherited from Late Latin sanguilentus, alternative form of sanguinolentus (whence sanguinolent).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek λεξικόν (lexikón), whence English lexicon.
From Latin corallium (“coral”), from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion, “coral”).

Borrowed from Latin benedīcite, a plural imperative of benedīcō (“to bless, to praise”) found as the first word of several grace prayers. Doublet of bénissez, second-person plural imperative of bénir.
Borrowed from Latin nocīvus, from noceō.
Borrowed from Latin allūsiōnem (“frolicking”), from allūdō (“to frolic”).
Learned borrowing from Latin indifferentia. By surface analysis, indifférent + -ence.

Inherited from Middle French large, from Old French large, from Latin largus, larga, largum (“abundant, plentiful, copious, large, much”). The feminine is inherited and even generalised for both genders, but for the old masculine, Latin largum (the masculine and neuter accusative) developed into Old French larc, which was discarded.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin putrefactiōnem.
Borrowed from Italian parapetto, from parare (“to shield”) + petto (“chest”).

From Occitan farfadet, from fadet, by addition of the expressive affix particle far- → see farfouiller,[1] with influence from Italian farfarello or Arabic فرفار, farfar ("inconsistent, fickle"), from farfara ("to agitate, stir")[2][3].

Inherited from Old French preface, borrowed from Medieval Latin prefatia, from Classical Latin praefātiō (“preface, prologue”), from praefor (“to speak beforehand”), from prae- (“beforehand”) + for (“to speak”).
Anglicism (English template). Possibly a doublet of templet.

Inherited from Old French sigue, cegue (13th c.), variant of cëue (12th c.), inherited from Latin cicūta. Irregular preservation or restoration of -g- < Latin -c- (as in aigre, aigu, égal etc.) may be due to southern Gallo-Romance influence, partial relatinisation, and/or the general desire for a fuller phonetic form.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intuītiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin creatūra (like English creature), from creo, creare (“to create”).
From Late Latin latria, from Ancient Greek λατρεία (latreía, “service; worship”).
Borrowed from New Latin ungulātus, with assimilation to ongle.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin solubilis, from Latin solvere.

From English market, from Old Northern French market (“commerce; marketplace; trade”) from Latin mercatus (“market; trade; trading; buying and selling”), from the past participle of mercari (“to deal in; to buy; to trade”), from merx (“merchandise; wares”), from the genitive mercis, from Proto-Italic *merk-, from Etruscan.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek προπᾰροξῠ́τονος (propăroxŭ́tonos, “paroxytone”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dissēminātiō. By surface analysis, disséminer + -ation.
From con + -erie; both semantically and lexically, a nearly exact parallel of English cuntery.
Inherited from Middle French repugnant, from Old French repugnant, borrowed from Latin repugnantem.
Learned borrowing from Latin impār. By surface analysis, im- + pair.
English sentimental. By surface analysis, sentiment + -al.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin offerenda, from Latin offerendus (literally “to be offered”), gerundive of offerō (“to offer”). Compare Catalan ofrena, Occitan and Romansh ufrenda, Portuguese oferenda, Spanish ofrenda.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin peccaminōsus. By surface analysis, Latin peccāmen (“sin”) + -eux.
Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Ecclesiastical Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion), diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”).
Borrowed from Latin agōnia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía).
Originally poitral, with change of suffix after -ail, from Latin pectoralis. Doublet of pectoral.
Learned borrowing from Latin impaenitēns. Morphologically analyzable as im- + pénitent.
From Late Latin rectitūdō (“straightness, uprightness”), from Latin rectus (“straight”), perfect passive participle of regō (“regulate, guide”).
Formed from the root of Latin discursus and the suffix -if. In part borrowed from Medieval Latin discursivus.
Learned borrowing from Latin complicātiō. By surface analysis, compliquer + -ation.
From Ancient Greek μακρόν (makrón), neuter form of μακρός (makrós, “long”).
Deverbal from changer (corresponding to Old French change). Compare Medieval and Late Latin cambium.
Borrowed from Latin aedificium, from aedificō (“to build”) (whence édifier).
Borrowed from Latin annālis, from annus (“year”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan cadenat, from Late Latin catēnātum, derived from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of chaîné.
From flambe + -er, replacing Old French flammer.
From Middle French and Old French archier, from Vulgar Latin *arcārius, from Classical Latin arcuārius, derived from Latin arcus (“bow”). Equivalent to arc + -er.
Inherited from Old French actif, from Latin āctīvus.
Inherited from Middle French occision, from Old French ocision, from Latin occīsiōnem, accusative of occīsiō.
Inherited from Middle French poltron, ultimately borrowed from Italian poltrone. Attested since 1509.
Inherited from Old French retencion, borrowed from Latin retentiōnem.
Formed from the root of Latin claustrum, claustra. See also cloîtrer.
From Late Latin heraldus, transposition of héraut (“herald”), with suffix -ique.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “pouch, bladder”).
Borrowed from English ketchup, from Malay kicap, from Hokkien 膎汁 (kê-chiap).
Learned borrowing from Latin recusātiōnem. By surface analysis, récuser + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin convalēscentia (“regaining of health”), from Latin convalēscō (“regain health, grow strong”).
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin fissūra.
From Italian saccheggiare, from sacco, from Latin saccus.
Borrowed from Latin antrum, from Ancient Greek ἄντρον (ántron).
Inherited from Middle French conte, from Old French conte, compte, derived from the verb conter, compter, or from Latin computus. See compte.
From mal- + heureux. Cognate with Piedmontese maleureus, maleuros.
Inherited from Old French agnel, aignel, agniau, from Latin agnellus (according to the TLFi, an early borrowing), diminutive of agnus.
Inherited from Middle French, formed from Old French fer (cf. fier) + -al, or borrowed from a Late Latin ferālis, from Latin ferus (“wild”).
Inherited from Old French constitucion, a learned borrowing from Latin cōnstitūtiō, from cōnstituō + -tiō. By surface analysis, constituer + -tion.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin deliciōsus.
From Middle French consanguinitéité, consanguinité, from Old French consanguinité, from Latin cōnsanguinitās. By surface analysis, consanguin + -ité.
Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Latin canonicatus.
Inherited from Middle French escouter, from Old French escouter, from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of ausculter, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Middle French election, borrowed from Latin ēlēctiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French intense, from Old French intense, which was borrowed from Latin intēnsus.
From Ancient Greek πολύχρηστος (polúkhrēstos, “multipurpose, highly useful”), from πολύς (polús) + χρηστός (khrēstós, “useful”).

Inherited from Middle French seigle, from Old French soigle, segle, seygle, from Latin sēcale. Possibly through the intermediate of Old Occitan segle (at least concerning this form; cf. regional variants seille, soile, Walloon swele, Old French soile, which were inherited).
Inherited from Middle French ventre, from Old French ventre, from Latin ventrem, from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-.
Borrowed from Arabic ظَهِير (ẓahīr), via Moroccan Arabic
From Old French esperoner, corresponding to éperon + -er.
From Ancient Greek καλάσιρις (kalásiris), likely from an unclear Egyptian source.
Inherited from Old French tiers, from Latin tertius.
From English hamburger, from German Hamburger.
From Latin adytum, from Ancient Greek ἄδυτον (áduton).
Learned borrowing from Latin annūlātiōnem. By surface analysis, annuler + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin ōrāculārius, from ōrāculum (whence oracle).
Inherited from Middle French esloigner, from Old French esloignier, itself probably from loing, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *exlongāre, from Latin longe.
Borrowed from Italian amaretto, from amaro (“bitter”) (from Latin amārus) + diminutive ending -etto.
Borrowed from Latin bimestris, or formed on the model of trimestre.
Inherited from Middle French barreaulx, equivalent to modern barre + -ot.
Borrowed from Latin hydromel, hydromeli, from hydro- (from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”)) + mel (“honey”).
Inherited from Middle French historial, from Latin historiālis. By surface analysis, histoire + -al.
Inherited from Old French montaingneus, from Late Latin montāniōsus, an adjective based on montānia, from Latin montem (“mountain”). By surface analysis, montagne + -eux.
Inherited from Middle French marmelade, from Galician or Portuguese marmelada (“jam, preserve”), from marmelo.
From enregistrer (“to register; to save; to record”) + -ment.

From Middle French metastase, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μετᾰ́στᾰσῐς (metắstăsĭs). By surface analysis, méta- + stase. Its use to refer to the spread of cancer was coined in 1829 by the French gynecologist Joseph Récamier (1774–1852).
From nombre + -eux, or from Latin numerōsus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θεραπευτής (therapeutḗs, “attendant”).
By surface analysis, banque + route. Calque of Italian bancarotta. First attested in the 15th century.
Borrowed from Latin plumbāgō. See also plombagine.
Learned borrowing from Latin immūtābilis. Compare immuable.
Learned borrowing from Latin faciēs. Doublet of face.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impassibilis. By surface analysis, im- + passible.
From Latin nāsīca (“large-noser”) Compare Spanish násico, Catalan nàsic.
Inherited from Middle French brocher, from Old French brochier. By surface analysis, broche + -er.
Inherited from Old French musique, borrowed from Latin mūsica, borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “art of the Muses”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin laicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós).
Inherited from Middle French vestir, from Old French vestir, from Latin vestīre.
Learned borrowing from Latin prōvīsiō (“preparation, foresight”), from prōvidēre (“provide”).

Inherited from Middle French chascun, from Old French chascun, from Vulgar Latin *cascunum, *casquunum, a conflation of quisque unum (“each one”) + *cata unum, a variant form showing a derivative of Ancient Greek κατά (katá) (this variant form survived into Old French as chaün). Compare Occitan cadun, chascun, Catalan cadascun, Italian ciascuno.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐμβολή (embolḗ).
From Latin exuō (“to draw out, take off, free”) (perfect passive participle exūtus) + -oire (suffix forming masculine nouns).
Learned borrowing from Latin calcārius, from calx.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin erēmīticus, from Latin erēmīta (whence French ermite).
From Latin Smyrna, from Ancient Greek Σμύρνα (Smúrna).
Calque of English diskette, as disque + -ette.
Inherited from Middle French pionnier, from Old French peonier (“infantryman”), from peon (“footman”) (modern French pion), from Latin pedōnem.
Borrowed from Latin pecūlātus, from Latin pecūlor (“to embezzle”).

Inherited from Middle French bastiment, from Old French bastiment (“act of building, fortification”), from bastir (“to build, make; to sew”), from Vulgar Latin *bastīre, borrowed from Frankish *bastijan (“to sew, weave”).
Learned borrowing from Latin diurnus. Doublet of jour.
From Old French, a borrowing from Latin scientem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin scrīptōrium. Doublet of écritoire.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”).

Inherited from Middle French carnage, itself probably from a Norman or Picard (Old Northern French) variant of Old French charnage, itself from char (see also chair (“flesh”)), or from a Medieval Latin carnāticum (“slaughter of animals”), from Latin carnem. See also Old Occitan carnatge, Italian carnaggio.
From a- + lune + -ir, by analogy with atterrir and amerrir. Compare Italian allunare, Portuguese alunar, alunissar, Romanian aluniza, and Spanish alunizar.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin laxativus.
Borrowed from Late Latin mēnsuālis (“monthly”), or derived from mensis (“month”) on the model of annuel from annus.
Borrowed from Latin nitidus. Doublet of net, which was inherited.
Past participle of Middle French endoulourir, from douleur.
From Middle French altercacion, altercation, from Old French altercation, borrowed from Latin altercātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French vervainne, verveine, from Latin verbēnae, plural of verbēna.
Inherited from Old French quiete (13th c.), borrowed from Latin quiētus. The masculine quiet is a Middle French backformation. Doublet of inherited coi and the earlier borrowing quitte.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin catalogus, itself from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “an enrollment, a register, a list, catalogue”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, to tell at length or in order, to make a list”), from κατα- (kata-, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to gather, to pick up, to choose for oneself, to pick out, to count”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin anacardus, from Latin anacardium, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “on, upon”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēfaecātiō. By surface analysis, déféquer + -ation.
Borrowed from Latin lumbus. Cf. Old French loigne, a doublet ultimately from the same origin.
Calque of English influencer, using influencer + -eur.

Inherited from Middle French sorbet, borrowed from Italian sorbetto, borrowed from Ottoman Turkish شربت (şerbet), borrowed from Classical Persian شَرْبَت (šarbat), borrowed from Arabic شَرْبَة (šarba), from شَرِبَ (šariba).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin manufactūra (“making by hand”); from manū (“by hand”) + factūra (“act of making”).
From Middle French absurde (16th c.), relatinized form of older absourde, from Old French absorde (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin absurdus (“discordant, incongruous”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek μετεωρολογικός (meteōrologikós, “relating to the study of celestial bodies or phenomena; skilled in meteorology”). By surface analysis, météorolog(ie) + -ique.
Borrowed from Latin patria, from pater (whence French père).
Learned borrowing from New Latin catharticus, from Ancient Greek καθαρτικός (kathartikós).
Inherited from Latin īnsignia, a neuter plural reinterpreted as a feminine singular. Doublet of insigne.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνεύρυσμα (aneúrusma).
From Latin monitor; in the sense of 'computer screen', calqued after English monitor.
From Middle French succes (16th c.), a borrowing from Latin successus. The verb succéder is older (13th c.).
Borrowed from Occitan arpioun, from arpa (“claw”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin mūsicālis. By surface analysis, musique + -al.
Derived from Old French bugle, itself borrowed from Latin buculus.
From Old French, from Latin ēnormitās. By surface analysis, énorme + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin philanthrōpia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
Learned borrowing from Latin patella. Doublet of poêle (“frying pan”).
Borrowed from Latin anathema, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνάθεμα (anáthema).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin praemonitōrius; pré- + monitoire.
From Old French croster and its variants, from Latin crusta (“crust, hard shell”).
Learned borrowing from Latin recipiēns, present participle of recipiō, from re- + capiō (“to catch”). Cognate with English recipient and Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish recipiente (“vessel”).
Inherited from Middle French societé, from Old French societé, borrowed from Latin societātem (“society”), from socius. Compare the inherited Old French doublet soisté.
Inherited from Old French pin, from Latin pīnus, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *poi- (“sap, juice”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin īrāscibilis, from īrāscor (“grow angry”), from īra (“anger”) (whence ire).
From é- + couler, or possibly from Vulgar Latin *excolāre, from Latin cōlāre. Compare Italian scolare, Portuguese escoar, Spanish escolar, Sicilian sculari.
Inherited from Old French speculatif, borrowed from Late Latin speculativus. By surface analysis, spéculer + -atif.
Inherited from Middle French Sclave, from Medieval Latin Sclavus, from Medieval Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. Doublet of esclave.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin superioritātem, from Latin superior. By surface analysis, supérieur + -ité.
Inherited from Middle French patricien, from patrice + -ien.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τρᾰπεζοειδής (trăpezoeidḗs). By surface analysis, trapèze + -oïde.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin repulsiō, from Latin repellō.
Learned borrowing from Latin sepulcrālis. By surface analysis, sépulcre + -al.
Inherited from Old French concevoir, from Vulgar Latin *concipēre, from Latin concipere.
From Middle French and Old French vi(c)toire, from earlier victorie, a borrowing from Latin victōria.

Inherited from Middle French chirurgien, from Old French cirurgiien (see also Old French surgien, inherited through Vulgar Latin), or simply formed from the root of chirurgie, borrowed from Latin chīrūrgia, from chīrūrgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).
Inherited from Middle French saingne, from Old French sainnie, from Latin saniēs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”).
Inherited from Old French esgratigner, from gratter.
From Old French legit(t)ime (13th c.), borrowed from Latin lēgitimus.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin supplicātiōnem.
Borrowed from English challenge, from Old French chalonge, from Latin calumnia. Doublet of calomnie.
From Late Latin substantīvum, neuter singular of substantīvus (“substantive”), from substantia (“substance, essence”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dērīsōrius.
Calque of Hindi हिंदुत्व (hindutva) / Bengali হিন্দুত্ব (hindutto, literally “Hinduness”): hindou + -ité.
