Inherited from Old French pendre, from Late Latin pendĕre (conjugation confused with or altered by pendere (“to suspend, hang”)) for Latin pendēre, present active infinitive pendeō, from Proto-Italic *pendēō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin”).
From métrer + -age. Compare Walloon metraedje. Compare typologically English footage.
From English sprue, from Dutch spruwe (“thrush”). Originally denoted a disease of the mouth characterised by ulcers.
Inherited from Middle French lunaire, from Latin lūnāris.
Inherited from Middle French barquette, first attested c. 1320 (discounting an adjective in nef barquette, 1238). By surface analysis, barque + -ette.
Inherited from Old French taster, from Vulgar Latin *tastāre, contraction of *taxitō, frequentative of Late Latin taxāre (“touch repeatedly”), from Latin taxus. Compare English taste.
Variation of fillâtre after fils, from Old French fillastre, from Latin filiaster.
From quitte + -er, or from Late Latin quietare (“acquit, discharge, release”), from Latin quiētāre (“to calm”).
Learned borrowing from Latin pellicula (“small skin or hide”).

Inherited from Old French aguisier, from Vulgar Latin *acutiāre, from Latin acūtus, the past participle of acuō. Compare Catalan agusar, Italian aguzzare, Occitan agusar, Portuguese aguçar, Spanish aguzar. The initial -ai- can probably be explained through a hypothetical proto-French or late Vulgar Latin intermediate form *ayguydzar(e), from assimilation of the palatal approximant in the second syllable of an earlier *aguydzare. In this hypothesis, the Old French form aguisier may be due to influence from agu (cf. aigu).
Borrowed from Latin adiacentem, present active participle of adiaceō (“adjoin, border”). Doublet of aise.

From Old French formatif, formative, from Medieval Latin formātīvus, from Latin fōrmātus + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘doing’ or ‘related to doing’). Fōrmātus is the perfect passive participle of fōrmō (“to form, to shape”); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a form, shape”) (see further at that entry). By surface analysis, former + -atif.

Inherited from Middle French oreille, from Old French oreille, from Vulgar Latin oricla, from Latin auricula, diminutive of auris, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws. Cognate with Catalan and Galician orella; Portuguese orelha; Italian orecchio; Occitan aurelha; Romanian ureche; and Spanish oreja. Compare zoreille, zorey.
From Latin antipathia, from Ancient Greek ἀντιπάθεια (antipátheia).
Inherited from Old French rapporter (attested since the mid-twelfth century), from Latin reportare.
Learned borrowing from Latin traumaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τραυματικός (traumatikós), from τραῦμα (traûma).
Borrowed from Latin tepidus. Doublet of tiède, which was inherited.
PIE word  *ḱóm From Middle French constellation, from Old French constellation, borrowed from Late Latin cōnstēllātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin perorātiōnem, and refashioned after oraison.
Borrowed from Spanish guano, from Quechua wanu.

Borrowed from Late Latin benna (“wicker carriage”), related to benne used in Norman and Lyonnais. The meaning of bâche (“covering, tarp”) is the same that connects bâche and basket, see also Latin bascauda.
Learned borrowing from Latin epanadiplōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναδίπλωσις (epanadíplōsis, “doubling, folding”).
Borrowed from Late Latin initiātor, from initiō, from Latin initium, from ineō.
Inherited from Middle French erythree, from Latin erythraeus, from Ancient Greek ἐρυθραῖος (eruthraîos).
From Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).
Inherited from Old French chevalerie. By surface analysis, cheval + -erie. Compare cavalerie.
Borrowed from Late Latin antiphrasis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀντίφρασις (antíphrasis). By surface analysis, anti- + phrasis.
Borrowed from Latin chirurgia, from chirurgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).
Inherited from Middle French apuyer, Old French apoiier, borrowed from Medieval Latin *appodiāre, from Latin podium. Compare Spanish apoyar, Portuguese apoiar, Italian appoggiare.
Inherited from Middle French costé, from Old French costé, from Latin costātus. Compare Spanish costado, Catalan costat.
Inherited from Old French antan, from Latin ante annum.
Inherited from Old French dissenterie, borrowed from Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diaphanus (“diaphanous”), from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) and φαίνω (phaínō, “show”).
From voisin + -age. Displaced Old French visné.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin līnum.
Borrowed from Latin dictamnum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek δίκταμνον (díktamnon).

Inherited from Middle French monstrer, from Old French monstrer, semi-learned form of older moustrer, mostrer, from Latin mōnstrāre, whence also English demonstrate. Cognate with Spanish mostrar, Italian mostrare, English muster.
Learned borrowing from Latin orīginālis. Doublet of originel.
Derived from Ancient Greek ὁμός (homós, “one and the same, common, joint”).
From Latin Hunni. Possibly a doublet of Xiongnu.
Inherited from Middle French baril, from Old French baril, bareil (“barrel”), of uncertain origin.
First attested in the 12 century. From Latin sardonyx.
From earlier hen, heim, from Latin hem (“eh?”).
Learned borrowing from Latin fragmentum (“a fragment, remnant”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin parentheticus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin distributivus.
Borrowed from Spanish canario (“canary, resident or native of the Canary Islands”).
Inherited from Middle French moyen, from Old French moien, earlier meien, inherited from Latin mediānus. Doublet of médian, a borrowing, and also of misaine.
19th century, derived from hôpital + -iser, using the Latinate form of the noun as retained in hospitalier.
Learned borrowing from Latin vexātiō. By surface analysis, vexer + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French vene, from Old French veine, from Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin.
Borrowed from Latin vitiōsus. See vice + -eux. Cf. also Old French voisos.
Inherited from Old French mule, from Latin mūla (“a she-mule, mule”), feminine of mūlus (“a mule”).
Inherited from Old French peiz, from Latin picem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pī́ts (“pitch; resin”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hypothecārius. By surface analysis, hypothèque + -aire.
From Latin artem, accusative singular of ars.
From dé- + bord + -er. Cognate with Catalan and Spanish desbordar.
Borrowed from Italian semola, from Latin simila.
Borrowed from New Latin suīcīdium, from suī (“oneself”) and -cīdium (“-cide”).
Learned borrowing from Latin irrītātiō. By surface analysis, irriter + -ation.
Borrowed from Portuguese mangostão, from Malay manggustan, a variant of manggis.
Learned borrowing from Latin dēportātiō. By surface analysis, déporter + -ation.
Borrowed from Spanish iguana, from Taíno *iwana.
From Middle French exemplaire, Old French essamplaire, from Latin exemplāris. Related to exemple.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek εμπύριος (empúrios, “that which is inflamed”), from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).
Learned borrowing from Latin rapiditās. By surface analysis, rapide + -ité.
Borrowed from Latin plumbaginem, as it resembled lead. Compare also plumbago.
From English tholin, with the suffix replaced by -ine.
From Vulgar Latin bīnāre (“to do something twice; to work the land twice”), from a derivative of Latin bīnī, from bis ("twice, two times"). Cognate with Spanish binar ("to plow over").
Borrowed from Latin thalamegus, itself from Ancient Greek θᾰλᾰμηγός (thălămēgós).
Borrowed from Latin stabilitātem, see stable, -ité.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνορεξία (anorexía).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin apostolicus (“apostolic”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀποστολικός (apostolikós, “apostolic”).
Borrowed from Spanish parangón, from Italian paragonare.

From stationner + -ment. The word has been in use in French for a long time. Only in the sense of "parking lot" or "parking space" is this a Quebecism (originally "parc de stationnement") coined by the Office québécois de la langue française to replace the anglicism "parking" within French in official use.

Uncertain, perhaps from cap + -oter, influenced by Spanish cabo (“cape”). Sometimes claimed to be derived from Italian explorer Sebastian Cabot (c. 1474–1557) or John Cabot (c. 1450–1500), but the Centre National de Ressources Textuelles et Lexicales describes this derivation as unsupported by the chronology.
From Old French, from Latin officiālis.
From Middle French augural, borrowed from Latin augurālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin vulgāris. Compare also Old and Middle French vulgal, inherited from a Vulgar Latin form *vulgālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin inculpātiō. By surface analysis, inculper + -ation.
From English shoot + -er. First attested in 1900.
Learned borrowing from Latin volātilis (“flying”). Doublet of volaille.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄφωνος (áphōnos). By surface analysis, a- + -phone.

Inherited from Middle French malin(g), backformation from Old French maligne m (12th c.), a borrowing from Latin malignus. Compare the same backformation in bénin and, on the other hand, the original common-gender form preserved in digne.
Inherited from Middle French hostile, hostif (this form with a change of suffix), borrowed from Latin hostilis.
Learned borrowing from New Latin polyedron, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πολύεδρος (polúedros, “having many seats”).

Inherited from Middle French vaisseau, from Old French vaissel, from Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of Latin vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vessel”). Compare Occitan vaissèl, Catalan vaixell, Italian vascello.
Inherited from Middle French bannir, from Old French bannir, banir, from Frankish *bannijan.
Inherited from Old French laitue, from Latin lactūca.
Inherited from Old French violence, from Latin violentia, from the adjective violentus, see violent.
Derived from pic(c)olo, from Italian piccolo.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin paradīsiacus.
From Latin animalculum. By surface analysis, animal + -cule.
From Middle French histoire, from Old French istorie (ca. 1100), borrowed from Latin historia, itself from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía).

Inherited from Middle French roial, from Old French roial, from earlier reial, real, from very early Old French (c. 880) regiel, from Latin rēgālis, from rēx (“king”) + -ālis. Equivalent to roi + -al.
Borrowed from Latin mandātum, from mandō (“put in one's hands, command”), from Proto-Indo-European *man- (“hand”) + *dʰeh₁- (“put”).
Inherited from Middle French asne, from Old French asne, from Latin asinus.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēvidentia. A false friend of evidence, which is better translated as preuve.
Inherited from Middle French écrin, from Old French escrin, from Latin scrīnium. Related to English shrine.
Inherited from Old French juin, from Latin iūnius.
Inherited from Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae (“relics”).
Borrowed from Spanish vigía, itself a borrowing from Portuguese vigia, from vigiar. Cognate with French veille.
From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-), from ἀνά (aná, “on, up, above, throughout”).
From Latin Mūsagetēs, from Doric Greek Μουσαγέτης (Mousagétēs), from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”) + Doric Greek ἀγέτης (agétēs, “leader”), literally “leader of the Muses”.
Inherited from Middle French alleage. By surface analysis, allier + -age.
Inherited from Old French enfler, from Latin īnflāre.

Clipping of rabiot (“(originally fishermen and military cant) excess, remainder; (earlier) (1831) excess of fish remaining after rations had been imparted to the mates, (1859) soup soldiers often left over in their mess tin, (1832) an extra something which one can enjoy”). Further unclear, probably from (Gascon) Occitan rabiot (“little fish; leftovers from fishing”).
Borrowed from Late Latin incomplētus, from Latin complētus.
Learned borrowing from Latin hieraticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís).
Inherited from Middle French meusnier, from Old French meunier, meulnier, munoiere, from Late Latin molīnārius, from molīnum (“mill”), from Latin molō (“to grind”). Compare moulinier.
Partly from Middle French obsolet, partly directly borrowed from Latin obsolētus (“worn out, gone out of use”).
Inherited from Old French pred, pré, from Latin prātum.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τετράχειρ (tetrákheir).
Borrowed from Latin Āsiarcha, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιάρχης (Asiárkhēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin partiālis. Doublet of partial.
From Latin thōrax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).
From Latin asteria, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.
From Latin ecloga, from Ancient Greek ἐκλογή (eklogḗ, “selection”).
From Late Latin modernus (“recent, actual”), from the adverb modo (“recently, just now”).
Borrowed from Late Latin veniālis, from Latin venia.

From Latin catēchīzāre (“to instruct in religion; to catechize”), from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō, “to instruct orally”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to resound, instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).
Inherited from Middle French truchement, from Old French drugement, borrowed from Arabic تُرْجُمَان (turjumān) during the crusades.
Inherited from Old French cedule, borrowed from Latin schedula, diminutive of scheda. Compare Portuguese and Spanish cédula.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cardō, from Latin carduus. Doublet of cardon and chardon.
Learned borrowing from Latin quotīdiānus, late spelling of Classical cottīdiānus, from cottīdiē (“daily”); cognate with English quotidian.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin cambium.
From aménager (“to lay out; to develop”) + -ment.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin spontāneus. In modern French, only words descending from Latin borrowings of Greek origin ending in the suffixes -ēus/-ēum, -aeus/-aeum (and exceptionally -ius/-ium, as in élysée/Élysée) are written with -ée in the masculine. Words descending from Latin words in -āneus (a different suffix, from -ānus + -eus), are now written with the ending -ané (as seen, for example, in méditerrané, momentané). The first four editions of the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française spelled these words with -anée before adopting the current spelling in the fifth edition.
Inherited from Old French dunc, from Vulgar Latin dunc, from a crossing of Latin tunc with dum. Compare Italian dunque, Occitan donc and Catalan doncs.
From Old French adjective journel + -ment; see also journal.

Inherited from Middle French endive, endivie, andive, indivie, from Medieval Latin endivia or Italian indivia~endivia, from Medieval Greek ἐντύβιον (entúbion), from Latin intibus (which see). The ultimate source is likely Semitic.
Borrowed from Late Latin melopoeia, from Ancient Greek μελοποία (melopoía).
From Late Latin sphēra, earlier Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), of unknown origin.
From Old French, from Latin absolūtiōnem (“acquittal”), from absolvō (“absolve”).
From Latin īnfēcunditās, from īnfēcundus + -tās. By surface analysis, infécond + -ité.
From Middle French, from Old French humain, umain, from Latin humanus (“of or belonging to a man, human, humane”), from homo (“man, human”).
From Latin mamma (“breast, udder, pap, teat, dug”) + -fère, from fero.
From ré- + incarnation or from réincarner + -ation.
From Old French poison f, inherited from Latin pōtiōnem f. Doublet of potion f, a borrowing. Cognate with English poison, potion.
Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Latin carnārium.

Inherited from Middle French banquet, from Italian banchetto (“light repast between meals, snack eaten on a small bench”, literally “a small bench”), from banco (“bench”), from Lombardic bank (“bench”) / Lombardic panch (“bench”), from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”). Akin to Old High German bank, banch (“bench”), Old English benc (“bench”). Compare Old French banquet, which only meant "small bench", from the same Proto-Germanic source.
From avant (“before”) + hier (“yesterday”). See also Italian avantieri.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek διαγνωστικός (diagnōstikós).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin schisma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “division”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”).
Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀδήν (adḗn) + -itis. By surface analysis, adén(o)- + -ite.
Learned borrowing from Latin paenitentia. Compare the inherited Old French peneance, penance.
From Old French beguer, besguer (compare bègue).

PIE word  *gʷṓws Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek βουστροφηδόν (boustrophēdón, literally “turning like an ox”), in reference to the back-and-forth course traced by boustrophedon text resembling the path taken by an ox ploughing a field.
Inherited from Middle French garniture, from Old French garneture, garnesture, from Old French garnir. Compare Anglo-Norman warnesture, warniture, whence Middle English warnestore, warnestoure.
Learned borrowing from Latin exsultātiō. By surface analysis, exulter + -ation.

Inherited from Middle French serement (1415, Charles d'Orléans), from Old French sairement (twelfth century), from earlier sagrament (842, Serments de Strasbourg), from Latin sacramentum. Doublet of sacrement.
Inherited from Old French logëiz. By surface analysis, loger (“to lodge”) + -is.
Derived from Latin horizōn (“horizon”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).
Inherited from Old French reson, raison, inherited from Latin ratiōnem. Compare the borrowed doublet ration.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “trainer of athletes”).
Inherited from Middle French fenestre, from Old French fenestre, from Latin fenestra.
Gallicization of Late Latin incessanter with the suffix -ment.

Inherited from Middle French compter, conter, from Old French compter, conter, cunter, from Latin computāre. Doublet of conter and computer. The learned spelling -mpt- was originally used interchangeably with the phonetic spelling -nt-. In modern French they have been split in such a way that the Latinizing form represents the sense “to count”, which was already present in Latin, while the native form represents the derived sense “to tell” (see conter).
From Late Latin discussiōnem, from Latin discutiōnem.
From Old French celidoine, from Medieval Latin celidonia, chelidonia.

Inherited from Middle French grappe, from Old French grappe, grape, crape (“cluster of fruit or flowers, bunch of grapes”), from graper, craper (“to pick grapes”, literally “to hook”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *krappo (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *grep- (“hook”), *gremb- (“crooked, uneven”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, end, twist”). Cognate with Middle Dutch krappe (“hook”), Old High German krapfo (“hook”) (German Krapfe). More at cramp.
Inherited from Middle French quantiesme, from Latin quantus + *-ĕsimus. By surface analysis, quant + -ième.
From héli- + port, calque of English heliport.

From fronce "frown, scowl" from Middle French fronce, from Old French fronces, fronche "frown, wrinkles, small creases in cloth", from Frankish *hrunkja "wrinkle" from Proto-Germanic *hrunkijō, *hrunkitō (“fold, wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *sker- (“to turn, bend”). Akin to Old High German runza "fold, wrinkle, crease" (German Runzel "wrinkle"), Middle Dutch ronse "frown", Old Norse hrukka "wrinkle, crease" (Icelandic hrukka "wrinkle, crease, ruck"). More at ruck₂.
Inherited from Old French bretesche, from Late Latin brittisca.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δημαγωγός (dēmagōgós, “popular leader, mob leader”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía).
Inherited from Middle French tube, from Latin tubus (“tube, pipe”).
From Latin collātīvus, from collātus, past participle of cōnferō (“confer”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin orthodoxus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “right”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ūsūrārius. Compare also usurier.
Inherited from Old French branche, from Late Latin branca, possibly of Gaulish origin.
From Late Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, departure”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ὁδός (hodós, “path, road”).
Inherited from Middle French deces, from Old French deces, from Latin dēcessus, past participle of dēcēdō (“depart, die”).
From Medieval Latin Lōthariānus, from Lōtharius + -iānus.
Borrowed from Latin dēdūcere, on the model of conduire (from condūcere).
From Latin alveus; according to the TLFi etymological dictionary, it was a (very early) borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin incestuōsus.
Inherited from Old French tant, from Latin tantum.
Borrowed from Italian opera, from Latin opera. Doublet of œuvre and opus.
Borrowed from Late Latin contrādictōrius (“contradictory”), from Latin contrādīcō (“to speak against; contradict”), from contrā (“against”) + dīcō (“to say, speak”).

Borrowed from Latin ēdictum (“proclamation, edict”), the neuter of ēdictus, perfect passive participle of ēdīcō (“to publish, proclaim”), itself from ex (“out of, from”) + dīcō (“say”); cognate with Dutch edict, German Edikt.
Borrowed (in this form) from Latin fascia. The Old French form faisse, fece, which underwent "re-Latinized" spelling in modern French, was popularly inherited.
Inherited from Middle French abeille, from Old Occitan abelha, from Latin apicula, diminutive of apis. Displaced Old French ef.
From Ancient Greek σωματικός (sōmatikós, “bodily”), from σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

Inherited from Middle French bourdon (“honeybee, bumblebee”), from Old French bordon (“bumblebee, drone, beetle, insect”), from Medieval Latin burdō (c. C.E. 1000), first recorded in the Homilies of King Ælfric, glossed by Old English dora (“bumblebee”). Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Frankish *boʀdō, *buʀdō (“beetle, insect”), from Proto-Germanic *buzdô (“beetle, grub”, literally “swelling”), from *būs- (“to erupt, burst, flow rapidly”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰūs- (“to move quickly”), related to Old English budda (“beetle”), Middle Low German buddech (“thick, swollen”), Low German budde (“louse, grub”). See bug.
Borrowed from Latin congelātiōnem, from congelo. By surface analysis, congeler + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French architecteur (“architect”), from Latin architector, variant of architectus.
From Latin rāna (“frog”) + culture, on the model of agriculture.
Borrowed from Latin dactylicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek δακτυλικός (daktulikós). By surface analysis, dactyle + -ique.

Either from Italian carnevale, from Medieval Latin carnelevale, from caro (“flesh”) + levo (“to lighten, to raise”), or directly from Medieval Latin. The alternative carne vale (“to flesh/meat, farewell”) is believed to be a folk etymology.

Inherited from Middle French chesne, from Old French chesne, chaisne, chasne, from Vulgar Latin *cassanus (attested in Medieval Latin as casnus), probably from Gaulish kassanos. Some Old French forms possibly influenced by fraisne, fresne (cf. modern frêne). Compare Occitan casse, Franco-Provençal châno. See also Spanish quejigo, Galician caxigo, Aragonese caixico.

Inherited from Middle French parole, from Old French parole, inherited from Vulgar Latin *paraula, from Late Latin, from Latin parabola (“comparison; (later) speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabole and palabre.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χθόνιος (khthónios, “in or under the ground”), from χθών (khthṓn, “ground”).
Inherited from Old French boure, borre, from Late Latin burra (“coarse fabric or material”).
Inherited from Middle French mieulx, from Old French mielz, mialz, miels, from Latin melius.
From Middle French araire (1443), a borrowing from Occitan araire, from Latin arātrum. Compare the inherited Old French arere, which had fallen out of use in favour of charrue.
Borrowed from Latin cannabis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). Doublet of chanvre.
Borrowed from Russian тайга́ (tajgá), from Turkic or Yakut тайга (tayga).
Inherited from Old French charnelment. By surface analysis, charnel + -ment.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek διακριτικός (diakritikós).
Borrowed from Italian allegro, itself borrowed from French allègre. Doublet of allègre.
Inherited from Middle French laine, from Old French lainne, lein, from Latin lāna.
Inherited from Middle French dire, from Old French dire, from Latin dīcō, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).
Borrowed from Late Latin glandulōsus, from Latin glandula.
Old French lod, from Late Latin levita, from levātus.
Learned borrowing from Latin capitulum. Doublet of chapitre.
Inherited from Middle French magicien. By surface analysis, magique (“magic”) + -ien.
Learned borrowing from Latin tyrannicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τυραννικός (turannikós). By surface analysis, tyran + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Latin quasi (“as if”).
Borrowed from Latin pigmentum (“pigment”), itself from pingō (“to paint”) + -mentum. Doublet of piment, a borrowing from Spanish.
Borrowed from Arabic اِنْتِفَاضَة (intifāḍa, “shaking off, uprising, insurrection”).
From furieux + -ax. The Latin word is unrelated.
From Latin lexis, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”) + -al.
Inherited from Middle French carobe, from Medieval Latin carrubium, from Arabic خَرُّوب (ḵarrūb).
Inherited from Old French pensif, from penser (“to think”), semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin pēnsō.
From Latin atheos, from Ancient Greek ἄθεος (átheos).
Learned borrowing from Latin multiplicātor. By surface analysis, multiplier + -ateur.
Inherited from Middle French heritier, from Old French eritier, from Latin hērēditārius. Doublet of héréditaire.
Inherited from Old French fabliau, diminutive of fable.
Borrowed from English grogram, from French gros-grain.
From Old French, from Latin conclūsiōnem, from the past participle stem of conclūdere (“conclude”).
Borrowed from Latin lepra, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra).
From Old French conforter, from Late Latin cōnfortāre (“strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (“strong”).
Inherited from Middle French latin, from Old French latin, borrowed from Latin latīnus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin chorion.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin episcopālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin callōsus. By surface analysis, cal + -eux.
Inherited from Old French degré, from Latin gradus, with the prefix de- (probably to avoid a conflation with gré).
Learned borrowing from Latin nōdulus (“small knot”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monasticus.
From débarder + -eur. The carnival figure usually wore a débardeur, or trousers.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin revolūtiō, from Latin revolvō.
Borrowed from New Latin vēlāris, from vēlum (whence French voile).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐφελκυστικός (ephelkustikós).

From Old French uistre, oistre, from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon). The h is unetymological (no h in the Latin ostrea), but it used to disambiguate the pronunciation in the times when u and v were variants of the same letter, cf. huit, huile.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin trānsfōrmātiōnem, from Latin trānsfōrmō.
Inherited from Old French perdiciun, borrowed from Late Latin perditiōnem, from Latin perdō.
Borrowed from Late Latin obligātōrius, from obligō (whence French obliger).

Latinate learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cogitātiōnem (“act of pondering; reflection”), supplanting or reshaping variant forms from Middle French cogitatiun, Old French cogitaciun, cogitacion, from Vulgar Latin cōgitātiōnem; compare Middle English cogitacioun, English cogitation. Ultimately from Latin cōgitō (“to turn over in the mind; think, consider, ponder, meditate”) from con- (“together, with”) + agitō (“to put in constant motion, drive at something; devise, plot, contrive”), verbal root from Proto-Italic *agō (“to drive, impel”) from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ-.
Inherited from Old French [Term?], probably from Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula), from Medieval Latin *vitula (“stringed instrument”). Compare Italian viola.
Inherited from Old French fae, from Vulgar Latin Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Catalan, Occitan, and Portuguese fada, Italian fata, Spanish hada.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin attractīvus.
From Provençal entamenar, from Latin intaminare, from Latin in- + tangere + -are.
Inherited from Middle French ouyr, from Old French oir, from Latin audīre.
From Medieval Latin Sina (“China”), from Latin Sinae (“the Southern Chinese; Southern China”), from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v.
Inherited from Old French juré, from Latin iūrātus. Doublet of jurat.
Inherited from Middle French hart, from Old French hart, hard, a borrowing from Frankish *heʀdā.
Clipping of application, probably a calque of English app.
Inherited from Middle French nourrisse, nourrice, from Old French nurrice, from Late Latin nūtrīcia, feminine of Latin nūtrīcius.
Learned borrowing from Latin intelligēns (“discerning”), present active participle of intellegō (“understand, comprehend”), itself from inter (“between”) + legō (“choose, pick out, read”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dēformātiō. By surface analysis, déformer + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French chapelle, from Old French chapele, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin cappella, diminutive of cappa.
From Latin faldistōrium. Doublet of fauteuil.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin assistentia.
Inherited from Middle French combustion, from Old French combustion, from Latin combustiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French tension, borrowed from Latin tensiō.
Inherited from Old French plenitude, borrowed from Latin plenitudō.
Borrowed from Latin sīc (“thus, so”). Doublet of si.
Learned borrowing from Latin copula. Doublet of couple.
Learned borrowing from Latin imprimātur (“let it be printed”).
Inherited from Middle French oncle, from Old French oncle, from Vulgar Latin *aunclum, from Latin avunculus.

Unadapted borrowing from Latin aberrātiō(n) (“relief, diversion”), from aberr(ā) (“wander away, go astray”) (from ab (“away”) + errō (“wander”)) + -tiō(n) (suffix forming nouns relating to actions or their results). Compare English aberration.
Inherited from Middle French, from Late Latin duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō.
Learned borrowing from Latin ātrium. Doublet of aître.
From front + -al; see also Medieval Latin frontalis, from Latin frōns, as well as fronteau and frontail.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin aptitūdō.
From Old French largesce, corresponding to large + -esse.
From en- + chaîne + -er. Possibly also corresponds to Vulgar Latin *incatēnāre, from Latin catēnāre. Compare Italian incatenare; Catalan, Occitan, and Catalan encadenar; and Portuguese encadear.
magasin + -er. Dénominal from magasin; possibly influenced by English shop.
From chambre + -ée. Compare camarade, a borrowing from Spanish.
From relation + -el. The noun sense probably arose by ellipsis from a noun phrase comprised of the adjective + some masculine noun (such as domaine or aspect).
From Middle French abyssal (16th c.), from Late Latin abyssālis. By surface analysis, abysse + -al, though the noun is younger in French than the adjective.
Inherited from Old French flaiel, flael, flayau, inherited from Latin flagellum.

From Middle French suffragant, from Old French suffragam, from Ecclesiastical Latin suffrāgāneus, from suffrāgium (“vote, support, intercession”) + -āneus, with the ‹t› added in Middle French under the influence of Latin suffrāgantem. Doublet of suffragané, the learned borrowing from Latin.
From Latin latentem, present participle of lateo (“lie hidden”).
Inherited from Middle French jouet, corresponding to jouer + -et.
Inherited from Middle French logement, loigement. By surface analysis, loger + -ment. Related to lodge, lobby, leaf.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intēnsīvus, from Latin intēnsus.
From transparent + -ence, or borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentia, from trānspārēns (“transparent”).
Inherited from Middle French recel, deverbal from receler.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá).
Inherited from Middle French sauvable, from Old French sauvable, salvable, from Medieval Latin salvābilis. By surface analysis, sauver + -able.

Inherited from Middle French souhaiter, itself (with /t/ through influence of the noun souhait) from Old French sohaidier, from Gallo-Roman Vulgar Latin *subhaitare (“to vow with little commitment”, literally “under-promise”), a hybrid of Latin subtus (“under”) + Frankish *haitan (“to order, promise”). Cognate with Picard souhédhier. For Germanic cognates see Proto-Germanic *haitaną.
Borrowed from Latin tangēntem, an ellipsis of [līnea] tangēns, "touching line".
Learned borrowing from Latin ēventuālis, from ēventus (“outcome, event”), past participle of ēveniō.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”).
Inherited from Old French impetueus, a borrowing from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“violence”).
Internationalism, from Ancient Greek ὤνιος (ṓnios, “for sale”) + -manie, after German Oniomanie.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūgubris (“mournful; gloomy”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin interstitium.
Borrowed from Latin hypothēca (“pledge given as surety for a loan”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē).
Inherited from Middle French sumptueux, from Latin sūmptuōsus, from sūmptus (“cost, charge, expense”), perfect passive participle of sūmō, sūmere (“take”).
From Latin prōscrīptiōnem, from prōscrībere (originally "publish in writing"), from prō- and scrībere.
Learned borrowing from Latin trāductiō (“transferring, translation”, literally “leading across”), from trādūcō (“to lead across”), from trāns (“across”) + dūcō (“to lead”).
Inherited from Middle French pyrenee, from Latin Pyrenaeus (“Pyrenean”), from Ancient Greek Πῡρηναῖος (Pūrēnaîos), from Πῡρήνη (Pūrḗnē, “Pyrene”) + -αῖος (-aîos). By surface analysis, Pyrène + -ée.
Inherited from Middle French expiration, borrowed from Latin exspīrātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin inaccessibilis. By surface analysis, in- + accessible.
From Latin pentagonus, which came from πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos). Morphologically penta- + -gone.
From nicher (“nestle”) + -on (because the breasts nestle in the blouse, or perhaps because the infant nestles against the breast).
Inherited from Old French prevost, inherited from Latin praepositus (“[one] placed in command”). Compare French préposé.

From Old French chelidre, chelydre, from Latin chelydrus (“fetid water serpent”), from Ancient Greek χέλυδρος (khéludros, “amphibious serpent”), from χέλυς (khélus, “tortoise”) + ὕδρος (húdros, “water serpent”). Cognate of English chelydre. The meaning of a snapping turtle by reanalysis back to the feminine noun χέλυς (khélus, “tortoise”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δημαγωγία (dēmagōgía, “demagogy”), from δημαγωγός (dēmagōgós, “demagogue”).
Borrowed from Occitan cabrit (“(goat) kid”), from Vulgar Latin capritus (“billy goat”). Doublet of chevri. Compare Spanish cabrito.
From change of suffix from Old French seculer, borrowed from Latin saeculāris (whence also séculaire, a later borrowing), from saeculum (“century”).
From Middle French ers (16th c.), from Occitan èrs, from Latin ervum (“vetch”).
From Old French coutel (cf. modern couteau) + the suffix -ier; cf. also Medieval Latin cultellārius.
Inherited from Middle French and Old French persan, from Perse + -an. Compare Middle French persien.
From électrique + -ifier, calque of English electrify.
Learned borrowing from Latin organicus. By surface analysis, organe + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνάμνησις (anámnēsis).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin hierarchicus. Morphologically, from hiérarchie + -ique.
From agri- + culture, or borrowed from Latin agricultūra.
Borrowed from Latin spicum < spica. Doublet of épi, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin collātiōnem (“gathering”). The sense "snack" derives from collātiō in the sense of "gathering of monks for a meal."
Borrowed from Ancient Greek συναλοιφή (sunaloiphḗ, “a coalescing, confluence”).

Inherited from Middle French gratter, from Old French gratter, grater, borrowed from Frankish *kratton, from Proto-Germanic *krattōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gred-, see also Albanian gërresë (“rasp, scraper”), German kratzen (“to scratch”), Swedish kratta (“to rake”).
Borrowed from Latin moderātiōnem (accusative singular moderātiōnem).
Inherited from Old French indicatif, a borrowing from Late Latin indicātīvus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “within the head”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).
Learned borrowing from Latin aliās (“at another time; elsewhere, under other circumstances, otherwise”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κράτος (krátos, “power, might”).
From Middle French glorieux, from Old French glorious, from Latin gloriosus.
Borrowed from Latin iūnctiōnem (accusative singular iūnctiōnem).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀκρόπολις (akrópolis).
Learned borrowing from New Latin epithēlium.
Inherited from Old French nonante, from Latin nōnāgintā, from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥dḱomt (“nine tens”).
Borrowed from Latin chlamys (genitive singular chlamydos, chlamydis).
Borrowed from English impeachment, originally to refer to the United States. Doublet of empêchement.
Borrowed from English poney (now pony), apparently from Middle French poulenet (“little foal”), ultimately from Late Latin pullānus (“young of an animal”).
From Old French pomel (“rounded knob”) (12th c.), diminutive of pom (“sword's hilt”), from Late Latin pomellum, from Latin pomum (“apple”).
From Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin *penicellus, alteration of Latin pēnicillum.
Inherited from Old French anelet, diminutive of anel (“ring”) (modern anneau).
From the stem of Ancient Greek πούς (poús).

Inherited from Old French guant, from Frankish *want (compare Middle Dutch want, Old High German wantus), from Proto-Germanic *wantuz (“glove”). Cognate with Italian guanto, Spanish guante, and Catalan guant.
From dégueuler (“to vomit”) + -asse. Compare English vomitrocious.
Borrowed from Latin clāvicula. Doublet of cheville, which was inherited.
Inherited from Middle French charge, from Old French charge, carge, equivalent to a deverbal from charger.
Learned borrowing from Latin dēsignātiō. By surface analysis, désigner + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin capitulāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).
From vesser (“to fart”), alteration of Old French vessir (probably under influence from péter), from Latin vissīre. Compare Italian vescia; cf. Romanian băși.
From Latin eleutheria, from Ancient Greek ἐλευθερία (eleuthería).
From Middle French corier, a borrowing of Italian corriere. Compare Medieval Latin currerius.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin baptistērium, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστήριον (baptistḗrion).
From Latin illūstrātiōnem, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Eurōpa, from Ancient Greek Εὐρώπα (Eurṓpa), a character in Greek mythology.
Inherited from Middle French mystere, a borrowing from Latin mystērium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μῠστήρῐον (mŭstḗrĭon). See also métier.
Learned borrowing from New Latin Gorilla, from Ancient Greek Γόριλλαι (Górillai).
From Ancient Greek βιβλίον (biblíon, “paper, document, tablet, small book”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin amalgama.
From Ancient Greek διαπειραίνω (diapeiraínō, “to pierce through”).

From alteration of Middle French tissir, from Old French tissir, formed analogically from the original tistre, itself from Latin texō, from Proto-Italic *teksō, either from Proto-Indo-European *tḗtḱ-ti or from *teḱ-se-ti, both from *teḱ- (“to beget, produce”). The original past participle was tissu.
Inherited from Latin amāritūdinem. Equivalent to amer + -tume.
From Latin Nīlōticus, from Ancient Greek Νειλώτης (Neilṓtēs) + -icus. By surface analysis, Nil + -ote + -ique.

Inherited from Old French ahan, from Vulgar Latin *afannō, of unknown origin. Indirectly attested by the Old French ahaner and the Old Occitan afanar. Since afannō is a verb, ahan is likely a deverbal of ahaner, although ahan is attested first.
Clipping of beuhère, verlan form of herbe (“grass”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma).
Inherited from Middle French espés, from Old French espés, from Latin spissus, from Proto-Indo-European *spidtos.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sola, from Latin solea.
From Middle French (sinthome, Bernard de Gordon). Borrowed from Latin symptōma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma).
Borrowed from Latin imprūdentia. Morphologically analyzable as imprudent + -ence.
From Old French galaxie, borrowed from Latin galaxiās, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “milky”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”).
Inherited from Middle French gratuitement. By surface analysis, gratuit + -ment.
From croy- (a stem of the verb croire) + -able.

From Middle French meschant (“bad; wrong”), from Old French mescheant (“hapless, unlucky; worthless”), from mescheoir (“to misfall, happen unfavourably”); equivalent to mé- + choir. For sense evolution, compare mauvais.
Learned borrowing from Latin pestis (“plague; pest”).
Inherited from Middle French erection, borrowed from Latin ērectiōnem.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀγνωσία (agnōsía, “ignorance”). Cognate with English agnosia.
Learned borrowing from Latin capitālis. Doublet of cheptel.
Learned borrowing from New Latin molybdaenum
Inherited from Old French tressaillir, from tres- (“across”) + saillir (“jump”).
Learned borrowing from Latin trāns. Doublet of très and trans.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pinnāculum. Doublet of panache.
Learned borrowing from Latin transalpīnus, equivalent to trans- + alpin.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin entelechīa, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).

Inherited from Middle French choix, from Old French chois, deverbal from choisir, coisir (“to differentiate, see distinctly”), from Frankish *keusan (see contemporary Dutch kiezen), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to choose”). Akin to Old High German kiosan (“to choose”) (whence German kiesen (“to choose”)), Old English ċēosan (“to choose”), Old Norse kjósa (“to choose”). More at English choose.
From Old French administration, from Latin administrātiōnem.
From Latin ethnicus (“pagan, heathen”), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”).
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French espiautre, espelte (“spelt, corn”), from Late Latin spelta (“spelt”).
From Medieval Latin iconographia. By surface analysis, icône + -o- + -graphie.
Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin praemeditātiō. Morphologically, from préméditer + -ation.

Inherited from Middle French riche (“rich”), from Old French riche (“rich, wealthy”), from Frankish *rīkī (“rich”), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“rich, powerful”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to straighten, direct, make right”). Akin to Old High German rīhhi (“rich”) (German reich (“rich”)), Old English rīċe (“rich”) (modern English rich). More at rich.
Inherited from Middle French horloge, from Old French orloge, oriloge, from Latin horologium, from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin minerālis, minerāle, from Latin minera.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἑτεροδοξία (heterodoxía). By surface analysis, hétérodoxe + -ie.
Inherited from Middle French sublime, borrowed from Latin sublimis.
From déléguer + -ation, or borrowed from Latin delegātiōnem, from delego.
Learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsitātem. By surface analysis, curieux + -ité.
Borrowed from Late Latin revēlātiōnem, from Latin revēlātum.
Inherited from Old French honorer, borrowed from Latin honorāre.
From Ancient Greek μύρμηξ (múrmēx). By surface analysis, myrméco- (“ant”) + -logie (“study of”).
Borrowed from Latin hypotēnūsa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνουσα (hupoteínousa).

Inherited from Middle French panique, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós), from Πάν (Pán). Pan, the Greek god of fields and woods, was believed to be the source of mysterious sounds that caused contagious, groundless fear in herds and crowds, or in people in lonely spots.
From Ancient Greek ἐπι- (epi-), from ἐπί (epí, “on top of”).
Inherited from Old French fort, from Latin fortem (“strong”), from Old Latin forctis, fortis.
Inherited from Middle French vif, from Old French vif, from Latin vīvus (“alive, living”), from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
From Ancient Greek βλαστός (blastós). Cognate with English -blast and Breton -blast.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lēgislātiō, lēgislātiōnem (“the giving of the law”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostolātus. See apôtre and -at.
Inherited from Middle French sel, from Old French sel, from Latin salem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂l-.
Semi-learned borrowing from New Latin ovārium, from Medieval Latin ovāria (“bird ovary”), from Latin ovum (“egg”).
Inherited from Middle French plier, from Old French pleier, ploiier, from Latin plicāre.
Inherited from Old French romans (“work in french”) + -ière (“-ess”, feminine noun-forming suffix).
Inherited from Middle French saluer, from Old French saluer, earlier saluder, from Latin salūtāre.
Borrowed from Latin arōma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma).
Borrowed from Latin scūtārius, from scūtum. Doublet of écuyer.
From espérer + -ance (Middle French and Old French esperance), or possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Compare Italian speranza, Spanish esperanza, Catalan esperança.
Learned borrowing from Latin collocātiōnem (“a putting together”).
From Middle French litigieux (14th c.), a borrowing from Latin lītigiōsus. By surface analysis, litige + -(i)eux.
Borrowed from English camping. The sense "campsite" is a pseudo-anglicism.
Learned borrowing from Latin indemnitās, from indemnis (whence indemne).
Borrowed from Spanish rancio. Doublet of rance.
Borrowed from Latin cōnfīdentia, altered after the noun fiance. Doublet of confidence.
Borrowed from Late Latin causālis, from Latin causa.
From condamner + -ation, or borrowed from Latin condemnātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin humiliātiō. By surface analysis, humilier + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French prytanee, from Latin prytanēum, from Ancient Greek πρυτανεῖον (prutaneîon). By surface analysis, prytane + -ée.
From Old Occitan sota, originally a preposition, from Late Latin subtus (“under”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek βρίζα (bríza, “rye”).
From Latin pressāre, present active infinitive of pressō, frequentative of premō.
Inherited from Middle French actrice, borrowed from Latin āctrīcem.
From Old French corageus, corresponding to courage + -eux.

Inherited from Middle French gauler (“to knock down with a pole”), from Old French gauler, wauller (“to fight with a pole”), from gaule, waulle (“long pole, rod”), from Frankish *walu (“stick”), from Proto-Germanic *waluz (“stick, root”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind, roll”). By surface analysis, gaule + -er. More at gaule.
Borrowed from Latin dissertātiōnem, from dissertō.
From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).
Borrowed from Italian fiasco. Doublet of flacon and flasque.
From Middle French timide, from Latin timidus.
Learned borrowing from Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis, “discontinuance”).
Borrowed from Late Latin rheuma, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin recapitulātiōnem. By surface analysis, récapituler + -ation.
Borrowed from Italian risotto, from riso (“rice”).
Inherited from Middle French enorme, borrowed from Latin ēnormis.
From Old French voer, vuer, from Late Latin vōtāre, denominal from vōtum; or simply formed from vœu + -er. Doublet of voter (from English). Compare also Italian votare, Spanish and Portuguese votar.
English neutron, a scientific coinage based on Latin neuter.
Clipping of football; pseudo-anglicism. Doublet of pied.
From co- + équipier (“player in a team”).
From Italian incarnato, from Latin incarnātus. Doublet of incarné. By surface analysis, incarner + -at.
Perhaps borrowed from English ultimate. Compare Spanish ulti, Portuguese ulti, Italian ulti, German Ulti.

Inherited from Late Latin troia. Cognate with Italian troia, Occitan truèja, Catalan truja, Walloon troye. Further origin uncertain: * It has been compared to Latin porcus Troiānus (literally “Trojan pig”), a singularly attested name for a stuffed roast of pork, so called by humorous comparison to the “filled” Trojan horse. * More likely of Celtic origin, from a Gaulish *trogja, from a root meaning “to pull” and thence also “fertile," Proto-Celtic *trāglo-, for which see Latin traho. * Finally it might be an imitative formation after the sound of a pig's grunt.
Borrowed from Latin immortālitātem. By surface analysis, in- + mortalité or immortel + -ité.
Inherited from Old French relacion, from Latin relātiōnem.
From conforme + -ment. An acute accent is added to the e of conforme to help the pronunciation.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀναιμία (anaimía).
From Latin dissolubilis, itself from dissolvere (“to dissolve”) (from dis- (“apart”) + solvere (“to solve”) + -bilis (“-able”).
Inherited from Middle French outil, from Old French ostil, ustil, from Vulgar Latin *usitilium, derived from Latin ūtēnsilia.
Inherited from Old French chalor, from Latin calōrem m.
Inherited from Middle French cervelle, from Old French cervele, from Latin cerebella, the plural of cerebellum (whence French cerveau) reinterpreted as a feminine singular.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin reminiscentia.
Inherited from Late Latin tortūra, from Latin tortus, from torqueō.
Borrowed from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”).
Borrowed from Latin daemon, from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn).
From Middle French estendard, from Old French estandart.
Borrowed from Italian vasca, from Vulgar Latin vāscula, from Latin vāsculum. Compare vaisseau.
Learned borrowing from Latin dehīscentis, present participle of dehīscō (“to divide, split open, gape”).
Learned borrowing from Latin oxymōrus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀξύμωρος (oxúmōros).
Inherited from Old French, from Latin hordeum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdeyom (“bristly”).
From Old French esciemment, equivalent to escient + -ment.
Learned borrowing from Latin speciālis; compare Old French especial.
From Medieval Greek στίγμα (stígma), likely coined by analogy with σίγμα (sígma).
Inherited from Middle French fors, from Old French fors, from Latin forīs, or more likely derived from dehors (in Middle and Old French defors).
Inherited from Old French dignité, borrowed from Latin dignitātem. Compare the inherited Old French deintié.
From Old French hospitalité (ca. 1200), a borrowing from Latin hospitālitās. It remained a learned word and therefore did not undergo the regular muting of preconsonantal /s/ (as in hôpital).
Inherited from Old French superior, borrowed from Latin superior.
From Late Latin sānātōrium (“giving health”) from Latin sānātus, past participle of sānō (“to cure, to heal”).
From Middle French facile (15th c.), a borrowing from Latin facilis (“easy”), likely under influence of Italian facile.
Clipping of vélocipède (“velocipede”), which is now obsolete.
English cosplay. The Office québécois de la langue française recommends the term costumade as its replacement.
Inherited from Old French continu, borrowed from Latin continuus.
Inherited from Middle French partir, from Old French partir, from Latin partīre.
Inherited from Middle French adamantin, from Latin adamantinus.
Inherited from Middle French cul, from Old French cul, from Latin cūlus.
Inherited from Old French fuerre, from Early Medieval Latin fodrum, from Frankish *fodar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂tróm (“food”). Cognate with English fodder.
From tribu + -al, possibly influenced by English tribal.
Inherited from Old French licence, borrowed from Latin licentia.
Inherited from Old French figure, borrowed from Latin figūra.
From Latin sex (“six”) by analogy with quatuor.
Inherited from Latin fistula. Doublet of fistule.
From ridicule + -iser, attested since 1675. Displaced older ridiculer and ridiculariser.
From Russian царь (carʹ), from Old East Slavic цьсарь (cĭsarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь, from a Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar. Doublet of César.
Borrowed from Latin cithara, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Doublet of guitare.
Inherited from Middle French femelle, from Old French femele, from Latin fēmella f.
Inherited from Middle French anse, from Late Old French anse, borrowed from Latin ānsa.
Learned borrowing from Latin peremptōrius (“deadly; decisive”), from perimō (“destroy”).

From Middle French brosse, from Old French broce, brosse, broisse (“brushwood, brush”), of unknown origin. Probably cognate with Catalan brossa and possibly with various other Romance words. Theories include: * From Vulgar Latin *broccia, from Proto-Celtic *wroikos (“heather”). * From Vulgar Latin *bruscia, itself from Latin brūscum (“knot, excrescence on a tree”), or Proto-Germanic *bruskaz (“underbrush”), or a confluence of these. * From Vulgar Latin *brustia, from Frankish *bursti, from Proto-Germanic *burstiz (“bristle”). This is considered least likely, because the Germanic word does not have the sense “brushwood” while the Romance word does not have the sense “bristle”.
Inherited from Middle French caverne, from Old French caverne, borrowed from Latin caverna.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impertinentem. Morphologically, from in- + pertinent.
Learned borrowing from New Latin hēpatītis, from hēpar (“liver”) + -ītis (suffix denoting diseases characterized by inflammation).
Learned borrowing from Latin vigilantia. By surface analysis, vigile + -ance.
Learned borrowing from Latin īnsalūbris. By surface analysis, in- + salubre.
From pesant + -eur (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns from adjectives).
Learned borrowing from Latin cachecticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek καχεκτικός (kakhektikós).
Directly from Italian minestrone, from minestra (“soup”, ultimately from Latin ministrō) + -one (augmentative suffix).

Inherited from Middle French travailler, from Old French travailler (“to toil, suffer, torment”), from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“to torture”), derived from Late Latin tripālium (“torture instrument”), from Latin tripālis (“having three stakes”).
Inherited from Middle French censer, from Old French censer, from Latin cēnsēre.
Learned borrowing from Latin vīcīnitātem. Compare voisin.
Learned borrowing from Latin tenācitās. By surface analysis, tenace + -ité.
From Russian хрущёвка (xruščóvka), named after Nikita Khrushchev, former leader of the Soviet Union.
Borrowed from Arabic فُلُوس (fulūs), from Aramaic פילס / ܦܠܣ / פולסא / ܦܘܠܣܐ (/⁠fuləsā, filas⁠/), from Ancient Greek φόλλις (phóllis), from Latin follis. Doublet of fou.
From dé- + con + -er, literally “to pull out of the cunt”.
Borrowed from Latin moderātōrem (“moderator, manager”), from moderor (“moderate”), from modus (“measure, mode”).
Inherited from Middle French language, from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”) (whence langue). By surface analysis, langue + -age.
Borrowed from Latin grandiloquus, remodelled after éloquent.
From Ancient Greek νευρο- (neuro-), combining form of νεῦρον (neûron, “sinew, tendon, cord”).
Inherited from Old French apercevoir (“to become aware of”), from percevoir.
From Latin eclīpsis (“eclipse”), from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”), from ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to abandon”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and λείπω (leípō, “to leave behind”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin expeditivus.
Learned borrowing from Latin imāginārius, from imāgō (“image”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύναψις (súnapsis, “conjunction”), from συνάπτω (sunáptō, “to clasp”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dēfēnsīvus.
Inherited from Old French moieul, from Latin modiolus. Compare Occitan mojol. Doublet of modiole, a borrowing.
Inherited from Old French gracieus, borrowed from Latin gratiōsus.

From Middle French mareschal, from Old French mareschal, marescal, from Medieval Latin mariscalcus, from Frankish *marhaskalk, from *marh (from Proto-Germanic *marhaz (“horse”)) + *skalk (from Proto-Germanic *skalkaz (“servant, knight”)). Compare also Italian maniscalco.
Learned borrowing from Latin imprūdens. Morphologically analyzable as im- + prudent.
Inherited from Middle French chatte, from Old French chate, from Late Latin catta, feminine of cattus. By surface analysis, chat + -e.
Inherited from Middle French porc, from Old French porc, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin immātrīculāre.
From Medieval Latin ducātus, from dux + -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns). Doublet of ducat and dogat. By surface analysis, duc (“duke”) + -é (“-ate”).
Borrowed from Italian salto. Doublet of saut.
Inherited from Middle French translateur, from Old French translateur /translator /translatour, from Latin trānslātor.
Inherited from Middle French absolut, replaced earlier asolu (c. 1100), from Latin absolūtus (“unconditional”), perfect passive participle of absolvō (“loosen, free; complete”).
Borrowed from Late Latin provocātiōnem, from Latin provocō.
Inherited from Old French vigur, borrowed from Latin vigorem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin syntagma, from Ancient Greek σύνταγμα (súntagma, “orderly arrangement”), from συντάσσω (“arrange together”, “to order”).
Inherited from Middle French corpulent, from Old French corpulent, a borrowing from Latin corpulentus.
Inherited from Old French joc (“chicken roost”).
From Latin masturbātōrem. By surface analysis, masturber + -ateur.
Learned borrowing from Latin purpura. Doublet of pourpre.
From Old French, corresponding to sur- + monter.
From Middle French inquiet (16th c.), a borrowing from Latin inquiētus. Earlier was the verb inquiéter (12th c.). By surface analysis, in- + quiet.
Inherited from Middle French epitaphe m or f, from Latin epitaphium.
Inherited from Middle French ligature, from Late Latin ligātūra, from Latin ligātus, past participle of ligō (“tie, bind”). Compare the popular Old French liüre.
Inherited from Old French volille, volleille, from Late Latin volātilia, from Latin volātilis. Doublet of volatil.
Learned borrowing from Latin ulcerāre. By surface analysis, ulcère + -er.
Inherited from Old French cotoun, coton, from Italian cotone, from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun), variants of Arabic قُطْن (quṭn); see cotton for more.
Formed from dis- + paraître, based on Late Latin disparere.
From Hebrew שֶׁקֶל (shékel, “shekel”), from שָׁקַל (shakál, “to weigh”).
Borrowed from Latin monticulus, diminutive of mons (“mountain”).
Borrowed from English anticyclone, etymologically analyzable as anti- + cyclone.

Inherited from Middle French gastine, from Old French gastine, guastine (“uncultivated land, deserted ground”), from Frankish *wōstini (“desert, wasteland”), from Proto-Germanic *wōstinī (“desert, waste, abandoned land”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂-stos (“empty, wasted”). Influenced in form by gâter. Cognate with Middle High German wuostinne, wuosten (“a desert, waste”), Saterland Frisian Wüüste (“a desert, waste”), Old English wēsten (“a waste, wilderness, desert”). More at waste.
Learned borrowing from Latin punctiō. Compare the inherited doublet poinçon.
Learned borrowing from Latin amphitheātrum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέᾱτρον (amphithéātron).
Borrowed from English Shavian, from Latin Shavi(us) + -ien (Latinised form of Shaw).
Inherited from Middle French théorème, a borrowing from Latin theōrēma, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θεώρημᾰ (theṓrēmă).
From Old French centre (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point”).
From Middle French silene, from Latin sīlēnus (“silen”), named after Sīlēnus (“Silenus”), from Ancient Greek Σῑληνός (Sīlēnós).
Inherited from Old French volage, from Latin volāticus.
Borrowed from English design. Doublet of dessein.
Inherited from Old French esquis, past participle of esquerre, from Latin exquirere with a change in conjugation. /k/ was originally lost and later reinserted per the Latin etymon.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin patristica, from Latin pater (“father”).
Inherited from Old French unifier, borrowed from Late Latin unificare.
Inherited from Middle French mutation, from Old French mutacion, borrowed from Latin mutātiōnem.
From Old French tablete, diminutive of table.
Inherited from Old French air, aire, from Latin āēr.
Inherited from Middle French, borrowed from Latin fallaciōsus.
Inherited from Old French bécher (“to bite”), from Latin beccus (“beak, bill”).
Inherited from Old French, from Latin dūrus.
Borrowed from German Talweg prior to the 1901 spelling reform (see etymology of English entry).
From Portuguese português, replacing earlier Portugalois.
Borrowed from Latin iris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris).
Borrowed from Latin Tocharus, from Ancient Greek Τόχαρος (Tókharos).
Inherited from Old French consoude, consoulde, consolde, from Latin cōnsolida.

From Old French gai, from Old Occitan gai, from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌴𐌹𐍃 (*gaheis, “impetuous”); or from Frankish *gāhi (“fast, sudden, impetuous”), Frankish *wāhi (“pretty”), both from Proto-Germanic *ganhuz (“lively, fast, quick”); or (per Liberman, Chance, Meier) from Latin vagus (“wandering, inconstant, flighty”), with *[w] → [ɡ] as in French gaine. Doublet of vague in that case. Cognate with English gay and Italian gaio.
From Ancient Greek δοκιμασία (dokimasía, “ordeal, strain, trial”).
From Italian cameriere. Doublet of chambrier.

Inherited from Old French porsivre, poursivre, porsuir, poursuire, porsivir, from Vulgar Latin *prosequere (attested in Vulgar or early Medieval Latin as prosevere and prosequire), from Latin prosequi. Most of the other Romance cognates (as well as the Old French parsivre, parsuivre) derived from the related persequor (which influenced the Old French in meaning); compare Occitan persegre, Spanish perseguir, Italian perseguire.
Borrowed from Latin frūmentārius, from frūmentum (whence froment).

Inherited from Old French molture, from moldre (“to grind”), later moudre, the same as Modern French. The Old French alternatively derives from a Vulgar Latin *molitūra, from Latin molitus (compare Spanish moltura, Friulian muldure).
Inherited from Old French deis, dois, inherited from Latin discus. Doublet of disque, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Middle French prurit, from Old French prurit (first attested in 1271), borrowed from Latin prūrītus.
Learned borrowing from Latin regiōnem. Compare the inherited Old French reiun, rëon, royon.
From Middle French oracle, from Old French oracle, from Latin ōrāculum (12th c.).
From Middle French echo, from Old French equo (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin ēchō.
Learned borrowing from Latin usurpatorius. By surface analysis, usurpation + -oire.
Borrowed from English demonize. Morphologically, from démon + -iser.
From Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin Messiās, from Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic [Term?].
Borrowed from Latin duplex, see above.

Semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin sūdārium (“handkerchief; napkin; shroud”), from sūdāre (“to sweat”) (ancestor of French suer). (If the Latin noun had been inherited by French, the ending would have regularly developed to -ier instead of -aire). By surface analysis, suer + -aire.
From Ancient Greek ὀστρακίζω (ostrakízō, “to ostracize, banish by voting with pot shards”), from ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “clay pot”).
Inherited from Old French pourcel, purcel, from Late Latin porcellus, diminutive of Latin porcus.
Learned borrowing from Latin minūtia. Doublet of menuise.
Borrowed from Late Latin lāticlāvium, with change of gender after lāticlāvus.
Inherited from Old French falcille, from Late Latin falcīcula, from Latin falcem. Compare Norman faûcil'ye.

Inherited from Old French mincier, of disputed origin. Often purported to be from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, a verb based on Latin minūtus, though the phonetic development poses several problems. The proper outcome of Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre is rather the Old French menusier, menuiser (“to reduce to small pieces”), modern French menuiser. Old French mincier, however, more likely derives from Frankish *minnistō (“smaller, finer”) or Frankish *minnisōn (“to make small, make smaller”), thus relating it to Old English ġeminsian (“to reduce, make smaller, lessen”), whence English mince.
Inherited from Old French erbe, herbe, from Latin herba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreH₁- (“to grow, become green”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin irrefutābilis. By surface analysis, in- + réfutable.
Inherited from Middle French eschole, from Old French escole, an early borrowing or semi-learned word taken from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).

Inherited from Middle French garnir, from Old French guarnir (“to protect (oneself), armour up”), from Frankish *warnijan (“to ward, take care of something”), from Proto-Germanic *warnijaną (“to worry, be careful, take heed, refuse, withhold”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *wer- (“to close, cover, protect, save, defend”). Compare Italian guarnire and Portuguese guarnir. Cognate with Middle Dutch waernen (“to provide, equip”), Middle Low German warnen, wernen (“to secure, arm”), Old English wiernan (“to withhold, be sparing of, deny, refuse, reject, decline, forbid, prevent”), Old Norse varna (“to prevent, refuse, protect”). Related to English warn.
Borrowed from Latin chiasmus, from Ancient Greek χιασμός (khiasmós).
Borrowed from Dutch kakkerlak, under the influence of cancre.
Inherited from Middle French integral, borrowed from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer.
Learned borrowing from Latin spatiōsus. See espace and -eux.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek παράταξις (parátaxis, “placement side by side”).
Borrowed from Latin medium. The sense of "person who contacts the dead" is probably a semantic loan from English medium. Doublet of mi-.
Borrowed from Latin fermentātiōnem. By surface analysis, fermenter + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Latin malleolus, from malleus (“hammer”) (whence mail).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin servitūdō, from Latin servus.
Inherited from Old French conception, concepcion, borrowed from Latin conceptiōnem (“comprehension, understanding”).
From German Spath, an obsolete spelling of Spat (“spar”).
Borrowed from English dance. First attested in 1994. Doublet of danse.
Borrowed from Arabic حَسّ (ḥass) or from Arabic حسد.
Inherited from Middle French nerfveux, from Old French nerveus, a borrowing from Latin nervōsus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Greek σχολιαστής (skholiastḗs).
Borrowed from Late Latin perinaeum, from Ancient Greek περίναιον (perínaion).
Inherited from Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”).

Inherited from Old French crevice, from Frankish *krebitja (“crayfish”), diminutive of Frankish *krebit (“crab”), from Proto-Germanic *krabitaz (“crab, cancer”), from Proto-Indo-European *grebʰ-, *gerebʰ- (“to scratch, crawl”). Non-etymological initial /e/ appears to be the result of rebracketing in the Old French plural les crevisses.
Inherited from Late Latin bibitiōnem, from Latin bibitus, from bibere (“to drink”).
Old (14th century), borrowed from Latin rancidus. Doublet of rancio.
Inherited from Old French don, from Latin dōnum.
Inherited from Middle French racheter, from Old French rachater. By surface analysis, re- (“re-”) + acheter (“to buy”).
Borrowed from Spanish mate, from Quechua mati (“gourd”).
Inherited from Middle French revenir, from Old French revenir, from Latin revenīre (“come back, return”).
Borrowed from Latin periphrasis < Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis).
Learned borrowing from Latin chiliarchia, from Ancient Greek χιλιαρχία (khiliarkhía).
Learned borrowing from New Latin staticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós).
Inherited from Middle French vent, from Old French vent, from Latin ventus, from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts < *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
Inherited from Latin vēra, neuter plural of vērus (“true”). Related to vrai (“true”), from Latin vērāx.
Borrowed from Portuguese banana, from a Niger-Congo language spoken in the Guinea region. See Portuguese banana for more information.
Formed from the root of Latin bellua (“wild beast, monster”) and the suffix -aire.
From the Latin orīginārius. Equivalent to origine + -aire.
Borrowed from Latin regente, singular ablative of regēns.
From Latin gentiana, possibly ultimately from Illyrian.

Inherited from Old French chapitel, from Late Latin capitellum (likely a semi-learned borrowing), from Latin capitulum, ultimately from caput (“head”), whence also French chef. Doublet of cadeau and cadet, borrowings from Occitan, and caudillo, a borrowing from Spanish.
Learned borrowing from Latin obtentiōnem, accusative of obtentiō.
From mixer + -eur, calque of English mixer.
Inherited from Old French prune, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin fornicātrīcem.

Inherited from Old French samedi, from Vulgar Latin *sambatum and *sambatī diēs, from Latin Sabbatī diēs, variant of diēs Sabbatī (“day of the Sabbath”), from sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton) (Modern Greek: Σάββατο (Sávvato)), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát). See also sabbat, chabbat.
Inherited from Middle French escueil, borrowed from Old Occitan escueyll, from Vulgar Latin *scoculum, from Latin scopulus, from Ancient Greek. Cognate with Italian scoglio.
Borrowed from English wafer. Doublet of gaufre.
Borrowed from Occitan aglandau, from agland (“acorn”), referring to its shape.

Derived from Latin laboratorium, from Medieval Latin labōrātōrius, from Late Latin labōrātor, from Latin labōrō (“toil, labor; strive”) + -tor (agentive suffix). Equivalent to Latin labōrō (“to labor”) (supine stem labōrāt-) + -oire (suffix forming masculine nouns).
Borrowed from Italian ricotta (literally “cooked again”), from Latin recocta.
From Latin cultivātōrem (“grower”), corresponding to cultiver + -ateur.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin allium.
Borrowed from Late Latin dēcrētālis, from Latin dēcrētum.
Borrowed from Dutch stadhouder (literally “placeholder”), calqued from Medieval Latin locum tenēns. Compare lieutenant.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin incursiōnem.
Inherited from Old French araigne, from Latin arānea.
From Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).
Inherited from Old French conscience, borrowed from Latin cōnscientia (“knowledge within oneself”), from consciens, present participle of conscire (“to know, to be conscious (of wrong)”).
From re- + cycler. Possibly a borrowing from English recycle.
Borrowed from English week-end (now more commonly weekend).
From Old French vuit, from Vulgar Latin *vocitum. The modern French form is due to generalisation of the feminine (Old French vuide) and assimilation vui- → vi-.
Inherited from Middle French chasse, from Old French chace, deverbal of chacier.
Inherited from Middle French More, respelled according to Latin Maurus.
Inherited from Middle French Volsque, from Latin Volscus.
Inherited from Old French furche, forche, from Latin furca (“pitchfork”).
Inherited from Middle French aisné, from Old French aisné, contraction of ainz (“before”) + né (“born”).
Inherited from Old French letre, inherited from Latin littera.
Inherited from Middle French mast, from Old French mast, from Early Medieval Latin mastus, from Frankish *mast, from Proto-Germanic *mastaz.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin angelus. Doublet of ange.
Inherited from Middle French tumbe, tombe, from Old French tumbe, tombe, from Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).
Learned borrowing from Latin Narcissus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Νάρκισσος (Nárkissos).
Deliberately humorous spelling of English English.
Borrowed from Italian palermitano, from Latin Panormitānus, from Panormus + -itānus.
Inherited from Middle French coste, from Old French coste, a learned borrowing from Latin costa.
Learned borrowing from Latin cooperātiō. By surface analysis, coopérer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French rai, inherited from Latin radius. Doublet of radius, a borrowing. Unrelated to raie.
Inherited from Middle French Æque, from Latin Aequus.
Borrowed from Arabic صَحْرَاوِيّ (ṣaḥrāwiyy, “of the desert”, from صَحْرَاء (ṣaḥrāʔ, “desert”)).
From Old French Orliens (“an Orléanais”), from Latin Aurēliānus (“a member of the gens Aurelia”), with the suffix -ais (Old French -eis, from Latin -ensis). Cf. Latin Aurelianensis
Learned borrowing from Late Latin patriōta (“fellow countryman”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “of the same country”).

Inherited from Middle French poisson, from Old French poisson, peisson, from an older form peis with suffix -on, from Latin piscem, see below. Alternatively, but less likely, through a Vulgar Latin *pisciō, pisciōnem.

An adaptation of the Castilian Spanish criollo (“homey, local yokel”), from Portuguese crioulo, diminutive of cria (“person raised in one’s house, servant”), from Portuguese criar (“to rear, to bring up”), from Latin creō (“to create”)

Inherited from Middle French verge, from Old French verge, vierge, virge, from a shortening of virgene, from Latin virgō, according to the Trésor de la Langue Française etymological dictionary, a borrowing.
From ἔρομαι (éromai). Akin to Old Norse raun (“trial, experience”).
From Ἑκᾰτόμβαῐᾰ (Hekătómbaĭă), a festival at which hecatombs were offered.
By surface analysis, a- + laccio + -are. Compare Neapolitan allazzare.
From contorcere; cf. Latin contortio. Cf. torsione.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from camping, which seems to have formerly had the meaning of "campsite". First attested in 1911.
From Θαργήλῐᾰ (Thargḗlĭă), a festival dedicated to Apollo and Artemis held at Athens.
From κρῠπτεύω (krŭpteúō, “hide oneself”), from κρῠπτω (krŭptō, “to hide”).
From Latin sphinx, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ (Sphínx).
From balzare (“to spring”). The meaning of impost alludes to the perceived capriciousness with which the tax was imposed.
From κεῖμαι (keîmai, “to lie down”), unrelated to Latin coitus.
From ἑτερόζυγος (heterózugos, “unevenly yoked”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, different”) + ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”).
From δαιδάλλω (daidállō, “work, craft”), itself of uncertain origin.
From Πῠᾰνέψῐᾰ (Pŭănépsĭă), a festival dedicated to Apollo, in which a dish of beans was cooked and offered.
Coined as a substitute term for sandwich during the Italianization process of Fascist Italy. By surface analysis, tramezzo (literally “in the middle”) + -ino (diminutive suffix).
From τροπαῖος (tropaîos, “of defeat”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “rout, turning of an enemy”).
Deverbal from planter. Doublet of plan (“plan, map”).
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from surfing. Note that the English noun surf only refers to an instance of surfing, and not the activity itself.
From ὅρμος (hórmos, “cord, chain”), with a suffix found also in γυργαθός (gurgathós) and κάλαθος (kálathos).
From Ἐλαφηβόλῐᾰ (Elaphēbólĭă), a festival dedicated to Artemis.
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + foglio (“sheet of paper”).
From ἐμβάλλω (embállō, “to put in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to put, place, throw”).
Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of spingere (“to push”).
Deverbal from danser (“to dance”). Doublet of dance.
From κροτέω (krotéō, “to rattle”), with a suffix -αλον found also in κύμβαλον (kúmbalon, “cymbal”) and ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club, mace”).
Derived from πρῠμνός (prŭmnós, “hindmost”), but with different accentuation.

From earlier *ἐπι-hίσταμαι (*epi-hístamai), with early loss of the breath *-h- and vowel contraction, with sense development "stand before something" > "be confronted with something" > "take knowledge of something" similar to that of Proto-West Germanic *frastandan (“to oppose; to understand”), which is partially cognate in the second component. By surface analysis, ἐπι- (epi-, “epi-, on-”) + ἵσταμαι (hístamai, “to stand, set up”). Compare ἐφῐ́στημῐ (ephĭ́stēmĭ), which is closely related in formation.
Deverbal from traîner. See also train.
Verb-object compound, composed of batti (“to beat, to strike”) + panni (“clothing”).
Verb-object compound, composed of tira (“to pull”) + pranzi (“meals”).
Verb-object compound, composed of gira (“to turn”) + arrosto (“roast”).
Verb-object compound, composed of segna (“to mark”) + accento (“stress”).
From the verb taxer. Cf. also Medieval Latin taxa.
Verb-object compound, composed of apri (“to open”) + porta (“door”).
From earlier sucidume. By surface analysis, sudicio + -ume.
Deverbal from ajouter. Neologism by André Gide, coined in his Journals in 1895.
Verb-object compound, composed of salva (“to save, to protect”) + motore (“motor”).
From calli (pl. of callo) + suffix -fugo (“remedy; cure”).
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + fogli (“sheets of paper”).
Verb-object compound, composed of para (“to protect; to block”) + lume (“light source”).
Verb-object compound, composed of mangia (“to eat”) + nastri (“tapes”).
Verb-object compound, composed of appoggia (“to support, to lean on”) + capo (“head”). Attested since 1865.
Verb-object compound, composed of cavalca (“to span”) + via (“way, road”).
Verb-object compound, composed of cala (“to lower”) + pranzi (“meals”).
Verb-object compound, composed of lancia (“to throw; to launch”) + fiamme (“flames”).
Verb-object compound, composed of mangia (“to eat”) + dischi (“disks”).
Verb-object compound, composed of para (“to protect; to block”) + urti (“crashes”).
Verb-object compound, composed of passa (“to pass”) + parola (“word”).
Verb-object compound, composed of cerca (“to look for”) + metalli (“metal(s)”).
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from aerobics. While aerobic exists in English to refer to aerobics, it is an adjective and not a noun.
Verb-object compound, composed of tergi (“to wipe clean”) + cristallo (“pane of glass”).
Verb-object compound, composed of guarda (“to guard, to watch”) + via (“way, street”).
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + uova (“eggs”).
Verb-object compound, composed of spara (“to shoot”) + chiodi (“nails”).
Verb-object compound, composed of strizza (“to squeeze, to squash”) + cervelli (“brains”).
