Verb-object compound, composed of segna (“to mark, to note down, to score”) + punti (“points”).
From canotto (“dinghy”) + -iera, because it was originally used by those who sailed on dinghies.
Verb-object compound, composed of batti (“to beat, to strike”) + carne (“meat”).
Verb-object compound, composed of cura (“to take care of”) + cari (“loved one(s)”).
Deverbal from demeurer. Akin to Italian dimora.
Verb-object compound, composed of accendi (“to light, to ignite”) + gas (“gas”).
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + bagagli (“baggage, luggage”).
Verb-object compound, composed of salva (“to save, to protect”) + schermo (“screen”).
Past participle of abbinare (“to match, to pair”).
Deverbal from relever. See also relief.
From passione (“passion”), probably used as a nickname.
From Macedonia, probably referring to the great ethnic variety that distinguished that region.
Deverbal of ciuffo (“herbs, foliage”), with the original meaning of 'collecting herbs'.
Back-formation from κοινωνέω (koinōnéō), after pairs like στρατηγέω (stratēgéō) and στρατηγός (stratēgós).
From παρθενών (parthenṓn, “women's chamber”), from παρθένος (parthénos, “maid, young woman”).
From σύρω (súrō, “to drag, sweep”), with enlargement in -φ-.
Verb-object compound, composed of caccia (“to hunt”) + torpediniere (“torpedo boats”).
From δόκῐμος (dókĭmos, “approved”), from δέχομαι (dékhomai, “I receive, I accept”).
From tinter (“to chime”) + a suffix of obscure origin.
Verb-object compound, composed of guida (“to guide, to drive”) + via (“way, street”).
From Βοηδρόμῐᾰ (Boēdrómĭă), the name of an Athenian festival in which was celebrated the help given by Theseus against the Amazons.
From Μαιμάκτης (Maimáktēs, “boisterous, stormy”), an epithet of Zeus at Athens.
From τρώγω (trṓgō, “to bite; to eat”), through the concept of an animal chewing a hole.
From μῡριάς (mūriás, “number of 10,000”), from μῡρίος (mūríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”).
From Hébert (the surname of the populist journalist Jacques Hébert (1757-1794)) + -isme.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from autocar. By surface analysis, auto- + car.
From οἴσω (oísō, “I will bear”) (future infinitive of φέρω (phérō, “to bring, bear”)) + ἔφαγον (éphagon, “I ate”).
Deverbal from élever (“to raise, bring up, elevate”).
From Σκῐροφόρῐᾰ (Skĭrophórĭă), the name of a festival.
From λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine, gleam”) and πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).
From αἴξ (aíx, “goat”) and ᾰ̓γρός (ăgrós, “land”) (compare with ἄγριος (ágrios, “wild”)).

Substantive noun from ὁρίζων κύκλος (horízōn kúklos, literally “separating circle”), from the present active participle of ὁρίζω (horízō, “to mark out a boundary”) and κύκλος (kúklos, “circle, sphere”).
Deverbal from entreposer (“to store goods in a warehouse”), with the ending influenced by dépôt (“store, warehouse, depot”).
Deverbal from montrer (“show”); the meaning 'watch' is a specialisation of the older meaning 'something shown; something which shows'.
Derived from πλάζω (plázō, “I turn aside, wander”).
From νεανίας (neanías) (ultimately from νέος (néos, “young, new”)) with the suffix -ίσκος (-ískos), diminutive in form but not necessarily in force.
Verb-object compound, composed of alza (“to raise”) + cristallo (“pane of glass”).
Verb-object compound, composed of strappa (“to snatch; to rip”) + lacrime (“tears”), literally “tear-snatcher”.
Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of leggere (“to read”).
Verb-object compound, composed of trita (“to grind, to crush”) + carne (“meat”).
Verb-object compound, composed of tira (“to throw”) + pugni (“fists, punches”).
Verb-object compound, composed of perdi (“to waste”) + tempo (“time”).
Verb-object compound, composed of scarica (“unload, dump”) + barile (“barrel”), literally “barrel-dumping”.
From cremasco (“of or from Crema”), a habitational surname for someone from Crema.
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + valori (“valuables”).
From motonautico. By surface analysis, moto- + nautica.
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + lampada (“lamp”).
Verb-object compound, composed of mangia (“to eat”) + fuoco (“fire”).
Verb-object compound, composed of para (“to protect; to block”) + fulmine (“lightning”).
Verb-object compound, composed of batti (“to beat, to strike”) + tappeto (“carpet”).
Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of scampagnare.
Verb-object compound, composed of guarda (“to guard, to watch”) + strada (“road, way”).
From truffare (“to swindle, deceive, cheat or dupe”).
From lupo (“wolf”), from its traditional use in wolf hunting.
Derived from arteriosclerosi (“arteriosclerosis”), with reference to the mental decline induced by the disease.
From gatto (“cat”), due to the shape and hairiness of the spikes, reminiscent of a cat's tail.
Verb-object compound, composed of attacca (“to attach”) + panni (“clothes”).
Verb-object compound, composed of apri (“to open”) + pista (“trail”).
Verb-object compound, composed of para (“to protect; to block”) + occhi (“eyes”).
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + mina (“pencil lead”).
Borrowed from Latin Oedipus, from Ancient Greek Οἰδίπους (Oidípous).
Verb-object compound, composed of calza (“to put on”) + maglia (“knitting, jersey”).
Verb-object compound, composed of cava (“to extract, to pull out”) + pietre (“stones”).
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from cross country. -cross exists in English to refer to cross country, but only as a suffix.
Verb-object compound, composed of lava (“to wash”) + macchini (“cars”).
Verb-object compound, composed of trincia (“to cut up”) + pollo (“chicken”).
Verb-object compound, composed of rileva (“to detect”) + metalli (“metal(s)”).
Verb-object compound, composed of caccia (“to drive away; to shove”) + pietre (“stones”).
Verb-object compound, composed of picchia (“to beat, to strike”) + duro (“hard”).
Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + provette (“test tubes”).
Verb-object compound, composed of castiga (“to punish”) + matti (“madmen”).
Verb-object compound, composed of guarda (“to guard, to watch”) + raglio (“rail”).
Verb-object compound, composed of tappa (“to plug”) + buchi (“holes”).
Verb-object compound, composed of mangia (“to eat”) + spaghetti (“spaghetti”).
From verde (“green”), with an influence from verza (“Savoy cabbage”).
Verb-object compound, composed of rompi (“to break”) + capo (“head”).
Deverbal from soutenir. (soutien-gorge): Compare typologically Russian подтя́жки (podtjážki) (distantly cognate vie Proto-Indo-European *ten-).
Verb-object compound, composed of macina (“to grind”) + caffè (“coffee”).
Verb-object compound, composed of lecca (“to lick”) + culo (“ass/arse”).
Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of parlare (“to talk, speak”).
Verb-object compound, composed of scopa (“to fuck, to shag”) + amico (“friend (male)”).
From sessantotto (“68, as in the year 1968”).
Pseudo-anglicism, from auto- (relating to cars) + English stop.
From ape (“bee”) in imitation of its sound (see also Vespa).
From lepre (“hare”), nickname for a fleet-footed or timid person.
From paese. Compare Neapolitan paisano, French paysan, Spanish paisano.
From σπέος (spéos, “cave, cavern”). Cognate with Latin spēlunca.
From μέγας (mégas); the original meaning was perhaps “to consider too great”.
Deverbal from rabaisser. Akin to Italian ribasso.
From disporre. Cognate with Piedmontese dispòst.
Past participle of vivere. Compare French vécu, Catalan and Occitan viscut.
From vegliare; cf. Latin vigila, French veille, Piedmontese vijà.
From palo; cf. palizzo. Compare French palissade, Piedmontese palissà.
From pesci (“fishes”), plural of pesce. Astronomy/Astrology sense is a calque of New Latin Pisces.
Past participle of contenere. Compare French contenu, Portuguese conteúdo.
From riconoscente. Cf. also Medieval Latin recognoscentia, French reconnaissance.
From fossa. Compare with Neapolitan fuosso.

From μεγαίρω (megaírō, “to grudge, to envy”). This was the name of one of the Furies or Ἐρινύες (Erinúes, “Erinyes”) in Greek mythology. The name is used as a word in several European languages to denote a shrewish, ill-tempered woman. Compare French mégère, Italian megera and Sicilian majara.
Past participle of rouer (“to break upon a wheel; to beat harshly”), from the belief that such individuals deserve such a punishment.

From the verb brocanter (“to deal in second-hand goods”), of obscure origin. Probably either from Dutch brok (“piece, fragment”), or from the same root as Middle French broqueur, abrokeur (“broker”), from Medieval Latin *brocator, abrocator (“broker”), from Old Dutch *brokere (“one who determines the usages of trade, manager”), from broke, bruyck, breuck (“use, usage, trade”), from Proto-Germanic *brūkiz (“use, custom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg- (“to use, enjoy”). More at broker.
From trattore (“host”), from trattare (“to treat”). Cognate with Piedmontese tratorìa.
Diminutive of orbo (“blind”). Compare French orvet.
From guardia, from guardare. Compare Medieval Latin guardianus; compare French gardien, Piedmontese guardian.
Augmentative of capra. Compare Spanish cabrón, Portuguese cabrão, Catalan cabró, Venetan cavron, Friulian cjavron.
From κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed, kernel”). Compare Ancient Greek Κώκαλος (Kṓkalos).
From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τομ-, o-grade of the root of τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”) + -ός (-ós).
From μᾰθ- (măth-, root of μᾰνθᾰ́νω (mănthắnō, “to learn”)) + -μᾰ (-mă, result noun suffix).

From μυέω (muéō, “to initiate into mysteries”), from μῡ́ω (mū́ō, “to shut”), + -της (-tēs). The sense development was probably "to shut" > "(one who) shuts one's eyes" > "one who is or is to be initiated (in the Eleusinian mysteries)".
Learned borrowing from Latin Athēnae, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀθῆναι (Athênai).
Learned borrowing from Latin Patroclus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Πάτροκλος (Pátroklos).
Learned borrowing from Latin Ēpīrus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἤπειρος (Ḗpeiros, “mainland”).
Unadapted borrowing from Ancient Greek Πάφος (Páphos). Doublet of Paphe.
Semi-learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μασσαλία (Massalía).
Borrowed from Latin Dracō, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Δρᾰ́κων (Drắkōn).
From Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios).
From Latin Tisiphone, ultimately from Ancient Greek Τισιφόνη (Tisiphónē).
Coined by Jules Dumont d'Urville, from Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “dark”) + νῆσος (nêsos, “island”), referring to the skin color of the inhabitants.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μασσαλία (Massalía).
From Ancient Greek πρωτεῖος (prōteîos, “of the first quality”) + -ique.
Borrowed from Latin Olympia, from Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπία (Olumpía).
Borrowed from Latin Parmenidēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Παρμενίδης (Parmenídēs).

Inherited from Latin Liger, itself borrowed from the native Gaulish name of the river, from *liga (“silt, sediment, deposit, alluvium”) (see also French lie, English lees), from Proto-Celtic *legyā, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie, lay”), the same source as many words in English such as lie, ledge, etc.
Inherited from Old French Mathieu, from Latin Matthaeus, from Ancient Greek Ματθαῖος (Matthaîos), from Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ (mattiṯyāhū, literally “gift of the Lord”).
From pectine + -ique, from Ancient Greek πηκτικός (pēktikós, “curdling”), from πηκτός (pēktós, “curdled”), from πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “stiffen”).
From Latin Sparta, from Ancient Greek Σπάρτη (Spártē).
From Latin Anastasius, from Ancient Greek Ἀναστάσιος (Anastásios).
From gué + -er, found in Old French as guaër; or less likely from Late Latin vadāre and altered by Germanic influence into a Vulgar Latin form *wadāre; compare however Italian guadare.

Borrowed from Latin Terentius. Itself borrowed from latin goddess Terensis, a goddess who presided over the threshing of wheat. Ultimately from Latin terō linked to the technic to separate cobs and seeds of wheat. Cognate with ancient greek τέρην, to make soft.
Borrowed from Latin Aquitania. Doublet of the inherited Guyenne and Guienne, from Old French Aguyenne.
Learned borrowing from Latin Attalīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀττάλεια (Attáleia).
From Latin Cybelē, from Ancient Greek Κυβέλη (Kubélē).
From Latin Oeneus, from Ancient Greek Οἰνεύς (Oineús).
From Latin Arabia; alternatively from arabe + -ie.
Borrowed from Latin Cythēra, from Ancient Greek Κύθηρα (Kúthēra).
From Latin Marcellus, diminutive of Marcus.
From Latin Orestheus, from Ancient Greek Ὀρεσθεύς (Orestheús).
From Latin Dioscūrī, from Ancient Greek Δῐόσκοροι (Dĭóskoroi).
From Latin Atropatia, from Ancient Greek Ἀτροπατία (Atropatía). By surface analysis, Atropatès + -ie.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin Scylla, from Ancient Greek Σκύλλα (Skúlla).
Borrowed from Latin Pharae, from Ancient Greek Φαραί (Pharaí).
From Latin Tēreus, from Ancient Greek Τηρεύς (Tēreús).
Borrowed from Latin Plūtarchus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Πλούταρχος (Ploútarkhos).
From Latin Olynthus, from Ancient Greek Ὄλυνθος (Ólunthos).
From frigide + -ité, or borrowed from Latin frigiditātem.
Learned borrowing from Latin Gabriel, from Koine Greek Γαβρῑήλ (Gabrīḗl), from Biblical Hebrew גַּבְרִיאֵל (gaḇrīʾḗl)
Borrowed from Latin Hēraclītus, from Ancient Greek Ἡράκλειτος (Hērákleitos).
Borrowed from Latin Gangēs, from Ancient Greek Γάγγης (Gángēs), from Sanskrit गङ्गा (gáṅgā, literally “swift-goer”).
From in- + humanité or from inhumain + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Latin Archimēdēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀρχιμήδης (Arkhimḗdēs).
Borrowed from Latin Tritaea, from Ancient Greek Τριταία (Tritaía).
From Latin Mithridātēs, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs).
From Latin Corcyraeus + -en. By surface analysis, Corcyre + -éen.
From Latin Pēleus, from Ancient Greek Πηλεύς (Pēleús).
*(Bouches-du-Rhône): Borrowed from Occitan Arle; from Latin Arelate. *(Pyrénées-Orientales): Borrowed from Catalan Arles; from Latin Arulas.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin Franciscus (from Francia + -iscus). Doublet of Français.
From Latin Crataeis, from Ancient Greek Κραταιΐς (Krataiḯs).
From Latin Andreās, from Ancient Greek Ἀνδρέας (Andréas).
From énumérer + -ation, or borrowed from Latin ēnumerātiōnem.
From Latin Phthīōtidem, accusative of Phthīōtis, from Ancient Greek Φθιῶτις (Phthiôtis).
From Latin Paeonia, from Ancient Greek Παιονία (Paionía).
From Latin Idomeneus, from Ancient Greek Ἰδομενεύς (Idomeneús).
Borrowed from Latin Stephanus m, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος m (Stéphanos), becoming popular beginning in the 1950s. Doublet of Étienne, which was inherited.
Learned borrowing from Latin Fortunatus. Doublet of Fortuné.
From farine + -eux, perhaps corresponding to Late Latin farīnōsus, from Latin farīna.
From lait + -eux, possibly corresponding to Latin lactōsus.
From Latin Hypsipylē, from Ancient Greek Ὑψιπύλη (Hupsipúlē).
Learned borrowing from Latin Nīcaea, from Ancient Greek Νίκαια (Níkaia). Doublet of Nice.
Borrowed from Latin Serāpis; ultimately from Ancient Greek Σέρᾱπις (Sérāpis).
Ultimately from Late Latin Cōnstantīnopolis, from Ancient Greek Κωνσταντινούπολις (Kōnstantinoúpolis).
From Latin Tēthȳs, from Ancient Greek Τηθύς (Tēthús).
Borrowed from Latin Athanasius, from Ancient Greek Ἀθανάσιος (Athanásios).
From a- + poser, with senses based on Latin appōnere.
From Latin Cyzicus, from Ancient Greek Κύζικος (Kúzikos).
Inherited from Middle French France, from Old French France, from Late Latin Francia, from Francī, the name of a Germanic tribe. Doublet of Francie.
Learned borrowing from Latin Thūcȳdidēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Θουκυδίδης (Thoukudídēs).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Lūdovīcus. Doublet of Louis, which was inherited, as well as Clovis, used as a historical term.
Learned borrowing from Latin Eusebius, borrowed from Ancient Greek Εὐσέβιος (Eusébios), from εὐσεβής (eusebḗs) + -ῐος (-ĭos).
From Latin Euneus, from Ancient Greek Εὔνηος (Eúnēos).
From Latin Cynthus, from Ancient Greek Κύνθος (Kúnthos).
Borrowed from Latin Eurīpidēs, from Ancient Greek Εὐρῑπῐ́δης (Eurīpĭ́dēs).
Borrowed from Latin Ulyssēs. The Roman name is commonly used for the Greek character, perhaps because a Greek-derived name would be rendered identically to Odyssée (“Odyssey”).
From essaim (“swarm”) + -er. Cf. older échemer. Less likely from Vulgar Latin exāminō, exāmināre, from Latin exāmen. Compare Italian sciamare, Catalan eixamar, Spanish enjambrar, Portuguese enxamear.
Borrowed from Latin Olenus, from Ancient Greek Ὤλενος (Ṓlenos).
From Latin Argolidem, accusative of Argolis, from Ancient Greek Ἀργολίς (Argolís).
From Ecclesiastical Latin Sīōn, from Koine Greek Σῑών (Sīṓn), from Biblical Hebrew צִיּוֹן (ṣiyyôn).
From Latin Lerna, from Ancient Greek Λέρνη (Lérnē).
Learned borrowing from Latin Cōnfūcius, from Mandarin 孔夫子 (Kǒng Fūzǐ).
Borrowed from Latin Polyphēmus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Πολύφημος (Polúphēmos).
Borrowed from Latin Prāxitelēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Πραξιτέλης (Praxitélēs).
Borrowed from Occitan Agde, from Latin Agatha.
From the Latin Alexius, a saint's name, from Ancient Greek Ἄλεξις (Álexis, “helper, defender”).
From Latin Pergamum, from Ancient Greek Πέργαμον (Pérgamon).

Inherited from Middle French Lotharingie, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Lotharingia, from Lōtharingus (“a member of the dynasty or of the people of King Lothair II; a Lotharing, a Lotharian”) + Latin -ia (suffix forming country names). By surface analysis, Lotharinge + -ie.
Borrowed from Latin Scythia, from Ancient Greek Σκυθία (Skuthía).
Borrowed from Late Latin Lazarus, from Ancient Greek Λάζαρος (Lázaros), the New Testament Greek form of Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר (ʾelʿāzār, literally “God has helped”). Doublet of ladre.
Inherited from Latin Brigantium, from Proto-Celtic *Brigantī.
Inherited from Latin Mogontiacum, the Roman name of the settlement, from a Celtic language.
Borrowed from Latin Theophilus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Θεόφιλος (Theóphilos).
Inherited from Middle French Napples, from Italian Napoli, from Latin Neāpolis, from Ancient Greek Νεᾱ́πολῐς (Neā́polĭs), from νέᾱ (néā, “new”) + πόλῐς (pólĭs, “city”).
Borrowed from Latin Nīcodēmus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Νικόδημος (Nikódēmos).
From Middle French Byzance, from Latin Byzantium, borrowed from Ancient Greek Βυζάντιον (Buzántion).
From Latin Anticythēra, from Ancient Greek Ἀντικύθηρα (Antikúthēra), from ἀντι- (anti-) + Κύθηρα (Kúthēra). By surface analysis, anti- + Cythère.
From pierre + -eux, or from Latin petrōsus. Doublet of pétreux, a later borrowing.
From dé- + noter. The sense “to stick out” arose from a confusion with détonner.
From Latin Naupactus, from Ancient Greek Ναύπακτος (Naúpaktos).
From vermine + -eux, or borrowed from Latin verminōsus.
Borrowed from Latin Patrae, from Ancient Greek Πάτραι (Pátrai).
From Latin Actaeōn, from Ancient Greek Ἀκταίων (Aktaíōn).
Borrowed from Latin Elysium n, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἠλῠ́σῐον n (Ēlŭ́sĭon).
From Latin Althaea, from Ancient Greek Ἀλθαία (Althaía).
Originally an adjective, borrowed from Latin Belgicus; morphologically, from Belge + -ique. Noun use arose by ellipsis of province belgique.
From Latin Proconnēsi(us) + -en. By surface analysis, Proconnèse + -ien.
From Latin Renātus, name of a legendary 5th century French saint, from renātus (“reborn”), with identical meaning in French (rené).
From the Roman name, Latin Valentia.
Borrowed from Latin Helicē, from Ancient Greek Ἑλίκη (Helíkē).
Borrowed from Latin Cerberus, from Ancient Greek Κέρβερος (Kérberos).
From Latin Aesculapius, from Ancient Greek Ἀσκληπιός (Asklēpiós).
From Latin Lycaonia, from Ancient Greek Λυκαονία (Lukaonía).
From labourer + -eur. Cf. also Medieval Latin laborator, and the Old French loreür.
Modern French pronunciation of Latin Carnūtēs, name of a Gaulish tribe, from a Celtic root for “rock, stone”.
Learned borrowing from Latin Theodōrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος (Theódōros), from θεός (theós, “god”) + δῶρον (dôron, “gift”).
From Latin Elephantīnē, from Ancient Greek Ἐλεφαντίνη (Elephantínē).
From Latin Phineus, from Ancient Greek Φινεύς (Phineús).
From Perse + -ique, or borrowed from Latin Persicus (hence a doublet of pêche).
From laver + -oir. Compare also Late Latin lavātōrium.
Learned borrowing from Latin Alemannia. Doublet of Allemagne.
From Latin Periboea, from Ancient Greek Περίβοια (Períboia).
From Latin Alcaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκαῖος (Alkaîos).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin Artemis, from Ancient Greek Ἄρτεμις (Ártemis).
From abjurer + -ation, copying Latin abiūrātiōnem (“forswearing, abjuration”).
Composed as herbe + -eux or borrowed from Latin herbōsus.
From Latin Proconnēsus f, from Ancient Greek Προκόννησος f (Prokónnēsos).
From Latin Cyriacus, from Koine Greek Κυριακός (Kuriakós, “Belonging to the Lord”).
Borrowed from Latin Elagabal, the unadapted variant of Elagabalus, from Semitic. Compare other unadapted Latin borrowings from Semitic languages: e.g. Chanaā̆n, Isrāēl.
From Latin Paphlagonia, from Ancient Greek Παφλαγονία (Paphlagonía).
From Latin Euryclēa, from Ancient Greek Εὐρύκλειᾰ (Eurúkleiă).
Borrowed from Latin Syene, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Συήνη (Suḗnē).
From Latin Thēbaidem, accusative of Thēbais, from Ancient Greek Θηβαΐς (Thēbaḯs).
Inherited from Latin sartor (“tailor”) via the nominative form. Compare Italian sarto.
From Latin Pelusium, from Ancient Greek Πηλούσιον (Pēloúsion).
From Latin Hierōnymus, from Ancient Greek Ἱερώνυμος (Hierṓnumos). Doublet of Hiéronyme.
From cercle + -er, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *circlāre, from Late Latin circulāre, from Latin circulārī (and therefore a doublet of the borrowed circuler). Compare Italian cerchiare.
From Latin Mauritania. Doublet of Maurétanie.
Derived from Latin Vincentius, from vincēns.
Borrowed from Latin Dȳmē, Dȳma, from Ancient Greek Δῡ́μη (Dū́mē).
Borrowed from Late Latin pentēcostē, from Ancient Greek πεντηκοστή (pentēkostḗ, “fiftieth (day)”).
From Latin Tȳdeus, from Ancient Greek Τῡδεύς (Tūdeús).
From Latin Eleutherae, from Ancient Greek Ἐλευθεραί (Eleutheraí).
From Latin Thebaeus + -en. By surface analysis, Thèbes + -éen.
From Latin Pellēnē, from Ancient Greek Πελλήνη (Pellḗnē).

From char + -ière, or from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Doublet of carrière (“career”), taken from Old Occitan. Compare Occitan carrièra, Catalan and Spanish carrera, Portuguese carreira, archaic Italian carraia, Romanian cărare.
Back-formation from urgent; compare Latin urgeō.
Inherited from Latin Desiderius, from desiderium (“desire, longing”).
From Latin Erebus, from Ancient Greek Ἔρεβος (Érebos).
From Latin Oeagrus, from Ancient Greek Οἴαγρος (Oíagros).
From Latin Cnidus, from Ancient Greek Κνίδος (Knídos).
Learned borrowing from Latin Aethiopia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπία (Aithiopía).
Borrowed from Latin Hēliodōrus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἡλιόδωρος (Hēliódōros).
Learned borrowing from Latin Commagēna, from Ancient Greek Κομμαγηνή (Kommagēnḗ).
Borrowed from Latin Fabricius, name of a plebeian Roman gens, of unknown origin, but often explained as from faber (“skillful, one who works with hands”).
From ciment + -ier or from Late Latin caementārius, from Latin caementum.
Borrowed from Latin Vercingetorix, from Gaulish [Term?].
Borrowed from Latin Hēsiodus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἡσίοδος (Hēsíodos).
From cire + -eux, possibly corresponding to Latin cērōsus.
From Latin Triptolemus, from Ancient Greek Τριπτόλεμος (Triptólemos).
From Latin Cyrēnē, from Ancient Greek Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē).
Borrowed from Latin Aeschylus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Αἰσχύλος (Aiskhúlos).
From évêque + -é (suffix forming abstract nouns), or from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin epīscopātus.
Inherited from Middle French, Old French, from Latin Pictāvus, after the Pictones, the Gaulish tribe inhabiting the region.
From Latin Borysthenēs, from Ancient Greek Βορυσθένης (Borusthénēs).
From Latin Phōcidem, accusative of Phōcis, from Ancient Greek Φωκίς (Phōkís).
Borrowed from Occitan Carpentràs, from Latin Carpentoracte, from Gaulish.
From Latin Ithaca, from Ancient Greek Ἰθάκη (Ithákē).
From Latin Phōcaea, from Ancient Greek Φώκαια (Phṓkaia).
From Latin Pylaemenēs, from Ancient Greek Πυλαιμένης (Pulaiménēs).
From Latin Semelē, from Ancient Greek Σεμέλη (Semélē).
Borrowed from Latin Hērostratus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos).
From Latin Pharsālus, from Ancient Greek Φάρσαλος (Phársalos).
Borrowed from Latin Sophoclēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Σοφοκλῆς (Sophoklês).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin Chalcis, from Ancient Greek Χαλκίς (Khalkís). Doublet of Chalcide.
Learned borrowing from Latin Lūsītānia. By surface analysis, Lusitan + -ie.
From Latin Catacecaumenē, from Ancient Greek Κατακεκαυμένη (Katakekauménē, literally “burnt land”).
Inherited from Old French, from an alteration of Latin Aegīdius.
From Latin Persis (stem: Persid-), from Ancient Greek Περσίς (Persís), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s).
Borrowed from Latin Sīdōn, from Ancient Greek Σιδών (Sidṓn), from Phoenician 𐤑𐤉𐤃𐤅𐤍 (ṣydwn).
From Latin Cytherēius + -en. By surface analysis, Cythère + -éen.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin Basilius, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος (Basíleios).
From Latin Lēnaeus (“Lenaeus”), from Ancient Greek Ληναῖος (Lēnaîos, “Lenaeus”), from ληναῖος (lēnaîos, literally “of or relating to the winepress”), from ληνός (lēnós, “winepress”) + -αῖος (-aîos).
Borrowed from Latin Aeschinēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Αἰσχίνης (Aiskhínēs).
From Latin Syrtis, from Ancient Greek Σύρτις (Súrtis), q.v.
Borrowed from Latin Arēs, from Ancient Greek Ἄρης (Árēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin Fortunatus. Doublet of Fortunat.
Borrowed from Latin Ida, from Ancient Greek Ἴδη (Ídē).
Borrowed from Latin Cornēlius. Alternatively from Breton Kornéli.
From Latin Mātrona (“Marne”), from Gaulish *Mātronā, from Proto-Celtic *Mātronā, a derivative of Proto-Celtic *mātīr (“mother”).
Borrowed from Latin Daedalus, itself from Ancient Greek Δαίδαλος (Daídalos).
Learned borrowing from Latin Frisia (“territory of the Frisians”).
Borrowed from Latin Manēs, from Ancient Greek Μάνης (Mánēs).
Inherited from Middle French Bourgoigne, from Old French Borgogne, Borgoigne, from Late Latin Burgundia. Related to root of burgh, borough. From the same root is Brie, via Gaulish.
From Latin Sīlēnus, from Ancient Greek Σῑληνός (Sīlēnós).
From Latin Idaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἰδαῖος (Idaîos).
From Latin Thebaeus + -en. By surface analysis, Thèbes + -éen.
